title: UT Level 2 Practice Questions 2026: 30 Exam-Quality MCQs with Answers
snippet: Free 2026 UT Level II practice exam with 30 multiple-choice questions, full explanations, ASME V Article 4 and ISO 17640 references, and study plan.
content:
This 2026 practice question bank for Ultrasonic Testing (UT) Level II certification covers the full body of knowledge tested by ASNT (SNT-TC-1A and CP-189), PCN, and CSWIP examination boards. The questions below reflect the format and difficulty of the actual closed-book general examination, the open-book specific examination, and the practical demonstration. All questions are referenced to ASME BPVC Section V Article 4, ISO 17640, EN 12668, and ASNT SNT-TC-1A paragraph 7.

UT Level II Exam Format Overview

Per ASNT SNT-TC-1A paragraph 7, the minimum exam composition for UT Level II is:

  • General Examination: 40 closed-book multiple-choice questions on UT principles, equipment, and physics. Minimum score 70%.
  • Specific Examination: 20 open-book questions on the employer's written procedures, applicable codes, and equipment. Minimum score 70%.
  • Practical Examination: Hands-on demonstration on at least one specimen. Minimum score 70%.
  • Composite Score: Average of all three must be at least 80%.

For PCN Level 2, the structure is similar but the general paper has 40 questions and the specific paper has 30 questions across two methods. See our ASNT vs PCN comparison for full details.

UT Level II Practice Questions

Question 1: Per ASME Section V Article 4, the minimum number of calibration reflectors required on a DAC curve is:

  • A. One
  • B. Two
  • C. Three
  • D. Four

Correct Answer: C

Explanation: ASME V Article 4 T-434.2.1 requires a minimum of three points on the DAC: 1/4T, 1/2T, and 3/4T side-drilled holes to establish the distance amplitude correction curve for weld inspection.

Question 2: The velocity of a longitudinal wave in steel is approximately:

  • A. 3,250 m/s
  • B. 5,920 m/s
  • C. 7,500 m/s
  • D. 1,480 m/s

Correct Answer: B

Explanation: Longitudinal wave velocity in carbon steel is approximately 5,920 m/s (5.92 mm/microsecond). This value is used in time-of-flight calculations and thickness measurements.

Question 3: Snell’s Law is used to calculate:

  • A. Beam divergence
  • B. Refraction angles between two media
  • C. Attenuation coefficient
  • D. Pulse repetition frequency

Correct Answer: B

Explanation: Snell’s Law (sinθ1/V1 = sinθ2/V2) calculates the refracted angle when an ultrasonic beam crosses an interface between two materials of different acoustic velocities. It is fundamental to angle beam wedge design.

Question 4: The first critical angle for a perspex-to-steel interface is approximately:

  • A. 27.5°
  • B. 57.7°
  • C. 90°
  • D. 33°

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: The first critical angle is the incident angle at which the refracted longitudinal wave reaches 90°, leaving only the refracted shear wave in the second medium. For perspex (2,730 m/s) to steel (5,920 m/s longitudinal), this is approximately 27.5°.

Question 5: Per ISO 17640, testing level B is used for:

  • A. Reduced testing
  • B. Basic testing
  • C. Enhanced testing
  • D. Special testing

Correct Answer: C

Explanation: ISO 17640 defines four testing levels: A (reduced), B (basic), C (enhanced), and D (special). Level B is the most commonly specified level for general weld inspection in pressure equipment, while level C provides enhanced sensitivity.

Question 6: A 60° angle beam shear wave probe is most commonly used for:

  • A. Thickness measurement
  • B. Lamination detection
  • C. Weld inspection in butt joints
  • D. Hardness testing

Correct Answer: C

Explanation: The 60° shear wave is the most widely specified angle for inspecting butt weld fusion faces in carbon steel between 10 and 40 mm thickness. 45° and 70° are also used to provide complete coverage of different fusion face orientations.

Question 7: DAC stands for:

  • A. Decibel Adjustment Curve
  • B. Distance Amplitude Correction
  • C. Defect Acceptance Criteria
  • D. Dynamic Angle Calibration

Correct Answer: B

Explanation: DAC = Distance Amplitude Correction. The curve compensates for the natural attenuation and beam spread of the ultrasonic signal as it travels through material, allowing consistent sizing of reflectors at different depths.

Question 8: TCG stands for:

  • A. Time Corrected Gain
  • B. Total Coverage Gain
  • C. Transverse Crack Gain
  • D. Transducer Calibration Gain

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: TCG = Time Corrected Gain. Unlike DAC which is a curve drawn on the screen, TCG electronically amplifies signals at increasing time/depth so reflectors of equal size produce equal screen height regardless of depth.

Question 9: The near field length N of a circular transducer is calculated as:

  • A. D² / (4λ)
  • B. D²f / (4V)
  • C. Both A and B are correct
  • D. λ / (4D)

Correct Answer: C

Explanation: Near field length N = D²/(4λ) where D = diameter and λ = wavelength. Since λ = V/f, this is equivalent to D²f/(4V). The near field is the region of complex interference where flaw sizing is unreliable.

Question 10: Beam divergence in the far field is reduced by:

  • A. Lower frequency
  • B. Smaller transducer diameter
  • C. Higher frequency and larger diameter
  • D. Increasing pulse width

Correct Answer: C

Explanation: The half-angle of beam divergence γ = 1.22λ/D for the 0-amplitude edge. Higher frequency (smaller λ) and larger diameter both reduce divergence, producing a more focused beam.

Question 11: Per EN 12668-1, which component is the pulser-receiver?

  • A. Part 1: Instruments
  • B. Part 2: Probes
  • C. Part 3: Combined equipment
  • D. Part 4: Cables

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: EN 12668 has three parts: Part 1 covers instruments (pulser-receiver, flaw detector electronics); Part 2 covers probes; Part 3 covers combined equipment performance.

Question 12: The IIW V1 calibration block is primarily used for:

  • A. Sensitivity setting only
  • B. Range calibration and angle verification
  • C. DAC construction
  • D. Couplant qualification

Correct Answer: B

Explanation: The IIW V1 block (International Institute of Welding) is the most common calibration block. It is used for range/sweep calibration, angle verification (using the 100 mm radius and the 1.5 mm hole), and basic sensitivity checks.

Question 13: A skip distance for a 60° probe inspecting a 20 mm thick plate is:

  • A. 17.3 mm
  • B. 34.6 mm
  • C. 69.3 mm
  • D. 20 mm

Correct Answer: C

Explanation: Full skip distance = 2 × thickness × tan(angle). For 60° and 20 mm: 2 × 20 × tan(60°) = 2 × 20 × 1.732 = 69.3 mm.

Question 14: Couplant is required to:

  • A. Reduce wear on the probe
  • B. Eliminate the air gap and transmit sound
  • C. Calibrate the instrument
  • D. Mark indication locations

Correct Answer: B

Explanation: Couplant (water, gel, glycerine, oil) displaces the air between the probe and the part surface. Air has an acoustic impedance so different from steel that nearly 100% of the sound would reflect at the interface without couplant.

Question 15: A signal that occurs after the backwall echo and at twice the path length is most likely:

  • A. A lamination
  • B. A second backwall (multiple)
  • C. A surface crack
  • D. Mode conversion

Correct Answer: B

Explanation: Multiple backwall echoes are normal in straight beam testing of thin plate with low attenuation. They occur at integer multiples of the thickness path length and confirm good coupling.

Question 16: The 6 dB drop sizing technique is used for:

  • A. Reflectors larger than the beam
  • B. Reflectors smaller than the beam
  • C. Calibration only
  • D. Couplant evaluation

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: The 6 dB drop technique sizes reflectors that are LARGER than the ultrasonic beam by scanning across the indication until the signal drops by 6 dB (half amplitude). For reflectors smaller than the beam, the 20 dB drop or maximum amplitude method is used.

Question 17: Per ASME V Article 4, system linearity verification should be performed:

  • A. Every shift
  • B. Every calibration
  • C. When cables, probes, or wedges are changed
  • D. Annually

Correct Answer: C

Explanation: ASME V Article 4 T-461 requires verification of system linearity and sensitivity when cables, probes, or wedges are changed because these components affect the calibrated response. Daily and pre-job checks are also required.

Question 18: A tandem technique is most useful for detecting:

  • A. Surface-breaking cracks
  • B. Vertically oriented planar flaws
  • C. Porosity clusters
  • D. Slag inclusions

Correct Answer: B

Explanation: The tandem technique uses two probes (one transmitting and one receiving) positioned to catch the corner-reflected signal from vertically oriented flaws (lack of side wall fusion) that single-probe pulse-echo would miss.

Question 19: Mode conversion refers to:

  • A. Switching between A-scan and B-scan
  • B. Conversion of a longitudinal wave to a shear wave at an interface
  • C. Changing test frequencies
  • D. Changing display gain

Correct Answer: B

Explanation: When an angled beam strikes an interface, part of the energy converts between longitudinal and shear wave modes. This is a normal physical phenomenon but can produce spurious indications if misinterpreted.

Question 20: The standard reference reflector specified in ASME V Article 4 for piping welds is:

  • A. Flat-bottomed hole
  • B. Side-drilled hole
  • C. Notch
  • D. V-notch

Correct Answer: B

Explanation: ASME V Article 4 specifies side-drilled holes (SDH) at 1/4T, 1/2T, and 3/4T depths in the basic calibration block as the primary DAC reference reflectors for weld inspection.

Question 21: Total internal reflection in UT occurs at:

  • A. The first critical angle
  • B. The second critical angle
  • C. Either critical angle
  • D. Above the second critical angle

Correct Answer: D

Explanation: Above the second critical angle (where the refracted shear wave reaches 90°), total internal reflection occurs and a surface (Rayleigh) wave is produced. This is used in surface wave inspection.

Question 22: A frequency of 5 MHz in steel produces a longitudinal wavelength of approximately:

  • A. 0.59 mm
  • B. 1.18 mm
  • C. 5.92 mm
  • D. 0.32 mm

Correct Answer: B

Explanation: Wavelength = Velocity / Frequency = 5,920 / 5,000,000 = 0.001184 m = 1.18 mm. Smaller wavelengths detect smaller flaws but attenuate more in the material.

Question 23: Per ISO 17640, the typical scanning gain above evaluation level is:

  • A. +3 dB
  • B. +6 dB
  • C. +12 dB
  • D. +20 dB

Correct Answer: B

Explanation: ISO 17640 specifies a scanning sensitivity typically +6 dB above the evaluation sensitivity to ensure detection. Evaluation is then performed at the reference level for sizing.

Question 24: The thickness of the dead zone in a contact transducer is most affected by:

  • A. Couplant viscosity
  • B. Pulse width and damping
  • C. Probe cable length
  • D. Material temperature

Correct Answer: B

Explanation: The dead zone (the region near the surface where reflectors cannot be detected) is governed by the pulse duration. Heavily damped probes with short pulses have smaller dead zones but lower sensitivity.

Question 25: A twin-crystal (TR) probe is used primarily for:

  • A. Angle beam weld inspection
  • B. Thin material thickness gauging and near-surface flaws
  • C. Through-transmission testing
  • D. Long-range guided waves

Correct Answer: B

Explanation: Twin-crystal (TR) probes separate the transmitter and receiver elements with an acoustic barrier. This eliminates the dead zone, making them ideal for thin-wall corrosion mapping and near-surface flaw detection in thin plate.

Question 26: Surface wave (Rayleigh wave) velocity in steel is approximately:

  • A. 2,720 m/s
  • B. 3,250 m/s
  • C. 5,920 m/s
  • D. 1,480 m/s

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: Rayleigh surface waves travel at approximately 0.9 times the shear wave velocity. For steel that gives roughly 0.9 × 3,250 = 2,925 m/s, commonly approximated as 2,720–2,900 m/s.

Question 27: Per ASNT SNT-TC-1A, the minimum recommended training hours for UT Level II total are:

  • A. 8 hours
  • B. 40 hours
  • C. 80 hours (40 Level I + 40 Level II)
  • D. 120 hours

Correct Answer: C

Explanation: SNT-TC-1A Table 6.3.1A recommends 40 hours of formal training at Level I plus 40 hours at Level II for ultrasonic testing, plus method-specific experience hours.

Question 28: A high amplitude signal that disappears when the probe is rotated 360° around the indication position suggests:

  • A. A spherical reflector (porosity)
  • B. A planar reflector (crack or LOF)
  • C. A volumetric reflector
  • D. Mode conversion

Correct Answer: B

Explanation: Planar reflectors (cracks, lack of fusion) are highly directional and only reflect strongly when the beam strikes them near perpendicular. Rotating the probe drops the signal sharply, distinguishing them from volumetric or spherical reflectors.

Question 29: The transfer correction (transfer loss) accounts for:

  • A. Difference in attenuation between calibration block and test piece
  • B. Probe wear
  • C. Couplant temperature
  • D. Cable loss

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: Transfer correction compensates for differences in surface condition, grain structure, and attenuation between the calibration block and the actual test piece. It is added to the gain before evaluation per ASME V and ISO 17640.

Question 30: For a UT Level II to certify a procedure, what additional approval is required?

  • A. Site safety officer
  • B. Level III review and approval
  • C. Customer signature
  • D. No further approval needed

Correct Answer: B

Explanation: Per ASNT SNT-TC-1A, only a Level III is authorized to write, approve, and audit NDT procedures. A Level II performs inspections and interprets results per approved procedures. See our Level II vs Level III article.

Study Tips for UT Level II

  • Master the formulas: Wavelength, near field, beam divergence, skip distance, Snell’s Law. Practice 20+ calculation problems per topic.
  • Know your codes: Read ASME V Article 4 cover to cover. Highlight T-432, T-434, and T-461. Practice with the actual code book you will use in the open-book specific exam.
  • Practical: Spend at least 40 hours scanning real welds. Calibrate from scratch every day until DAC, TCG, and angle verification become muscle memory.
  • Question bank: Aim to solve 500+ practice questions before exam day. Track which topics you miss and re-study them.
  • Time management: The general exam typically allows 90 minutes for 40 questions, less than 2.5 minutes per question. Pace yourself.

Recommended Study Materials

  • ASNT Recommended Practice SNT-TC-1A (2024 edition)
  • ASNT UT Classroom Training Book by Davis & Hagemaier
  • ASME BPVC Section V (current edition)
  • ISO 17640:2018 NDT of welds — Ultrasonic testing
  • EN 12668 Parts 1, 2, 3 — NDT — Characterization and verification of ultrasonic test equipment
  • Krautkrämer Ultrasonic Testing of Materials (Springer)
  • Atlantis NDT UT Level II training course (40-hour classroom + 40-hour practical)

Frequently Asked Questions

Q: How many hours of experience do I need before I can take the UT Level II exam?

A: Per ASNT SNT-TC-1A, you need 400 hours of UT Level I experience before progressing to Level II training. Some employers require an additional 400 hours of Level II experience before certification.

Q: Can I skip Level I and go directly to Level II?

A: Direct-entry Level II is allowed under SNT-TC-1A only if the candidate completes the cumulative training and experience for both levels (typically 80 hours of training and 800 hours of experience). PCN allows direct-entry Level 2 only for candidates with documented prior experience.

Q: How long is the UT Level II certification valid?

A: ASNT employer-based certification under SNT-TC-1A is valid for up to 5 years with annual eye exams and continuous activity. ASNT Central Certification (ACCP) and PCN are valid for 5 years with renewal exam at 10 years.

Q: What is the pass rate for UT Level II?

A: First-attempt pass rates vary by training provider but typically range from 60 to 75 percent for the composite exam. Atlantis NDT students average 85 percent first-attempt pass rate with our 80-hour blended program.

Q: Is PAUT covered in standard UT Level II?

A: No. Phased Array UT (PAUT) is a separate certification under SNT-TC-1A. You must hold standard UT Level II first and then complete an additional PAUT-specific training and exam.

Q: Can a UT Level II inspector approve procedures?

A: No. Only a UT Level III may write, approve, and audit procedures. See our Level II vs Level III comparison for full authority scope.

Q: What is the difference between ASME V Article 4 and ISO 17640?

A: ASME V Article 4 is the US code for ultrasonic weld inspection in pressure vessels and piping. ISO 17640 is the international (European) equivalent. Both require similar calibration but differ in acceptance criteria reference and reporting format.

Q: Do I need to know AWS D1.1 for UT Level II?

A: AWS D1.1 is required if you will inspect structural welds. The exam code (ASME, AWS, API) is chosen at certification time. Many inspectors hold dual certifications for ASME and AWS coverage.

Q: What couplant is recommended for hot surfaces above 50°C?

A: High-temperature couplants such as Sonotech Ultratherm or Echotrace HT are rated to 540°C. Below 50°C, standard glycerine, water-based gel, or cellulose paste is adequate.

Q: How does Atlantis NDT prepare candidates for the UT Level II exam?

A: Our 80-hour blended program covers 40 hours of theory (general + specific code training), 40 hours of supervised practical, four proctored mock exams, and a personalized study plan. We also include a copy of ASME V and ISO 17640 in the course fee. Enroll here or call +1 (281) 840-8969.

We deliver accredited NDT training, technical consulting, certification preparation, and digital inspection software trusted by oil & gas, fabrication, EPC, and power generation clients. title: RT Level 2 Practice Questions 2026: 30 ASME V & ISO 17636 MCQs
snippet: 2026 RT Level II practice questions: 30 MCQs with answers, ASME V Article 2 references, ISO 17636 coverage, radiation safety, plus FAQ and study plan.
content:
Welcome to the 2026 Radiographic Testing (RT) Level II practice exam bank. The questions below mirror the format of the ASNT general examination, the employer-administered specific examination, and the practical demonstration required by SNT-TC-1A paragraph 7. All questions reference ASME BPVC Section V Article 2, ISO 17636 Parts 1 and 2, and ASTM E94 (Standard Guide for Radiographic Examination).

RT Level II Exam Format Overview

RT Level II under SNT-TC-1A consists of three examinations:

  • General: 40 closed-book questions on radiation physics, equipment, film, image quality, and radiation safety. Pass mark 70%.
  • Specific: 20 open-book questions on the employer's written practice, applicable codes (ASME V, AWS D1.1, API), and procedures. Pass mark 70%.
  • Practical: Setup, exposure, processing, and interpretation of at least one radiograph. Pass mark 70%.
  • Composite: Average of all three at or above 80%.

Note: Radiation safety training (often 32 hours) is mandatory in most jurisdictions before any RT exam. Many countries also require a separate Radiation Protection Officer (RPO) license. For the bigger picture see our ASNT vs PCN comparison.

RT Level II Practice Questions

Question 1: The SI unit of absorbed dose is the:

  • A. Roentgen
  • B. Gray
  • C. Sievert
  • D. Becquerel

Correct Answer: B

Explanation: The Gray (Gy) is the SI unit of absorbed dose, equal to 1 joule of energy absorbed per kilogram of material. The Roentgen measures exposure in air, the Sievert measures equivalent dose, and the Becquerel measures activity.

Question 2: Per ASME V Article 2, the minimum source-to-film distance (SFD) is determined by:

  • A. Tube voltage
  • B. Geometric unsharpness (Ug) formula
  • C. Film type
  • D. Radiation type

Correct Answer: B

Explanation: ASME V T-274.2 limits geometric unsharpness Ug = f × t / d, where f = focal size, t = source-to-object distance, and d = object-to-film distance. The minimum SFD is calculated to keep Ug at or below the limit (typically 0.51 mm or less depending on thickness).

Question 3: A penetrameter (IQI) is used to:

  • A. Measure film density
  • B. Verify radiographic sensitivity
  • C. Calculate exposure time
  • D. Determine source decay

Correct Answer: B

Explanation: The Image Quality Indicator (IQI) — hole-type or wire-type — is placed on the source side of the part to demonstrate that the radiographic technique can detect a specified percentage of the test object thickness. ASME V uses 2-2T sensitivity (2% essential hole visible).

Question 4: The half-life of Ir-192 is approximately:

  • A. 30 years
  • B. 5.27 years
  • C. 74 days
  • D. 60 days

Correct Answer: C

Explanation: Iridium-192 has a half-life of 73.83 days. Cobalt-60 has a half-life of 5.27 years. Selenium-75 has a half-life of 119.8 days. Half-life governs source replacement intervals and exposure time calculations.

Question 5: Per ASME V Article 2, the acceptable film density range for the area of interest is:

  • A. 1.0 to 2.0 H&D
  • B. 1.8 to 4.0 H&D (composite up to 4.0)
  • C. 0.5 to 1.5 H&D
  • D. 3.0 to 5.0 H&D

Correct Answer: B

Explanation: ASME V T-282 requires film density of 1.8 to 4.0 in the area of interest for single-film viewing. For composite (two films viewed together), the through-density limit may extend higher, with each film between 1.3 and 4.0.

Question 6: Geometric unsharpness Ug is reduced by:

  • A. Larger focal spot
  • B. Shorter SFD
  • C. Larger SFD and smaller focal spot
  • D. Higher kV

Correct Answer: C

Explanation: Ug = f × t / d. Reducing focal spot size (f) and increasing source-to-object distance (so that d, object-to-film, is small relative to t) both reduce geometric unsharpness. This is why panoramic shots use long SFD when possible.

Question 7: The inverse square law states that radiation intensity:

  • A. Decreases linearly with distance
  • B. Decreases as 1/d
  • C. Decreases as 1/d²
  • D. Increases with distance

Correct Answer: C

Explanation: Inverse square law: I1/I2 = (d2/d1)². Doubling the distance from a point source reduces intensity to one quarter. This is fundamental to time-distance-shielding radiation safety practice.

Question 8: A diffraction mottle pattern on a radiograph indicates:

  • A. Defective film
  • B. Coarse grain structure in the part
  • C. Light leak
  • D. Backscatter

Correct Answer: B

Explanation: Diffraction mottling appears as a swirly low-contrast pattern caused by large crystalline grains in cast or coarse-grained materials (some austenitic stainless steels). It can mask real defects and is typically addressed by changing kV or using a different technique.

Question 9: A lead letter B on the back of a film cassette is used to detect:

  • A. Film fogging
  • B. Backscatter radiation
  • C. Source decay
  • D. Density variation

Correct Answer: B

Explanation: Per ASME V T-223, a lead letter B (typically 13 mm high, 1.6 mm thick) is placed on the back of the cassette. If the B appears as a light image on the developed film, backscatter is present and the technique must be modified (typically by adding lead screens or backing).

Question 10: Per ISO 17636-1, the wire IQI is placed:

  • A. On the film side, perpendicular to the weld
  • B. On the source side, parallel to the weld with finest wire outward
  • C. In the weld center
  • D. Between the film and the screen

Correct Answer: B

Explanation: ISO 17636-1 (and EN ISO 19232) require the wire IQI on the source side, placed parallel to the weld axis with the smallest wire furthest from the weld center. Sensitivity is determined by the smallest visible wire.

Question 11: Tube voltage (kV) primarily controls:

  • A. Radiation intensity
  • B. Beam penetrating power and contrast
  • C. Film density only
  • D. Focal spot size

Correct Answer: B

Explanation: Higher kV produces higher-energy (more penetrating) photons but reduces subject contrast. Lower kV produces softer, more contrasty radiographs but cannot penetrate thick sections. kV selection balances penetration vs. contrast.

Question 12: Tube current (mA) primarily affects:

  • A. Penetrating power
  • B. Beam quality
  • C. Quantity of radiation (intensity)
  • D. Wavelength

Correct Answer: C

Explanation: mA controls the number of electrons hitting the target per second, which is directly proportional to X-ray photon output. mA × time (mAs) controls film density without changing contrast.

Question 13: The reciprocity law states that:

  • A. Density depends on mAs only
  • B. kV and mA are interchangeable
  • C. Film responds equally to long-low and short-high exposures
  • D. Distance and time are reciprocal

Correct Answer: C

Explanation: Reciprocity law: film density depends on total exposure (intensity × time). Long exposures at low intensity should produce the same density as short exposures at high intensity. Some films show reciprocity failure at extreme times.

Question 14: A wire IQI with wires 0.10, 0.13, 0.16, 0.20, 0.25, 0.32 mm in an 8 mm part requires visible wire of:

  • A. 0.32 mm
  • B. 0.20 mm (closest to 2%)
  • C. 0.10 mm
  • D. 2.0 mm

Correct Answer: B

Explanation: For 2% sensitivity (Class A typical), the required wire diameter is 2% of 8 mm = 0.16 mm. Since 0.16 mm is in the set, that is the minimum visible wire; the 0.20 mm wire would correspond to a slightly relaxed sensitivity if 0.16 mm cannot be resolved.

Question 15: Cobalt-60 emits gamma rays primarily at:

  • A. 1.17 and 1.33 MeV
  • B. 0.30 to 0.61 MeV
  • C. 0.066 MeV
  • D. 0.27 MeV

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: Co-60 emits two gamma rays at 1.17 and 1.33 MeV — high energy suitable for steel up to 200 mm thick. Ir-192 emits a spectrum 0.21–0.61 MeV (effective approximately 0.4 MeV). Se-75 emits 0.066–0.40 MeV.

Question 16: A lead intensifying screen does what for the film?

  • A. Reduces contrast
  • B. Reduces exposure time and enhances image
  • C. Filters radiation
  • D. Eliminates backscatter

Correct Answer: B

Explanation: Lead foil screens (typically 0.13 mm front, 0.25 mm back) emit secondary electrons when struck by gamma photons, increasing film exposure. They reduce required exposure time and improve image quality. They also filter low-energy scatter.

Question 17: A dark, fuzzy, narrow line in the root of a single-V butt weld radiograph is most likely:

  • A. Tungsten inclusion
  • B. Lack of root penetration (LOP)
  • C. Slag
  • D. Concavity

Correct Answer: B

Explanation: Lack of root penetration appears as a dark, sharp, straight line in the root of a single-V butt weld where the original root face was not melted. Slag is irregular and dark; tungsten inclusion is a small bright (light) spot; concavity is a darker root contour.

Question 18: Per ASTM E94, “shooting through” multiple layers in a single exposure requires:

  • A. No special consideration
  • B. IQI on source side and verification of sensitivity at each layer
  • C. Always two separate exposures
  • D. A different film type

Correct Answer: B

Explanation: When a single exposure radiographs multiple thicknesses (e.g., DWDI — double wall double image), an IQI is placed on the source side and the technique must achieve required sensitivity at both layers. ASTM E94 provides guidance.

Question 19: The annual dose limit for a radiation worker per ICRP 103 (and US 10 CFR 20) is:

  • A. 1 mSv
  • B. 5 mSv
  • C. 50 mSv with a 5-year average of 20 mSv
  • D. 500 mSv

Correct Answer: C

Explanation: ICRP 103 and US 10 CFR 20 set occupational limits at 50 mSv per year with a 5-year running average of 20 mSv/yr. Public limit is 1 mSv/yr. Lens of the eye limit was reduced to 20 mSv/yr by ICRP 118.

Question 20: A digital radiography system uses what to capture the image?

  • A. Silver halide film
  • B. Photostimulable phosphor plate (CR) or flat panel detector (DDA)
  • C. Lead screen
  • D. Penetrameter

Correct Answer: B

Explanation: Digital RT replaces film with either Computed Radiography (CR) phosphor plates that are scanned after exposure, or Direct Digital Arrays (DDA) such as flat-panel detectors that produce a live image. See our DR vs film comparison.

Question 21: Per ASME V Article 2 (2021), digital radiography (CR/DDA) is:

  • A. Not permitted
  • B. Permitted with qualification and Article 2 Mandatory Appendix III/IV/V
  • C. Permitted only on aluminum
  • D. Permitted only for tubular sections

Correct Answer: B

Explanation: ASME V Article 2 was expanded with Mandatory Appendices for CR (App. III), DDA (App. IV), and computed tomography (App. V). Each requires demonstration of equivalent or superior performance to film.

Question 22: The basic spatial resolution (SRb) of a CR system is determined by:

  • A. Pixel size only
  • B. Pixel size and detector unsharpness (typically 2× effective pixel size)
  • C. Source size
  • D. kV

Correct Answer: B

Explanation: For CR, SRb depends on the phosphor plate properties, laser scanning resolution, and pixel size, typically 2 times the effective pixel size. SRb is measured per EN 14784 / ISO 17636-2 using a duplex wire IQI.

Question 23: A typical Class B sensitivity per ISO 17636-1 corresponds to:

  • A. Lower sensitivity than Class A
  • B. Higher sensitivity than Class A
  • C. Same as Class A
  • D. No defined limit

Correct Answer: B

Explanation: ISO 17636-1 defines Class A (basic) and Class B (improved). Class B requires longer SFD, finer-grained film, and demonstrates a smaller wire/hole IQI. Class B is typically required for safety-critical welds.

Question 24: A double-wall double-image (DWDI) technique is used for:

  • A. Pipe at or below 76 mm OD
  • B. Pipe greater than 76 mm OD
  • C. Flat plates only
  • D. Castings only

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: DWDI is used on small-diameter pipe (typically at or below 76 mm or 3 in OD) where the source is offset to produce an elliptical projection showing two opposite weld regions simultaneously. For larger pipe, single-wall single-image is used.

Question 25: Per ASME V T-276, the IQI hole “2T” means:

  • A. Hole diameter equal to 2× IQI thickness
  • B. IQI is 2 mm thick
  • C. Hole at 2 inches from edge
  • D. Two thicknesses of test piece

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: In ASME V hole-type IQI, the holes are designated 1T, 2T, and 4T, where T is the IQI thickness. A “2-2T” sensitivity means a 2% IQI (2% of part thickness) showing the 2T hole visible — standard Level 2 sensitivity.

Question 26: The ALARA principle stands for:

  • A. As Low As Reasonably Achievable
  • B. Always Lower Allowed Radiation Average
  • C. Acceptable Limit And Reasonable Action
  • D. Annual Limit And Required Approval

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: ALARA — As Low As Reasonably Achievable — is the foundational radiation safety principle. Even below regulatory limits, exposures should be minimized using time, distance, and shielding.

Question 27: The HVL (half value layer) of Ir-192 in steel is approximately:

  • A. 2 mm
  • B. 13 mm
  • C. 50 mm
  • D. 100 mm

Correct Answer: B

Explanation: The half value layer of Ir-192 in steel is approximately 13 mm (0.5 in). For Co-60 the HVL in steel is about 22 mm. HVL is used to calculate shielding for radiation safety and exposure time for thickness changes.

Question 28: A typical Ir-192 source for industrial RT has activity of:

  • A. 1 GBq
  • B. 10 MBq
  • C. 0.5–3.7 TBq (15–100 Ci)
  • D. 50 mCi

Correct Answer: C

Explanation: Industrial Ir-192 source projectors typically carry 0.5–3.7 TBq (15–100 Curies). Higher activity reduces exposure time but increases handling hazard. License conditions limit maximum activity per device.

Question 29: Per ISO 17636-1, the minimum SFD for a class A technique is determined by:

  • A. A simple rule of 10×t
  • B. The nomogram in Annex B based on focal spot size and Ug limit
  • C. Always 1 m
  • D. Always 50 mm

Correct Answer: B

Explanation: SFD is calculated from the nomogram in ISO 17636-1 Annex B based on focal spot size, geometric unsharpness limit, and part thickness. Generic answers like 10 times thickness are not correct; always use the nomogram.

Question 30: A Level II RT inspector’s responsibilities include:

  • A. Writing the procedure
  • B. Setting up exposures, processing, and interpreting radiographs per approved procedure
  • C. Approving new procedures
  • D. Training Level IIIs

Correct Answer: B

Explanation: Per SNT-TC-1A, Level II personnel may set up and calibrate equipment, perform the test per a procedure, interpret and evaluate results, and train Level I personnel. Procedure writing and approval is Level III only.

Study Tips for RT Level II

  • Radiation safety first: Many candidates fail because they underestimate the safety questions. Master ALARA, time-distance-shielding, HVL/TVL, dose limits, and source handling.
  • Practice film interpretation: Look at 200+ real radiographs before exam day. Recognize porosity (round dark), slag (irregular dark), tungsten (bright spot), LOF (straight dark), LOP (sharp dark line), and cracks (sharp dark zig-zag).
  • Calculate exposure: Practice the relationship between mAs, distance, density, and time. The exam often requires re-calculation when distance or kV changes.
  • Source decay: Memorize Ir-192 (74 days) and Co-60 (5.27 years). Practice calculating remaining activity after N half-lives.

Recommended Study Materials

  • ASNT Radiographic Testing Classroom Training Book
  • ASME BPVC Section V Article 2 + Mandatory Appendices III, IV, V
  • ISO 17636-1 (film) and 17636-2 (digital)
  • ASTM E94 Standard Guide for Radiographic Examination
  • ASTM E1742 / E2033 / E2698 for digital radiography
  • Atlantis NDT RT Level II training with radiation safety officer module

Frequently Asked Questions

Q: Do I need a radiation safety license to take the RT Level II exam?

A: A radiation safety license is required to OPERATE radioactive sources or X-ray equipment, but not strictly to take the certification exam. However, most reputable training programs include the 32-hour radiation safety training as part of RT Level II.

Q: Can I use my phone calculator during the exam?

A: Most exam boards provide a basic calculator or allow only non-programmable scientific calculators. Phones, smart watches, and devices with internet access are prohibited.

Q: What is the difference between RT Level II for film and for digital?

A: Standard RT Level II covers film. Digital radiography (CR/DDA) requires additional method-specific training and an addendum exam. ASNT now offers DR endorsements.

Q: How long is the RT Level II exam?

A: General: 90 to 120 minutes for 40 questions. Specific: 60 to 90 minutes for 20 questions. Practical: 4 to 6 hours including setup, exposure, processing, and report writing.

Q: What is the most common reason for failing the RT specific exam?

A: Inability to navigate the code book quickly. The specific exam is open book, candidates fail when they have not tabbed and indexed their ASME V book. Atlantis NDT provides a pre-tabbed code in our course.

Q: Can I take RT Level II if I am colour blind?

A: RT does not rely on colour, only on grayscale density. Near vision and contrast sensitivity (Jaeger 2 at 12 in) are required. See SNT-TC-1A para 8 on physical requirements.

Q: Is digital RT replacing film?

A: Digital RT is rapidly growing in oil & gas, aerospace, and pipeline inspection. Film is still widely used in heavy fabrication and where archival regulatory submission requires hard copies. See our DR vs film article.

Q: How does Atlantis NDT prepare candidates for RT Level II?

A: We offer an 80-hour blended program with 40 hours classroom, 32 hours radiation safety, 8 hours mock exam, plus 40 hours practical with real sources at our Houston darkroom. Group rates available for corporate cohorts. Call +1 (281) 840-8969 to enroll.

Q: What is the salary difference between RT Level I and Level II?

A: In the US, RT Level I averages a modest cost to a modest cost; RT Level II averages a modest cost to a modest cost, with experienced offshore inspectors earning $130,000+. See also our Level II vs III salary comparison.

About Atlantis NDT

Atlantis NDT is a global NDT technology and services company headquartered in Houston, Texas with operations across India and the Middle East. We deliver accredited NDT training, technical consulting, certification preparation, and digital inspection software trusted by oil & gas, fabrication, EPC, and power generation clients. Our team of ASNT Level III instructors has trained thousands of inspectors worldwide.

title: MT Level 2 Practice Questions 2026: 30 ASME V Article 7 MCQs
snippet: Free 2026 MT Level II practice exam with 30 multiple-choice questions, full explanations, ASME V Article 7, ASTM E709/E1444 and ISO 9934 references.
content:
This 2026 question bank for Magnetic Particle Testing (MT) Level II certification follows the format of the ASNT general exam (40 closed-book questions), the specific code-and-procedure exam (20 open-book), and the practical demonstration. All questions reference ASME BPVC Section V Article 7, ASTM E709 (Standard Guide for MT), ASTM E1444 (Standard Practice for Wet Fluorescent MT), and ISO 9934 Parts 1, 2, 3.

MT Level II Exam Format Overview

  • General: 40 closed-book questions, 90 minutes, 70% pass mark.
  • Specific: 20 open-book questions on the employer's procedure and applicable code (ASME, AWS, API, ISO).
  • Practical: Demonstration on at least one item with both AC and DC techniques, dry and wet methods.
  • Composite: 80% average across the three.

MT Level II Practice Questions

Question 1: MT can only detect flaws that are:

  • A. Internal to the part
  • B. At or near the surface of a ferromagnetic material
  • C. In any material
  • D. Subsurface in any material

Correct Answer: B

Explanation: MT detects surface and near-surface flaws (typically within 3 mm of the surface) in ferromagnetic materials. It cannot detect deep subsurface flaws and cannot be used on austenitic stainless steel, aluminum, copper, or other non-ferrous materials.

Question 2: Per ASME V Article 7, the minimum tangential magnetic field strength is:

  • A. 1–2 kA/m
  • B. 2.4 kA/m (30 Oe) measured with a gauss meter
  • C. 10 kA/m
  • D. Not specified

Correct Answer: B

Explanation: ASME V T-754 requires a tangential field of at least 30 Oersted (2.4 kA/m or 24 Gauss) measured with a gauss meter on the part surface, or alternatively verified by a magnetic field indicator (pie gauge or shim).

Question 3: A longitudinal magnetic field is produced by:

  • A. A central conductor
  • B. A coil or solenoid wrapped around the part
  • C. Head shot (direct contact)
  • D. Yokes only at side

Correct Answer: B

Explanation: A longitudinal field, used to detect transverse cracks, is produced by a coil with the part inside or by encircling magnetizing cable. Yokes can also produce longitudinal fields along the axis between the two poles.

Question 4: A circular magnetic field is best for detecting:

  • A. Transverse cracks
  • B. Longitudinal cracks aligned with the current
  • C. Subsurface porosity
  • D. Laminations

Correct Answer: B

Explanation: A circular field, produced by passing current through the part (head shot) or through a central conductor, detects cracks oriented parallel to the current flow (i.e., perpendicular to the magnetic flux lines).

Question 5: The right-hand rule states:

  • A. Current direction determined by thumb, flux direction by fingers
  • B. Flux is perpendicular to current
  • C. AC produces no flux
  • D. Field strength is independent of current

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: When the thumb of the right hand points in the direction of current flow, the fingers curl in the direction of the magnetic flux lines. This is fundamental to predicting field direction in MT.

Question 6: AC magnetization is best for detecting:

  • A. Subsurface flaws
  • B. Surface flaws (due to skin effect)
  • C. Internal porosity
  • D. Lack of fusion at root

Correct Answer: B

Explanation: Due to the skin effect, AC concentrates the magnetic field near the surface (within roughly 1.5 mm depth in carbon steel at 50/60 Hz). This makes AC ideal for surface crack detection but unable to detect subsurface flaws.

Question 7: DC or full-wave rectified (FWDC) magnetization penetrates:

  • A. Only the surface
  • B. Several millimeters into the part
  • C. The entire cross-section uniformly only with HWDC
  • D. Only at high amperage

Correct Answer: B

Explanation: DC and FWDC produce fields that penetrate several millimeters into the part, allowing detection of slightly subsurface flaws. HWDC (half-wave) produces a pulsed field that is intermediate between AC and FWDC.

Question 8: Per ASTM E709, residual magnetism after MT is typically required to be:

  • A. Less than 3 G (240 A/m)
  • B. Less than 10 G
  • C. Less than 50 G
  • D. Not required

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: After MT, residual magnetism must be removed for parts that will be welded, machined, or have moving magnetic components. ASTM E709 typically requires less than 3 Gauss (240 A/m) measured with a field indicator, though customer specs may be tighter.

Question 9: A pie gauge (octagonal pie-shaped indicator) is used to:

  • A. Calibrate the gauss meter
  • B. Verify field direction and approximate strength on the part surface
  • C. Replace the IQI
  • D. Measure couplant

Correct Answer: B

Explanation: The pie gauge consists of eight pie-shaped pieces of steel brazed together with a copper plate on top. When placed on a magnetized part, the joints show indications, confirming both field strength and direction.

Question 10: For a longitudinal field by coil shot, an empirical formula for amp-turns is:

  • A. NI = 45,000 / (L/D) for L/D between 4 and 15
  • B. NI = 100
  • C. NI = 1000/D
  • D. Not calculable

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: ASTM E1444 and ASME V give empirical formulas based on the length-to-diameter (L/D) ratio of the part. For 4 at or below L/D at or below 15, NI = 45,000/(L/D). Different formulas apply for short parts (low L/D) or with end pieces.

Question 11: Wet fluorescent MT inspection is performed under:

  • A. White light
  • B. UV-A (black light) of at least 1000 μW/cm²
  • C. Red light
  • D. Daylight only

Correct Answer: B

Explanation: Wet fluorescent MT particles fluoresce under UV-A (320–400 nm) light. ASTM E1444 and ASME V require at least 1000 μW/cm² of UV-A on the part surface, with ambient white light at or below 20 lux (2 ftc).

Question 12: A bath concentration for wet fluorescent MT is typically:

  • A. 0.1–0.4 mL/100 mL settled in pear tube
  • B. 5 mL/100 mL
  • C. 20 mL/100 mL
  • D. Not measured

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: ASME V T-732 requires bath concentration of 0.1–0.4 mL settled particles per 100 mL of bath for fluorescent particles, measured in a pear-shaped centrifuge tube after 30 minutes settling. Visible (non-fluorescent) particles use 1.2–2.4 mL/100 mL.

Question 13: A yoke (electromagnetic yoke) has lifting power requirements of:

  • A. 10 lb for any yoke
  • B. 40 lb for DC and 10 lb for AC at maximum pole spacing
  • C. 100 lb for any yoke
  • D. Not specified

Correct Answer: B

Explanation: ASME V T-762 requires lifting power tests: AC yokes must lift 10 lb (4.5 kg), DC/permanent yokes must lift 40 lb (18 kg) at maximum pole spacing. Verified daily or per shift on a known steel weight.

Question 14: A common non-relevant indication on MT is caused by:

  • A. Sharp geometry changes (fillets), surface roughness, magnetic writing
  • B. Internal porosity
  • C. Hydrogen
  • D. High temperature

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: Non-relevant indications include sharp geometry changes (where flux leakage occurs naturally), surface roughness and machining marks, magnetic writing (transferred field from contact with magnetized tools), and grain boundaries in cold-worked material.

Question 15: The continuous method of MT means:

  • A. Current is on while particles are being applied and during indication formation
  • B. Current is on continuously for hours
  • C. Method used only on continuous welds
  • D. Particles applied continuously after demag

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: In the continuous method, magnetizing current is on while particles are applied (or just after, for the residual method). The continuous method gives better sensitivity for low-retentivity steels.

Question 16: The residual method requires:

  • A. High-retentivity steel
  • B. Low-retentivity steel
  • C. Aluminum parts
  • D. Non-magnetic material

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: The residual method magnetizes the part, removes the current, then applies particles to the residual magnetic field. It works only on high-retentivity steels (typically tool steel, hardened steel, ferritic stainless) that hold a field after the current is removed.

Question 17: A central conductor through a hollow part produces:

  • A. Circular field in the wall
  • B. Longitudinal field
  • C. No field
  • D. Reversed field

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: A central conductor carries current through the bore of a tubular part. By the right-hand rule, the resulting circular field in the part wall detects longitudinal cracks on both inside and outside surfaces simultaneously.

Question 18: Per ISO 9934-1, magnetic particle suspension viscosity should be:

  • A. Low (kerosene-like, less than 5 mPa·s)
  • B. 50 mPa·s
  • C. 200 mPa·s
  • D. Not relevant

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: ISO 9934-1 and ASTM E1444 require a thin, low-viscosity carrier (typically a refined kerosene-based oil less than 5 mPa·s at 38°C) so particles can mobilize to flaw locations. Water-based with surfactant is also common.

Question 19: A typical MT defect indication for a surface fatigue crack appears as:

  • A. A sharp, well-defined line of particles
  • B. A diffuse cloud
  • C. Round dots
  • D. Streaks following the current

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: Fatigue cracks produce tight, sharp, often slightly raised particle build-ups along the crack edge. Subsurface flaws produce broader, fuzzier indications because the leakage field spreads.

Question 20: Demagnetization is performed by:

  • A. Cooling the part below Curie point
  • B. Slowly reducing the alternating field while moving away from a coil
  • C. Hitting the part
  • D. Adding a magnet

Correct Answer: B

Explanation: Demagnetization is achieved by subjecting the part to a continuously reversing field of decreasing amplitude — either AC of decreasing amplitude, DC reversed and decreased, or moving the part away from an AC coil at low speed.

Question 21: Per ASME V Article 7, the white-light intensity for visible particle MT is:

  • A. At least 100 fc (1076 lx) at surface
  • B. At least 50 fc
  • C. At least 1000 μW/cm² UV
  • D. No requirement

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: ASME V T-777.1 requires at least 100 footcandles (1076 lux) for visible (dry or wet non-fluorescent) inspection, measured at the part surface. UV-A requirements apply only to fluorescent inspection.

Question 22: The Curie temperature of carbon steel (above which it loses magnetic properties) is approximately:

  • A. 100°C
  • B. 770°C
  • C. 1500°C
  • D. 50°C

Correct Answer: B

Explanation: The Curie point of iron and carbon steel is approximately 770°C. Above this, the material becomes paramagnetic and cannot be magnetized for MT. This is why hot welds (just out of the arc) cannot be MT-tested directly.

Question 23: A QQI (quantitative quality indicator) shim is used to:

  • A. Replace the pie gauge
  • B. Verify field direction and adequacy on the part itself
  • C. Calibrate amperage
  • D. Test particle concentration

Correct Answer: B

Explanation: QQI shims (thin flexible steel shims with EDM-machined crosses) are placed directly on the part. They verify both field strength and direction in the area of interest, which is more representative than a pie gauge placed nearby.

Question 24: A typical MT Level II training duration per SNT-TC-1A is:

  • A. 8 hours total
  • B. 12 hours Level I + 8 hours Level II = 20 hours total
  • C. 40 hours
  • D. 80 hours

Correct Answer: B

Explanation: SNT-TC-1A Table 6.3.1A recommends 12 hours formal training for MT Level I and 8 hours additional for Level II, totaling 20 hours. Many employers exceed these minimums.

Question 25: In the residual method, the application of particles should be:

  • A. While the current is on
  • B. After the magnetizing current has been removed
  • C. Before any magnetization
  • D. Only in a coil

Correct Answer: B

Explanation: The residual method depends on the material retaining magnetism after the current is removed. Particles are applied AFTER the current is shut off, relying on the remaining residual field to develop indications.

Question 26: Prods are used to magnetize:

  • A. Castings and weldments by direct current passage
  • B. Only thin sheets
  • C. Only fluorescent applications
  • D. Tubes only

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: Prods are pointed contact electrodes pressed onto the part to pass current locally for a circular field around each prod tip. Common on castings and heavy weldments. Prod spacing typically 75–200 mm; amperage 100 A/inch (4 A/mm) of prod spacing.

Question 27: Burning of the part by prod contact is mitigated by:

  • A. Sharper prods
  • B. Clean copper tips, firm contact, and breaking contact only after current is off
  • C. Higher amperage
  • D. Using AC only

Correct Answer: B

Explanation: Arc burns from prods can cause weld defects in critical components. Prevention: clean tips, firm pressure before current-on, current off before lift-off, and avoid prod use on finished machined surfaces.

Question 28: For a multidirectional MT setup, current vectors must be:

  • A. Perpendicular and applied alternately fast enough that particles see both directions
  • B. Always parallel
  • C. DC only
  • D. Not allowed by ASME

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: Multidirectional magnetization applies two or three magnetization currents in rapid succession (within seconds) so that particles see effective fields in multiple directions, eliminating the need for two separate shots.

Question 29: ISO 9934-2 covers:

  • A. Magnetic particle products (detection media)
  • B. General principles
  • C. Equipment
  • D. Acceptance criteria

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: ISO 9934 is structured: Part 1 General principles, Part 2 Detection media (particles), Part 3 Equipment. Acceptance criteria are typically in the product code (ISO 23278 for welds, etc.).

Question 30: A Level II inspector finding a borderline (3 mm) linear indication on a Class 1 weld should:

  • A. Reject immediately
  • B. Re-clean and re-inspect; if confirmed, evaluate against the applicable acceptance code; consult Level III if ambiguous
  • C. Ignore
  • D. Re-magnetize with higher current

Correct Answer: B

Explanation: Best practice: clean the surface (to eliminate false indications), re-magnetize, re-inspect. If the indication is confirmed, compare to the applicable acceptance criteria (e.g., ASME VIII Div 1 Appendix 6, AWS D1.1, API). Consult Level III for ambiguous calls.

Study Tips for MT Level II

  • Understand the physics: Flux leakage, hysteresis, skin effect, Curie point. Many exam questions test underlying physics not just procedure.
  • Practice formulas: NI = 45,000/(L/D), prod amperage 4 A/mm of spacing, central conductor 12 A/mm of bore diameter. Know when each formula applies.
  • Indication identification: Study reference photographs of cracks vs. magnetic writing vs. surface roughness vs. fillets.
  • Code knowledge: Memorize ASME V Article 7 key tables (lifting power, dwell, concentration) and the applicable acceptance criteria of your industry code.

Recommended Study Materials

  • ASNT Magnetic Particle Testing Classroom Training Book
  • ASME BPVC Section V Article 7
  • ASTM E709 (Standard Guide), ASTM E1444 (Standard Practice for Wet Fluorescent)
  • ISO 9934 Parts 1, 2, 3
  • Atlantis NDT MT Level II training course

Frequently Asked Questions

Q: Can MT be used on stainless steel?

A: Only on ferritic and martensitic stainless steels (400 series) that are ferromagnetic. Austenitic stainless (300 series, 304/316) is non-magnetic and cannot be tested by MT — use PT instead.

Q: What is the minimum surface preparation for MT?

A: Surfaces must be clean, dry, and free of scale, paint, oil, grease, or loose particles. Maximum paint thickness allowed (when MT through paint is permitted) is typically 0.05 mm verified by a known-flaw shim test.

Q: Is MT faster than PT for production parts?

A: Yes, MT is significantly faster on ferromagnetic parts. A yoke shot takes seconds vs. 10 to 60 minutes for full PT sequence. See our MT vs PT comparison.

Q: Can MT detect cracks under paint or plating?

A: Up to about 0.05 mm coating thickness, MT can detect cracks if calibrated against a known shim flaw. Thicker coatings reduce sensitivity significantly. Always remove coatings for critical inspections.

Q: What is the difference between dry powder and wet method?

A: Dry powder is best for hot surfaces (up to 320°C with high-temperature particles) and rough surfaces (castings, weldments). Wet method gives higher sensitivity for fine cracks on smoother surfaces and is the standard for fluorescent inspection.

Q: How often must yokes be tested for lifting power?

A: ASME V requires lifting power verification at least once per day of use, or whenever the yoke is suspected of being damaged. AC yokes 10 lb, DC yokes 40 lb at max pole spacing.

Q: Is MT acceptable instead of PT for surface inspection per ASME?

A: ASME generally allows MT or PT for surface examination when the material is ferromagnetic. For non-ferromagnetic materials only PT is allowed. Always check the construction code (e.g., ASME VIII, B31.1, B31.3) for specific requirements.

Q: How long is MT certification valid?

A: Same as other methods: 5 years under SNT-TC-1A with annual eye exam, 5 years under PCN with renewal exam at 10 years, 5 years under ACCP. See our ASNT vs PCN comparison.

Q: How does Atlantis NDT train MT Level II students?

A: Our 24-hour MT Level II program covers all magnetization techniques (yoke, prod, coil, central conductor, head shot, multidirectional), both visible and fluorescent inspection, ASME V Article 7 and acceptance to ASME, AWS D1.1, API, and ISO 23278. content:
This 2026 question bank for Liquid Penetrant Testing (PT) Level II certification mirrors the ASNT general (40 closed-book), specific (20 open-book), and practical examination. Questions reference ASME BPVC Section V Article 6, ASTM E165 (Standard Practice for Liquid Penetrant Examination), and ISO 3452 Parts 1 to 6.

PT Level II Exam Format Overview

  • General: 40 closed-book questions on physics, materials, and procedure principles. 70% to pass.
  • Specific: 20 open-book questions on employer's procedure and applicable code.
  • Practical: Demonstration on at least one item using the candidate's chosen technique (Type I or II, Method A/B/C/D).
  • Composite: 80% average.

PT Level II Practice Questions

Question 1: PT detects flaws that are:

  • A. Subsurface only
  • B. Open to the surface only
  • C. Any internal flaw
  • D. Only in welds

Correct Answer: B

Explanation: Liquid penetrant testing detects discontinuities that are open to the surface of the test material. Subsurface flaws and surface flaws filled with foreign matter (paint, oxide) cannot be detected without proper surface preparation.

Question 2: Per ASME V Article 6 and ISO 3452-1, Type I penetrant is:

  • A. Visible (color contrast)
  • B. Fluorescent
  • C. Post-emulsified
  • D. Solvent-removable

Correct Answer: B

Explanation: ISO/ASME classification: Type I = Fluorescent, Type II = Visible (color contrast, typically red). Methods are then A (water-washable), B (post-emulsifiable lipophilic), C (solvent-removable), D (post-emulsifiable hydrophilic).

Question 3: The action that draws penetrant into a flaw is:

  • A. Pressure
  • B. Capillary action
  • C. Gravity
  • D. Magnetism

Correct Answer: B

Explanation: Capillary action results from the balance of surface tension and adhesive forces between liquid and solid. Penetrants are formulated with low surface tension and good wetting properties to maximize capillary draw-in.

Question 4: Per ASME V T-672, the minimum dwell time for penetrant is:

  • A. Always 30 minutes
  • B. Per manufacturer instructions, typically 5 to 60 minutes
  • C. 2 minutes
  • D. Not specified

Correct Answer: B

Explanation: ASME V T-672 requires the penetrant dwell (penetration time) per the manufacturer's instructions, with typical industry minimums of 5 to 10 minutes for cracks in metals and longer (30+ minutes) for tight fatigue cracks or porous ceramics.

Question 5: Method A (water-washable) penetrant contains:

  • A. Built-in emulsifier so it washes off with water spray
  • B. Oil only
  • C. Solvent only
  • D. No emulsifier

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: Method A penetrants contain a self-emulsifier so they can be removed by direct water spray. They are faster than post-emulsified methods but tend to over-wash and lose sensitivity if rinse is not controlled.

Question 6: Method C (solvent-removable) penetrant excess is removed by:

  • A. Water rinse
  • B. Wiping with dry cloth, then clean with lightly dampened solvent cloth
  • C. Air blast only
  • D. No removal needed

Correct Answer: B

Explanation: ASME V T-673 (Method C): wipe excess with a dry cloth, then a clean cloth lightly dampened with solvent. NEVER spray solvent directly on the part — this washes penetrant out of the flaw.

Question 7: Developer types include:

  • A. Form a (dry), Form b (water-soluble), Form c (water-suspendible), Form d (non-aqueous wet)
  • B. Only dry
  • C. Only wet
  • D. No types

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: ISO 3452-1 / ASME V developer forms: Form a = dry powder, Form b = water-soluble, Form c = water-suspendible, Form d = non-aqueous wet (solvent suspension, typically used for high-sensitivity Type I-D combinations).

Question 8: Fluorescent PT must be inspected under:

  • A. UV-A 320 to 400 nm at minimum 1000 μW/cm²
  • B. White light only
  • C. Red light
  • D. No special light

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: ASME V T-676 requires UV-A light intensity of at least 1000 μW/cm² at the part surface for fluorescent PT, with ambient white light at or below 20 lux (2 ftc). Operator must dark-adapt for at least 1 minute before evaluation.

Question 9: For visible (Type II) PT, white-light intensity must be:

  • A. At least 100 fc (1076 lux)
  • B. At least 50 fc
  • C. At least 10 fc
  • D. No requirement

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: ASME V T-676 requires minimum 100 footcandles (1076 lux) of white light at the part surface for visible inspection. Most workshop areas already meet this; outdoor work in good daylight greatly exceeds it.

Question 10: A row of bleed-out dots aligned in a line is most likely:

  • A. A crack
  • B. Porosity
  • C. A linear indication that may indicate a tight crack with intermittent surface opening
  • D. Lack of fusion

Correct Answer: C

Explanation: A row of dots can be either porosity (round) or a tight intermittent crack. Per ASME V/VIII Appendix 8, any aligned indications separated by less than 1.6 mm are evaluated as continuous and treated as a linear indication.

Question 11: Per ASTM E165, the standard surface temperature range for PT is:

  • A. Below freezing only
  • B. 10 to 52°C standard, with qualification outside this range
  • C. Only above 25°C
  • D. Only above 50°C

Correct Answer: B

Explanation: Standard penetrants are formulated for 10 to 52°C (50 to 125°F). Use outside this range requires qualification per ASTM E165 Annex (using a reference comparator). Low-temperature penetrants extend the range down to about −5°C.

Question 12: The penetrant must be removed completely from the surface before:

  • A. Penetrant application
  • B. Developer application
  • C. Pre-cleaning
  • D. No removal needed

Correct Answer: B

Explanation: After dwell, excess surface penetrant must be removed (rinse or wipe) so the developer can pull only the penetrant that was drawn into discontinuities. Over-removal washes out flaw indications; under-removal causes high background that masks indications.

Question 13: Pre-cleaning purposes include:

  • A. Remove dirt, oil, paint, scale; open flaw entrances; ensure surface compatibility
  • B. Decoration
  • C. Marking the part
  • D. Heat treatment

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: Pre-cleaning removes contaminants that could block flaw entrances or react with the penetrant. Methods include solvent wipe (most common), alkaline cleaning, vapor degreasing. Mechanical cleaning (grit blast) is avoided because it can close flaw openings.

Question 14: A typical Level 2 sensitivity Type I-A penetrant detects cracks as small as:

  • A. 100 μm
  • B. 10 to 20 μm
  • C. 1 mm
  • D. Not measurable

Correct Answer: B

Explanation: Modern fluorescent Type I-A penetrants achieve Level 3 high sensitivity, detecting cracks 5 to 10 μm wide. Solvent-removable Level 2 typically detects 10 to 20 μm. Sensitivity is qualified by reference panels per ISO 3452-2.

Question 15: Per ISO 3452-3, reference test panels are:

  • A. Aluminum with thermal cracks of known width
  • B. Painted plywood
  • C. Magnetized steel
  • D. No reference panels exist

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: ISO 3452-3 specifies aluminum reference blocks with controlled crack widths produced by quenching. Type 2 panels have five panels with cracks of progressively smaller size, used to qualify penetrant system sensitivity.

Question 16: A relevant indication on a forging is one that:

  • A. Is more than 1.6 mm in any dimension and is from an actual discontinuity
  • B. Has any size
  • C. Only fluorescent indications
  • D. Only linear indications

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: ASME V/VIII Appendix 8 generally considers any indication with major dimension greater than 1.6 mm as relevant. Non-relevant indications include those from surface roughness, fillets, or part configuration.

Question 17: After developer application, the part should be evaluated:

  • A. Immediately
  • B. After 10 to 60 minutes per manufacturer
  • C. After 24 hours
  • D. Without developer

Correct Answer: B

Explanation: ASME V T-674 specifies developer dwell of 10 minutes minimum, with most procedures using 15 to 30 minutes. After dwell, bleed-out indications reach their maximum visibility before fading.

Question 18: Re-testing the same part with PT requires:

  • A. Just re-applying penetrant
  • B. Thorough cleaning to remove all previous penetrant from flaws
  • C. Heating only
  • D. Not allowed by code

Correct Answer: B

Explanation: Re-test requires removing all residual penetrant from prior application, typically by vapor degrease, ultrasonic cleaning, or thorough solvent wash. Residual penetrant in flaws gives muted, unreliable indications on re-test.

Question 19: Per ASME V Article 6, typical acceptance criteria for class 1 weld surfaces are:

  • A. No relevant linear indications greater than 1.6 mm
  • B. No relevant linear indications; rounded indications limited per construction code
  • C. All indications allowed
  • D. Determined by Level II

Correct Answer: B

Explanation: Typical ASME VIII Div 1 Appendix 8 acceptance: no relevant linear indications (3 times width); rounded indications limited (e.g., at or below 5 mm acceptable per spacing rules). Exact criteria vary by class.

Question 20: Penetrant testing on titanium and high-nickel alloys requires:

  • A. Low halogen and low sulfur content penetrants
  • B. Standard penetrants
  • C. No special considerations
  • D. Magnetic penetrant

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: Halogens (chlorine, fluorine) and sulfur can cause stress corrosion cracking in nickel alloys and titanium at elevated service temperature. Penetrants for these materials are certified low-halogen and low-sulfur (less than 1% by weight typically).

Question 21: A flat indication on a casting that follows a grain or shrinkage pattern is most likely:

  • A. Crack
  • B. Porosity
  • C. Shrinkage or non-metallic inclusion stringer
  • D. Lack of fusion

Correct Answer: C

Explanation: Casting defects include shrinkage cavities, gas porosity (round), cold shuts (smooth linear), and inclusion stringers (irregular linear). PT can detect all surface-breaking versions but cannot distinguish them without metallurgical knowledge.

Question 22: An indication that bleeds out and grows during developer dwell suggests:

  • A. A small flaw
  • B. A large flaw with substantial penetrant volume
  • C. Surface roughness
  • D. Developer error

Correct Answer: B

Explanation: Indications that bleed out and grow during developer dwell indicate larger volume cavities or wider/deeper cracks. Tight, small flaws produce small static dots; large or deep flaws bleed broadly.

Question 23: PT cannot be used effectively on:

  • A. Porous materials (unfired ceramics, sintered metals)
  • B. Smooth steel
  • C. Aluminum
  • D. Stainless steel

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: Highly porous materials absorb penetrant into the bulk, producing high background that masks real surface flaws. PT is also problematic on parts with surface coatings, oil contamination, or extreme roughness.

Question 24: Per SNT-TC-1A, the recommended training for PT Level II totals:

  • A. 12 hours (4 hours Level I + 8 hours Level II)
  • B. 40 hours
  • C. 80 hours
  • D. 160 hours

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: SNT-TC-1A Table 6.3.1A recommends 4 hours formal training at PT Level I and 8 hours additional at Level II, total 12 hours. Method-specific experience hours are also required (typically 70 hours Level I + 140 hours Level II).

Question 25: PT is sometimes preferred over MT because:

  • A. Higher sensitivity to subsurface flaws
  • B. Works on all materials (ferrous and non-ferrous)
  • C. Lower cost
  • D. Faster than MT on castings

Correct Answer: B

Explanation: PT works on virtually all non-porous materials — stainless steel, aluminum, titanium, ceramics, polymers. MT is restricted to ferromagnetic materials. See our MT vs PT comparison.

Question 26: A reference panel comparator block (TAM panel) is used to:

  • A. Demonstrate procedure suitability
  • B. Verify penetrant system sensitivity each work day
  • C. Calibrate the lamp
  • D. Test surface roughness

Correct Answer: B

Explanation: The TAM/CRC panel has controlled cracks of known size. Per ASME V and ISO 3452, verification of system performance on the comparator is required at intervals (e.g., daily, before re-use, or whenever consumables change).

Question 27: Excessive developer thickness:

  • A. Improves sensitivity
  • B. Masks fine indications
  • C. Has no effect
  • D. Required by code

Correct Answer: B

Explanation: Developer must form a thin, uniform white coating. Excessive developer (especially aqueous) covers small bleed-out indications and reduces visibility of fine cracks. Apply developer in short bursts to a dry surface.

Question 28: Maximum hold time after pre-cleaning before applying penetrant should be:

  • A. Per procedure, but typically minimized to prevent re-contamination and oxidation
  • B. No limit
  • C. 24 hours
  • D. Always 1 hour

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: Industry good practice: apply penetrant as soon as the part is dry after pre-cleaning. Long delays risk dust, fingerprints, or oxidation re-contaminating the surface and blocking flaw entrances.

Question 29: A Level II inspector witnesses an indication that does not bleed back after a developer wipe-test. The indication is likely:

  • A. Real
  • B. Non-relevant (surface contamination or pre-existing dye)
  • C. Subsurface
  • D. Always rejectable

Correct Answer: B

Explanation: The wipe-and-redevelop test: gently wipe the indication; if it reappears as developer pulls more penetrant, it is real. If it does not, it was likely surface contamination or pre-existing dye from another source.

Question 30: Per ASTM E165 and ISO 3452, periodic system contamination tests include:

  • A. Water content for water-based, contamination by oil/grease/other penetrant type
  • B. Color only
  • C. Viscosity only
  • D. No testing

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: Periodic system contamination tests: water content (water-based emulsifiers), fluorescence brightness (Type I), color (Type II), removability, and absence of cross-contamination between Type I and Type II materials.

Study Tips for PT Level II

  • Know the classifications: Type I vs II, Methods A/B/C/D, Forms a/b/c/d. Combinations like Type II Method C Form d are very common exam questions.
  • Process steps: Pre-clean, apply penetrant, dwell, remove excess, developer, evaluate, post-clean. Memorize minimum times for each step.
  • Recognize indications: Look at 100+ real PT photographs to distinguish cracks, porosity, fillet bleed-back, and non-relevant indications.
  • Code knowledge: ASME V Article 6, ASTM E165, ISO 3452-1. Tab your code books before the specific exam.

Recommended Study Materials

  • ASNT Liquid Penetrant Testing Classroom Training Book
  • ASME BPVC Section V Article 6
  • ASTM E165 (Standard Practice for Liquid Penetrant Examination)
  • ISO 3452 Parts 1 to 6
  • Atlantis NDT PT Level II training course

Frequently Asked Questions

Q: Can PT be performed on hot surfaces?

A: Standard penetrants are limited to about 52°C (125°F). High-temperature penetrants extend operation up to 150 to 175°C with qualification. Above this, the penetrant evaporates from the flaw before developer can pull it out.

Q: Is PT acceptable instead of MT for ferromagnetic steel?

A: Yes, PT can be used on any non-porous material, including carbon steel and ferritic stainless steel. However, MT is usually faster and more sensitive for surface-breaking flaws in ferromagnetic materials. See MT vs PT.

Q: How long after a weld can PT be performed?

A: Allow the weld to cool below the maximum penetrant temperature (52°C standard, 150°C high-temp). Some weld defects develop only after cool-down (delayed hydrogen cracking), so PT 24 to 48 hours after welding is often specified.

Q: What is the difference between water-washable and post-emulsified penetrant?

A: Water-washable has built-in emulsifier; faster process but lower sensitivity due to over-wash risk. Post-emulsified (Methods B/D) applies a separate emulsifier before water rinse, giving better sensitivity but more processing steps.

Q: Can PT detect cracks under paint?

A: No. Paint must be removed in the inspection area. The exception is some thin MT-through-paint applications, which do not apply to PT.

Q: Why do some PT procedures specify a separate dwell time for developer?

A: Developer dwell allows the developer to absorb and amplify the bleed-out from flaws. Minimum 10 minutes per ASME V; typical 15 to 30. Inspect during dwell, not after fading begins.

Q: How are PT consumables certified?

A: PT material families are certified together as a system per ISO 3452-2 (sensitivity classification 1 to 4) and tested on reference panels. Mixing materials from different families is generally not allowed without re-qualification.

Q: How long is PT certification valid?

A: 5 years under SNT-TC-1A with annual eye exam, 5 years under PCN with renewal exam at 10 years. See our ASNT vs PCN article.

Q: Does Atlantis NDT include code books in PT Level II training?

A: Yes — our PT Level II course includes pre-tabbed copies of ASME V Article 6 and ASTM E165. Students also receive practice with TAM reference panels and real production hardware. Enroll here or call +1 (281) 840-8969.

About Atlantis NDT

Atlantis NDT is a global NDT technology and services company headquartered in Houston, Texas with operations across India and the Middle East. We deliver accredited NDT training, technical consulting, certification preparation, and digital inspection software trusted by oil & gas, fabrication, EPC, and power generation clients. Our team of ASNT Level III instructors has trained thousands of inspectors worldwide.

Whether you are preparing for ASNT certification, API 510, API 570, or API 653, our exam preparation programs combine classroom theory, hands-on practical training, and proctored mock exams that mirror the real test environment.

Call us at +1 (281) 840-8969 or email sales@atlantisndt.com to enroll in the next training cohort. Same-day quotes for corporate group training in Houston, Dubai, Riyadh, Hyderabad, and on-site at your facility.
