title: CSWIP 3.1 Exam Prep 2026: Format, 25 Practice MCQs, Study Guide
snippet: Complete 2026 CSWIP 3.1 welding inspector prep: exam format, 25 practice MCQs, defect identification, code references (AWS D1.1, ASME IX, EN ISO 5817), FAQ.
content:
The CSWIP 3.1 Welding Inspector certification is one of the most widely recognized welding inspector qualifications worldwide. Administered by TWI Certification Ltd (UK), it covers welding inspection of structural and pressure equipment in line with international codes. This 2026 guide explains the exam, gives 25 practice questions, and provides study and reference material guidance.

CSWIP 3.1 Exam Format Overview

CSWIP 3.1 is a 5-day course concluding with multiple examinations:

  • General Theory (Paper 1): 50 multiple-choice questions, 1 hour, 70% pass mark. Covers welding processes, terminology, defects, materials, NDT awareness.
  • Specific Theory (Paper 2): 60 multiple-choice questions, 1 hour 15 minutes, 70%. Covers a chosen code/standard (e.g., AWS D1.1, BS EN ISO 5817, ASME IX) applied to inspection.
  • Practical Plates and Pipes: Two practical examinations: visual inspection of a butt-welded plate and butt-welded pipe, report findings. 70% on each.
  • Macro Examination: Identify weld features and defects from polished and etched macro sections. 70%.
  • Overall: All sections must be passed to gain CSWIP 3.1.

Certification valid for 5 years; renewal at 5 years requires renewal exam (re-test of theory) and continued practice records. Full re-exam at 10 years.

CSWIP 3.1 Practice Questions

Question 1: SMAW is the abbreviation for:

  • A. Shielded Metal Arc Welding (stick welding, MMA)
  • B. Submerged Metal Arc Welding
  • C. Single Metal Arc Welding
  • D. Stainless Metal Arc Welding

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: SMAW (AWS designation) = Shielded Metal Arc Welding, also known as Manual Metal Arc (MMA) in UK/European usage. Uses a consumable flux-coated electrode. Versatile, simple, widely used.

Question 2: GTAW is also known as:

  • A. TIG (Tungsten Inert Gas) welding
  • B. MIG welding
  • C. Stick welding
  • D. Brazing

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: GTAW = Gas Tungsten Arc Welding = TIG. Uses a non-consumable tungsten electrode and inert shielding gas (argon, helium). Filler is added separately. Produces high-quality welds in stainless, aluminum, and root passes on pipe.

Question 3: Lack of fusion at the side wall is caused by:

  • A. Insufficient heat, poor electrode angle, contamination
  • B. Too much penetration
  • C. Cold weather only
  • D. Excessive cleaning

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: Lack of side-wall fusion (LOF) occurs when the molten pool does not melt the parent metal at the joint side. Caused by insufficient heat input, wrong electrode angle, fast travel speed, slag/contamination on side wall. Critical defect, usually rejected.

Question 4: A weld defect that appears as a thin line of slag entrapment between weld passes is:

  • A. Inter-run slag (slag inclusion)
  • B. Porosity
  • C. Crack
  • D. Undercut

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: Slag inclusions between weld runs (inter-run slag) occur when slag is not properly cleaned between passes in SMAW, FCAW, or SAW. Appears on RT as irregular dark indications usually following the bead.

Question 5: Undercut is:

  • A. A groove melted into the parent material adjacent to a weld toe
  • B. Excess weld metal
  • C. Porosity
  • D. Internal flaw

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: Undercut is a surface flaw: a groove melted into the parent metal adjacent to the weld toe, not filled by weld metal. Common in high-current GMAW and SMAW. Acceptance limits in BS EN ISO 5817 are based on weld class.

Question 6: BS EN ISO 5817 quality level B is:

  • A. Stringent (most strict)
  • B. Moderate
  • C. Loose
  • D. No requirements

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: BS EN ISO 5817 defines three quality levels: B (stringent), C (intermediate), D (moderate). Higher levels have tighter acceptance criteria on every defect type. Most pressure equipment specifies B or C.

Question 7: A weld procedure specification (WPS) per ASME IX must include:

  • A. Essential and non-essential variables for the process
  • B. Only the welder’s name
  • C. Material thickness only
  • D. Visual inspector only

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: ASME IX QW-200 requires the WPS to list essential, supplementary essential, and non-essential variables (process, base metal, filler metal, position, preheat, PWHT, gas, electrical, technique). Changes to essential variables require requalification (new PQR).

Question 8: A PQR (Procedure Qualification Record) is:

  • A. Documentation of the actual welding parameters and mechanical tests used to qualify a WPS
  • B. A pre-job checklist
  • C. Material spec
  • D. Welder ID card

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: The PQR records the actual values used (current, voltage, travel speed, preheat, etc.) during qualification welding and the test results (tensile, bend, impact, hardness). The WPS is derived from the PQR.

Question 9: A welder performance qualification (WPQ) per ASME IX is:

  • A. The record that the welder produced a sound test coupon meeting acceptance criteria
  • B. A union card
  • C. The WPS
  • D. A heat treatment record

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: WPQ (QW-300) demonstrates the welder’s skill. Welder welds a coupon per the WPS; the coupon is tested (RT or bend tests). Acceptance qualifies the welder for a range of positions, materials, and thicknesses per the essential variables.

Question 10: A welder continuity period per ASME IX is:

  • A. Maximum 6 months between welds in the qualified process to maintain certification
  • B. No limit
  • C. 12 months
  • D. Forever

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: Per QW-322, a welder must weld using the qualified process at least every 6 months to maintain qualification. If gap exceeds 6 months, requalification is required (or limited recertification per QW-322.2).

Question 11: A typical preheat temperature for carbon steel above 25 mm thick is:

  • A. 100 to 150°C, with higher for higher carbon equivalent
  • B. No preheat needed
  • C. Above 500°C
  • D. Cool below ambient

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: Preheat reduces cooling rate to prevent hard HAZ and hydrogen cracking. AWS D1.1, ASME B31.3, ISO/TR 17671 provide preheat tables based on material, thickness, carbon equivalent, and heat input.

Question 12: A solidification crack (hot crack) typically:

  • A. Forms in the weld metal during solidification, usually centerline
  • B. Forms cold in the HAZ
  • C. Forms after PWHT
  • D. Does not occur

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: Hot cracks form at high temperature during solidification, typically along grain boundaries at the weld centerline. Driven by tensile stress and segregation of impurities (sulfur, phosphorus). Mitigated by reducing restraint, decreasing heat input, controlling impurities.

Question 13: A cold crack (hydrogen crack) in HAZ typically appears:

  • A. Hours or days after welding, in hard microstructure with hydrogen and tensile stress
  • B. During welding only
  • C. Never
  • D. Always at root

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: Hydrogen-assisted cold cracking requires hydrogen, hard microstructure (martensite), and tensile stress. Develops typically 48 hours after welding. Prevention: low-hydrogen consumables, preheat, hydrogen bake-out, controlled cooling, soft microstructure (PWHT).

Question 14: A weld root concavity is:

  • A. A shallow groove at the weld root, less than parent metal level
  • B. Excess penetration
  • C. Slag
  • D. Porosity

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: Root concavity is a depression at the root surface caused by excessive penetration heat or insufficient filler. Acceptance depends on code; usually limited to 1 to 2 mm depending on wall thickness.

Question 15: A weld toe is:

  • A. The junction between weld face and parent metal
  • B. The root
  • C. The weld cap
  • D. The heat source

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: The weld toe is where the weld surface meets the base metal. Stress concentrates here, making toes preferential sites for fatigue cracks. Toe grinding/peening is a common fatigue improvement technique.

Question 16: Per AWS D1.1, visual inspection of welds is performed:

  • A. Always — mandatory for all welds
  • B. Optional
  • C. Only on completed pressure vessels
  • D. Never

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: Visual inspection is the most universal NDT method. AWS D1.1, ASME IX, and BS EN ISO 17637 all mandate visual inspection on all welds. CSWIP 3.1 is fundamentally a visual inspector qualification.

Question 17: A weld with high crown reinforcement:

  • A. Creates stress concentration and is typically limited in height
  • B. Improves strength
  • C. Is required
  • D. Has no effect

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: Excess weld metal (overfill) creates a notch at the weld toe, raising stress concentration. Codes typically limit cap height to 3 mm for thin sections and up to 5 mm for thicker plates. Grinding flush is common for fatigue-critical applications.

Question 18: PWHT (post-weld heat treatment) of carbon steel typically holds at:

  • A. 580 to 620°C for stress relief
  • B. Above melting
  • C. Below freezing
  • D. Room temperature

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: PWHT for carbon steel holds at 580 to 620°C for typically 1 hour per inch of thickness. Reduces residual stress, tempers HAZ, helps hydrogen diffusion. Heating/cooling rate controlled to limit thermal stress.

Question 19: A fillet weld leg length is measured:

  • A. From the toe to the root along each fusion face
  • B. Diagonal of the weld
  • C. Width only
  • D. Not measured

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: Fillet weld leg = distance from the joint root to the toe along each fusion face. Throat = shortest distance from the root to the weld face. Most acceptance criteria specify minimum leg length.

Question 20: Gas tungsten arc welding (GTAW/TIG) shielding gas is typically:

  • A. Argon, or argon-helium mixtures
  • B. CO2
  • C. Air
  • D. Nitrogen for steel

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: TIG uses inert gas to protect the tungsten and weld pool. Argon is the most common (cleaner arc, easier control); helium adds heat (deeper penetration). CO2 is reactive and not used for TIG. Nitrogen used for duplex stainless backing in limited applications.

Question 21: A welder qualified on plate (PA position) by ASME IX is also qualified for:

  • A. Plate flat (PA) position only, per essential variable position
  • B. All positions
  • C. Pipe in all positions
  • D. No position

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: Position is an essential variable for welder qualification. Plate PA qualifies only flat. To qualify for vertical/overhead, the welder must test in those positions. Pipe 6G qualifies all positions.

Question 22: A typical filler metal classification AWS A5.1 E7018 indicates:

  • A. 70 ksi tensile, all positions, low-hydrogen iron-powder iron-powder coating, AC/DCEP
  • B. Aluminum
  • C. Stainless steel
  • D. Cast iron

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: AWS A5.1 SMAW electrode classification: E = electrode, 70 = 70 ksi tensile, 1 = all positions, 8 = iron-powder iron-powder low-hydrogen flux. E7018 is the workhorse low-hydrogen electrode for carbon steel pressure work.

Question 23: A weld macro examination requires:

  • A. Cut section, polish, etch with appropriate reagent, examine at low magnification
  • B. Microscopic only
  • C. Photograph weld surface
  • D. Heat treat the weld

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: CSWIP 3.1 macro exam: cut weld coupon transverse to the weld, polish with progressively finer papers (220, 400, 600 grit), etch with 2% Nital (carbon steel), examine the cross-section for fusion, defects, HAZ size, and pass sequence. Magnification typically 5x to 10x.

Question 24: A weld inspection report should include:

  • A. Job ID, welder, WPS, NDT performed, indications with location and acceptance status, inspector ID and date
  • B. Verbal report only
  • C. Sketch only
  • D. Welder name only

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: Standard weld inspection report includes traceability (job, drawing, weld number), welder identification, WPS/PQR reference, NDT performed, all indications with size and location, acceptance per code, repair recommendations, and inspector identification.

Question 25: A CSWIP 3.1 inspector’s primary role is:

  • A. Verify welding is performed per WPS and that the resulting weld meets the acceptance code
  • B. Welding
  • C. Designing welds
  • D. Heat treatment

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: CSWIP 3.1 inspectors check that the WPS is used, parameters are within limits, joint preparation is correct, NDT is performed, and the finished weld meets the visual and NDT acceptance criteria. They do not weld or design.

Study Tips for CSWIP 3.1

  • Memorize defect morphology: Use the TWI defect chart, read BS EN ISO 6520-1 (defect classification). Be able to identify every common weld defect from a photo or macro.
  • Master the code: Choose your code (AWS D1.1, ASME IX, BS EN ISO 5817) and study it cover to cover. The Specific Theory paper is open-book for some codes.
  • Practical practice: Spend 20+ hours visually inspecting real welded plates and pipes before the exam. Practice writing concise, accurate inspection reports.
  • Macro etching: Practice etching and identifying features on sample sections. Most candidates fail the macro paper because they cannot identify all weld passes.
  • Time management: The General Theory is 50 questions in 60 minutes; less than 1.5 minutes per question. Pace yourself.

Recommended Study Materials

  • TWI CSWIP 3.1 Course Notes (provided at training)
  • BS EN ISO 5817 Quality levels for imperfections in welded joints
  • BS EN ISO 6520-1 Classification of geometric imperfections
  • ASME BPVC IX Welding qualification
  • AWS D1.1 Structural Welding Code
  • BS EN ISO 17637 Visual testing of fusion welds
  • Atlantis NDT CSWIP 3.1 prep course (5-day course aligned with TWI syllabus)

Frequently Asked Questions

Q: How is CSWIP 3.1 different from CSWIP 3.0?

A: CSWIP 3.0 is the entry-level Visual Welding Inspector (limited to visual inspection of butt and fillet welds in plate). CSWIP 3.1 expands to pipes and adds the macro examination. CSWIP 3.2 (Senior Welding Inspector) is the next step up.

Q: Is CSWIP 3.1 recognized in the USA?

A: CSWIP 3.1 is widely recognized globally, including in many US oil & gas, pipeline, and offshore contracts. AWS CWI (Certified Welding Inspector) is the closest US equivalent and is sometimes preferred for AWS-driven structural work.

Q: What experience is required to sit CSWIP 3.1?

A: Documented experience in welding inspection, with formal training of at least one week prior. Typical candidates have 1+ year of welding/inspection background.

Q: How long does CSWIP 3.1 certification last?

A: 5 years initial certification, renewable at 5 years with continued practice records and a re-examination. Full reset exam at 10 years.

Q: How does CSWIP 3.1 differ from API 510/570?

A: CSWIP 3.1 is a welding inspection certification, focused on construction-stage QA/QC. API 510/570/653 are in-service inspection certifications. Many inspectors hold both for full life-cycle coverage.

Q: Does Atlantis NDT offer CSWIP 3.1 prep courses?

A: Yes — our 5-day intensive CSWIP 3.1 prep course mirrors the TWI syllabus, includes 300+ practice questions, mock macro exams, and real plates/pipes for practical practice. Cohorts run quarterly in Houston, Dubai, Hyderabad. Call +1 (281) 840-8969.

Q: What is the CSWIP 3.1 pass rate?

A: First-attempt pass rate averages 65 to 75%. The macro paper has the highest failure rate. Atlantis prep students average 90%+.

Q: Can I take CSWIP 3.1 without prior welding experience?

A: It is allowed but very challenging. We recommend at least 1 year of welding QC/QA experience before attempting CSWIP 3.1.

Q: Is CSWIP 3.1 valid for NDT inspection?

A: CSWIP 3.1 covers visual inspection of welds. For NDT methods (UT, RT, MT, PT), separate ASNT or PCN certifications are required. See our ASNT vs PCN article.

Q: How does CSWIP 3.1 compare to AWS CWI?

A: Both are welding inspector certifications. CSWIP is UK-origin, internationally recognized in oil & gas and offshore. AWS CWI is US-origin, dominant in US structural and pipeline. Many inspectors hold both.

About Atlantis NDT

We deliver accredited NDT training, technical consulting, certification preparation, and digital inspection software trusted by oil & gas, fabrication, EPC, and power generation clients. Our team of ASNT Level III instructors has trained thousands of inspectors worldwide.

Whether you are preparing for ASNT certification, API 510, API 570, or API 653, our exam preparation programs combine classroom theory, hands-on practical training, and proctored mock exams that mirror the real test environment.

title: PCN Level 2 Exam Guide 2026: Format, 25 Practice MCQs, ISO 9712
snippet: 2026 PCN Level 2 NDT exam guide: ISO 9712 alignment, exam structure, 25 practice MCQs, sectors, vision rules, recertification, study tips, and FAQ.
content:
The Personnel Certification in Non-destructive Testing (PCN) scheme, administered by the British Institute of Non-Destructive Testing (BINDT), is one of the most widely recognized third-party NDT certifications globally. PCN is fully aligned with ISO 9712, and a PCN Level 2 certificate is accepted across Europe, the Middle East, Asia, and increasingly North America. This 2026 guide explains the PCN Level 2 exam structure, gives practice questions for the most common methods (UT, RT, MT, PT), and provides recommended study material.

PCN Level 2 Exam Format Overview

PCN Level 2 follows ISO 9712 closely. The certification structure has three components:

  • General Examination: 40 closed-book MCQ on NDT principles for the chosen method. 1 hour 30 minutes. Pass mark 70%.
  • Specific Examination: 30 closed-book MCQ covering codes/standards and product technology relevant to the candidate’s industry sector. 1 hour 30 minutes. Pass mark 70%.
  • Practical Examination: Hands-on demonstration including instrument setup, calibration, inspection of two or three specimens, written report on findings, and writing an NDT instruction. 80% pass mark on practical (separate elements: instruction writing, setup, indication detection, evaluation, reporting).

All three components must be passed in the same window (typically 1 year). Certification valid for 5 years with annual employer verification of practice, renewal exam at 5 years, full recertification at 10 years.

PCN Industry Sectors

PCN organizes certifications by industry sector. Common Level 2 sectors include:

  • Welds: Pressure equipment, structural welds, pipelines
  • Castings: Steel, aluminum castings
  • Forgings: Steel, aluminum forgings
  • Wrought: Plate, rod, bar inspection
  • Aerospace: Combination of welds, castings, composites
  • Railway: Wheel/axle inspection, rail integrity
  • In-service inspection: Pressure equipment, pipelines, tanks

PCN Level 2 Practice Questions

Question 1: PCN is administered by:

  • A. BINDT (British Institute of Non-Destructive Testing)
  • B. ASNT
  • C. TWI
  • D. ISO directly

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: BINDT, headquartered in Northampton UK, administers the PCN scheme. PCN is fully ISO 9712 aligned and accredited by UKAS (UK Accreditation Service).

Question 2: PCN Level 2 certification follows which international standard?

  • A. ISO 9712
  • B. ASNT SNT-TC-1A
  • C. EN 473 (now obsolete)
  • D. ASME Section V

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: ISO 9712 is the international standard for NDT personnel qualification. PCN is one of several ISO 9712-compliant schemes (others include COFREND, DGZfP, ACCP). EN 473 was the former European standard, now harmonized with ISO 9712.

Question 3: How long is PCN Level 2 certification initially valid?

  • A. 5 years
  • B. 10 years
  • C. 1 year
  • D. 3 years

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: ISO 9712 sets the certification cycle at 5 years initial validity, renewal at 5 years (administrative renewal with annual eye exam and continuous practice), and full recertification exam at 10 years.

Question 4: PCN UT Level 2 weld sector requires what minimum experience?

  • A. 480 hours UT experience documented (after Level 1) before sitting Level 2
  • B. No experience required
  • C. 10 years
  • D. 100 hours

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: ISO 9712 Table 2 / PCN appendix sets experience: typically 480 hours UT Level 2 documented after Level 1 certification, plus 80 hours formal training. Direct-entry Level 2 requires combined Level 1 + 2 training and experience.

Question 5: For a PCN UT Level 2 weld inspection at 60°, the skip distance on 25 mm plate is:

  • A. ~86.6 mm full skip (2 × 25 × tan 60°)
  • B. 50 mm
  • C. 25 mm
  • D. 100 mm

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: Full skip = 2 × thickness × tan(angle) = 2 × 25 × 1.732 = 86.6 mm. Half skip = 43.3 mm. Skip distances are critical for marking the scanning range for full coverage of the weld volume.

Question 6: A PCN UT Level 2 specific examination weld sector uses what standard for acceptance?

  • A. EN ISO 11666 or EN ISO 23279, depending on contract
  • B. ASNT only
  • C. No standard
  • D. AWS only

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: European weld acceptance standards: EN ISO 11666 (acceptance for amplitude-based UT), EN ISO 23279 (characterization of indications), EN ISO 17640 (general UT of welds). ASME and AWS are also recognized depending on contract.

Question 7: A PCN RT Level 2 candidate must demonstrate competence in:

  • A. Setup, exposure calculation, processing, IQI sensitivity verification, interpretation, reporting
  • B. Only film handling
  • C. Only safety
  • D. Only writing

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: PCN RT Level 2 practical demonstration covers the full workflow: technique selection, IQI placement, exposure setup, film processing or DR/CR acquisition, interpretation, and final report. All must reach 80% to pass.

Question 8: PCN Level 2 in MT requires understanding of:

  • A. Magnetization methods, field strength verification, particle systems, indication interpretation, acceptance criteria
  • B. Only one technique
  • C. Only welds
  • D. Only forgings

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: PCN MT Level 2 covers all magnetization techniques (yoke, prod, coil, central conductor, head shot, multidirectional), particle types (visible/fluorescent, wet/dry), field strength verification, and acceptance to applicable standards (e.g., EN ISO 23278).

Question 9: A PCN PT Level 2 practical exam typically includes:

  • A. Pre-clean, penetrant, dwell, removal, developer, evaluate, report on 2 to 3 specimens
  • B. Only spray penetrant
  • C. Only visual
  • D. No specimens

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: PCN PT Level 2 practical follows the full penetrant sequence on 2 or 3 specimens (typically with planted defects). Candidates must identify and characterize indications, evaluate to the chosen acceptance standard (EN ISO 23277 etc.).

Question 10: PCN Level 2 certificate is recognized in:

  • A. UK, Europe, Middle East, Asia, increasingly worldwide oil & gas
  • B. UK only
  • C. US only
  • D. Nowhere

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: PCN is globally recognized in oil & gas (Shell, BP, ADNOC, Aramco accept PCN), offshore, pipelines, manufacturing, and aerospace. ISO 9712 alignment makes PCN portable across borders.

Question 11: A PCN written NDT instruction is:

  • A. A document a Level 2 prepares from an approved procedure, specifying step-by-step how to perform an inspection on a specific item
  • B. The same as a procedure
  • C. A welding spec
  • D. A safety document

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: Per ISO 9712 / PCN, Level 2 personnel are authorized to write NDT instructions from approved procedures. The instruction is item-specific and lists exact parameters, scope, and acceptance. Level 2 cannot write procedures (that is Level 3).

Question 12: PCN vision requirements per ISO 9712 are:

  • A. Near vision Jaeger 1 or equivalent at 30 cm, plus color vision triennial
  • B. Color only
  • C. No requirements
  • D. Distance vision only

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: ISO 9712 / PCN requires near vision capable of reading Jaeger 1 or Times Roman N4.5 letters at 30 cm (one or both eyes, corrected if needed), and color vision sufficient to distinguish colors used in the method (triennial test).

Question 13: PCN recertification at 10 years requires:

  • A. Re-examination (general, specific, and practical)
  • B. Document review only
  • C. No action
  • D. Just experience hours

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: ISO 9712 specifies 10-year recertification by re-examination, similar to the initial qualifying exams. Renewal at 5 years is by document review (continued practice, eye exam, employer endorsement) with no exam.

Question 14: PCN practical examination for UT Level 2 typically includes how many specimens?

  • A. Two or three specimens of the chosen sector (e.g., two weld specimens + one cast)
  • B. One
  • C. Ten
  • D. None

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: ISO 9712 Annex A and PCN procedures specify the minimum 2 specimens for many sectors, with extra for multi-process sectors. Weld sector typically requires plate butt weld and pipe butt weld specimens.

Question 15: PCN Level 2 specific paper open-book or closed?

  • A. Closed-book by default (some sectors may allow access to specific standards)
  • B. Always open-book
  • C. No specific paper
  • D. Verbal only

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: PCN specific exams are closed-book in most sectors (candidates must memorize key acceptance values), although some sectors allow restricted reference material. Always verify with the current PCN syllabus.

Question 16: A PCN Level 2 weld sector candidate must know acceptance to which European standards?

  • A. EN ISO 5817 (visual quality levels), EN ISO 11666 (UT acceptance), EN ISO 10675 (RT), EN ISO 23277 (PT), EN ISO 23278 (MT)
  • B. Only ASME
  • C. AWS only
  • D. No standards

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: The European/ISO acceptance standards form the spec backbone of PCN weld sector exams. Candidates must memorize quality levels (B, C, D) and key acceptance values.

Question 17: A PCN training course must be conducted by:

  • A. A PCN-approved training organization (ATO)
  • B. Any company
  • C. Self-study only
  • D. Online only

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: ISO 9712 requires training by an approved training organization. PCN maintains a register of ATOs that have demonstrated trainer qualifications, syllabus alignment, and facilities. Atlantis NDT is working toward formal ATO status; for now we deliver pre-PCN preparation training in partnership with ATOs.

Question 18: PCN Level 2 UT training duration is typically:

  • A. 80 hours (40 Level 1 + 40 Level 2) total
  • B. 8 hours
  • C. 200 hours
  • D. No formal training

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: ISO 9712 Table 1 specifies 40 hours UT Level 1 + 40 hours UT Level 2 = 80 hours total formal training. Other methods have different durations (e.g., MT 12 + 8, PT 4 + 8, RT 40 + 40).

Question 19: PCN Level 2 in PAUT (Phased Array UT) sector is:

  • A. Separate from standard UT — requires its own training and exam
  • B. Same as standard UT
  • C. No certification exists
  • D. Only Level 3

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: PCN treats PAUT as a separate method requiring its own qualifying exam (general, specific, practical). Candidates typically must hold PCN UT Level 2 in the same sector first. See our PAUT vs TOFD article.

Question 20: PCN compared to ASNT employer-based certification is:

  • A. Third-party (independent of employer), generally more portable internationally
  • B. Same as ASNT
  • C. Inferior
  • D. Only US

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: PCN is third-party certification (BINDT, not the employer, issues the certificate). ASNT employer-based (SNT-TC-1A) is issued by the employer and is tied to that employer. ACCP and ASNT Central Certification are third-party schemes. See ASNT vs PCN article.

Question 21: A PCN candidate’s vision results must be:

  • A. Verified by a qualified medical examiner annually
  • B. Self-declared
  • C. Only at certification
  • D. Not required

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: Vision must be verified by an optometrist, occupational physician, or other competent medical examiner annually. Color vision is verified every 3 years. The results are recorded and submitted to BINDT.

Question 22: A failed PCN specific exam can be re-sat:

  • A. Twice within the validity period (typically 1 year), then re-training required
  • B. Once only
  • C. Unlimited
  • D. Never

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: ISO 9712 allows re-examination of failed components twice within the qualifying period. After two failures, re-training is required before another attempt. Practical and theory papers can be re-sat independently.

Question 23: A PCN certificate identifies:

  • A. Method, level, sector, expiry date, and unique certificate number
  • B. Only the candidate name
  • C. Only the employer
  • D. No information

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: PCN certificate clearly states method (UT, RT, MT, PT, ET, VT), level (1, 2, 3), sector (welds, castings, etc.), holder name and ID, issue date, expiry date, and unique certificate number for verification on the BINDT portal.

Question 24: To upgrade from PCN Level 2 to Level 3 requires:

  • A. Additional formal training, accumulated experience as Level 2, and passing the Level 3 Basic + Method exams
  • B. Document review only
  • C. Self-declaration
  • D. Time alone

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: PCN Level 3 (like ASNT Level III) requires Basic exam (cross-method knowledge) and Method exam (depth in one method). Experience after Level 2 (typically 1 to 2 years) is a prerequisite. See our Level 2 vs 3 comparison.

Question 25: A PCN Level 2 inspector’s primary scope of authority is:

  • A. Set up equipment, perform tests per a procedure, interpret indications, write NDT instructions, train Level 1
  • B. Write and approve procedures
  • C. Approve all NDT methods
  • D. Train Level 3

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: ISO 9712 / PCN Level 2 scope: equipment setup, calibration, test execution, indication interpretation, evaluation to acceptance criteria, instruction writing from procedures, training Level 1. Procedure writing and approval is Level 3 only.

Study Tips for PCN Level 2

  • Use a PCN-approved training organization (ATO): Your training must come from a registered ATO for the syllabus and hours to count. BINDT maintains the list at bindt.org.
  • Practice the practical: The practical exam has the highest failure rate. Spend 50+ hours on real specimens before exam day. Practice writing instructions until you can produce a complete one in 30 minutes.
  • Tab the standards: EN ISO 17640 (UT of welds), EN ISO 17636 (RT), EN ISO 5817 (visual quality), EN ISO 23277/23278 (PT/MT acceptance).
  • Closed-book preparation: Unlike ASNT specific (open-book), PCN specific is closed-book. Memorize key acceptance values and parameter limits.
  • Practice 500+ questions: Atlantis prep program delivers 500+ questions across general and specific for each method.

Recommended Study Materials

  • ISO 9712:2021 NDT — Qualification and certification of NDT personnel
  • PCN General Requirements (PCN/GEN) latest edition
  • PCN Method-Specific syllabi (CP-7 UT, CP-8 RT, etc.)
  • EN ISO 5817, 11666, 10675, 23277, 23278 (acceptance standards)
  • EN ISO 17640, 17636, 9712, 9934 (method standards)
  • BINDT NDT Yearbook for industry context
  • Atlantis NDT PCN Level 2 preparation course (in partnership with approved ATO)

Frequently Asked Questions

Q: What is the main difference between PCN and ASNT certification?

A: PCN is third-party (BINDT issues the certificate). ASNT (under SNT-TC-1A) is employer-based. ASNT also offers third-party certification (ACCP / ASNT Central Certification). See our full ASNT vs PCN comparison.

Q: Is PCN accepted in the USA?

A: Increasingly yes, especially in oil & gas and offshore. Some US codes (ASME) still default to ASNT, but PCN holders are widely accepted in international and multinational contracts.

Q: How long does the full PCN Level 2 process take?

A: Typically 6 to 12 months: training (1 to 2 weeks), accumulating required experience hours (often during work between training and exam), then 1 to 2 days of exams.

Q: Does PCN expire if I don’t work in NDT for a year?

A: PCN requires continuous practice. Gaps over 12 months may invalidate certification. Always verify with BINDT and your employer.

Q: What is the PCN Level 2 cost?

A: Training fees vary (typically £1,500 to £2,500 per method) plus BINDT exam fees (~£500 to £700 per method). Total cost £2,000 to £3,500 per method.

Q: Does Atlantis NDT offer PCN preparation?

A: Yes — we deliver PCN preparation in partnership with approved ATOs. Our 80-hour blended program covers theory, practical, and mock exams. Call +1 (281) 840-8969 to discuss the next cohort.

Q: Can I hold both PCN and ASNT certifications?

A: Yes, many international inspectors hold both. They are complementary — ASNT for US work and PCN for international.

Q: How does PCN Level 2 in welds relate to CSWIP 3.1?

A: CSWIP 3.1 is a visual welding inspector qualification. PCN Level 2 weld sector is an NDT method qualification (UT, RT, MT, PT) applied to welds. Many inspectors hold both for complete fabrication inspection coverage.

Q: What is the PCN Level 2 pass rate?

A: First-attempt averages 60 to 75%. The practical exam has the highest failure rate. Structured prep raises pass rates to 85%+.

Q: How does PCN compare to API 510/570/653?

A: PCN certifies you in NDT methods. API 510/570/653 certify you as an in-service inspector of vessels, piping, or tanks. Many inspectors hold both PCN (for NDT skill) and API (for in-service inspection role).

About Atlantis NDT

Atlantis NDT is a global NDT technology and services company headquartered in Houston, Texas with operations across India and the Middle East. We deliver accredited NDT training, technical consulting, certification preparation, and digital inspection software trusted by oil & gas, fabrication, EPC, and power generation clients. Our team of ASNT Level III instructors has trained thousands of inspectors worldwide.

Whether you are preparing for ASNT certification, API 510, API 570, or API 653, our exam preparation programs combine classroom theory, hands-on practical training, and proctored mock exams that mirror the real test environment.

Call us at +1 (281) 840-8969 or email sales@atlantisndt.com to enroll in the next training cohort. Same-day quotes for corporate group training in Houston, Dubai, Riyadh, Hyderabad, and on-site at your facility.

title: UT vs RT 2026: Complete Comparison Guide for Inspectors & Engineers
snippet: 2026 ultrasonic vs radiographic testing comparison: physics, defect detection, safety, cost per inspection, training, code coverage, when to use which.
content:
Ultrasonic Testing (UT) and Radiographic Testing (RT) are the two dominant volumetric NDT methods. Both find buried flaws inside welds, castings, and forgings, but they work on fundamentally different physics and have very different operational, safety, and cost profiles. This 2026 guide compares UT and RT across 12 dimensions so engineers, inspectors, and project managers can pick the right method for the right job — or know when to combine both.

UT vs RT at a Glance

DimensionUltrasonic Testing (UT)Radiographic Testing (RT)
PhysicsHigh-frequency sound waves (typically 1 to 15 MHz) reflected from flawsIonizing radiation (X-ray or gamma) absorbed differently by flaws & material
Defect detection biasBest for planar flaws (cracks, LOF) oriented to reflect the beamBest for volumetric flaws (porosity, slag, voids)
SafetyNo ionizing radiation; operator can work next to othersRadioactive sources or X-ray tubes; exclusion zones required
Image recordA-scan (digital data), B-scan, C-scan, encoded scans archivedFilm or digital image; classical archival 2D image of weld
Operator skillHigh — calibration, interpretation, sizing all skill-dependentModerate to high for interpretation; setup is more procedural
Speed (per weld)Fast with encoded PAUT; slower with manualSlower exposure + processing time; longer with film
Cost per inspectionLower running cost; instrument capex high, no consumablesHigher running cost (film, sources, decay) and licensing
Thickness range3 mm to 1 m+ depending on probe and materialTypically 6 mm to 200 mm steel; Co-60 for very thick
Material constraintsCoupling required; coarse-grain austenitic problematicDensity contrast required; uniform thickness preferred
Defect sizingThrough-wall sizing with TOFD/PAUTLength and width; through-wall depth limited
Code coverage (ASME)Section V Article 4 (manual), Article 5 (immersion), App. IV (PAUT)Section V Article 2 + Mandatory Appendices III/IV/V (CR/DDA/CT)
Training timeUT L2: 80 hours formal training + 400 hrs experienceRT L2: 80 hours formal + 32 hours radiation safety + experience

1. Physics — How Each Method Works

UT sends high-frequency longitudinal or shear waves into the material via a piezoelectric transducer and a couplant. Reflections from internal interfaces (flaws, geometry, back wall) return to the transducer and produce a time-vs-amplitude (A-scan) trace. The depth of a flaw is calculated from the time-of-flight; the size is estimated from amplitude (DAC/TCG) or from sizing techniques (6 dB drop, 20 dB drop, TOFD, S-scan).

RT exposes the part to a beam of X-rays or gamma rays. Where the part is thinner or contains a void, more radiation reaches the detector (film, CR plate, or DDA), producing a darker image. The radiographic image is fundamentally a 2D shadow of the part’s density distribution, similar in nature to a medical chest X-ray.

2. Defect Detection — What Each Sees

UT excels at planar flaws oriented to reflect the beam:

  • Lack of fusion (LOF) at the side wall
  • Lack of root penetration (LOP)
  • Crack initiation and propagation (fatigue, SCC, HIC)
  • Laminations parallel to the surface
  • Hydrogen-induced cracking with TOFD or AUBT

RT excels at volumetric flaws:

  • Porosity (round dark indications)
  • Slag inclusions (irregular dark)
  • Tungsten inclusions in GTAW (bright spot)
  • Cluster porosity
  • Concavity/excess penetration on root surface (depending on technique)

Both can miss flaws oriented unfavorably to the beam (RT) or to the radiation path. The classic case: a tight, vertically oriented LOF can be invisible to RT (no significant density difference) but easily detected by UT angle beam.

3. Safety

UT is intrinsically safe — sound waves carry no health hazard. Inspectors can work in occupied areas and near other crafts. Couplant management (slip hazard, environmental) is the main concern.

RT is a regulated hazard. Ionizing radiation requires:

  • Licensed operators and radiation safety officers (RSOs)
  • Site survey and exclusion zone (typically 0.3 to 1 mSv/hr boundary)
  • Shielding, badges, dosimeters, alarming dose ratemeters
  • Source storage and transport per IATA / DOT
  • Shutdown of adjacent work, often nights/weekends

The result: RT productivity drops dramatically in busy plants. UT can keep running 24/7 alongside other crews.

4. Cost Comparison (Typical 2026 Figures)

ItemUTRT (film)RT (DR)
Instrument cost (entry)a modest cost to a modest costa modest cost source projector + a modest cost darkrooma modest cost to a modest cost DDA
Per-weld consumablesMinimal (couplant)Film a modest cost to 20/exposureNone
Setup time / weld5 to 10 min30 to 60 min15 to 30 min
Exposure / scan time2 to 20 min5 to 30 min1 to 5 min
Processing timeNone (real time)10 to 30 min (chemistry)None (real time)
Crew size1 to 22 to 3 (RT crew with RSO)2 (radiographer + assistant)
Effective $/weld (typical 25 mm CS)a modest cost to a modest costa modest cost to a modest costa modest cost to a modest cost

5. Speed

Manual UT is slower per weld than experienced PAUT; encoded PAUT with corrosion mapping can survey 1 to 2 m/min, outpacing film RT by 5 to 10x. Per ASME Section V Mandatory Appendix XI, PAUT can replace RT in many code applications. See our PAUT vs TOFD article for advanced UT options.

6. Code Coverage

ASME BPVC Section V: Article 4 (UT general), Article 5 (immersion UT), Appendix IV (PAUT, encoded scans), Appendix III (TOFD). Article 2 covers RT with Mandatory Appendices III (CR), IV (DDA), V (CT).

ISO/EN: ISO 17640 (UT of welds), ISO 13588 (PAUT), ISO 10863 (TOFD). ISO 17636-1 (RT film), 17636-2 (RT digital).

API: Both methods are accepted as the volumetric exam under API 510, API 570, and API 653 for in-service inspection.

Recent code changes have explicitly allowed UT/PAUT as an RT replacement in many cases when properly qualified per ASME V Mandatory Appendix XI.

7. Training and Certification

Both methods require UT Level 2 or RT Level 2 certification. UT generally has a steeper learning curve due to live calibration and 3D mental visualization. RT adds the radiation safety training and licensing burden — in many countries an RT inspector must also hold a radiation safety officer (RSO) certificate before operating sources.

8. Documentation and Archival

Traditional film RT produces a hard-copy radiograph that can be archived for decades and audited 30 years later. This is still highly valued in nuclear, aerospace, and some refineries.

Modern UT (especially encoded PAUT and TOFD) produces digital scan data that can also be archived — with the advantage of being computer-readable, searchable, and overlaid for trending. Industry is gradually moving from film to digital UT/RT for this reason.

9. Environmental / Geometry Constraints

UT struggles with:

  • Coarse-grained austenitic stainless (extreme scatter)
  • Cast iron (porous, dispersive)
  • Very thin material (less than 2 to 3 mm)
  • Complex geometries that prevent good coupling

RT struggles with:

  • Very thick steel (> 100 mm needs Co-60 and long exposures)
  • Tight planar flaws perpendicular to the beam
  • Sites without exclusion zones (urban refineries during operation)
  • Materials with similar density to defects (e.g., aluminum porosity in thick aluminum)

10. Defect Sizing

UT (especially TOFD and PAUT) can directly measure through-wall extent of a flaw, critical for engineering critical assessment (ECA) and fitness-for-service per API 579. Film RT gives length and width but the through-wall depth must be inferred from indication density — less precise.

11. When to Use Which (Decision Guide)

  • Choose UT when: Working in occupied plants, fatigue-critical welds, looking for cracks/LOF, need real-time results, need through-wall sizing for FFS, working around other crafts, thick sections.
  • Choose RT when: Customer or code mandates film records, looking for porosity/slag/inclusions, working in cleared shop environments (e.g., fabrication shops), unfamiliar weld geometry needing a global 2D image.
  • Use both when: Critical pressure equipment where neither alone gives full confidence; new construction often requires both for first-of-class welds, then transitions to UT-only based on PAUT qualification.

12. Future Outlook

UT — especially encoded PAUT and full-matrix capture (FMC/TFM) — is rapidly replacing RT in many construction and in-service applications. Drivers: safety, productivity, no consumables, digital archival. RT remains essential for porosity-sensitive welds, regulatory submission, and where customer specifications mandate film. Digital radiography (DDA/CR) is closing the productivity gap. Expect a long coexistence with UT growing share.

Frequently Asked Questions

Q: Can UT completely replace RT?

A: In many applications yes — especially with PAUT qualified per ASME V Mandatory Appendix XI. Some customers and codes still mandate film RT for specific welds (e.g., nuclear class 1).

Q: Which is more accurate for sizing?

A: UT (TOFD and PAUT) provides more accurate through-wall sizing. RT is more accurate for length and porosity counts.

Q: Can UT detect porosity?

A: Yes, but with lower sensitivity than RT. Small clustered porosity (<1 mm) is easier to see on a radiograph than on an A-scan.

Q: How does cost compare over a project?

A: Over a 1,000-weld project, UT is typically 40 to 60% cheaper than film RT, including capex amortization. Digital RT closes the gap.

Q: Are both methods accepted internationally?

A: Yes. UT and RT are universally accepted under ASME, ISO, AWS, API. The specific procedure must match the applicable code.

Q: What certifications do I need to perform UT or RT?

A: Level 2 in the relevant method (ASNT or PCN), plus method-specific endorsements (TOFD, PAUT, DR). RT also requires radiation safety qualification. See our ASNT certification page.

Q: How does PAUT differ from standard UT?

A: PAUT uses multi-element probes with electronic beam steering for faster, encoded inspection with imaging output. See our PAUT vs TOFD comparison.

Q: How does DR compare to film RT?

A: Digital radiography offers real-time imaging, no chemicals, lower per-shot cost long-term, but higher capex. See our DR vs film article.

Q: Can Atlantis NDT help us choose and qualify a UT or RT procedure?

A: Yes — our consulting team writes and qualifies UT, PAUT, TOFD, and RT procedures to ASME V, ISO 17640, AWS D1.1, API standards. Call +1 (281) 840-8969 or visit our consulting page.

Q: What is the training timeline for a UT vs RT inspector?

A: UT Level 2 = 80 hours formal training + 400 hours experience. RT Level 2 similar plus 32 hours radiation safety. Most inspectors take 6 to 12 months from Level 1 to Level 2 certification.

title: MT vs PT 2026: Magnetic Particle vs Liquid Penetrant Comparison
snippet: 2026 comparison of magnetic particle (MT) vs liquid penetrant (PT) testing: materials, sensitivity, speed, cost, temperature, codes, when to use which.
content:
Magnetic Particle Testing (MT) and Liquid Penetrant Testing (PT) are the two dominant surface NDT methods. Both find surface-breaking flaws — cracks, lack of fusion, porosity, laps, seams — but they work on fundamentally different physics and have very different material, speed, and sensitivity envelopes. This 2026 guide compares MT and PT across the dimensions that matter to inspection planners, QC managers, and NDT inspectors.

MT vs PT at a Glance

DimensionMagnetic Particle (MT)Liquid Penetrant (PT)
MaterialsFerromagnetic only (carbon steel, ferritic stainless, nickel iron)Any non-porous material (steel, stainless, aluminum, titanium, ceramic, plastic)
Flaws detectedSurface + slightly subsurface (up to ~3 mm)Surface only (must be open to surface)
SensitivityHigh for tight surface cracks; less sensitive subsurfaceVery high for tight surface cracks (5 to 10 μm visible)
Speed per partVery fast (yoke shot: seconds)Slower (full process 30 to 90 min)
Cost per partLowerHigher (consumables, time)
Surface prepClean dry; coatings < 0.05 mm OK with shim verifyClean, dry, paint-free; surface must be open
Temperature rangeUp to ~320°C (dry powder with HT particles)10 to 52°C standard; HT penetrants to 175°C with qualification
Equipment costa modest cost to a modest cost (yoke / coil / bench unit)a modest cost to a modest cost (spray cans / portable kit)
Operator skillModerate — magnetization geometry mattersModerate — process discipline matters
Coded by ASMESection V Article 7; ASTM E709/E1444; ISO 9934Section V Article 6; ASTM E165; ISO 3452
Acceptance standards (welds)ISO 23278, ASME VIII App 6, AWS D1.1ISO 23277, ASME VIII App 8, AWS D1.1
HazardsStrong magnetic field; arc burn from prodsSolvents (flammable); UV light for fluorescent

1. Physics — How Each Method Works

MT magnetizes the test part and applies finely divided ferromagnetic particles (dry powder or wet suspension). Surface or near-surface discontinuities perpendicular to the magnetic flux distort the field, causing a leakage field at the surface. The particles are attracted to this leakage, accumulating over the discontinuity as a visible indication.

PT applies a low-viscosity colored or fluorescent liquid (penetrant) to a thoroughly cleaned surface. The penetrant is drawn into any surface-breaking discontinuity by capillary action over a controlled dwell time. Excess surface penetrant is then removed, and a developer is applied which draws (blots) the penetrant out of the discontinuity, producing a visible indication.

2. Material Compatibility (the Biggest Decision Driver)

MT works only on ferromagnetic materials:

  • Carbon and low-alloy steel — primary use case
  • Ferritic stainless steel (400 series, e.g., 410, 430)
  • Martensitic stainless
  • Some nickel-iron alloys (e.g., 9% Ni cryogenic)
  • Cast iron (lower sensitivity due to porosity)

MT does NOT work on: Austenitic stainless (304/316), aluminum, titanium, copper, brass, plastics, ceramics.

PT works on all non-porous materials regardless of magnetic properties. PT is the only NDT option for surface inspection on most stainless and non-ferrous components. This is the single biggest factor in choosing between the two methods.

3. Speed and Productivity

MT is dramatically faster on ferromagnetic parts:

  • Yoke shot: 5 to 15 seconds per shot, two orthogonal shots per area — under a minute total per square foot of weld
  • Stationary bench MT: 30 seconds to 2 minutes per part for production work

PT requires the full sequence:

  • Pre-clean: 5 to 30 minutes (often the longest step)
  • Penetrant application + dwell: 5 to 60 minutes
  • Penetrant removal: 5 to 15 minutes
  • Developer application + dwell: 10 to 30 minutes
  • Evaluation: 5 to 20 minutes
  • Post-clean: 5 to 15 minutes

Total: 30 to 90 minutes per inspection area. For a production shop running ferromagnetic parts, this 10x to 30x speed difference is the deciding factor.

4. Sensitivity

Both methods can find very tight cracks if applied correctly. Quantitatively:

  • PT Level 3 (high sensitivity Type I-A fluorescent): 5 to 10 μm crack width
  • PT Level 2 (medium sensitivity): 10 to 20 μm
  • MT wet fluorescent: ~10 μm (similar to PT Level 2)
  • MT dry powder: ~25 μm

Both methods are highly operator-dependent. Sensitivity drops if dwell, particle concentration, magnetization direction, or surface prep are wrong.

5. Subsurface Detection

MT detects flaws up to about 3 mm below the surface (depending on field strength and material). PT can only detect flaws open to the surface. For mildly subsurface flaws — e.g., LOF beneath a slightly bowed cap — MT has the advantage on ferromagnetic parts.

6. Surface Preparation

MT is more tolerant of imperfect surface conditions:

  • Tolerates clean paint up to 0.05 mm with shim verification
  • Tolerates light rust and scale (with reduced sensitivity)
  • Can be performed through thin non-ferromagnetic coatings

PT requires the surface to be:

  • Completely paint-free over the inspection area
  • Free of oil, grease, dirt, water
  • Open at the surface (machining or shot-peening can close cracks — etch may be needed)

For coated or partially-cleaned welds, MT typically wins. For freshly machined or finished components, PT can be applied directly.

7. Temperature Range

MT is much more flexible for hot work:

  • Wet method up to ~52°C (standard) or ~125°C (HT carriers)
  • Dry powder with high-temperature particles up to ~320°C

PT standard penetrants are limited to ~52°C. High-temperature penetrants extend operation to ~175°C with qualification. Beyond this, penetrant evaporates before developer can pull it out. Many in-process weld inspections on hot piping rely on MT for this reason.

8. Cost Per Inspection

For ferromagnetic parts, MT is dramatically cheaper:

Cost itemMT (per weld)PT (per weld)
Consumablesa modest cost to a modest cost (particles, demag spray)a modest cost to a modest cost (penetrant + remover + developer)
Labor (15-min weld)a modest cost to a modest costa modest cost to a modest cost (90-min cycle)
Equipment amortizationa modest cost to a modest cost (yoke)a modest cost (spray cans)
Typical total per welda modest cost to a modest costa modest cost to a modest cost

9. Standards and Acceptance

MT codes: ASME BPVC Section V Article 7, ASTM E709 (Standard Guide), ASTM E1444 (Standard Practice for Wet Fluorescent), ISO 9934 Parts 1/2/3. Acceptance: ASME VIII Appendix 6, AWS D1.1, ISO 23278.

PT codes: ASME BPVC Section V Article 6, ASTM E165 (Standard Practice), ISO 3452 Parts 1 to 6. Acceptance: ASME VIII Appendix 8, AWS D1.1, ISO 23277.

Most construction codes allow either method for surface examination of ferromagnetic materials, leaving the choice to the inspector/manufacturer. Non-ferromagnetic materials default to PT.

10. Decision Guide — When to Use Which

Choose MT when:

  • The material is ferromagnetic (carbon steel, ferritic stainless)
  • You need high production throughput (e.g., 100+ welds/day)
  • You want near-surface flaw detection in addition to surface
  • The surface has light coatings or is hot
  • You need indication-detection in seconds, not minutes

Choose PT when:

  • The material is non-ferromagnetic (austenitic stainless, aluminum, titanium, ceramics)
  • The geometry makes magnetization difficult (very complex shapes)
  • You need the highest possible surface sensitivity (Type I-A high sensitivity)
  • You cannot risk arc burn or residual magnetism (precision machined components, electronics)
  • The inspection is one-off and a yoke is not available

11. Common Failure Modes

MT false rejects:

  • Magnetic writing from tool contact
  • Sharp geometry (fillets, threads) leakage
  • Grain boundary indications in cold-worked material

PT false rejects:

  • Bleed-back from porous surface treatments
  • Fillets retaining penetrant
  • Inadequate removal of excess (high background)

Both methods require re-inspection with surface cleaning to confirm whether an indication is relevant.

12. Training and Certification

Both methods are taught at ASNT or PCN Level 1 and Level 2. Training is short:

  • MT Level 2: 12 + 8 = 20 hours formal training under SNT-TC-1A
  • PT Level 2: 4 + 8 = 12 hours formal training under SNT-TC-1A

See our MT Level 2 practice questions and PT Level 2 practice questions for exam prep.

Frequently Asked Questions

Q: Can MT and PT be performed on the same part?

A: Yes — sometimes both are specified for high-criticality welds (e.g., nozzle attachments in pressure vessels). Demag and clean between methods.

Q: Is MT or PT more sensitive overall?

A: High-sensitivity Type I-A fluorescent PT is generally the most sensitive surface NDT method. MT wet fluorescent is comparable. Dry powder MT is less sensitive but faster.

Q: Can PT replace MT on carbon steel?

A: Yes — code-wise both are accepted. Operationally MT is preferred for ferromagnetic parts due to speed and lower cost.

Q: Why can’t MT be used on austenitic stainless steel (304/316)?

A: Austenitic stainless is non-magnetic at room temperature. There is no flux to leak at flaws. Some cold-worked 304 develops some magnetism but is not reliable for MT.

Q: What is wet fluorescent MT vs dry powder MT?

A: Wet fluorescent uses a liquid carrier (oil or water) with fluorescent particles inspected under UV light — higher sensitivity. Dry powder is applied directly to dry hot surfaces — better for rough surfaces and high temperature.

Q: Does PT work through paint?

A: No. Paint must be removed in the inspection area.

Q: Can MT detect cracks under thin paint?

A: Yes, up to about 0.05 mm coating with calibration on a shim test piece. Thicker coatings reduce sensitivity.

Q: How do I demagnetize a part after MT?

A: Apply a decaying alternating field (AC of decreasing amplitude or DC reversed and decreased). Verify residual less than 3 G with a field indicator.

Q: Are there environmental concerns with PT?

A: Penetrants and cleaners may contain volatile organic compounds (VOCs). Many countries require VOC-compliant materials. Disposal of used penetrant/wipes follows local hazardous waste rules.

Q: Does Atlantis NDT offer MT and PT training?

A: Yes — our combined MT/PT Level 2 program runs in 24 hours classroom plus practical. Cohorts monthly in Houston, Dubai, and on-site. Call +1 (281) 840-8969 or visit our training page.

We deliver accredited NDT training, technical consulting, certification preparation, and digital inspection software trusted by oil & gas, fabrication, EPC, and power generation clients. Our team of ASNT Level III instructors has trained thousands of inspectors worldwide.

Whether you are preparing for ASNT certification, API 510, API 570, or API 653, our exam preparation programs combine classroom theory, hands-on practical training, and proctored mock exams that mirror the real test environment.

title: PAUT vs TOFD 2026: Phased Array vs Time-of-Flight Diffraction
snippet: 2026 PAUT vs TOFD comparison: physics, defects, blind zones, sizing accuracy, cost, code coverage, when to combine. Full advanced UT decision guide.
content:
Phased Array Ultrasonic Testing (PAUT) and Time-of-Flight Diffraction (TOFD) are the two most powerful advanced UT techniques in use today. Both are routinely deployed as alternatives or supplements to film radiography on welds. They use different physical principles, have different strengths and blind zones, and increasingly are combined on a single instrument for full weld coverage. This 2026 guide compares PAUT and TOFD across the dimensions that matter to NDT planners, inspection engineers, and procedure writers.

PAUT vs TOFD at a Glance

DimensionPAUT (Phased Array)TOFD (Time of Flight Diffraction)
PhysicsMulti-element probe, electronic beam steering, pulse-echoTwo probes (pitch-catch), detects diffraction from flaw tips
Primary outputS-scan, E-scan, sectorial images; C-scan with encoderD-scan grayscale image of diffraction signals
Best forSurface-breaking + volumetric flaws, defect type ID, sizing larger flawsThrough-wall sizing of mid-thickness planar flaws (cracks, LOF)
Detection thresholdAmplitude-based; tight cracks may be missed if angle is wrongIndependent of amplitude; sensitive to tight crack tips
Near-surface dead zone~1 to 2 mmLateral wave masking ~3 to 5 mm
Far-surface dead zoneMinimalBackwall masking ~2 to 4 mm
Through-wall sizing accuracy1 to 2 mm (with calibration)0.5 to 1 mm (tip diffraction)
Speed of inspectionEncoded line scan 100 to 300 mm/secEncoded line scan 100 to 300 mm/sec (single pass)
Hardware costa modest cost to a modest cost (instrument + probes + wedges)a modest cost to a modest cost (often combined with PAUT)
Operator trainingUT L2 + PAUT endorsement (40+ hrs)UT L2 + TOFD endorsement (32+ hrs)
Code coverage (ASME V)Appendix IV (PAUT), Mandatory Appendix XI (RT alternative)Appendix III (TOFD), Mandatory Appendix XI (RT alternative)
ISO/EN standardsISO 13588, ISO 19285ISO 10863

1. Physics — How Each Method Works

PAUT uses an array of 16, 32, 64, or 128 piezoelectric elements arranged in a linear or matrix pattern. By firing the elements with controlled time delays, the resulting wavefronts superimpose to form a steered, focused beam at angles and focal depths chosen electronically — no physical wedge change needed. Reflections are received by the same array, processed, and displayed as sectorial scans (S-scans, multiple angles in one image) or linear electronic scans (E-scans, multiple parallel beams).

TOFD uses two probes facing each other across the weld, transmitting and receiving longitudinal waves at oblique angles. A defect’s upper and lower tips diffract the energy, producing weak but characteristic signals. The time-of-flight of these diffraction signals reveals the through-wall position of the tips, allowing accurate sizing independent of signal amplitude.

2. Defect Detection Capability

PAUT excels at:

  • Surface-breaking flaws (with appropriate scan angles)
  • Volumetric flaws (porosity, slag, inclusions)
  • Defects perpendicular to scan direction (good reflectors)
  • Defect type identification through image interpretation
  • Sizing of large flaws (using 6 dB drop, S-scan visualization)

TOFD excels at:

  • Through-wall sizing of vertical or near-vertical planar flaws
  • Detection of mid-wall LOF and lack of side wall fusion
  • Detection of cracks regardless of orientation (because tip diffraction is independent of amplitude)
  • Monitoring of crack growth over time (very repeatable measurements)

3. Blind Zones (Critical to Understand)

TOFD has two blind zones that PAUT does not:

  • Lateral wave (near-surface) blind zone: The strong direct wave from transmitter to receiver masks flaws within the first 3 to 5 mm below the scan surface.
  • Backwall blind zone: The backwall echo masks flaws within 2 to 4 mm of the opposite surface.

This is the primary reason PAUT and TOFD are combined: TOFD covers the mid-wall efficiently and accurately, while PAUT covers the near and far surface zones. Together they achieve full weld coverage.

4. Through-Wall Sizing Accuracy

Accurate through-wall sizing is critical for fitness-for-service (FFS) evaluations per API 579-1 / ASME FFS-1. TOFD typically achieves 0.5 to 1 mm sizing accuracy on mid-wall flaws — better than any other commonly available NDT method short of metallography. PAUT achieves 1 to 2 mm with proper calibration, especially using S-scan visualization.

5. Productivity

Both PAUT and TOFD are encoded scans — the operator pushes the probe along the weld and an encoder records position. Typical scan speeds 100 to 300 mm/sec. A 1-meter weld is scanned and saved in under 10 seconds, then analyzed offline. This is dramatically faster than manual UT (5 to 10 minutes per meter of weld) and competitive with or faster than film RT once exposure + processing time is included.

6. Cost Comparison

Cost itemPAUT-onlyTOFD-onlyCombined PAUT + TOFD
Instrument capexa modest cost to a modest costa modest cost to a modest costa modest cost to a modest cost
Probe and wedge kita modest cost to a modest costa modest cost to a modest costa modest cost to a modest cost
Scanner and encodera modest cost to a modest costa modest cost to a modest costa modest cost to a modest cost (shared)
Inspection cost / meter welda modest cost to a modest costa modest cost to a modest costa modest cost to a modest cost (full coverage)

7. Training and Certification

Both PAUT and TOFD require additional certification beyond standard UT Level 2:

  • PAUT endorsement: Typically 40 hours formal training + practical demonstration. ASNT, PCN, CSWIP all offer PAUT certifications.
  • TOFD endorsement: Typically 32 hours formal training + practical. Often paired with PAUT in a combined training course.

Atlantis NDT offers an 80-hour PAUT + TOFD combined program designed to ASME V Mandatory Appendix XI requirements.

8. Code Coverage

Both methods are codified:

  • ASME V: Appendix IV (PAUT), Appendix III (TOFD), Mandatory Appendix XI (RT alternative qualification)
  • ISO: ISO 13588 / 19285 (PAUT), ISO 10863 (TOFD), ISO 22825 (PAUT for austenitic)
  • API: Both accepted under API 510 and API 570 as volumetric NDT
  • Pipeline: API 1104 mainline weld inspection commonly uses combined PAUT + TOFD systems with specific procedural requirements

9. When to Use PAUT Only

  • Thinner welds (less than 6 mm) where TOFD blind zones consume too much volume
  • Geometry constraints preventing two-probe TOFD setup (fillet welds, nozzle welds, T-joints)
  • Coarse-grained austenitic stainless where TOFD diffraction signals are buried in noise
  • Defect type identification is more important than precise sizing

10. When to Use TOFD Only

  • Wall thickness 12 to 50 mm where mid-wall is the primary concern
  • Long-term monitoring of known flaws for growth (TOFD repeatability is excellent)
  • Critical engineering critical assessment where through-wall sizing accuracy is paramount

11. When to Combine PAUT + TOFD (Most Common)

For most production weld inspection on pipelines, pressure vessels, and structural welds 6 mm thick or more, the standard configuration is combined PAUT + TOFD on a single instrument:

  • PAUT covers the near-surface and far-surface (the TOFD blind zones)
  • TOFD covers the mid-wall efficiently with accurate sizing
  • Single pass with multiple data sets saved simultaneously

This combined approach is the foundation of code-qualified RT-replacement procedures under ASME V Mandatory Appendix XI.

12. Common Applications

  • Pipeline girth welds: Combined PAUT + TOFD with multi-zone discrimination (per API 1104 Appendix A)
  • Pressure vessel longitudinal/circumferential welds: PAUT + TOFD under ASME V
  • Wind turbine tower welds: Combined for full-height coverage
  • Nuclear primary loop welds: ENIQ-qualified PAUT + TOFD per ASME XI
  • Aerospace bond inspection: PAUT (TOFD less common)
  • Refinery in-service weld monitoring: TOFD for crack growth monitoring

Frequently Asked Questions

Q: Can PAUT replace radiography?

A: Yes, in many applications, when qualified per ASME V Mandatory Appendix XI. The combined PAUT + TOFD configuration is the common path. See our UT vs RT comparison.

Q: Why is TOFD often paired with PAUT rather than used alone?

A: TOFD has near-surface and backwall blind zones that PAUT can cover. Together they give full weld volume coverage.

Q: Can PAUT detect porosity?

A: Yes, but with somewhat lower sensitivity than RT. Small isolated porosity may produce weak signals; larger clusters are easily detected.

Q: How long does a PAUT calibration take?

A: For an experienced operator with a pre-configured setup, 15 to 30 minutes including DAC/TCG, focal law verification, and wedge delay. Initial procedure qualification takes much longer.

Q: Is TOFD accurate enough for fitness-for-service?

A: Yes — TOFD’s 0.5 to 1 mm through-wall sizing is widely accepted for API 579-1/ASME FFS-1 Level 2 and 3 assessments.

Q: Can PAUT inspect austenitic stainless welds?

A: Yes, but coarse-grained austenitic scatters and attenuates UT energy heavily. Specialized low-frequency probes and TFM (full matrix capture with total focusing method) techniques per ISO 22825 are used.

Q: What is TFM/FMC and how does it relate to PAUT?

A: Total Focusing Method (TFM) uses Full Matrix Capture (FMC) data — every transmit/receive combination — reconstructed in software to focus at every point in the image. TFM is an extension of PAUT with superior image quality, especially for coarse-grain materials.

Q: Does PAUT need couplant?

A: Yes, just like standard UT — water, gel, or glycerine. Encoded scans typically use continuous water irrigation.

Q: How long is PAUT procedure qualification per ASME V Mandatory Appendix XI?

A: 30 to 120 days depending on weld variety. Demonstration scans on blocks containing known flaws are required; the procedure is signed off when the procedure consistently detects/sizes all required flaw types.

Q: Does Atlantis NDT offer PAUT/TOFD training and procedure development?

A: Yes — our 80-hour PAUT + TOFD training and our procedure qualification service is delivered in Houston, Dubai, and on-site. Call +1 (281) 840-8969 or visit our consulting page.

We deliver accredited NDT training, technical consulting, certification preparation, and digital inspection software trusted by oil & gas, fabrication, EPC, and power generation clients. title: Digital Radiography vs Film 2026: CR, DDA & Film RT Comparison
snippet: 2026 digital radiography vs film comparison: CR, DDA/DR vs film. Resolution, dynamic range, throughput, cost, ASME V coverage, when each wins.
content:
For 100+ years, industrial radiography meant exposing silver halide film, processing in a chemistry darkroom, and viewing the resulting negative on a light box. Today, two digital alternatives have arrived: Computed Radiography (CR) uses re-usable photostimulable phosphor (PSP) plates scanned after exposure; Direct Digital Radiography (DDA/DR) uses flat-panel detectors that produce a near-real-time image. This 2026 guide compares all three across the dimensions that matter for procurement, productivity, and code compliance.

Digital RT vs Film at a Glance

DimensionFilm RTComputed Radiography (CR)Direct Digital (DDA / DR)
DetectorSilver halide film (single use)Reusable PSP phosphor plateReusable flat-panel detector
Image readoutWet chemistry processing (10 to 30 min)Laser scanner (1 to 3 min per plate)Real-time (seconds)
Spatial resolution (typical)50 to 100 line-pairs/mm5 to 15 lp/mm (depending on pixel size)4 to 10 lp/mm
Dynamic rangeNarrow (~100:1)Wide (~10,000:1)Very wide (~10,000 to 100,000:1)
Exposure time vs film1x baseline0.25x to 0.5x (faster)0.1x to 0.3x (much faster)
Consumables per exposurea modest cost to a modest cost film + chemistryNone (plate reusable thousands of cycles)None
Capexa modest cost darkroom + processora modest cost to a modest cost (scanner + plates)a modest cost to a modest cost per detector
Image archivalPhysical film, 30+ year life with careDICONDE / DICOM digital filesDICONDE / DICOM digital files
Field portabilityExcellent (lead-foil cassettes)Good (sealed reusable cassettes)Limited (panel + cables + workstation)
ASME V coverageArticle 2 baselineArticle 2 Mandatory Appendix IIIArticle 2 Mandatory Appendix IV
Reading expertise requiredConventional film readersDigital reviewer trained on CRDigital reviewer trained on DDA
Image enhancementNone (fixed once developed)Brightness, contrast, sharpening, ROI windowingSame as CR plus higher SNR enables more aggressive enhancement

1. Physics — How Each Method Works

Film: Silver halide crystals embedded in gelatin emulsion. Radiation strips electrons that produce a latent image; chemical development reduces silver crystals to metallic silver. Density (darkness) correlates with absorbed exposure. Lead foil intensifying screens enhance sensitivity.

CR: Photostimulable phosphor (typically BaFBr:Eu) absorbs radiation and stores it as trapped electrons. A laser scanner stimulates the trapped electrons, releasing light that is captured by a photomultiplier tube. The light intensity correlates with exposure. The plate is erased (bright light) and re-used.

DDA / DR: Scintillator (cesium iodide or gadolinium oxysulfide) converts X-rays to light; underlying photodiode array (amorphous silicon or CMOS) converts light to electrical signals digitized into pixel values. Image appears within seconds on a monitor.

2. Image Quality — Resolution and Dynamic Range

Film holds the spatial resolution crown — modern fine-grain industrial films can resolve well over 50 line-pairs/mm. CR and DDA are typically limited to 5 to 15 lp/mm by pixel size and detector unsharpness.

However, digital systems have far higher dynamic range. A single digital exposure captures thicknesses that would require multiple film exposures bracketed at different kV/mA settings. Combined with image post-processing (contrast enhancement, edge sharpening, region-of-interest windowing), a single CR or DDA exposure often delivers equal or better diagnostic information than film for the same defect.

Per ISO 17636-2 / EN 14784, digital systems must demonstrate a basic spatial resolution (SRb) measured with a duplex wire IQI. SRb of 100 to 200 μm is achievable, sufficient for the standard 2-2T sensitivity.

3. Throughput

Throughput is where digital wins decisively:

  • Film cycle: Setup → exposure (1 to 30 min) → develop chemistry (10 to 30 min) → dry → read on viewer → archive. 30 to 90 minutes per shot.
  • CR cycle: Setup → exposure (shorter than film) → scan plate (1 to 3 min) → review on monitor. 10 to 30 minutes per shot.
  • DDA cycle: Setup → exposure (seconds) → image appears in real time. 5 to 15 minutes per shot.

A 100-weld project that takes 4 to 5 days with film can be done in 1 to 2 days with CR and under 1 day with DDA.

4. Exposure Time and Source Activity

Digital detectors are far more sensitive than film, requiring 25 to 90% less exposure for the same image quality. This translates to:

  • Smaller, cheaper radioactive sources (or shorter X-ray duty cycle)
  • Smaller exclusion zones
  • Lower operator dose per shot
  • Less site disruption

5. Cost Analysis — Capex vs Opex

ScenarioFilmCRDDA
System capexa modest cost to a modest costa modest cost to a modest costa modest cost to a modest cost
Annual consumables (5,000 shots/yr)a modest cost to a modest costa modest cost (plate replacement)a modest cost to a modest cost
Operator hours per shot1.0 to 1.50.5 to 0.80.2 to 0.4
5-year total cost (5,000/yr)a modest cost to a modest costa modest cost to a modest costa modest cost to a modest cost

For high-volume RT shops, payback for CR or DDA over film is typically 2 to 4 years. For low-volume one-off jobs, film may remain cheaper short-term but loses on productivity.

6. Regulatory Acceptance

All three are accepted by every major code:

  • ASME V: Film under Article 2 (baseline); CR under Mandatory Appendix III; DDA under Appendix IV; computed tomography under Appendix V
  • ISO: ISO 17636-1 (film), ISO 17636-2 (digital with both CR and DDA)
  • ASTM: E1742 (film), E2033 (CR), E2698 (DDA)
  • API/AWS/Pipeline: All major codes have added digital provisions

Some customers and jurisdictions still require film for regulatory submission — especially in legacy nuclear and certain government applications. Always verify the specific contract requirement.

7. Archival

Film, stored properly (cool, dry, dark), has demonstrated multi-decade archival life. Digital files require active management:

  • DICONDE (NDT extension of DICOM) is the dominant archival format
  • RAID-protected storage and offsite backup
  • Migration to new storage media as formats evolve (typical 5 to 10 year cycles)
  • Audit trail metadata (operator, instrument, time, parameters)

For 30+ year archival in regulated industries, digital is more reliable than film IF the IT discipline is maintained.

8. Field Portability

Film cassettes are the most portable: rugged, no electronics, work in any environment. CR plates and cassettes are similarly portable; the scanner stays in a truck or trailer. DDA panels are sensitive electronic equipment, require cables back to a workstation, are heavier, and are vulnerable to drops — making them more challenging in field and offshore applications.

9. Operator Skill

Film reading is an art — experienced film readers have decades of mental pattern matching. Digital images can be enhanced and re-windowed in software, which is both a benefit (better defect detection) and a risk (over-processing can hide real defects or create artifacts). Digital RT inspectors require specific training on image processing tool limits and acceptance.

Both require RT Level 2 certification plus method-specific endorsements for CR and DDA per ASNT and PCN schemes.

10. When Film Still Wins

  • One-off shots where capex amortization fails
  • Remote sites without reliable power for digital workflows
  • Customer or regulatory mandate for film records
  • Inspections where the highest possible spatial resolution is essential and time/cost permit film
  • Underwater RT (specialized waterproof film cassettes)

11. When CR Wins

  • Mid-volume shops with mixed inspection requirements
  • Field crews needing rugged reusable cassettes
  • Transition path from film (workflow change is moderate)
  • Variable thickness welds where wide dynamic range matters

12. When DDA Wins

  • High-volume RT (pipeline mainline, in-shop production)
  • Real-time inspection workflows (rapid acceptance decisions)
  • Lowest exposure budget (smallest sources, shortest duty cycles)
  • Integration with other digital QA/QC systems (DICONDE archival, weld traceability)

Frequently Asked Questions

Q: Is CR or DDA more like film in workflow?

A: CR is closer — you still load cassettes, expose, then process. DDA is fundamentally different (real-time digital).

Q: Can I read old film on a digital viewer?

A: Yes — film digitizers scan radiographs to DICONDE for digital review and archival. Useful for legacy records.

Q: Does digital RT still need the IQI/penetrameter?

A: Yes — per ASME V and ISO 17636-2, IQI is mandatory. Additionally, the duplex wire IQI is used to verify the digital basic spatial resolution.

Q: What is the typical pixel size for industrial CR?

A: 50 to 200 μm, selectable. Smaller pixels = higher resolution but larger files and slower scan time. 100 μm is a common compromise.

Q: Are DDA detectors damaged by high doses?

A: Modern flat-panel detectors withstand typical industrial NDT exposures for thousands of shots. Direct beam exposure (no part) at high dose can degrade the scintillator over time — manufacturers specify limits.

Q: Can DDA do real-time radiography (fluoroscopy)?

A: Yes — many DDA systems capture 30 frames/sec real-time imaging for assembly inspection, casting flow analysis, and weld pool monitoring. This is closer to medical fluoroscopy than to conventional RT.

Q: What is computed tomography (CT) in NDT?

A: CT acquires hundreds or thousands of DDA projections at incremental angles around the part, then reconstructs a full 3D volume image. Covered under ASME V Mandatory Appendix V. Standard for casting and additive manufacturing inspection.

Q: Will film disappear?

A: Film usage is declining 5 to 10% per year globally. It will remain for certain niches (high resolution one-offs, certain regulatory submissions, very thick castings) for the foreseeable future, but the trajectory is digital.

Q: What is the typical training gap from film RT to digital?

A: 24 to 40 hours of method-specific training covers detector physics, basic spatial resolution measurement, image processing limits, file management, and code-specific procedures for CR/DDA qualification.

Q: Does Atlantis NDT offer DR/CR procedure development and training?

A: Yes — our RT Level 2 program includes both film and digital tracks. We also write and qualify CR and DDA procedures to ASME V Appendices III and IV. Call +1 (281) 840-8969 or visit our training page.

About Atlantis NDT

Atlantis NDT is a global NDT technology and services company headquartered in Houston, Texas with operations across India and the Middle East. We deliver accredited NDT training, technical consulting, certification preparation, and digital inspection software trusted by oil & gas, fabrication, EPC, and power generation clients. Our team of ASNT Level III instructors has trained thousands of inspectors worldwide.

Whether you are preparing for ASNT certification, API 510, API 570, or API 653, our exam preparation programs combine classroom theory, hands-on practical training, and proctored mock exams that mirror the real test environment.

Call us at +1 (281) 840-8969 or email sales@atlantisndt.com to enroll in the next training cohort. Same-day quotes for corporate group training in Houston, Dubai, Riyadh, Hyderabad, and on-site at your facility.
