title: ASNT vs PCN Certification 2026: Complete NDT Comparison Guide
snippet: 2026 ASNT vs PCN NDT certification comparison: model, recognition, exam structure, training hours, costs, salary, mutual recognition, when to hold each.
content:
The two dominant international NDT personnel certification schemes are ASNT (American Society for Nondestructive Testing) and PCN (Personnel Certification in Non-destructive Testing, administered by BINDT). Both certify Level 1, 2, and 3 NDT inspectors in UT, RT, MT, PT, VT, ET, and other methods, but they operate on different philosophies, exam formats, and bodies of recognition. This 2026 guide compares ASNT and PCN across the dimensions that matter to inspectors, employers, and project managers.

ASNT vs PCN at a Glance

DimensionASNT (SNT-TC-1A / CP-189 / ACCP)PCN (ISO 9712 via BINDT)
Certification modelPrimarily employer-based (SNT-TC-1A); also third-party (ACCP / ASNT Central Certification)Third-party (BINDT issues certificate independent of employer)
Origin / HQUSA — Columbus, OhioUK — Northampton (BINDT)
Underlying standardSNT-TC-1A (recommended practice), CP-189 (standard), ANSI/ASNT CP-105ISO 9712:2021 (international standard)
Geographic recognition (strong)USA, North America, ASME-driven industries globallyUK, Europe, Middle East, Asia, oil & gas globally
Body of knowledgeASNT BOK per method & level; Written Practice (employer-tailored)ISO 9712 + PCN method documents (CP-7 UT, CP-8 RT, etc.)
Exam administrationEmployer-administered under SNT-TC-1A; ASNT-administered for ACCP/CentralBINDT-approved authorized qualifying bodies and exam centers
Certificate ownershipEmployer holds the certificate (SNT-TC-1A); ASNT for ACCPIndividual holds the certificate (portable to any employer)
Validity period5 years; renewal at 5; re-exam at 105 years; renewal at 5 (document review); full re-exam at 10
LevelsTrainee, Level I, II, IIILevel 1, 2, 3
Industry sectorsNot formally sectorized; written practice may specifyFormal sectors: welds, castings, forgings, wrought, aerospace, railway, in-service
Training requirementsPer Table 6.3.1A of SNT-TC-1APer ISO 9712 Table 1 (often very similar hours)
Vision requirementsAnnual near vision (Jaeger J1 at 12 in), triennial colorAnnual near vision (Jaeger 1 at 30 cm), triennial color
Cost per certificationa modest cost to a modest cost per method (employer-borne for SNT-TC-1A)£700 to £1,500 per method (individual-borne typically)

1. Certification Model — Employer-Based vs Third-Party

The most important distinction:

ASNT SNT-TC-1A: The employer certifies the inspector based on training, experience, and exams administered by the employer’s Level III (or contracted Level III). The certificate is tied to that employer. If the inspector changes employer, the new employer must re-evaluate and reissue certification under their own Written Practice.

PCN: BINDT certifies the individual through approved authorized qualifying bodies (AQBs). The certificate is the individual’s property and is portable to any employer worldwide. The new employer verifies the certificate but cannot revoke it.

ASNT also offers third-party certification via ACCP (ASNT Central Certification Program) and the ASNT Level III certificate. These are portable, similar to PCN. ASME, API, and many specifications recognize ASNT Level III certificate.

2. Underlying Standards

ASNT operates under three main documents:

  • SNT-TC-1A: Recommended practice. Not mandatory unless invoked by contract. Employer adapts via Written Practice.
  • ANSI/ASNT CP-189: Standard. Mandatory when invoked. More prescriptive than SNT-TC-1A.
  • ANSI/ASNT CP-105: Topical outlines for training and examination.

PCN operates under ISO 9712, the international standard for NDT personnel certification. ISO 9712 is mandatory and prescriptive: it sets exam structure, training hours, experience hours, vision requirements, and recertification cycles.

3. Geographic Recognition

Rough rule of thumb:

  • USA, Canada, Mexico: ASNT dominant. ASME / API contracts default to ASNT.
  • UK, Europe: PCN (or other ISO 9712 schemes like COFREND, DGZfP) dominant. Aerospace prime contractors require PCN or equivalent.
  • Middle East (Aramco, ADNOC, etc.): Both accepted; PCN more common for international contractors.
  • Asia (India, SE Asia): Both common; PCN growing in oil & gas; ASNT in ASME-driven work.
  • Australia / NZ: Local AINDT scheme similar to ISO 9712; PCN well-recognized.
  • South America: Mixed; both recognized.

For international inspectors, holding both ASNT and PCN provides the broadest employment access.

4. Exam Structure

Both schemes have General, Specific, and Practical exams at Level 2. Differences:

ComponentASNT (typical)PCN
General Exam40 closed-book MCQs40 closed-book MCQs
Specific Exam20 open-book MCQs (employer’s procedures + applicable code)30 closed-book MCQs on chosen sector codes/standards
Practical ExamDemonstration on at least 1 specimen; 70%Demonstration on 2 to 3 specimens with separate scoring on each step; 80%
Written instructionNot always requiredRequired at Level 2 (write a method-specific instruction from a procedure)
Composite80% average across general, specific, practicalAll components must individually meet pass marks

PCN is generally stricter on the practical, with its higher pass mark (80% vs 70%) and explicit instruction-writing component.

5. Industry Sectors

PCN formally sectorizes Level 2 certification:

  • Welds
  • Castings (ferrous, non-ferrous)
  • Forgings
  • Wrought products (plate, rod)
  • Aerospace (composites, multilayer)
  • Railway (wheels, axles, rail)
  • In-service inspection (pressure equipment, pipelines)

A PCN UT Level 2 (Welds) inspector cannot inspect castings without a separate Castings sector certification. ASNT does not formally sectorize; the employer’s Written Practice may specify product scope.

6. Training and Experience Requirements

Both schemes require similar formal training hours and experience hours. Examples for Level 2:

MethodSNT-TC-1A (L1 + L2 hours)ISO 9712 / PCN (L1 + L2 hours)
UT40 + 40 = 80 training; 210 + 630 = 840 experience40 + 40 = 80 training; 320 + 640 = 960 experience
RT40 + 40 = 80 training; 210 + 630 = 840 experience40 + 40 = 80 training; 320 + 640 = 960 experience
MT12 + 8 = 20 training; 70 + 140 = 210 experience16 + 8 = 24 training; 130 + 260 = 390 experience
PT4 + 8 = 12 training; 70 + 140 = 210 experience16 + 8 = 24 training; 130 + 260 = 390 experience

PCN/ISO 9712 generally requires more documented experience hours than SNT-TC-1A.

7. Cost and Time to Certification

Total cost (training + exam + materials) per method, Level 2:

  • ASNT (under SNT-TC-1A): a modest cost to a modest cost. Often employer-paid.
  • ASNT ACCP / Central Certification: a modest cost to a modest cost.
  • PCN: £2,000 to £3,500 (training + BINDT exam fees). Often individual-paid.

Timeline from zero NDT to Level 2: typically 6 to 18 months, depending on experience accumulation.

8. Salary and Recognition Impact

Both certifications yield similar salaries. In the US, employers tend to view ASNT Level III certificate and ACCP as the gold standard. In international oil & gas, PCN Level 3 is often preferred. Holding both opens the broadest career path. Typical 2026 salaries:

  • Level 2 inspector (single method): $60,000 to a modest cost USA; a modest cost to a modest cost/month Middle East
  • Level 2 multi-method (UT + RT + MT + PT): a modest cost to a modest cost USA; a modest cost to a modest cost/month ME
  • Level 3: a modest cost to a modest cost USA; a modest cost to a modest cost/month ME (see L2 vs L3 article)

9. Recertification

Both schemes use a 5-year primary cycle and 10-year re-examination cycle. Key differences:

  • SNT-TC-1A: Recertification by re-examination every 5 years (employer-administered). Annual eye exam.
  • PCN: Renewal at 5 years (document review — no exam) if continuous practice and current eye exam. Re-examination at 10 years.
  • ACCP / ASNT Central: Recertification by structured CEUs or re-examination at 5 years.

The PCN 5-year administrative renewal is generally easier than the SNT-TC-1A 5-year re-exam.

10. When to Choose Which

Choose ASNT (SNT-TC-1A) when:

  • Working primarily in the USA, Canada
  • Employer pays for and administers certification
  • ASME / API contracts driving the work
  • You will stay with one employer for the long term

Choose ASNT ACCP / Central Certification when:

  • You want US-recognized portable certification
  • You contract or work for multiple employers

Choose PCN when:

  • Working internationally, especially UK, Europe, Middle East
  • You want a portable individual certificate
  • You work in oil & gas, offshore, aerospace contracts
  • Customer specifications mandate ISO 9712-aligned scheme

Hold both when:

  • Working in international oil & gas with both US and European prime contractors
  • Career flexibility across continents matters
  • Senior Level III roles where customer mix demands either

11. Mutual Recognition

There is no automatic mutual recognition between ASNT and PCN. To gain the other, the inspector typically:

  • Demonstrates equivalent training and experience hours
  • Sits the General and Specific exams of the new scheme
  • Sits the Practical (sometimes waived with strong documented evidence)

BINDT publishes an Aerospace Equivalency policy and some bridging exams; check the latest with each body.

12. Other Certifications to Know

  • CSWIP 3.1 / 3.2: TWI welding inspector certifications (visual inspection) — see our CSWIP 3.1 article
  • AWS CWI: US welding inspector certification
  • API ICP (510/570/653): In-service inspection (vessels/piping/tanks)
  • NACE/AMPP: Coating and corrosion inspector
  • COFREND, DGZfP, AINDT, JSNDI: National ISO 9712 schemes equivalent to PCN

Frequently Asked Questions

Q: Is PCN better than ASNT?

A: Neither is better; they are different models. PCN portability is preferred by international contractors; ASNT is the US default.

Q: Can I convert ASNT to PCN or vice versa?

A: There is no automatic conversion. You sit the new scheme’s exams with credit for documented training/experience.

Q: Do US employers recognize PCN?

A: Some do, especially in oil & gas. ASME and most US codes still default to ASNT.

Q: Do Middle East employers recognize ASNT?

A: Yes — both ASNT and PCN are widely accepted by Aramco, ADNOC, KOC, QatarEnergy, Sonatrach. Specification language varies.

Q: What is the difference between SNT-TC-1A and CP-189?

A: SNT-TC-1A is a recommended practice (guidance). CP-189 is a standard (mandatory when invoked). CP-189 has stricter Level III qualification requirements (must hold ASNT Level III).

Q: What is the easiest scheme for a new inspector?

A: SNT-TC-1A is often easier to enter because the employer pays and administers. PCN gives stronger long-term portability.

Q: Does Atlantis NDT prepare candidates for both ASNT and PCN?

A: Yes — our combined training program covers both bodies of knowledge. Candidates can sit either exam after the program. See our training page or call +1 (281) 840-8969.

Q: Do I need a Level III to administer SNT-TC-1A exams?

A: Yes — SNT-TC-1A requires a Level III to develop and administer the Written Practice exams. CP-189 requires ASNT Level III certificate specifically.

Q: Is the practical exam harder for PCN?

A: Yes — PCN practical has 80% pass mark with separate scoring on instruction writing, setup, detection, sizing, and reporting. ASNT practical is typically 70% on overall demonstration.

Q: How do I find a PCN ATO or ASNT-approved trainer?

A: BINDT publishes the ATO register; ASNT lists Approved Training Organizations on its site. Atlantis NDT delivers in partnership with both networks. Contact us for the next cohort.

About Atlantis NDT

Atlantis NDT is a global NDT technology and services company headquartered in Houston, Texas with operations across India and the Middle East. We deliver accredited NDT training, technical consulting, certification preparation, and digital inspection software trusted by oil & gas, fabrication, EPC, and power generation clients. Our team of ASNT Level III instructors has trained thousands of inspectors worldwide.

Whether you are preparing for ASNT certification, API 510, API 570, or API 653, our exam preparation programs combine classroom theory, hands-on practical training, and proctored mock exams that mirror the real test environment.

Call us at +1 (281) 840-8969 or email sales@atlantisndt.com to enroll in the next training cohort. Same-day quotes for corporate group training in Houston, Dubai, Riyadh, Hyderabad, and on-site at your facility.

title: API 510 vs API 570 2026: Vessels vs Piping Inspector Comparison
snippet: 2026 API 510 vs API 570 comparison: scope, code references, inspection intervals, damage mechanisms, exam, salary, prerequisites, career paths, FAQ.
content:
The American Petroleum Institute (API) Individual Certification Programs (ICP) include three foundational in-service inspector certifications: API 510 (Pressure Vessels), API 570 (Piping), and API 653 (Storage Tanks). Of these, API 510 and API 570 are the most commonly held by refinery, petrochemical, and pipeline inspectors. They are similar in structure but cover different equipment with different code drivers, damage mechanisms, and inspection workflows. This 2026 guide compares API 510 and API 570 across the dimensions that matter to inspectors, employers, and project managers.

API 510 vs API 570 at a Glance

DimensionAPI 510 (Pressure Vessels)API 570 (Piping)
Equipment scopeIn-service pressure vessels (typically >15 psig design)In-service metallic piping systems
Construction code referenceASME BPVC VIII Div 1 / Div 2 / Div 3ASME B31.3 Process Piping (and B31.1 Power Piping)
Key inspection intervalsExternal 5 yr; internal 10 yr or 1/2 remaining lifeClass 1 piping ext 5 yr; Class 2 ext 5 yr; Class 3 ext 10 yr
Risk-based extensionAPI 580 / 581 RBI; up to many years for low-PoF / low-CoFAPI 580 / 581 RBI; similar extension philosophy
Repair / alteration codeAPI 510 Sections 7 & 8API 570 Section 8 & ASME B31.3 Chapter V
Primary damage mechanismsWall thinning, brittle fracture, fatigue, SCC, HTHA, creepSame + CUI, MIC, injection-point corrosion, dead leg, NAC, sulfidation
Number of TMLsPer-vessel, often 50 to 500Per-circuit, often thousands across a unit
NDT mixInternal entry VT, UT thickness, PT/MT, RT/PAUTExternal UT (lots of it), GWUT, PEC, RT, PAUT, PMI
Exam structureClosed-book (50 Q, 2h45) + Open-book (60 to 80 Q, 4h45)Closed-book (50 Q) + Open-book (~80 Q); 7.5 hrs total
Recertification cycle3 yr (reduced) and 6 yr (full)3 yr (reduced) and 6 yr (full)
Industry rolesRefinery / petrochemical / chemical plant inspectorRefinery / pipeline / process plant inspector
Body of knowledge size~300 pages of effective study material~350 pages (more code documents)

1. Scope — What Each Code Covers

API 510 covers in-service pressure vessels that are typically designed and built to ASME BPVC Section VIII (Divisions 1, 2, and 3). Scope includes shells, heads, nozzles, manways, internals, and pressure-relief devices on the vessel. Heat exchangers, columns, drums, separators, and reactors all fall under API 510 when in pressure-vessel service.

API 570 covers in-service metallic piping systems designed and built to ASME B31.3 Process Piping (or B31.1 Power Piping). Scope includes pipe, fittings, flanges, valves, and supports of process piping. Pipelines under regulatory authority (e.g., DOT pipelines) often follow API 1160 / API 1163 with API 570 supplementally.

2. Inspection Interval Strategy

Vessels and piping have similar concepts but different practical implementations:

  • API 510 vessels: External inspection every 5 years. Internal (or on-stream) inspection every 10 years (or 1/2 remaining life). RBI per API 580/581 can extend intervals.
  • API 570 piping: Classified by consequence (Class 1 highest, Class 4 lowest). Class 1 external 5 yr; Class 2 ext 5 yr; Class 3 ext 10 yr; Class 4 optional. Thickness intervals similar.

For piping, inspection emphasizes thickness mapping at TMLs because internal entry is rarely possible. For vessels, internal entry is the gold standard but on-stream NDT increasingly substitutes.

3. Key Damage Mechanisms

Both certifications require thorough knowledge of API 571 damage mechanisms. Many mechanisms apply to both, but emphasis differs:

API 510 (vessels):

  • Wall thinning (general corrosion, erosion)
  • Brittle fracture (MDMT considerations)
  • Fatigue (pressure/thermal cycling)
  • Creep (high-temperature service)
  • Stress corrosion cracking (chloride SCC of stainless, caustic SCC, amine cracking)
  • HTHA (Nelson curves)
  • Hydrogen induced cracking, blistering, SOHIC in wet H2S

API 570 (piping): All of the above PLUS:

  • CUI (corrosion under insulation) — piping has vastly more insulated length than vessels
  • Injection-point corrosion (downstream of chemical injection)
  • Mixing-point corrosion (where two streams meet)
  • Dead-leg corrosion
  • Microbiologically influenced corrosion (MIC, especially in firewater)
  • Naphthenic acid corrosion (crude unit)
  • Sulfidation (high-temperature sulfur attack)

Piping inspectors generally face a wider damage-mechanism diversity per shift than vessel inspectors.

4. Inspection Workflow Differences

API 510 vessel internal: Out-of-service shutdown, isolation, blinding, draining, gas freeing, confined-space entry, VT internal, UT thickness, PT/MT critical welds, RT/PAUT as needed.

API 510 on-stream: External NDT (UT thickness, PAUT corrosion mapping, profile RT, AUBT for HTHA). Reduces shutdown costs.

API 570 piping: Almost entirely external, on-stream. UT thickness at hundreds of TMLs per unit. Guided wave UT for screening long lengths. PEC for through-insulation CUI screening. Profile RT at elbows for erosion. PAUT or RT at welds when needed.

5. Exam Format

Both exams follow the same API ICP structure:

  • Closed-book: ~50 multiple-choice questions, 2 hours 45 minutes. Tests memorized fundamentals.
  • Open-book: ~60 to 80 questions, 4 hours 45 minutes. Tests code navigation skill and applied calculation.
  • Pass mark: 70% (combined or by section depending on cycle).
  • Test center: Prometric worldwide.

The open-book paper requires the candidate to navigate API 510 / 570, ASME VIII / B31.3, ASME IX, API 571, RP 572/574, RP 577, RP 580, API 579-1 in real-time. Tab indexing is critical.

6. Body of Knowledge — Reference Material Differences

API 510:

  • API 510 Pressure Vessel Inspection Code
  • API RP 572 Inspection of Pressure Vessels
  • API RP 576 Inspection of Pressure-Relieving Devices
  • API RP 577 Welding Inspection and Metallurgy
  • API RP 580 Risk-Based Inspection
  • API 571 Damage Mechanisms
  • ASME BPVC V, VIII Div 1, IX

API 570:

  • API 570 Piping Inspection Code
  • API RP 574 Inspection of Piping
  • API RP 577 Welding Inspection and Metallurgy
  • API RP 578 Material Verification Program
  • API RP 580 RBI
  • API 571 Damage Mechanisms
  • ASME B31.3 Process Piping
  • ASME BPVC V, IX

API 570 candidates typically have a slightly heavier study load due to B31.3 being a thicker reference than ASME VIII Div 1.

7. Calculations Tested

Both exams test similar calculations with different code formulas:

  • Vessel minimum thickness: ASME VIII Div 1 UG-27 (t = PR / (SE − 0.6P) for shells; UG-32 for heads)
  • Piping minimum thickness: ASME B31.3 Eq. 3a (t = PD / (2(SE + PY)))
  • Remaining life: Same concept — (t-current − t-min) / corrosion rate
  • MAWP / MAOP: Solve t-formula for P using current measured thickness
  • Joint efficiency E: Per UW-12 (vessels) or Table A-1B (piping)
  • Branch reinforcement: UG-37 (vessels) or B31.3 304.3 (piping)

8. Roles and Career Paths

API 510 inspectors typically work in:

  • Refinery and petrochemical plants (turnaround crews)
  • Chemical plants
  • Power generation (boilers + pressure vessels)
  • OEM vessel manufacturers (as third-party authorized inspectors)

API 570 inspectors typically work in:

  • Refinery and petrochemical piping inspection programs
  • Pipeline operating companies (mid- and downstream)
  • EPC contractors during commissioning
  • RBI program development teams

Most senior inspectors hold both API 510 and API 570 (and often API 653 for tank-yard work). Stacking certifications dramatically increases earning potential and employability.

9. Compensation

2026 typical salaries (US base; Middle East tax-free monthly):

  • API 510 only: a modest cost to a modest cost USA; a modest cost to a modest cost/mo ME
  • API 570 only: a modest cost to a modest cost USA; a modest cost to a modest cost/mo ME
  • API 510 + 570: a modest cost to a modest cost USA; a modest cost to a modest cost/mo ME
  • API 510 + 570 + 653: a modest cost to a modest cost USA; a modest cost to a modest cost/mo ME
  • Senior inspectors with all three + RBI experience top end can reach a modest cost USA

10. Experience Prerequisites

API ICP requires combinations like (verify current API ICP rules):

  • BS engineering + 1 year inspection/NDT experience
  • AS engineering + 2 years
  • HS diploma + 3 years
  • No diploma + 5 years

The experience must be in NDT or inspection of fixed equipment. Welding, design, and operations alone do not count.

11. Which to Take First?

If you can only take one initially, choose based on your current job:

  • Refinery turnaround inspector: API 510 is the daily tool
  • Plant piping inspector / RBI engineer: API 570 is the daily tool
  • Pipeline integrity: API 570 (DOT pipelines often add API 1163 ICP)
  • Vessel OEM / new construction: API 510
  • Tank farm / terminal: API 653 first, then 570

If you have time and budget, take API 510 and API 570 in the same year (typical 12 to 18-month plan).

12. Where Atlantis NDT Fits

Atlantis NDT does not run API 510 or API 570 exam-preparation courses. What we do on the API side is inspection work: ASNT Level III technical support for owner-operator vessel and piping programmes — RBI per API 581, fitness-for-service per API 579 and independent inspection-data review — alongside employer-based NDT training and certification under SNT-TC-1A. See API 510 pressure vessel inspection support and API 570 piping inspection support; the API 510, API 570 and API 653 guides cover the exams themselves.

Frequently Asked Questions

Q: Can I take API 510 and API 570 on the same day?

A: No — API typically schedules each exam on separate dates within the same cycle. You can register for both in one window.

Q: Does API 510 include piping?

A: Vessel nozzles and internal piping within the vessel boundary fall under API 510. External process piping connecting vessels falls under API 570.

Q: Which is harder, API 510 or API 570?

A: First-attempt pass rates are similar (50 to 65% industry average). API 570 has more code documents to navigate; API 510 has more calculation problems. Both require structured prep.

Q: What is the typical preparation time?

A: 200 to 300 hours of focused study over 3 to 6 months, plus a 5-day intensive prep course.

Q: Is API 510 enough to inspect heat exchangers?

A: Yes — heat exchangers under VIII Div 1 are vessels. Some specialized exchangers (e.g., TEMA) add operational considerations not in API 510 alone.

Q: Do I need API 653 if I have API 510?

A: Yes — tanks are not vessels under API 510. API 653 is the tank-specific certification.

Q: How does API certification interact with ASNT/PCN NDT certifications?

A: API certifies you as an inspector (code role); ASNT/PCN certify you in NDT methods (UT, RT, MT, PT). Many inspectors hold both. API 510/570/653 are role certifications; ASNT/PCN are method certifications.

Q: Is API recognized in the Middle East?

A: Yes — Aramco, ADNOC, KOC, QatarEnergy, Sonatrach, OQ all explicitly recognize API 510/570/653 in their inspection contracts. Many tenders require dual API + ASNT/PCN.

Q: How does API 510 / 570 relate to API 653?

A: All three are API ICP certifications. 510 = vessels; 570 = piping; 653 = tanks. Inspectors commonly stack all three.

Q: Does Atlantis NDT offer recertification courses?

A: Yes — 2-day refresh courses for 3-year and 6-year recertification cycles. Call +1 (281) 840-8969 to schedule.

About Atlantis NDT

Atlantis NDT is a global NDT technology and services company headquartered in Houston, Texas with operations across India and the Middle East. We deliver accredited NDT training, technical consulting, certification preparation, and digital inspection software trusted by oil & gas, fabrication, EPC, and power generation clients. Our team of ASNT Level III instructors has trained thousands of inspectors worldwide.

Whether you are preparing for ASNT certification, API 510, API 570, or API 653, our exam preparation programs combine classroom theory, hands-on practical training, and proctored mock exams that mirror the real test environment.

Call us at +1 (281) 840-8969 or email sales@atlantisndt.com to enroll in the next training cohort. Same-day quotes for corporate group training in Houston, Dubai, Riyadh, Hyderabad, and on-site at your facility.

title: NDT Level 2 vs Level 3 2026: Authority, Salary, Career Comparison
snippet: 2026 NDT Level 2 vs Level 3 comparison: authority scope, procedure writing, exam structure, training hours, salary, lifestyle, career paths, FAQ.
content:
NDT certification at Level 2 qualifies an inspector to perform tests and interpret results to approved procedures. Level 3 is the senior tier — the procedure writer, the trainer, the auditor, the technical authority. The leap from Level 2 to Level 3 is much larger than the leap from Level 1 to Level 2, and it changes the inspector’s daily work, authority, and career trajectory. This 2026 guide compares Level 2 and Level 3 across the dimensions that matter to NDT professionals planning their careers and to employers structuring NDT teams.

Level 2 vs Level 3 at a Glance

DimensionLevel 2Level 3
Primary rolePerform tests per a procedure, interpret indications, write reportsDevelop and approve procedures, audit programs, train and qualify Level 1/2/3
Procedure authorityCannot write or approve procedures; can write instructions from procedures (PCN)Writes, approves, and audits procedures
Personnel authorityTrain Level 1; cannot certify any levelTrain and certify Level 1, 2, and 3; develop Written Practice (SNT-TC-1A)
Code interpretationApply code per procedure; consult Level 3 for ambiguityAuthority on code interpretation; liaise with customer/AHJ
Typical hours of experience prerequisite~840 hours total (UT, RT); fewer for surface methodsAdditional 1 to 2 years as Level 2 (plus formal training)
Training prerequisiteSNT-TC-1A or ISO 9712 Level 2 programLevel III formal training + Basic + Method exams
Exam structureGeneral + Specific + Practical for chosen methodBasic (cross-method) + Method (deep dive)
Multiple methods at onceEach method separately certifiedSame — but cross-method Basic is reusable across all method exams
Salary (USA, 2026)$60,000 to $115,000 single-to-multi methoda modest cost to a modest cost
Salary (Middle East, monthly)$5,000 to $12,000 tax-freea modest cost to a modest cost tax-free
Continuing educationAnnual eye exam; CEUs encouragedActive practice; recertification at 5/10 years
RecognitionOperates within employer’s NDT programRecognized industry-wide; often signs procedures used at many sites

Where Does Level 1 Fit In?

Level 1 is the foundation both Level 2 and Level 3 are built on, and it's worth covering explicitly rather than assuming it as background. A Level 1 technician performs specific NDT tasks under a written procedure and the direct supervision of a Level 2 or Level 3 — setting up equipment, running the test, and recording results — but does not independently interpret findings or make accept/reject calls. Per SNT-TC-1A, Level 1 certification typically requires around 40 hours of classroom training plus roughly 300 hours of documented on-the-job experience, and it does not require any prior NDT experience to begin: it's the standard entry point for someone new to the field.

The jump from Level 1 to Level 2 is the first major step up in independence: Level 2 can work unsupervised, interpret and evaluate results against acceptance criteria, and train Level 1 personnel, none of which Level 1 is authorized to do alone. That gap is real, but it's smaller than the Level 2-to-Level 3 gap covered in detail below — Level 1 to Level 2 is mostly about earning the right to work independently within an existing procedure, while Level 2 to Level 3 is about gaining the authority to write the procedure itself. For the full beginner path into Level 1, see How to Become an NDT Technician: Step-by-Step Career Guide, and for realistic timelines across all three levels, see How Long Does NDT Training Take?.

1. Day-to-Day Work

A typical Level 2 day looks like:

  • Daily equipment checks and calibration
  • Performing inspections per approved procedure
  • Interpreting indications, sizing, evaluating to acceptance code
  • Writing inspection reports
  • Discussing borderline calls with Level 3
  • Training Level 1 personnel on the job

A typical Level 3 day looks like:

  • Writing or revising NDT procedures for new applications
  • Reviewing and approving inspection records
  • Auditing field inspections and procedure compliance
  • Liaising with customers, AIs, AHJ, and engineering
  • Investigating failure cases and writing technical reports
  • Developing training plans and conducting Level 2 exams
  • Qualifying new procedures (PAUT, TOFD, DDA) per ASME V Mandatory Appendix XI
  • Supporting bids, technical proposals, and code negotiations

Level 3 is fundamentally a leadership and technical authority role. Time at the inspection bench drops; time at the desk and on calls rises.

2. Authority Scope

Level 2 cannot:

  • Write or approve NDT procedures
  • Certify Level 1 or Level 2 inspectors
  • Approve customer-specific technique variations
  • Conduct procedure qualification per ASME V Mandatory Appendix XI
  • Sign off on the Written Practice (SNT-TC-1A para 5)

Level 2 can:

  • Set up and calibrate equipment
  • Perform tests per approved procedure
  • Interpret and evaluate indications
  • Write inspection reports
  • Train Level 1 informally (on the job)
  • Under PCN/ISO 9712 only: write method-specific written instructions derived from a procedure

Level 3 can do all of the above PLUS:

  • Develop, qualify, write, and approve procedures
  • Establish acceptance criteria when not specified by code
  • Designate the NDT method and technique for a given inspection scope
  • Examine and certify Level 1, 2, and 3 candidates (in the employer’s Written Practice)
  • Audit the employer’s NDT program
  • Interpret code and resolve ambiguity
  • Liaise as the company’s NDT technical authority with customers and regulators

3. Training and Experience Requirements

Per SNT-TC-1A and ISO 9712:

  • Level 2 prerequisites: Level 1 certification + additional training (typically 8 to 40 hours method-dependent) + additional experience hours (typically 200 to 700 hours method-dependent).
  • Level 3 prerequisites: Level 2 certification + additional training (varies by scheme; ASNT requires study to pass Basic + Method exams; PCN requires formal Level 3 training) + 1 to 2 years experience as Level 2.

ASNT Level III certificate (third-party) is widely required even for SNT-TC-1A employer-based Level III practice. The ASNT Level III Basic + Method exams are challenging closed-book CBT tests.

4. Exam Structure Differences

Level 2 exam (ASNT or PCN):

  • General (closed-book, ~40 questions): physics, principles of the method
  • Specific (~20 questions, often open-book under ASNT): codes and procedures
  • Practical: hands-on demonstration on real specimens

Level 3 exam (ASNT):

  • Basic Exam: 135 questions, 3 hours, closed-book, covers personnel qualification, all NDT methods (cross-method), materials/fabrication/product technology, and NDT applications. See our Level III Basic prep article.
  • Method Exam: 135 questions, 4 hours, closed-book, deep dive into chosen method (UT, RT, MT, PT, VT, ET, LT, AE, IR, NR).
  • Pass mark 70% on each.

The Basic exam tests breadth across all methods, not just the candidate’s primary expertise. Many candidates fail the Basic on the first attempt because they over-focus on their primary method.

5. Salary Difference

Level 3 salaries are dramatically higher than Level 2:

RegionLevel 2 (single method)Level 2 (multi-method)Level 3 (single method)Level 3 (multi-method)
USA base salary$60,000 to $85,000$80,000 to $115,000a modest cost to a modest costa modest cost to a modest cost
Middle East monthly (tax-free)a modest cost to a modest costa modest cost to a modest costa modest cost to a modest costa modest cost to a modest cost
India monthly₹80,000 to ₹150,000₹120,000 to ₹250,000₹200,000 to ₹400,000₹350,000 to ₹600,000+

A 60 to 100% salary uplift on certification to Level 3 is typical, with multi-method Level 3s at the top of the NDT pay scale. Senior Level 3s in consulting and litigation support can earn far more.

6. Career Paths from Level 2

Common paths from Level 2:

  • Vertical: Level 2 → Level 3 (technical authority career)
  • Lateral expansion: Level 2 in one method → Level 2 in additional methods (multi-method inspector premium)
  • Code certifications: Add API 510, API 570, API 653 (becomes in-service inspector)
  • Specialized: Add PAUT, TOFD, DDA, AUBT endorsements (advanced UT/RT premium)
  • Management: NDT Coordinator → QA/QC Manager → Inspection Manager (managerial path)
  • Consulting: Independent NDT consultant or expert witness (typically requires Level 3 + 10+ years experience)

7. Hours and Lifestyle

  • Level 2: Typically shift work, turnarounds, outage rotations. Field-heavy. Physical demands (climbing, scaffolding, hot/cold, weight of equipment).
  • Level 3: More office-based, normal business hours. Travel for audits, customer meetings, training delivery. Less physical strain but more cognitive load.

Many Level 3s value the lifestyle change; others miss the field work and split time between desk and bench.

8. Multiple Methods Strategy

Holding Level 2 or Level 3 in multiple methods compounds value:

  • UT + RT covers volumetric inspection (welds, castings, forgings)
  • MT + PT covers surface inspection on ferrous + non-ferrous
  • VT (visual) is foundational to all weld inspection
  • ET (eddy current) opens conductivity, sorting, tube inspection
  • Advanced: PAUT, TOFD, DDA, AUBT, AE

A “four-method Level 2” (UT + RT + MT + PT) is a common all-around inspector profile. A “four-method Level 3” commands top salary across continents.

9. Cost of Reaching Level 3

Typical cost from Level 2 to Level 3 in one method:

  • Basic exam training: a modest cost to a modest cost (Atlantis NDT 5-day Basic prep)
  • Method exam training: a modest cost to a modest cost per method
  • ASNT exam fees (Basic + Method): ~a modest cost to a modest cost combined
  • Study materials: a modest cost to a modest cost
  • Total per method: ~a modest cost to a modest cost
  • Multi-method Level 3 (UT + RT + MT + PT): a modest cost to a modest cost total over 1 to 2 years

Payback is usually under a year given the salary uplift.

10. Common Pitfalls Going Level 2 to Level 3

  • Underestimating the Basic exam — candidates over-prepare their primary method and under-study the cross-method content
  • Insufficient procedure-writing experience — classroom theory does not substitute for shadowing a real Level 3
  • Weak code interpretation — need to be conversant with ASME V/VIII/IX, ISO codes, API codes, AWS
  • Failing to maintain practice in primary method while studying for Level 3

11. Choosing the Right Scheme

See our ASNT vs PCN article for full detail. Brief summary:

  • ASNT Level III certificate (third-party): Universally recognized in USA; widely respected internationally.
  • PCN Level 3: Strongly preferred in UK/Europe/Middle East; portable third-party.
  • SNT-TC-1A employer Level III: Functional only with that employer.

Most ambitious Level 3s hold the ASNT Level III certificate (or PCN Level 3) regardless of employer.

12. Atlantis NDT Level III Preparation

We offer comprehensive Level III preparation:

  • Level III Basic 5-day prep course (covers all five subject areas)
  • Method-specific Level III courses (UT, RT, MT, PT, VT)
  • 500+ practice MCQs per exam
  • Proctored mock exams
  • One-on-one tutoring for retake candidates
  • Cohorts in Houston, Dubai, Hyderabad, on-site for corporate groups

Visit our ASNT certification page or call +1 (281) 840-8969 to schedule.

Frequently Asked Questions

Q: How many years from Level 2 to Level 3?

A: Minimum 1 to 2 years of Level 2 experience (per SNT-TC-1A and ISO 9712). Most candidates take 2 to 5 years to feel exam-ready.

Q: Is Level III the highest NDT qualification?

A: Yes for personnel certification. Specialty endorsements (PAUT Level 3, TOFD Level 3, AUBT, AE) add depth but are within the Level 3 framework.

Q: Can a Level 2 audit another inspector?

A: Day-to-day field oversight, yes. Formal NDT program audits per the Written Practice are a Level 3 function.

Q: Can a Level 2 sign procedures?

A: No — only Level 3 can write and approve procedures. Level 2 can sign written instructions derived from approved procedures (PCN/ISO 9712).

Q: What if my employer doesn’t need a Level 3?

A: Some employers have no in-house Level 3 and contract one. As a Level 2 holder, you can become a contracted Level 3 once certified, even for your current employer.

Q: Are Level III exams open-book?

A: ASNT Level III Basic and Method exams are closed-book. PCN Level 3 has both open and closed-book components depending on the scheme update.

Q: How many Level 3s does a typical NDT company have?

A: Small companies: 1 to 2 (often the owner). Mid-size: 3 to 6. Major service providers: 20 to 50+ across all methods and regions.

Q: Is the salary jump worth the study effort?

A: Yes — the 60 to 100% salary uplift typically pays back the study time and exam fees within the first year of Level 3 employment.

Q: Can I go directly from Level 1 to Level 3?

A: No. Level 2 is a required intermediate step under all major schemes (ASNT, PCN, ISO 9712, ASME V).

Q: How does Level III relate to API 510/570/653?

A: Different certifications. NDT Level III is the method authority (UT, RT, etc.). API 510/570/653 are in-service inspector certifications (vessels/piping/tanks). Many senior inspectors hold Level III + multiple APIs.

About Atlantis NDT

Atlantis NDT is a global NDT technology and services company headquartered in Houston, Texas with operations across India and the Middle East. We deliver accredited NDT training, technical consulting, certification preparation, and digital inspection software trusted by oil & gas, fabrication, EPC, and power generation clients. Our team of ASNT Level III instructors has trained thousands of inspectors worldwide.

Whether you are preparing for ASNT certification, API 510, API 570, or API 653, our exam preparation programs combine classroom theory, hands-on practical training, and proctored mock exams that mirror the real test environment.

Call us at +1 (281) 840-8969 or email sales@atlantisndt.com to enroll in the next training cohort. Same-day quotes for corporate group training in Houston, Dubai, Riyadh, Hyderabad, and on-site at your facility.

title: ASME Section V Article 2 — Radiographic Testing (RT) Requirements Explained
author: Anoop Rayavarapu
metaDescription: ASME Section V Article 2 RT requirements decoded — IQI placement, density limits, source-to-film distance, geometric unsharpness, weld coverage, technique sheets. ASNT Level III practical guide.
snippet: ASME Section V Article 2 sets the rules for radiographic testing of weldments and castings. This 2026 guide explains IQI selection, geometric unsharpness limits, technique qualification, and how Article 2 ties into ASME Section VIII, B31.3, and API 510/570/653 acceptance.
content:
ASME Section V Article 2 — Practical Industry Guide

ASME Section V Article 2 is the foundational ASME nondestructive examination standard for radiographic testing of welds, castings, and forgings. It is referenced by ASME Section VIII (pressure vessel construction), ASME B31.1 (power piping), ASME B31.3 (process piping), API 510, API 570, API 653, AWS D1.1, NAVSEA T9074-AS-GIB-010, and dozens of international jurisdictional codes. Without Article 2 compliance, a radiograph cannot be used to support code acceptance of a welded joint, period.

Scope and Applicability of Article 2

Article 2 (T-210 through T-292) covers conventional radiography using X-ray sources up to 1 MeV and gamma radiation sources (Iridium-192, Cobalt-60, Selenium-75, Ytterbium-169). It addresses both single-wall single-image (SWSI) and double-wall double-image (DWDI) viewing techniques and applies to welds, castings, fabrications, and bonded composites. Computed radiography (CR) and digital detector array (DDA) techniques are addressed in companion Articles 22 and 27 — but Article 2 remains the baseline for film-based RT.

Equipment owners running multi-code inspection programs RBI program design should be aware that ultrasonic testing is the preferred alternative for many in-service inspections under API 510 § 5.6 and API 570 § 5.7 because of access, throughput, and ALARA radiation considerations — but Article 2 RT remains mandatory for original construction acceptance on most ASME-VIII Class 1 and B31.3 Category M services.

Image Quality Indicators (IQIs) — T-233

IQIs are the most-rejected element of any radiograph. Article 2 (T-233.1, T-233.2, T-276) allows two IQI types: hole-type per ASTM E1025 (the diamond-shaped plaque with three drilled holes 1T, 2T, 4T in diameter where T is the IQI thickness), or wire-type per ASTM E747 (a sequence of six wires of graduated diameter encased in low-attenuation plastic). The IQI is normally placed on the SOURCE side of the weld; placing it film-side requires marking with the letter F and using one designation thinner per T-277.

Selection of IQI designator is based on the radiographic-thickness range tables in T-276. For nominal 25 mm (1-inch) weld thickness with no reinforcement, the typical IQI is designator 25, with required hole 2T essential. The required sensitivity of 2-2T means the 2T hole on a thickness-25 IQI must be visible on the radiograph. Failure to demonstrate the essential hole or wire is an automatic technique rejection — re-shoot required.

Geometric Unsharpness (Ug) Limits — T-274.2

Geometric unsharpness Ug = F · t / d, where F = source size (mm), t = specimen-to-film distance (mm), d = source-to-specimen distance (mm). Article 2 sets the upper limit: 0.020 in. for material thickness ≤ 2 in., 0.030 in. for 2–3 in., 0.040 in. for 3–4 in., 0.070 in. for > 4 in. A 4 mm × 4 mm Ir-192 source at d = 600 mm, t = 50 mm yields Ug = 0.013 in. — within the 0.020 limit. Cobalt-60 sources (much larger physical dimension, 3–5 mm) require longer SFD to stay within Ug limits.

Source-to-film distance calculation is the most common technique-sheet error caught by qualified Level III reviewers. The Ug equation MUST be in the documented technique sheet, with the worst-case geometry called out. Atlantis NDT Reporting Software auto-calculates Ug from the technique inputs and flags non-compliant geometry before the shoot.

Density and Penetrameter Sensitivity — T-282 + T-283

Film density (D = log₁₀ (Io/I)) per T-282 must be 1.8–4.0 for X-ray and 2.0–4.0 for gamma sources, measured through the area of interest (weld) NOT the parent metal. Density variation across a single radiograph must not exceed −15 % / +30 % of the IQI density. A densitometer calibrated against an NIST-traceable step wedge is mandatory in the lab.

Sensitivity per T-283 is the IQI essential hole/wire that must be visible. Cracks, lack of fusion, lack of penetration, and slag inclusions in the weld are interpreted only after demonstrating that the radiograph meets the density and sensitivity requirements. Order matters — never call indications on a radiograph that fails the IQI check.

Single-Wall vs Double-Wall Techniques

Article 2 addresses three viewing geometries:

  1. Single-Wall Single-Image (SWSI) — T-271.1: source outside, film inside (or vice versa); one weld interrogated per exposure. Preferred for pressure vessels and any pipe > 3.5 inch NPS where access permits.
  2. Double-Wall Single-Image (DWSI) — T-271.2: source outside, film outside; only the far-side weld is interpreted (near-side weld is too unsharp). Used on small-bore piping where SWSI is impractical.
  3. Double-Wall Double-Image (DWDI) — T-271.3: source offset 90° to weld plane; both near and far welds visible, offset elliptically on the film. Limited to NPS ≤ 3.5 in. Minimum two shots at 90° spacing required for full circumferential coverage.

Article 2 Cross-References — ASME Section VIII, B31.3, B31.1, AWS D1.1, API

Article 2 is referenced (not duplicated) by every downstream construction code. ASME Section VIII Div 1 § UW-51 requires "full RT" per Article 2 for Class 1 lethal-service and some thicknesses; Div 2 § 7.4.7 specifies fluorescent screen / lead-screen rules. ASME B31.3 § 344.5 calls out Article 2 for Category M (severe cyclic / hazardous) and Category K services. ASME B31.1 § 136.4 calls out 100 % RT for Class 1 components > 19 mm wall.

AWS D1.1 Clause 8 and Annex G map to Article 2 with adjusted acceptance criteria for structural welds (cumulative slag, porosity, undercut limits). API 510 § 8 + API 570 § 5.7 + API 653 § 12 reference Article 2 for spot-RT on alterations and repairs. API 510 Pressure Vessel Inspector, API 570 Piping Inspector, API 653 Tank Inspector all expect inspectors to read and interpret an Article 2 radiograph.

Technique Sheet, Procedure Qualification, and Records — T-291 + T-292

Every radiograph requires a written technique sheet (T-292.5) capturing: source type and strength, source-to-film distance, exposure time, film type, screens, IQI designator and location, geometric unsharpness calculation, density measurements, identification marks, weld identification, joint geometry sketch, and personnel qualifications.

The procedure must be qualified per ASME Section V Mandatory Appendix when a "Demonstration" approach is required by the referencing code. The Procedure Qualification Record (PQR) bundles a worst-case shot, the IQI achieved, the density measured, and the demonstrated coverage. Atlantis NDT Reporting Software ships a built-in Article 2 technique-sheet template with Ug auto-calculation, IQI-table lookup, and PDF auto-generation per shot.

Common Article 2 Audit Findings

  • IQI essential hole/wire NOT visible — most common rejection
  • Density < 1.8 or > 4.0 (over- or under-exposure)
  • Ug calculation missing from technique sheet
  • SFD inconsistency between technique sheet and field shot
  • Source-side / film-side IQI marking missing the F stamp when film-side
  • Multi-shot circumferential coverage gaps on DWDI (less than 2 shots at 90°)
  • SNT-TC-1A guide Level II RT certification expired on the interpreting inspector
  • Calibration block / step-wedge traceability not documented

Personnel Qualification — Article 2 + ASNT SNT-TC-1A / ISO 9712

Article 2 itself does not certify personnel — it references ASNT SNT-TC-1A, CP-189, ACCP, ISO 9712, or an employer-approved equivalent (e.g., NAS 410 for aerospace). For pressure-equipment work in the US, the dominant scheme is SNT-TC-1A Level II RT. For European / Middle Eastern projects, ISO 9712 Level 2 RT is more common.

Annual eye exam (near-vision Jaeger J1 + colour-perception Ishihara) is required by both ASNT SNT-TC-1A § 8.2 and ISO 9712 § 7.4 — and is the second most common audit finding when missing from the Level II cert pack. ASNT Level III consulting provides written-practice authoring, training-hour audit, and exam administration to keep your RT roster Article 2-compliant year-round.

Frequently Asked Questions

Q1: Can I use digital radiography (DR) under Article 2?

A: No — Article 2 is film-only. Computed Radiography is Article 22; Digital Detector Arrays are Article 27. If your specification calls out "Article 2", you must shoot film unless the referencing code or contract amends the technique. Many recent ASME VIII fab specs allow either Article 2 OR Article 22/27 by mutual agreement; check the contract carefully.

Q2: What sensitivity does Article 2 require?

A: Hole-type IQIs require the 2T hole to be visible (2-2T sensitivity); wire-type IQIs require a specific wire diameter visible per the table in T-276 (typically wire 8 or smaller depending on thickness). The required IQI designator is determined by the radiographic thickness, which is the weld thickness plus reinforcement.

Q3: Is Ir-192 still allowed for thin pipe under 0.5-inch wall?

A: Yes, but the Ug equation governs. A 3 mm × 3 mm Ir-192 source at SFD 600 mm gives Ug = 0.005 in. on a 0.5 in. weld — well within limits. The bigger concern on thin wall is contrast — Ir-192 spectrum (avg ≈ 380 keV) gives flatter contrast than X-ray, so density and IQI sensitivity become harder to achieve. Many fabricators prefer 160–200 kV X-ray for pipe < 0.5 in. wall.

Q4: How does Article 2 compare with ISO 17636-1?

A: ISO 17636-1 (RT of metallic materials, film-based) is the European / international equivalent. Both define IQI placement, Ug limits, and density ranges, but ISO 17636-1 uses single-wire EN ISO 19232 IQIs by default (Article 2 allows wire OR hole). For projects accepted under both ASME and EN, dual-IQI exposures are common. The acceptance criteria are NOT in Article 2 / ISO 17636 — they live in the construction code (ASME VIII, B31.3, ISO 5817).

Q5: Does Article 2 cover acceptance criteria for porosity, slag, and cracks?

A: No. Article 2 is the WORKMANSHIP standard for HOW to shoot the radiograph; the acceptance criteria for the indications come from the construction code being used. ASME VIII Div 1 § UW-51 (no crack-like flaws), ASME B31.3 § 341.3.2 (Table 341.3.2A), AWS D1.1 Table 8.1 (slag length per inch), and API 1104 § 9 each define their own pass/fail rules. Always pair Article 2 with the construction code's acceptance section.

Q6: How long must Article 2 radiographs be retained?

A: Article 2 itself does not specify retention. Most referencing codes require a minimum of 5 years (ASME VIII § UW-52), often longer for life-of-equipment retention (typical for nuclear, offshore platforms, and LNG service). Digital archive of scanned films with SHA-256 hash chain is now widely accepted — Atlantis NDT Reporting Software auto-generates the archive bundle.

Q7: Are crawler / crawler-fed isotope cameras allowed under Article 2?

A: Yes, provided source size, SFD, and Ug calculations meet T-274.2. Pipeline pigging-crawler isotope shots are extremely common for cross-country pipeline construction (B31.4, B31.8) — and they are still Article 2 RT in spirit. The technique sheet must call out the crawler geometry, source size, and Ug calc for the worst weld position.

Q8: How does Article 2 interact with API 1104 for pipeline welds?

A: API 1104 § 11.1 references "an approved radiographic procedure". For US pipelines, that's almost always Article 2. The acceptance criteria are in API 1104 § 9 (image quality, indication length limits, cluster rules), NOT Article 2 — so Article 2 governs HOW you shoot, API 1104 governs PASS/FAIL on the pipeline weld.

title: ASME Section V Article 5 — Ultrasonic Thickness Measurement Requirements (2026)
author: Anoop Rayavarapu
metaDescription: ASME Section V Article 5 ultrasonic thickness measurement decoded — calibration, transducer selection, T-min calculation, corrosion grid mapping, API 510/570/653 cross-reference. ASNT Level III guide.
snippet: ASME Section V Article 5 is the UT thickness measurement standard for in-service pressure equipment. This 2026 guide explains transducer selection, calibration, corrosion-rate calculation, T-min remaining-life math, and how Article 5 plugs into API 510/570/653 inspection workflows.
content:
ASME Section V Article 5 — Practical Implementation Guide

ASME Section V Article 5 is the ASME nondestructive examination standard for ultrasonic thickness measurement. It is the single most-referenced ASME Section V article in operating-plant inspection — every API 510 external survey, every API 570 piping circuit reading, and every API 653 tank-shell thickness profile traces back to Article 5. Without Article 5 compliance, the thickness data cannot be used to calculate corrosion rate or remaining life under API 579 FFS (API 579-1 / ASME FFS-1).

Scope and Applicability

Article 5 (T-510 through T-590) covers ultrasonic thickness measurement of metallic materials including carbon steel, low-alloy steel, austenitic stainless, duplex, and clad construction. It is not used for crack detection (that's Article 4) or flaw sizing — Article 5 is purely about remaining-wall measurement. The standard applies to surfaces from 0 °C to 540 °C (above 540 °C use special hot-couplant + delay-line techniques).

Applicability examples: external CML grid on a 10-year API 510 pressure vessel inspection, API 570 Piping Inspector TML circuit on Class-1 piping, API 653 Tank Inspector 5-year tank shell course thickness profile, API 510 Pressure Vessel Inspector field external survey, refractory-clad fired-heater tube measurement, and pipeline integrity-management thickness mapping.

Equipment Qualification — T-530

Article 5 requires the ultrasonic instrument to demonstrate ±0.1 mm or ±0.004 in. accuracy across the operating range, verified on a calibrated step wedge (ASTM E797). Common qualified instruments: Olympus 38DL Plus, Olympus EPOCH 650 (in thickness mode), Sonatest Master Scan / Sitescan, GE USM Go +, Modsonic Einstein III. The instrument calibration certificate (ISO/IEC 17025 traceable) must be in date for the inspection.

Transducer selection is the most common source of measurement error:

  • Dual-element transducers (5 MHz typical): required for thin wall 3–25 mm, corroded surfaces, and curved geometries. Olympus D790, D791, D7227 series, or equivalent.
  • Single-element transducers (5–10 MHz, 0.25 in. element): for clean surfaces and walls > 25 mm.
  • High-temperature delay-line transducers: for surfaces 150–540 °C with appropriate hot couplant (silicone-based, IRT-X, or Sonotrace HT-260).
  • EMAT (electromagnetic-acoustic transducer): couplant-free, used for hot/dry surfaces and through-coating measurement.

Calibration Blocks and Procedure — T-561 + T-563

Calibration MUST bracket the expected wall thickness. A two-point calibration on a step-wedge with steps spanning the expected range (e.g. 5 mm + 25 mm steps for piping 6–20 mm wall) is required at the start of every shift AND every two hours during the survey. Velocity input must match the material (carbon steel ≈ 5,920 m/s; austenitic SS ≈ 5,740 m/s; titanium ≈ 6,070 m/s).

Coupling on rough or coated surfaces is the dominant accuracy killer. Surface prep (wire-brush + light grinding to bright metal, removal of paint where measurement on bare steel is required) is mandatory before the calibration shot and every CML reading. For external service with intact coating, "through-coating" UT-T techniques exist (subtracting coating thickness from the gross reading), but require documented procedure-qualification per T-563.

Condition-Monitoring Location (CML) Grid Design

Article 5 doesn't dictate CML grid design — that comes from API 510 § 5.6 / API 570 § 5.7 / API 653 § 6. But the UT-T technique used at each CML must be Article 5-compliant. Typical grid practices:

  • Pressure vessels (API 510): 1 CML per ft² on shell, 3-5 CMLs around each nozzle, 1 CML at each weld crossing; minimum 4 readings per CML, record min/avg/max.
  • Piping (API 570): CMLs at 10/2 / 4/8 / 6/12 o'clock at TML stations; spaced every 50 ft on Class-1 piping straight runs; intensified at elbows + tees + valves + reducers.
  • Tanks (API 653): shell course gridded 6 ft circumferential × full height; floor MFL scanning with UT-T verification on indications.

The CML readings flow into the corrosion-rate calculation: long-term (LT) corrosion rate = (initial − current) / years-in-service; short-term (ST) rate = (previous − current) / interval. Inspection interval = min(remaining life / 2, max interval per code). Atlantis NDT NDT reporting software auto-calculates LT/ST rates per CML, plots the trend, and flags any CML approaching T-min ≤ 12 months ahead.

T-min, Remaining Life, and Article 5 Limits

Article 5 produces the thickness data; API 510 Pressure Vessel Inspector/API 570 Piping Inspector/API 653 Tank Inspector or API 579 FFS calculates the disposition. T-minimum per ASME B31.3 § 304 for piping: t = PD / (2(SE + PY)); per ASME VIII Div 1 § UG-27 for cylindrical shells: t = PR / (SE − 0.6P). Once measured (Article 5) and design T-min (code) are known, remaining life = (t_actual − T-min) / corrosion rate.

If the actual thickness ever drops below code T-min, the equipment requires immediate FFS assessment under API 579 / ASME FFS-1 (Level 1, 2, or 3). Level 1 is a screening assessment — Atlantis NDT Level III consultants routinely run Level 2 / 3 evaluations for refineries and offshore operators globally.

Surface Conditions and Article 5 Limitations

Article 5 has known limitations that the inspector must understand:

  • Pitting: a single deep pit may not be detected by a CML grid; bunched pits cause back-wall echo loss. Pitting-aware techniques (corrosion mapping with PA, B-scan automated UT) supplement Article 5 spot readings.
  • Lamellar (mid-wall) cracking / hydrogen blistering: a mid-wall crack reflects the signal early; what looks like a thinning reading is actually a flaw. Always confirm with Article 4 (UT for flaws) when a CML reads "too thin".
  • Refractory or insulation: requires removal of a cup-shaped section for surface access, or specialised through-insulation techniques (pulsed-eddy current Atlantis Digital Twin platform layers are the modern complement).
  • Hot service > 540 °C: outside Article 5 scope; use refractory-line creep monitoring techniques per API 579 Part 10.

Article 5 Personnel Qualification

Article 5 inspections require ASNT SNT-TC-1A Level II UT (or ISO 9712 Level 2 UT, or NAS 410 Level 2 UT for aerospace). The same eye-test requirement (Jaeger J1 + Ishihara) applies as Article 4. UT-T-specific training emphasises calibration discipline, velocity correction, and CML-grid interpretation. ASNT Level III consulting provides written-practice and procedure approval for UT-T programs at refineries and offshore operators globally.

Frequently Asked Questions

Q1: How often must I calibrate during an Article 5 survey?

A: At minimum at the start of each shift AND every two hours during use. T-561 says "as often as necessary to assure accuracy" — most inspector procedures pin this at 2-hour intervals or after any transducer / cable change.

Q2: Can I use Article 5 readings for fitness-for-service assessment?

A: Yes — Article 5 thickness data feeds directly into API 579 FFS (API 579 Level 1/2/3). The FFS report must reference the Article 5 procedure used, the calibration certificates, the CML grid sketch, and the inspector's Level II UT credentials.

Q3: What's the difference between Article 4 UT and Article 5 UT-T?

A: Article 4 is flaw detection (cracks, LOF, slag, porosity) using angled-beam, PAUT, TOFD. Article 5 is wall-thickness measurement using normal-beam dual or single-element transducers. Different transducers, different calibration, different acceptance — same Code (Section V), different articles.

Q4: Does Article 5 cover composite / non-metallic materials?

A: No. Article 5 is for metallic. Composite thickness measurement uses ASME Section V Article 30 (Phased-Array Ultrasonic Testing — Composite-Specific) or ASTM E2580 / E2581 for aerospace.

Q5: How does Article 5 interact with API 510 / 570 / 653?

A: The API in-service standards REFERENCE Article 5 for thickness technique. API 510 § 8.3, API 570 § 8.2, and API 653 § 12.3 each call out "ultrasonic thickness measurement per ASME Section V Article 5 or equivalent." So you cannot do API external inspection without Article 5-qualified UT-T procedure.

Q6: How long must CML data be retained?

A: Life-of-equipment minimum. Trending requires historical baseline — losing the 1990 baseline CML reading kills the 2026 remaining-life calc. Atlantis NDT Reporting Software stores SHA-256-hashed CML records with PDF/A-3 archive bundles.

Q7: Is automated UT thickness mapping covered by Article 5?

A: Article 5 covers single-point spot readings. Automated UT corrosion mapping (with positional encoding, B-scan / C-scan output) is addressed in ASME Section V Article 4 (when used for sizing) and Article 5 (when used for thickness only). Most Class-1 fab specs accept automated thickness mapping under Article 5 if the inspection procedure is qualified per T-563.

Q8: How does Article 5 integrate with digital-twin platforms?

A: Article 5 CML readings are the heartbeat input to a corrosion-aware digital twin. Atlantis NDT Atlantis Digital Twin platform pulls Article 5 CML data per inspection, layers the 3D corrosion map onto the asset model, calculates remaining life per API 579 FFS, and forecasts re-inspection dates. This is the operational version of "smart" inspection.

title: ASME Section V Article 6 — Liquid Penetrant Testing (PT) Requirements Explained
author: Anoop Rayavarapu
metaDescription: ASME Section V Article 6 liquid penetrant testing requirements decoded — penetrant family selection, dwell time, developer, lighting, acceptance, ASNT/ISO 9712 personnel. ASNT Level III practical guide.
snippet: ASME Section V Article 6 governs liquid-penetrant testing for surface-breaking discontinuities. This 2026 guide explains penetrant family selection, dwell time, developer application, lighting requirements, acceptance, and cross-reference to ASME VIII, B31.3, and AWS D1.1.
content:
ASME Section V Article 6 — Practical PT Guide

ASME Section V Article 6 is the ASME nondestructive examination standard for liquid-penetrant testing (PT or LPI). It is the most-used surface NDT method for non-magnetic materials — austenitic stainless steel, duplex, nickel alloys, titanium, aluminum, and copper — and it complements magnetic particle testing (Article 7) for ferromagnetic materials. Article 6 is referenced by ASME Section VIII Div 1 § UW-51, B31.3 § 344.4, AWS D1.1 Annex M, API 510 / 570 / 653 alterations sections, and dozens of jurisdictional codes.

Scope and Applicability — T-610

Article 6 covers liquid-penetrant testing on non-porous metallic, ceramic, and some plastic surfaces. PT detects discontinuities OPEN TO THE SURFACE — cracks, laps, seams, lack of fusion, lack of penetration on the open root, porosity that breaks through. PT cannot detect subsurface flaws (use ultrasonic testing Article 4 or RT Article 2). Surface temperature limits: 5 °C to 50 °C standard; higher / lower requires specially-qualified penetrant per Mandatory Appendix III.

Applicability examples: post-weld surface inspection of austenitic-SS pressure vessels (Article 6 is the workhorse since MT doesn't work on non-ferro), root-pass inspection on B31.3 process piping, finish-pass inspection on aerospace welds, fitness-for-service crack confirmation on API 579 FFS Level 2 assessments, and API 653 Tank Inspector bottom-plate weld inspection on austenitic-clad tanks.

Penetrant Family Selection — T-621 + T-622

Article 6 recognises 6 process combinations (Type × Method):

  • Type I (Fluorescent) — Method A (Water-Washable): highest sensitivity for tight cracks; quick on production lines; needs UV-A inspection booth (100 µW/cm² minimum, 1000 µW/cm² standard).
  • Type I — Method B (Post-Emulsifiable): hydrophilic or lipophilic emulsifier post-applied; highest sensitivity of all combinations; longer process, lab-quality results. Aerospace standard.
  • Type I — Method C (Solvent-Removable): portable, field-friendly; fluorescent kits used at heights and confined spaces.
  • Type II (Visible Dye) — Method A: water-washable visible; less sensitive than fluorescent but no UV needed.
  • Type II — Method C (Solvent-Removable Visible Dye): the workhorse field method — Magnaflux SPOTCHECK or equivalent; aerosol penetrant + cleaner + developer; portable, low-cost, 5–10 min process.

Sensitivity classification per ASTM E165: Level ½ (low), Level 1 (medium), Level 2 (high), Level 3 (ultra-high), Level 4 (ultra-high). Aerospace work typically requires Level 3 fluorescent post-emulsifiable; pressure-equipment work most commonly uses Level 1 or 2 visible solvent-removable.

Dwell Time, Removal, and Developer — T-672 + T-673 + T-674

Penetrant dwell (T-672): minimum 5 minutes for most penetrants on most discontinuity types; up to 60 minutes for tight fatigue cracks or stress corrosion cracking (SCC). At temperatures below 16 °C, dwell time must be doubled. Article 6 mandates the dwell be documented for every shot.

Penetrant removal (T-673): solvent-removable uses a lint-free cloth dampened with remover (NEVER spray remover directly on the surface — washes penetrant out of cracks). Water-washable uses a low-pressure (≤ 50 psi / 350 kPa) low-temperature (≤ 43 °C) water spray at 30° angle, not normal to surface. Over-washing is the dominant cause of false negatives.

Developer (T-674): non-aqueous wet developer is the most common (Magnaflux SKD-S2, Met-L-Chek E-59A). Apply uniform, light coat 15–30 cm from surface. Developer dwell: 7–60 minutes minimum, never less than penetrant dwell. The developer draws penetrant out of the discontinuity and produces a visible indication width proportional to defect depth.

Lighting Requirements — T-676 + T-680

Visible-dye PT (Type II) requires 100 fc (1000 lux) minimum illumination at the surface, measured with a calibrated photometer. Fluorescent PT (Type I) requires:

  • Ambient white light ≤ 2 fc (20 lux) — dark booth
  • UV-A radiation ≥ 1000 µW/cm² at the surface (320–400 nm peak), measured with a calibrated radiometer
  • Inspector dark-adapted 5 min minimum before reading
  • UV lamp warm-up 5 min minimum before measurement

Light verification is the second most-common audit finding after dwell-time documentation gaps.

Acceptance Criteria — Comes from the Construction Code

Article 6 itself defines HOW to perform PT but NOT what is acceptable. Acceptance criteria come from the referencing code:

  • ASME VIII Div 1 § UW-51: no cracks, no linear indications ≥ 1.5 mm length, no rounded indications ≥ 5 mm
  • ASME B31.3 § 344.4 + Table 341.3.2A: Severe-Cyclic / Category M tighter limits
  • AWS D1.1 Clause 8 + Annex M: no cracks; no linear indications > 1/16 in. on weld surfaces
  • ASME Section III (nuclear): no cracks, no linear indications > 1/16 in., no rounded > 1/8 in.
  • API 1104 § 9.6: pipeline-specific acceptance — no crack-like indications, defined length limits per joint thickness

Personnel Qualification

SNT-TC-1A guide Level II PT (or ISO 9712 Level 2 PT; NAS 410 Level 2 PT for aerospace) is required for personnel interpreting Article 6 examinations. PT is often the first cert in a multi-method inspector's path because of the lower training-hour requirement (8 hrs for Level I, 8 additional for Level II per SNT-TC-1A 2024). Pair with annual eye test (J1 + Ishihara). ASNT Level III consulting provides written-practice and recertification audit support.

Frequently Asked Questions

Q1: Why use PT instead of MT on a stainless-steel weld?

A: Austenitic stainless is non-magnetic — MT (Article 7) cannot magnetise it, so no flux leakage, no indication. PT is the only ASME-accepted surface method on non-ferro materials.

Q2: Can I use water-washable penetrant outdoors in the field?

A: Possible but rare. Water source + over-wash risk make it impractical. Field PT is dominated by Type II Method C (solvent-removable visible dye) — the SPOTCHECK aerosol kit is the global standard.

Q3: How does dwell time change at low temperatures?

A: Below 16 °C the penetrant viscosity rises and capillary action slows — Article 6 requires doubling the documented dwell. Below 5 °C, use a low-temperature qualified penetrant per Mandatory Appendix III (or condition the surface with localised heating).

Q4: How do I distinguish a real indication from a false / non-relevant one?

A: Re-clean and re-test the area. Real crack indications reappear (the crack still holds penetrant after cleaning). Non-relevant indications from surface roughness, dirt, or porous oxide layers do not reappear after thorough cleaning.

Q5: What's the difference between Article 6 PT and ASTM E165?

A: ASTM E165 is the materials/process standard (defines the chemistry, sensitivity levels, and qualification of penetrant FAMILIES). Article 6 is the EXAMINATION standard (defines how the inspector applies it on a real part). For most pressure-equipment work, the inspector follows Article 6, using consumables qualified per E165. The two are complementary, not redundant.

Q6: How is Article 6 PT used in API 579 FFS assessments?

A: Surface-breaking cracks identified by Article 6 PT are characterised (length, sometimes etched depth) and fed into API 579 Level 1 / 2 / 3 crack-like flaw assessment. Atlantis NDT Level III consultants regularly use Article 6 PT confirmations to support FFS dispositions on refining and offshore equipment.

Q7: What records must I keep for Article 6 PT?

A: Technique sheet (penetrant batch + lot, developer batch + lot, dwell, lighting), inspector cert, surface temperature, calibration certificates for white-light + UV-A meters, sketch of inspected area with indication locations, accept/reject record per the referencing code. Atlantis NDT Reporting Software auto-bundles all of these per shot.

Q8: Are aerosol PT kits acceptable for Class-1 pressure equipment?

A: Yes, as long as the penetrant family is qualified per ASTM E165 sensitivity Level 1+ and the application meets Article 6. Many fabricators standardise on Magnaflux SPOTCHECK or Met-L-Chek VP-30 because both are Level 2 qualified and aerosol-applied. Always check shelf life + batch traceability on the aerosol cans.

title: ASME Section V Article 7 — Magnetic Particle Testing (MT) Requirements Explained
author: Anoop Rayavarapu
metaDescription: ASME Section V Article 7 magnetic particle testing requirements decoded — yoke vs prods vs central conductor, AC vs DC magnetisation, wet vs dry particles, fluorescent vs visible, acceptance. ASNT Level III guide.
snippet: ASME Section V Article 7 governs magnetic-particle testing of ferromagnetic materials. This 2026 guide explains magnetisation technique, particle media, lighting, demagnetisation, and how Article 7 maps to ASME VIII, B31.3, AWS D1.1, and API 510/570/653 acceptance.
content:
ASME Section V Article 7 — Practical MT Guide

ASME Section V Article 7 is the ASME nondestructive examination standard for magnetic-particle testing (MT, MPI). It is the workhorse surface + near-surface inspection method for ferromagnetic materials — carbon steel, low-alloy steel, ferritic stainless, ductile iron, nickel-iron alloys. Article 7 is referenced by ASME Section VIII Div 1 § UW-51, B31.1 § 136.4, B31.3 § 344.3, AWS D1.1 Clause 8.14, API 1104 § 9.5, and API 510 / 570 / 653 alterations sections.

Scope and Applicability — T-710

Article 7 covers MT on ferromagnetic materials only (austenitic stainless and aluminum require liquid penetrant testing per Article 6). MT detects surface and slightly subsurface discontinuities — cracks, laps, seams, cold shuts, lack of fusion on the open root, hot cracking in welds. Penetration depth is typically 1–6 mm depending on current type, frequency, and material magnetic permeability.

Applicability examples: post-weld surface inspection of carbon-steel pressure-vessel welds (the dominant surface NDT method since carbon steel is ferro), heavy-fabrication structural welds per AWS D1.1, pipeline girth welds per API 1104, drilling-equipment inspection, API 510 Pressure Vessel Inspector alterations on carbon-steel vessels, and API 653 Tank Inspector tank-shell weld inspection.

Magnetisation Techniques — T-720 + T-740

Article 7 recognises 7 magnetisation techniques; the most common in pressure-equipment work:

  • Yoke (T-721.1): portable electromagnet; AC or DC; pole spacing 75–300 mm; lift test 4.5 kg (AC) / 18 kg (DC). The single most common field technique. Examples: Magnaflux Y-7 / Y-8, Magnatech 5C.
  • Prods (T-721.2): two contact electrodes; AC, HWDC, or DC; produces longitudinal magnetisation. Risk of arc burns — requires controlled contact, copper/brass tips, and post-test grinding of contact areas.
  • Central conductor (T-721.3): non-magnetic conductor through hollow part; circumferential magnetisation; preferred for bolts, hollow castings, and short pipe pieces.
  • Direct current induction / cable wrap: for long pipe lengths or large vessels; cable wrapped around the part energised with HWDC.
  • Multidirectional (T-721.5): simultaneous longitudinal + circumferential magnetisation; production-shop bench unit standard.

Current type matters: AC produces strongest surface field (skin effect concentrates current at surface), best for fine surface cracks. DC / HWDC penetrates 3–6 mm subsurface for incomplete-penetration root flaws and just-subsurface inclusions.

Field-Strength Verification — T-754 + T-764

The single most-rejected Article 7 audit point. Article 7 requires field-strength verification on every shift, on every part orientation, using one of:

  • ASTM E709 pie-gauge: 8-piece copper-clad slotted plate; place on the part being tested; magnetise; observe particle build-up across the eight slots. All eight must reveal indications for adequate field.
  • Ketos ring / Betz ring (T-764): reference ring with through-drilled holes at known depths; particles must reveal the required number of holes per the technique procedure (typically 3 holes for medium sensitivity, 5+ for high).
  • Hall-effect gaugemeter: reads tangential field strength in gauss / millitesla; requires 30 G / 3 mT minimum at the surface during indication build-up.

Particle Media — T-761

Article 7 recognises wet and dry particle systems:

  • Wet fluorescent (Magnaflux 14HF, 20B, 25B): highest sensitivity; bench-unit production standard; requires UV-A booth (1000 µW/cm² + dark booth ≤ 2 fc ambient). Suspended in oil or water-based carrier.
  • Wet visible (Magnaflux 7HF, Met-L-Chek WCP): easier field application; doesn't need UV; lower sensitivity than fluorescent.
  • Dry visible (Magnaflux Grey 8A, Black 1, Red 3): field workhorse for heavy-fabrication and structural-weld MT; particles applied via puffer-bottle or shaker; surface contrast critical (white-contrast paint or clean steel).

Lighting Requirements — T-776

Visible-particle MT: 100 fc (1000 lux) white light at the surface, photometer-verified. Fluorescent MT: ≤ 2 fc ambient + ≥ 1000 µW/cm² UV-A, radiometer-verified, with inspector dark-adapted 5 min before reading.

Demagnetisation — T-771

Post-MT demagnetisation is required when residual magnetism would interfere with subsequent operations (machining, welding, assembly). Methods: AC step-down (gradually reducing field), DC reverse with step-down, or thermal (above Curie point — 770 °C for carbon steel; rarely practical). Residual field measurement with field-indicator: typical maximum 3 gauss (0.3 mT) for assemblies that will be re-welded or machined.

Acceptance Criteria — From the Construction Code

Article 7 defines HOW to perform MT but not what's acceptable. Acceptance comes from:

  • ASME VIII Div 1 § UW-51: no cracks; linear indications ≤ 1/16 in. acceptable; rounded ≤ 1/8 in.
  • ASME B31.3 § 344.3 + Table 341.3.2A: stricter for Category M / Severe Cyclic
  • AWS D1.1 Clause 8.14: no cracks; specific length limits on linear indications per weld thickness
  • API 1104 § 9.5: pipeline-specific acceptance — defined per joint thickness

Personnel Qualification

Same path as Article 6 PT: SNT-TC-1A guide Level II MT, ISO 9712 Level 2 MT, or NAS 410 Level 2 MT for aerospace. Annual eye test (Jaeger J1 + Ishihara) mandatory. ASNT Level III consulting provides written-practice and procedure-approval support for combined MT + PT + UT + RT programs.

Frequently Asked Questions

Q1: Why does AC give a stronger surface indication than DC?

A: Skin effect — alternating current concentrates near the conductor surface (depth ∝ 1/√frequency). 60 Hz AC penetrates ≈ 0.3 mm in carbon steel, producing very high tangential field at the surface, ideal for fine fatigue cracks. DC distributes through the cross-section, penetrating ≈ 3–6 mm — better for just-subsurface flaws but lower tangential field at the surface itself.

Q2: When must I use a Ketos ring vs a pie-gauge?

A: Pie-gauge for technique verification on the actual part (every shift, every orientation). Ketos ring for procedure qualification — proves the technique can resolve known reference flaws at known depths. Most fab specs require both.

Q3: Are prods allowed on pressure equipment in service?

A: Yes, but with caution. Article 7 requires controlled contact pressure, copper/brass tips, and post-test grinding of contact marks to prevent micro-cracks from arc burn. Many refineries forbid prods on high-strength alloys (P91, 2.25Cr-1Mo) because arc burn can initiate stress-corrosion cracks. Yoke is the safer choice in service.

Q4: Can I MT a stainless-steel weld?

A: Only if it's ferritic stainless (e.g., 410, 430). Austenitic SS (304, 316) is non-magnetic — use liquid penetrant testing per Article 6 instead. Duplex (2205, 2507) is partly ferritic — MT may work but PT is the safer choice.

Q5: How does Article 7 MT integrate with API 579 FFS?

A: Surface cracks detected by MT are characterised and fed into API 579 FFS Level 1/2/3 crack-like flaw assessment. The flaw length from MT, the depth from follow-up ultrasonic testing Article 4, and the local material properties feed into the API 579 disposition — fitness-for-service or repair.

Q6: What's the difference between wet fluorescent and wet visible MT?

A: Fluorescent particles are coated with a fluorescent dye that emits visible light under UV — far higher contrast and sensitivity, especially for tight fatigue cracks. Visible particles rely on coloured particles + contrast paint — lower sensitivity but no UV booth needed. Aerospace + nuclear default fluorescent; pressure-equipment field work often defaults visible.

Q7: Are dry-particle aerosol cans accepted for Article 7?

A: Yes — most field MT uses Magnaflux 8A grey or 1B black aerosol applied via puffer bulb or shaker. Verify shelf life and batch traceability. The aerosol is essentially the same particle as bulk; only the carrier differs.

Q8: How long must I retain Article 7 MT records?

A: Life-of-equipment for pressure equipment; minimum 5 years per most referencing codes. Atlantis NDT Reporting Software stores SHA-256-hashed MT records with technique sheet, pie-gauge verification, particle batch + lot, lighting verification, and accept/reject record in a PDF/A-3 audit bundle.
