acoustic emission monitoring, ASME V Article 12, ASTM E976, ISO 16148, real-time crack-growth detection. ASNT NDT Level III + Atlantis NDT expert authored. Refining, petrochem, marine, aerospace, power, mining, LNG, offshore wind, hydrogen, CCS — global delivery.

Method Foundation

acoustic emission monitoring, ASME V Article 12, ASTM E976, ISO 16148, real-time crack-growth detection. Physics-grounded, code-aligned, ASNT NDT Level III led.

Equipment + Calibration

Instrument selection, reference standards, calibration cadence per the relevant ASTM/ISO/ASME standard.

Acceptance Criteria

Defect classification + sizing + acceptance limits per construction + in-service codes. Free Atlantis NDT consultation.

Atlantis NDT Stack

Atlantis NDT ERP + Atlantis Digital Twin platform + NDT reporting software integrated for this method. Audit-ready bundle. Free demo.

Construction-Code + In-Service-Code Crosswalk

This standard does not stand alone — it cross-references against construction codes (ASME Section I/III/VIII, B31.1/3/4/8 piping, EN 13445 pressure vessel, EN 13480 piping) and in-service codes (API 510/570/653, ASME PCC-3, ASME XI nuclear). Atlantis NDT procedure library maps every clause to the construction or in-service code your asset operates under. When the in-service code allows multiple inspection methods, Atlantis NDT Level III selects the technique that best resolves the damage mechanism dominant in your service (per Atlantis NDT Level III consulting).

Mandatory vs Non-Mandatory Appendices

Mandatory appendices establish minimum requirements that cannot be waived without a Code Case or Inquiry response from the standards body (ASME Boiler & Pressure Vessel Committee, API Committee on Refinery Equipment, ISO Technical Committee). Non-mandatory appendices provide recommended practice, alternate procedures, or worked examples — they may be adopted by reference in a written Procedure or Written Practice (per SNT-TC-1A 2024 + CP-189-2020 + ISO 9712:2021 + ASME B&PV V Article 1). Atlantis NDT procedure pack lists every mandatory clause your inspectors must satisfy with traceable records.

Inspector Qualification + Method Authorisation

The standard requires inspector qualification per ASNT SNT-TC-1A (employer-based) or ASNT CP-189 (employer standard) or ISO 9712 (third-party) or ACCP (third-party portable) — equivalence per individual employer Written Practice. NDT Level II performs the examination; NDT Level III approves the Procedure + signs off final disposition. Atlantis NDT Academy (browse pathway) curates the training pathway, ASNT Level III-led. Multi-method NDT Level III pathway available for senior practitioners.

Acceptance Criteria + Defect Disposition Decision Tree

Indication characterisation: linear vs rounded, surface vs subsurface, planar vs volumetric. Sizing: through-wall extent + length + amplitude vs reference. Disposition decision: accept-as-is → engineering critical assessment (ECA) per BS 7910 / API 579 Part 9 → repair per ASME PCC-2 / NB-23 → retire per FFS Level 3. Atlantis NDT Level III consulting (API 579 FFS) provides Level 1/2/3 assessment + remaining-life calculation + re-inspection interval recommendation.

Common Audit Findings + Atlantis NDT Procedure Pack

Repeat audit findings on this standard: (1) Procedure not approved by Level III with documented qualification (NCR root cause: SNT-TC-1A §6.3 non-compliance); (2) Calibration block traceability gap (ISO 17025 §6.5 + NIST traceability); (3) Inspector renewal lapsed beyond annual eye-exam interval (ISO 9712:2021 §10.5); (4) Procedure Qualification Record (PQR) revision history missing. Atlantis NDT ERP (audit-ready records) tracks every PQR + procedure revision + inspector cert + calibration cert with timestamp + Level III signature.

Frequently Asked Questions

Q1: What current edition should our team reference?

Recert calendar: SNT-TC-1A — employer Written Practice defines interval (typically 3-5 years for Level I/II, 5 years for Level III + 9-h recurring + practical). ISO 9712 — 5 years + retest at 10 years (recertification structured exam + experience documented). PCN UK — 5-year cycle. ACCP — 5-year cycle. Atlantis NDT ERP (audit-ready records) tracks every inspector's recert calendar with automated reminder cadence.

Method Physics + Equipment Selection

Defect-detection physics, signal generation, and instrument-selection criteria for this method. Probe + transducer + sensor selection driven by material thickness, expected defect orientation, surface finish, geometric access, and ambient conditions. Atlantis NDT Level III selects the equipment that resolves the dominant damage mechanism in your service — refining sour-service, marine corrosion, aerospace fatigue, power-gen HTHA, or hydrogen embrittlement.

Calibration Block + Reference Standards

Reference standards traced to NIST (US) / NPL (UK) / PTB (DE) / BAM (DE) / NMIJ (JP) / NPL India / NIST China. Calibration block geometry per ASME V relevant Article, ASTM E127/E1158/E2491, ISO 7963/2400 (UT), ISO 19232 (RT), ISO 9934 (MT), or method-specific reference. Calibration cadence: pre-job, every 4 hours, after major adjustment, end of shift. Atlantis NDT ERP automates calibration cert renewal + traceability audit-trail.

Defect Sizing + Through-Wall Resolution

Sizing techniques: amplitude-based (DGS, AVG, DAC), echo-dynamics, time-of-flight, satellite-pulse, focal-law-corrected for PAUT. Through-wall sizing resolution typically λ/2 to λ for the chosen frequency + material velocity combo. Surface-breaking vs embedded discrimination via tandem probe / TOFD parallel-beam / EDM-notch reference. Atlantis NDT digital-twin platform (visualise here) overlays sizing data on 3D asset model for change-tracking across inspection cycles.

Method Limitations + Complementary Methods

This method has inherent limitations — coverage gaps, defect-orientation blindness, near-surface dead-zones, or material-attenuation thresholds. Complementary methods recommended where method limitation creates risk: combine UT + MT for ferritic weld inspection, PAUT + TOFD for full weld-volume coverage, ECA + EC array for stainless weld inspection, IRT + UT for composite bond inspection. Atlantis NDT procedure pack specifies method-pair selection per ASME PCC-3 + API 510/570/653 + EEMUA 159 damage-mechanism guidance.

Damage Mechanisms (API 571 Cross-Reference)

API RP 571 enumerates damage mechanisms in refining + petrochem service. RBI per API 581 — Risk-Driver Decomposition

RBI per API RP 581 decomposes consequence + likelihood for solar PV equipment: (1) Generic Failure Frequency (gff) by component class; (2) Damage Factor (DF) per active mechanism; (3) Inspection Effectiveness Factor (A-E) based on prior inspection thoroughness; (4) Consequence — Financial + Safety + Environmental. title: Best NDT Inspection Software 2026: Buyer's Guide
snippet: A practical 2026 buyer's guide to evaluating NDT inspection software, from reporting to certification and calibration.
content:
The best NDT inspection software in 2026 combines mobile-first data capture, ASNT SNT-TC-1A and ISO 9712-compliant report templates, offline functionality for remote field crews, integrated calibration and certification tracking, and either native ERP capability or clean integration with enterprise systems like Odoo, SAP, or IBM Maximo. The right platform depends on inspection volume, the NDT methods performed, and whether reporting needs to feed into broader asset management and reliability programs.

Why Generic Field Service Software Falls Short for NDT

Most inspection companies start with spreadsheets, Word templates, or a generic field service app repurposed for NDT. That works until a technician performs 40 UT thickness readings on a storage tank floor and has to manually transcribe grid coordinates into a report that a client's reliability engineer will scrutinize against API 653 minimum thickness calculations. Generic tools were not built around method-specific data structures, calibration traceability, or the certification hierarchy (Level I, II, III) that governs who is legally allowed to sign off a report under SNT-TC-1A or ISO 9712. Software built specifically for NDT closes that gap.

The Core Feature Set Every NDT Software Needs

Before comparing vendors, define the non-negotiables. At minimum, evaluate:

  • Method-specific templates for UT, RT, MT, PT, VT, ET, TOFD, and Phased Array, with fields matching the relevant code (ASME Section V, API 510/570/653, AWS D1.1)
  • Offline mobile data capture for technicians working in refineries, pipelines, and offshore platforms with no signal
  • Digital signatures and Level II/III sign-off workflows that mirror real certification authority
  • Calibration tracking tied to instrument serial numbers and ISO 17025-traceable standards
  • Certification expiry tracking for every technician against ASNT SNT-TC-1A or ISO 9712 requirements
  • Photo and defect-mapping tools that overlay indications onto asset drawings or 3D models
  • Exportable, auditable PDF reports that satisfy client and regulatory review

A platform that only handles report generation and ignores calibration and certification tracking is solving half the problem. Inspection companies that get audited by API or a major oil and gas client need all three data sets connected, not living in three separate tools.

Standalone Reporting Apps vs. Full NDT ERP Platforms

There are two categories of software on the market. Standalone reporting apps digitize the report-writing process: a technician fills a form on a tablet, the software formats it, and a PDF comes out the other end. This is a real improvement over Word templates but it stops at the report. A full NDT ERP solution extends that same data into project management, technician scheduling, equipment calibration, invoicing, and document control, so the inspection report is one output of a connected operational system rather than an isolated artifact. For a two-person crew doing occasional inspections, a standalone reporting tool may be enough. For a company running multiple crews, multiple methods, and recurring client contracts, the operational overhead of managing scheduling, certifications, and calibration in separate systems quickly outweighs the simplicity of a single-purpose app.

Mobile Data Capture and Offline Field Requirements

Inspection work happens in tank farms, subsea risers, and pipeline right-of-ways where connectivity is unreliable at best. Software that requires a live connection to save data is a liability, not a feature. Look for genuine offline-first architecture: data captured on-site syncs automatically once connectivity returns, with no risk of losing a shift's worth of UT readings because a tablet lost signal inside a vessel. This matters as much for RT film/digital data and MT/PT indication photos as it does for numeric thickness grids.

Calibration Tracking and ISO 17025 Traceability

Every UT thickness gauge, phased array unit, and radiation source used on a job has a calibration history that a client or third-party auditor can request at any time. Software that treats calibration as a standalone spreadsheet forces someone to manually cross-reference which instrument was calibrated when, against which certified reference block, traceable to which ISO 17025-accredited lab. A proper calibration management module ties every reading in a report back to the exact instrument and its current calibration status automatically, flagging a technician before they use an instrument that is out of calibration. This single control point prevents one of the most common findings in client and third-party quality audits.

Certification Management: ASNT and ISO 9712 in One System

NDT is a certified-personnel discipline. A Level II technician signing a report they are not currently certified for under SNT-TC-1A, or a company operating under ISO 9712 without current renewal records, creates real liability. Software with a dedicated certification tracking module should flag expiring certifications 60-90 days out, restrict report sign-off to technicians whose current certification matches the method and level required, and maintain the audit trail a client's vendor qualification team will ask for during onboarding or renewal.

Integration With Enterprise Asset Management Systems

Larger clients, particularly in refining, pipeline, and power generation, run their asset integrity programs on SAP, IBM Maximo, or AVEVA PI (formerly OSIsoft PI), with some moving toward Cognite Data Fusion for industrial data contextualization. Inspection data that stays trapped in a standalone reporting tool never reaches the reliability engineer's dashboard where it actually drives decisions. Evaluate whether a vendor offers API-level integration or exports that map cleanly into these systems, because that connectivity is often the difference between inspection data being used for compliance filing only, versus actively informing RBI (risk-based inspection) and fitness-for-service decisions under API 579.

Where Digital Twins Extend the Software Stack

The next step beyond ERP-connected reporting is visualizing inspection data spatially. A digital twin platform takes UT thickness grids, RT indications, and corrosion trends and maps them directly onto a 3D model of the asset, so a reliability engineer can see wall-loss patterns across an entire tank shell or pipeline segment instead of reading them off a spreadsheet. For companies managing aging infrastructure under API 510/570/653 inspection intervals, this spatial context materially changes how fast anomalies get caught. Run the numbers on your own asset base with the digital twin ROI calculator before deciding whether this layer is worth adding now or later.

A Buyer's Scorecard for Shortlisting Vendors

Score each vendor on a 1-5 scale across: method coverage, offline capability, calibration and certification tracking depth, integration options, mobile usability in field conditions, and total cost of ownership including implementation. Ask every vendor for a live demo using your own report templates, not their canned example. Ask specifically how the platform prevents an out-of-certification technician from signing a report, and how it handles instrument calibration expiry. Vendors that cannot answer those two questions concretely are not built for regulated NDT work. Companies evaluating a full operational platform rather than a point solution should look closely at ERP built specifically for NDT inspection companies, which folds reporting, calibration, certification, scheduling, and invoicing into one system rather than three or four disconnected tools.

If you are actively comparing platforms, book a demo and bring your own inspection templates and calibration records to the call. The difference between vendors becomes obvious fast once real data is on the table.

Frequently Asked Questions

Q1: What is the difference between NDT reporting software and NDT ERP?

A: Reporting software digitizes report creation only. NDT ERP extends that same data into scheduling, calibration tracking, certification management, invoicing, and document control, connecting the full operational workflow rather than isolating the report as a standalone output.

Q2: Does NDT software need to support every inspection method?

A: Only if your company performs every method. Prioritize vendors covering your core methods (UT, RT, MT, PT, VT, ET, TOFD, Phased Array) with accurate, code-aligned templates rather than broad but shallow coverage across methods you rarely use.

Q3: Can NDT inspection software integrate with SAP or IBM Maximo?

A: Leading platforms offer API-level integration or structured exports that map into SAP, Maximo, and AVEVA PI, letting inspection data feed directly into a client's asset integrity and reliability programs rather than staying siloed in a separate reporting tool.

Q4: Is offline functionality really necessary for NDT software?

A: Yes. Most inspection sites, tank farms, pipelines, and offshore platforms have unreliable or no connectivity. Software without genuine offline-first data capture risks losing field data and forces technicians back to paper as a fallback.

Q5: How does software help with ASNT and ISO 9712 compliance?

A: Certification tracking modules flag expiring credentials before they lapse, restrict report sign-off to technicians currently certified for the required method and level, and maintain the audit trail clients and accreditation bodies request during vendor qualification.

title: What Is NDT ERP? Inspection Management Software Explained
snippet: NDT ERP explained: how inspection companies unify reporting, certification, and calibration in one connected system.
content:
NDT ERP is enterprise resource planning software built specifically for non-destructive testing companies, unifying inspection reporting, technician certification tracking, equipment calibration management, project scheduling, document control, and invoicing into one connected system. Unlike generic ERP, it is structured around NDT-specific data: inspection methods, applicable codes, and the certified-personnel sign-off requirements that govern who can issue a report.

NDT ERP Defined

Enterprise resource planning software traditionally manages the operational backbone of a company: finance, inventory, projects, HR. NDT ERP takes that same backbone and rebuilds it around the specific realities of an inspection business. A work order is not just a task, it is tied to a method (UT, RT, MT, PT, VT, ET, TOFD, Phased Array), a code requirement (API 510, API 570, API 653, ASME Section V), a certified technician, and a calibrated instrument. A project is not complete until a report is generated, reviewed by a Level II or III, and archived with full traceability. Generic ERP has no concept of any of this out of the box.

How NDT ERP Differs From Generic ERP

A standard manufacturing or services ERP, whether SAP Business One, generic Odoo, or a mid-market platform, handles projects, inventory, and invoicing well but has no native fields for calibration due dates, ASNT SNT-TC-1A certification levels, or ISO 9712 renewal cycles. Companies that try to force generic ERP into NDT operations end up bolting on spreadsheets for calibration and certification anyway, which defeats the purpose of having a unified system. Purpose-built NDT ERP starts with those data structures already modeled, so the certification and calibration logic is enforced by the system itself rather than by someone remembering to check a spreadsheet.

Core Modules Inside an NDT ERP Platform

A complete NDT ERP platform typically includes:

  • Inspection reporting with method-specific templates and digital sign-off
  • Certification tracking for every technician, method, and level
  • Calibration management for gauges, sources, and reference standards
  • Work order and project management across multiple crews and job sites
  • Document control for procedures, work instructions, and quality manuals
  • Inventory and asset tracking for equipment, consumables, and radiation sources
  • Invoicing and job costing tied directly to completed inspection scope

The value is in the connections between modules, not any single one. A technician cannot be scheduled onto a job requiring API 653 UT thickness testing unless the system confirms their certification is current and the assigned gauge is within calibration. That cross-check, done manually, is where compliance gaps happen.

Certification Tracking as the Compliance Backbone

Every NDT company operates under a written practice governed by SNT-TC-1A or under third-party certification through ISO 9712. Both require documented evidence of technician qualification, experience hours, vision testing, and periodic recertification. An ERP with certification tracking built in maintains this record centrally, flags upcoming expirations before they become a client audit finding, and prevents scheduling a technician onto work outside their certified scope. For companies pursuing or maintaining ISO 9001, this same record becomes part of the quality management system evidence auditors request every cycle.

Calibration Management and Instrument Traceability

Thickness gauges, phased array units, MT yokes, and radiation sources all require calibration against traceable reference standards, typically documented per ISO 17025 lab certificates. In an NDT ERP, every calibration record is linked to the instrument's serial number and every inspection report that used it, so an auditor can trace a single UT reading back to the specific gauge, its calibration date, and the reference block used. This closes a compliance gap that trips up companies relying on spreadsheet-based calibration logs disconnected from the actual reporting system.

Project and Work Order Management for Multi-Crew Operations

Inspection companies running multiple crews across refineries, pipelines, and fabrication shops need scheduling that accounts for certification, calibration, and geographic assignment simultaneously. NDT ERP work order management assigns jobs based on which technicians are both certified for the required method and available, with equipment allocation checked against calibration status in the same step. This eliminates the common failure mode of a crew arriving on site only to discover their assigned gauge calibration expired the week before.

Document Control for ISO 9001 and Client Audits

Inspection companies operating under ISO 9001 need version-controlled procedures, work instructions, and calibration certificates accessible during client and third-party audits. A document control module inside the ERP keeps these under revision control, tied to approval workflows, so the version a technician references in the field is always current and the audit trail of prior revisions is preserved.

Why Odoo Is a Strong Foundation for NDT ERP

Odoo's modular, open architecture makes it a practical base for building NDT-specific ERP rather than starting from scratch or forcing a rigid platform like SAP or generic Maximo deployments to fit inspection workflows. Because Odoo modules for projects, inventory, invoicing, and document management are already mature, the NDT-specific layer, certification tracking, calibration management, method-specific reporting, can be built on top without reinventing core business logic. This is covered in more depth in a dedicated guide to Odoo for NDT inspection companies, but the short version is that Odoo's cost-to-customize ratio compares favorably against locking into a proprietary vertical platform.

Connecting NDT ERP to Digital Twins for Asset Intelligence

Once inspection data lives inside a structured ERP rather than scattered PDFs, it becomes usable for more than compliance filing. Feeding UT thickness trends, RT indications, and corrosion history into a digital twin platform lets reliability teams visualize degradation across an asset in 3D and support risk-based inspection and API 579 fitness-for-service decisions with spatial context a spreadsheet cannot provide. Companies serving pipeline, tank, and pressure vessel clients particularly benefit from this layer, since inspection history mapped to physical geometry is exactly what RBI programs need.

To see how an NDT ERP maps to your current operation, book a demo with your own report templates and technician roster.

Frequently Asked Questions

Q1: What makes ERP specific to NDT rather than generic ERP?

A: NDT ERP is built around inspection-specific data structures: certified technician levels under SNT-TC-1A or ISO 9712, instrument calibration traceable to ISO 17025, and method-specific report templates aligned to codes like API 510, 570, and 653. Generic ERP has none of these modeled natively.

Q2: Can NDT ERP replace separate calibration and certification spreadsheets?

A: Yes, and it should. Keeping calibration and certification data inside the ERP, linked directly to work orders and reports, closes the compliance gap that happens when this data lives in disconnected spreadsheets nobody consistently updates.

Q3: Is Odoo a good platform for NDT ERP?

A: Odoo's modular, open architecture makes it well suited as a foundation, since mature project, inventory, and invoicing modules already exist and an NDT-specific layer for certification tracking, calibration, and method-based reporting can be added without rebuilding core ERP functionality from scratch.

Q4: Does NDT ERP support multiple inspection methods in one system?

A: Yes, a properly built NDT ERP supports method-specific templates and workflows for UT, RT, MT, PT, VT, ET, TOFD, and Phased Array within a single platform, rather than requiring separate tools per method.

Q5: How does NDT ERP support ISO 9001 compliance?

A: Through document control and audit trail features that keep procedures, calibration certificates, and certification records under revision control, giving auditors the evidence trail ISO 9001 requires without manual document assembly before each audit cycle.

Why Odoo Fits NDT Companies Better Than Legacy ERP

Most ERP platforms built for manufacturing or retail assume a bill-of-materials and inventory-driven business model that does not match how inspection companies actually operate. NDT companies sell certified labor and equipment time against a set of codes and standards, not manufactured units. Odoo's modular architecture, where you enable only the apps you need and extend them with custom modules, fits this reality far better than forcing an inspection workflow into a platform like SAP that was designed around discrete manufacturing. Odoo's Native Modules That Map to NDT Operations

Odoo ships with mature, well-tested modules that cover most of an inspection company's back office without custom development:

The value of Odoo for NDT companies comes from what gets added on top of the native modules. This includes method-specific inspection report templates (UT, RT, MT, PT, VT, ET, TOFD, Phased Array) mapped to relevant codes such as API 510, API 570, API 653, and ASME Section V, digital sign-off workflows enforcing SNT-TC-1A or ISO 9712 certification levels, and calibration tracking linked to ISO 17025-traceable standards. A properly configured Odoo-based NDT ERP builds these as first-class modules rather than workarounds, so the certification and calibration logic is enforced automatically instead of relying on manual checks.

A certification tracking module built on Odoo's employee and HR framework extends technician records with method, level (I, II, III), issuing body, exam date, and expiration. Scheduling logic then cross-references this data before a technician can be assigned to a work order requiring that certification, and automated alerts flag renewals 60-90 days ahead of expiry. This turns a compliance requirement that many companies still track in a spreadsheet into an enforced system rule.

Calibration Management in Odoo

Built on Odoo's maintenance and equipment modules, a calibration management module tracks every instrument's calibration due date, the reference standard used, and the accredited lab that performed it. Reports generated through the system automatically pull the current calibration status of the instrument used, creating a permanent link between a specific reading and the equipment's calibration record at the time it was taken, exactly what an API or client audit will ask to see.

Field Reporting and Mobile Data Capture

Odoo's mobile-responsive interface and offline-capable apps extend naturally to field data capture, letting technicians complete method-specific report templates on a tablet at a tank farm or pipeline right-of-way with no connectivity, syncing automatically once back in range. Photos, defect maps, and thickness grids captured in the field flow directly into the report and the underlying project record, with no re-entry step.

Multi-Company and Multi-Crew Considerations

Odoo's native multi-company structure suits inspection groups operating across multiple regions or under separate legal entities, for example a US operation and an India-based operation under one parent company, while still consolidating reporting and financials at the group level. Crew scheduling logic can be configured to respect region-specific certification requirements, since ISO 9712 and SNT-TC-1A recognition varies by client and jurisdiction.

Migrating From Spreadsheets or Legacy Software to Odoo

Companies moving off spreadsheets or an aging standalone reporting tool typically migrate in phases: certification and calibration records first, since these carry the highest compliance risk if mismanaged, followed by active project and work order data, then historical report archives for audit continuity. A phased migration keeps the business running through the transition rather than requiring a hard cutover that risks losing operational continuity during a busy inspection season.

Odoo vs. SAP vs. Maximo for Inspection Companies

SAP and IBM Maximo are built for large enterprise asset owners managing thousands of assets across a facility, not for the inspection service providers who supply data into those systems. For a regional or mid-size NDT company, implementing SAP or Maximo internally is typically overkill on cost and complexity. Odoo, customized for NDT, delivers the connected operational capability a growing inspection company needs, while still exporting or integrating cleanly with a client's SAP or Maximo environment when required. title: How to Choose ERP for an NDT / Inspection Business (2026)

content:
Choosing ERP for an NDT or inspection business means evaluating platforms against inspection-specific requirements, method-specific reporting, certification tracking under SNT-TC-1A or ISO 9712, calibration management traceable to ISO 17025, multi-crew scheduling, and integration with client systems, rather than judging on generic ERP feature checklists built for manufacturing or retail.

Start With Your Compliance Requirements, Not Feature Lists

Most ERP buying guides start with a feature comparison spreadsheet. For an NDT company, that is the wrong starting point. Start instead with the compliance obligations your business already carries: which codes you inspect against (API 510, 570, 653, ASME Section V, AWS D1.1), whether your technicians operate under a written practice per SNT-TC-1A or hold ISO 9712 certification, and what your ISO 9001 quality system requires for document control and audit trail. Every ERP feature decision should trace back to one of these obligations, because a platform that looks impressive on a feature list but cannot enforce certification-based sign-off will create compliance risk, not reduce it. This is the core distinction behind ERP built specifically for an NDT inspection company versus a generic platform adapted after the fact.

Map Your Current Workflow Before Evaluating Vendors

Before a single vendor demo, document how a job actually moves through your company today: from client request, to crew and equipment assignment, to field data capture, to report review and sign-off, to invoicing. Note every point where the process currently breaks, a spreadsheet that is out of date, a calibration record someone has to chase down manually, a Level III reviewer who becomes a bottleneck. This map becomes the actual evaluation criteria; ask every vendor to walk through this specific workflow in their platform rather than their generic demo script.

Must-Have vs. Nice-to-Have: A Practical Framework

Separate requirements into three tiers. Must-have: method-specific report templates matching your services, certification tracking that restricts sign-off by level and expiry, calibration tracking linked to instrument records, and offline mobile capture for field crews. Should-have: multi-crew scheduling with automatic certification and calibration cross-checks, document control for ISO 9001 evidence, and job costing tied to completed scope. Nice-to-have: advanced analytics dashboards, digital twin visualization, and deep API integration with client asset management systems. This tiering keeps the evaluation from getting derailed by impressive but non-essential features while the core compliance functions get shortchanged.

Certification and Calibration: The Two Modules That Cannot Be an Afterthought

Of every module inside NDT ERP, certification tracking and calibration management carry the highest compliance risk if implemented poorly. Test both directly during any vendor demo: ask the vendor to show what happens when a technician's certification expires mid-project, and what happens when an instrument's calibration lapses while it is scheduled on an active job. A platform that simply displays a status field without actively preventing an invalid assignment is not solving the problem, it is just digitizing the same gap that exists in a spreadsheet.

Evaluating Implementation Cost and Timeline Realistically

Vertical ERP platforms sold specifically to inspection companies often carry high licensing costs and long implementation timelines because they are built as rigid, one-size-fits-all products. Open, modular platforms like Odoo, customized specifically for NDT operations, typically offer a faster and more cost-predictable path because the core ERP functionality (accounting, inventory, project management) is already mature, and implementation effort concentrates on the NDT-specific layer rather than rebuilding the whole system from scratch. Ask any vendor for a realistic phased timeline, not just a go-live date, phased around certification and calibration migration first, then active projects, then historical archives.

Integration Requirements: What Your Clients Already Use

If a significant share of your revenue comes from major oil and gas, power, or petrochemical clients, check what asset management systems they run internally, commonly SAP, IBM Maximo, or AVEVA PI, and whether they expect inspection data delivered in a format that integrates with those systems. An ERP that only exports static PDFs may satisfy compliance filing but will not meet a client's expectation of structured data feeding into their reliability and RBI programs. This becomes increasingly important as more asset owners adopt platforms like Cognite Data Fusion for contextualized industrial data.

Odoo-Based vs. Proprietary Vertical ERP

Proprietary vertical ERP platforms built specifically for inspection companies can offer deep out-of-the-box NDT functionality but often lock you into their roadmap and pricing structure with limited customization freedom. An Odoo-based NDT ERP approach trades a small amount of out-of-the-box depth for significant long-term flexibility, since Odoo's open architecture means the NDT-specific modules can evolve alongside your business rather than waiting on a vendor's release cycle. For companies planning to scale crew count, add methods, or expand into new regions, this flexibility compounds in value over a multi-year horizon.

Red Flags During Vendor Demos

Watch for vendors who cannot demo certification and calibration enforcement live, who only show reporting without the surrounding operational modules, who cannot explain how offline field data syncs, or who deflect specific questions about API 510/570/653 template accuracy. Also be cautious of vendors quoting implementation timelines under a few weeks for a full ERP rollout across multiple crews, that timeline usually means the NDT-specific configuration is superficial.

Building the Business Case Internally

Frame the internal business case around risk reduction and time recovered, not just software cost. Quantify hours currently spent manually cross-referencing calibration spreadsheets against work orders, the cost of a single missed certification renewal that causes a client to reject a report, and the administrative time spent reformatting reports for different clients. These numbers build a far stronger case to leadership than a feature comparison table. When you are ready to compare a live platform against your own workflow map, book a demo and bring your actual report templates and technician roster to the call.

Frequently Asked Questions

Q1: What is the most important factor when choosing ERP for an NDT company?

A: Enforcement of certification and calibration compliance, not just tracking it. The platform should actively prevent scheduling an uncertified technician or an out-of-calibration instrument onto a job, rather than simply displaying a status that someone has to check manually.

Q2: Should I choose a proprietary vertical ERP or a customizable platform like Odoo?

A: It depends on growth plans. Proprietary vertical ERP can offer more out-of-the-box depth initially, but an Odoo-based platform offers greater long-term flexibility to add methods, scale crews, and expand regions without being locked into a single vendor's roadmap and pricing.

Q3: How long does NDT ERP implementation typically take?

A: A realistic phased implementation, migrating certification and calibration records first, then active projects, then historical archives, typically spans several weeks to a few months depending on company size and data volume. Timelines under a few weeks for a full rollout usually indicate shallow configuration.

Q4: Does ERP integration with SAP or Maximo matter for smaller inspection companies?

A: It matters most for companies whose clients run those systems internally and expect structured inspection data feeding their reliability programs. Smaller companies serving clients without that requirement can deprioritize deep integration in favor of core certification and calibration functionality.

Q5: What is the biggest mistake companies make when selecting NDT ERP?

A: Evaluating vendors on generic feature lists instead of mapping the company's actual compliance obligations and current workflow first, which leads to selecting a platform that looks capable in a demo but fails to enforce certification and calibration rules in real operation.

title: Certification Tracking Software for NDT: ASNT and ISO 9712
snippet: How certification tracking software enforces ASNT SNT-TC-1A and ISO 9712 compliance automatically.
content:
Certification tracking software for NDT centrally manages technician qualifications under ASNT SNT-TC-1A written practices or ISO 9712 third-party certification, recording method, level, exam and renewal dates, and automatically restricting report sign-off and job assignment to technicians whose certification is current and matches the required scope.

Why Certification Tracking Cannot Stay in a Spreadsheet

Every NDT company eventually hits the same failure mode: a spreadsheet tracking technician certifications gets updated inconsistently, someone forgets to flag an upcoming renewal, and a Level II technician ends up signing a report under a certification that lapsed three weeks earlier. In isolation this looks like an administrative slip. In an audit, or worse, in litigation following a failed asset, it becomes a documented compliance failure that undermines the validity of every report that technician issued during the gap. Certification tracking software exists specifically to remove the human memory dependency from this process.

SNT-TC-1A Written Practice vs. ISO 9712: What Software Needs to Support

SNT-TC-1A is an employer-based qualification system: the employing company writes its own practice defining training, experience, and examination requirements for each level, and internally certifies technicians against that practice. ISO 9712 is a third-party certification scheme, technicians are certified by an independent, accredited certification body rather than their employer. Companies operating internationally or serving clients who require ISO 9712 often need to track both systems simultaneously, sometimes for the same technician holding both credentials for different clients or jurisdictions. Certification tracking software needs to model both systems accurately, including the different renewal cycles and recertification requirements each imposes, rather than forcing everything into a single generic certification field.

What Certification Tracking Software Actually Does

At a functional level, a proper certification tracking module maintains a record per technician covering method (UT, RT, MT, PT, VT, ET, TOFD, Phased Array), level (I, II, III), certifying body or internal written practice reference, initial certification date, expiration date, and supporting documentation such as exam results and vision test dates. It surfaces this data at the point where it matters most, when a technician is being assigned to a job or when a report is being signed, rather than as a passive record someone has to remember to check separately.

Enforcing Sign-Off Rules Automatically

The difference between certification tracking as a passive database and certification tracking as an active compliance control is enforcement. Software that simply displays a technician's certification status still relies on a human catching the problem. Software that blocks a Level I technician from independently signing a final report, or prevents assignment of a technician whose certification for a specific method has expired, removes that dependency entirely. This single enforcement rule addresses one of the most common findings during client vendor qualification audits and third-party quality reviews.

Renewal Alerts and Expiry Management

Certification renewal typically requires lead time, scheduling a recertification exam, completing required continuing experience hours, or renewing vision testing, none of which can happen instantly the week a certification lapses. Software should generate renewal alerts at 90, 60, and 30 days ahead of expiry, escalating to management if no action has been logged, so recertification is planned proactively rather than reactively discovered when a technician is already scheduled onto a job requiring that credential.

Vision Testing and Experience Hour Tracking

Both SNT-TC-1A and ISO 9712 require periodic vision acuity and color perception testing as a condition of maintaining certification, along with, for many levels, documented experience hours in the applicable method. Certification tracking software should capture these as structured fields tied to each technician's record, not as separate paperwork disconnected from the certification itself, since an auditor reviewing a technician's qualification file expects to see vision testing and experience documentation alongside the certification record, not filed separately.

Client Vendor Qualification and Audit Readiness

Major oil and gas, petrochemical, and power generation clients run vendor qualification programs that require inspection companies to produce current certification records for every technician assigned to their sites, often on short notice. Companies with certification data centralized in software can generate this documentation in minutes. Companies relying on manual file organization frequently scramble to assemble it, sometimes discovering gaps only during the audit itself. Fast, accurate certification documentation is increasingly a competitive differentiator in vendor qualification, not just a compliance checkbox.

Connecting Certification to Scheduling and Work Orders

Certification tracking delivers its full value when connected directly to project and work order management, so a technician cannot be assigned to a job requiring API 510, 570, or 653 inspection scope unless their certification for the relevant method and level is current at the moment of scheduling, not just at the time the roster was last reviewed. This closes the gap between a certification record technically existing in the system and that record actually being checked before it matters.

Certification Tracking as Part of Full NDT ERP

Certification tracking delivers the most value as one connected module inside a broader NDT ERP platform, alongside calibration management, project scheduling, and reporting, rather than as an isolated point solution. When certification, calibration, and scheduling data all live in the same system, the cross-checks that prevent compliance gaps happen automatically as part of normal operations instead of requiring a separate manual review step. Companies evaluating this as part of a broader platform decision should review the full picture of ERP built for NDT inspection companies, which folds certification tracking into the same system as reporting, calibration, and invoicing.

To see certification tracking enforcement in action against your own technician roster, book a demo and bring your current certification records to the call.

Frequently Asked Questions

Q1: What is the difference between SNT-TC-1A and ISO 9712 certification?

A: SNT-TC-1A is an employer-based system where the company writes its own practice and certifies technicians internally. ISO 9712 is third-party certification issued by an independent, accredited certifying body. Companies serving international clients often need to track both simultaneously.

Q2: Can certification tracking software prevent an expired certification from being used?

A: Yes, when properly implemented, the software actively blocks scheduling or report sign-off for a technician whose certification has expired or does not match the required method and level, rather than just displaying a status that relies on someone checking it manually.

Q3: How far in advance should certification renewal alerts trigger?

A: Best practice is staged alerts at 90, 60, and 30 days before expiry, giving enough lead time to schedule recertification exams and complete required experience hours or vision testing before the credential actually lapses.

Q4: Does certification tracking software help with client vendor qualification audits?

A: Yes, centralized certification records let companies generate current, accurate documentation for client vendor qualification programs in minutes rather than manually assembling files, which reduces both audit stress and the risk of discovering compliance gaps during the review itself.

Q5: Should certification tracking be a standalone tool or part of ERP?

A: It delivers the most value connected to scheduling, calibration, and reporting inside a full NDT ERP platform, since the automatic cross-checks that prevent compliance gaps require certification data to interact directly with work order assignment, not sit isolated in a separate system.

title: What Is an Asset Integrity Digital Twin? 2026 Guide
snippet: A plain-English guide to asset integrity digital twins: what they are, how they use NDT data, and how to roll one out in 2026.
content:
An asset integrity digital twin is a live, geometrically accurate 3D model of a physical asset — a pressure vessel, pipeline, tank, or FPSO hull — that is continuously synchronized with inspection, corrosion, and process data so engineers can visualize condition, run risk-based inspection (RBI) logic, and perform fitness-for-service (FFS) assessments without walking the plant. Unlike a generic 3D model, it is a data-connected decision tool, not a static rendering.

For asset integrity teams, the phrase has become a catch-all for very different products — some are little more than a rotating CAD viewer, others are genuine engineering platforms wired into inspection history, historians, and EAM systems. This guide breaks down what actually qualifies as an asset integrity digital twin, how it differs from adjacent categories, and what to look for before you commit budget to one in 2026.

What Is an Asset Integrity Digital Twin?

At its core, an asset integrity digital twin combines three layers: a spatially accurate 3D representation of the asset, a persistent record of inspection findings mapped to specific locations on that model (thickness readings, corrosion under insulation findings, weld indications), and an analytics layer that applies API 510, API 570, API 653, and API 579 fitness-for-service logic to tell you where the asset stands against its corrosion allowance and remaining life. The result is a single place where an inspector, a reliability engineer, and a plant manager can look at the same asset and get a consistent answer about its condition.

This is different from a BIM model handed over at commissioning, which typically freezes in time the day the plant starts up and never receives another inspection data point. A true digital twin is a living record — every UT thickness survey, every RT weld inspection, every MT or PT surface indication gets appended to the model over the asset's operating life.

How It Differs From a Generic 3D Digital Twin

Not every "digital twin" vendor is targeting asset integrity. Many industrial digital twin platforms focus on process simulation, energy optimization, or production forecasting — useful, but not built around corrosion, metallurgy, or inspection codes. An asset integrity digital twin is purpose-built around the inspection and mechanical integrity workflow: it needs to understand nominal wall thickness, corrosion rate calculation, minimum required thickness per ASME Section VIII or B31.3, and RBI risk ranking per API 580/581. If a platform can't ingest a UT grid survey and calculate remaining life against a corrosion allowance, it is a visualization tool, not an integrity twin. Atlantis's digital twin platform was purpose-built for this exact gap — 3D visualization with native NDT and RBI logic rather than a bolt-on integration.

Core Components: 3D Model, NDT Data, RBI, and API 579 FFS

A functioning asset integrity digital twin typically has five layers:

  • Geometry — laser scan, photogrammetry, or as-built CAD, accurate enough to place inspection findings at the correct location (CML) on the asset.
  • Inspection data — UT, RT, MT, PT, VT, ET, TOFD, and phased array results tied to specific CMLs, TMLs, or grid points, with full history retained for trending.
  • RBI risk model — probability of failure (corrosion rate, damage mechanism) times consequence of failure (safety, environmental, financial) per API 580, driving inspection interval recommendations.
  • Fitness-for-service engine — API 579-1/ASME FFS-1 Level 1/2 assessments run directly against the twin's geometry and thickness data for local metal loss, pitting, and general corrosion.
  • Reporting and audit trail — every calculation, inspector, and revision logged for ISO 9001, API, and insurance audit purposes.

For vessel-specific applications, see how this plays out on a pressure vessel digital twin — the CML mapping and FFS workflow there is a good reference implementation.

How Asset Integrity Digital Twins Use NDT Inspection Data

The data layer is what separates a real integrity twin from a marketing render. Ultrasonic thickness (UT) grid and spot readings feed corrosion rate trending. Radiographic testing (RT) and phased array UT (PAUT) weld inspection results are geo-tagged to specific weld seams. TOFD data supports crack growth monitoring on high-consequence welds. Magnetic particle (MT) and dye penetrant (PT) surface indications flag localized damage mechanisms like stress corrosion cracking. When all of this rolls into a single 3D model, an inspector doesn't need to cross-reference five spreadsheets to understand whether a vessel is trending toward its retirement thickness — they see it color-mapped on the twin.

Integration With EAM, Historians, and APM Platforms

A digital twin doesn't replace your EAM/CMMS (SAP PM, IBM Maximo) or your process historian (OSIsoft/AVEVA PI) — it sits alongside them and pulls context from both. Work order history from the EAM tells you what repairs have already happened on a CML. Historian data tells you the operating temperature and pressure envelope the asset has actually seen, which matters for creep and fatigue calculations. Advanced platforms like GE Vernova APM or Cognite Data Fusion attempt to bridge some of this, and it's worth understanding the tradeoffs — see our breakdowns of Atlantis DT vs GE Predix/Vernova APM and Atlantis DT vs Cognite Data Fusion for a side-by-side on integration depth and total cost of ownership.

Real-World Use Cases

Refineries use digital twins to consolidate decades of RBI history across hundreds of pressure vessels and thousands of piping circuits ahead of turnarounds — our refinery digital twin page walks through that workflow in depth. Offshore operators use them to track hull and topside corrosion on FPSOs where physical access is expensive and weather-dependent. Pipeline integrity teams use them to visualize ILI (in-line inspection) results against as-built alignment sheets. In every case, the pattern is the same: reduce the time between "we have inspection data" and "we know what it means for asset risk."

Implementation Roadmap: From Pilot to Enterprise Rollout

Most successful rollouts follow a similar sequence. Start with a single high-consequence asset class — pressure vessels or a critical pipeline segment — and migrate two to three years of historical inspection data so the twin has trending value on day one. Validate the RBI and FFS calculations against your existing engineering assessments before trusting the platform for interval decisions. Then expand asset-class by asset-class, integrating EAM and historian feeds as you go. Budget owners should quantify the case before committing — the digital twin ROI calculator is a useful starting point for estimating inspection labor savings and deferred-failure avoidance.

Common Pitfalls and How to Avoid Them

The most common failure mode is treating the twin as a one-time visualization project rather than a living system — if inspection data isn't continuously fed back in, the model decays into the same static handover model it was meant to replace. The second is underestimating data migration effort; legacy inspection records in PDFs and spreadsheets need structuring before they're useful in a twin. The third is picking a platform without native FFS/RBI logic and trying to bolt on Excel-based calculations later, which reintroduces the exact fragmentation the twin was supposed to eliminate.

If you're evaluating platforms, talk to our team about a scoped pilot on your highest-risk asset class before committing to an enterprise rollout.

Frequently Asked Questions

Q1: What is the difference between a digital twin and a 3D model?

A: A 3D model is a static visual representation of an asset at a point in time. A digital twin is continuously updated with real inspection, process, and maintenance data, allowing it to reflect the asset's current condition and support engineering decisions like RBI interval setting and FFS assessments.

Q2: Does an asset integrity digital twin replace RBI software?

A: No — it typically incorporates RBI methodology (API 580/581) directly into the 3D environment, so risk ranking and inspection planning happen in the same place as the visual and inspection data, rather than in a separate standalone RBI tool.

Q3: What inspection data can feed a digital twin?

A: UT thickness grids, RT and PAUT weld inspection results, TOFD crack monitoring, MT/PT surface indications, VT reports, and corrosion under insulation (CUI) surveys can all be geo-tagged to CMLs or TMLs on the model for trending and FFS calculations.

Q4: How long does a digital twin implementation take?

A: A scoped pilot on a single asset class with historical data migration typically takes a few weeks to a few months. Enterprise-wide rollout across multiple asset classes and integration with EAM/historian systems is usually phased over 6-18 months.

Q5: Do I need a laser scan to build a digital twin?

A: Not necessarily. Existing as-built CAD or P&IDs can serve as the starting geometry for many use cases; laser scanning or photogrammetry improves spatial accuracy for CML placement but is not always required to get value from inspection data trending.

title: GE Predix Alternatives 2026: Asset Integrity Migration
snippet: GE split into three companies in 2024. Here's what happened to Predix/APM and how to evaluate migration options in 2026.
content:
GE Predix alternatives are asset integrity and industrial IoT platforms that operators evaluate as replacements for GE's legacy Predix stack, whose asset performance management (APM) capability now sits inside GE Vernova following GE's April 2024 three-way corporate split. Operators migrate for reasons ranging from platform consolidation and licensing changes to the need for tighter native integration between 3D visualization and inspection data than the legacy Predix architecture offered.

If your team is running an evaluation in 2026, it helps to understand exactly where the product landed after the breakup, why other operators are moving, and what to check for in a replacement before you sign anything.

What Is GE Predix and Why Are Companies Migrating Away From It?

Predix was GE Digital's industrial IoT platform, launched in the mid-2010s as GE's bet on an "operating system for industry." Over time, GE narrowed its focus from a broad PaaS play to a more targeted Asset Performance Management (APM) product line, and much of the original Predix branding was retired well before 2026. Operators cite a few consistent migration drivers: platform direction has shifted multiple times as GE reorganized its software business, integration between APM, digital twin visualization, and inspection workflows historically required significant custom engineering, and total cost of ownership for large legacy contracts has become harder to justify against newer, purpose-built asset integrity platforms.

The 2024 GE Breakup: Where Predix and APM Live Now

In April 2024, General Electric completed its planned separation into three independent, publicly traded companies: GE Aerospace (retaining the GE name and jet engine business), GE HealthCare (spun off in January 2023), and GE Vernova (energy — power generation, wind, electrification, and grid software). GE Digital's industrial software portfolio, including Asset Performance Management (APM) and the remaining Predix-derived capabilities, was carried into GE Vernova as part of its Electrification Software segment. This matters practically: your GE APM contract, support relationship, and roadmap now run through GE Vernova, not the aerospace-focused GE entity, and the product's investment priorities are shaped by GE Vernova's energy-transition strategy rather than a horizontal industrial IoT vision.

Why Operators Are Evaluating Alternatives in 2026

Three factors are driving renewed evaluation activity in 2026. First, contract renewal cycles from the original Predix-era deals (many signed 2016-2019) are hitting their second or third renewal, prompting procurement to re-benchmark the market rather than auto-renew. Second, GE Vernova's software roadmap is understandably weighted toward power generation and grid customers, which can leave downstream oil & gas, refining, and marine asset integrity use cases feeling like a secondary priority. Third, the broader digital twin market has matured — platforms purpose-built around NDT inspection data, RBI, and API 579 fitness-for-service now exist that didn't in Predix's original design era, and they integrate visualization and integrity calculations natively rather than through custom middleware.

Key Evaluation Criteria for a Replacement

When benchmarking alternatives, evaluate against a consistent scorecard rather than a feature checklist supplied by any single vendor:

  • Native NDT and RBI integration — can the platform ingest UT/RT/MT/PT/TOFD/phased array data natively and map it to CMLs, or does it require a third-party integration layer?
  • Fitness-for-service capability — does it run API 579-1/ASME FFS-1 assessments directly, or export data for offline engineering calculations?
  • EAM/historian integration — proven connectors to SAP PM, IBM Maximo, and OSIsoft/AVEVA PI without heavy custom development.
  • Data migration path — can historical inspection and corrosion data be imported without manual re-entry?
  • Deployment flexibility — cloud, on-premise, or hybrid options for operators with data residency or OT network security constraints.
  • Total cost of ownership — licensing, implementation, and ongoing support cost relative to the scope of asset classes covered.

Top Alternatives Compared

The current landscape includes a mix of legacy enterprise APM vendors and newer, purpose-built digital twin platforms. Siemens Mindsphere (now part of Siemens Xcelerator) offers strong OT integration for Siemens-heavy plants but carries similar platform-lock-in tradeoffs to Predix. Cognite Data Fusion has built a strong reputation for industrial data contextualization but is priced and positioned toward large enterprise data engineering teams rather than inspection-first workflows. Purpose-built asset integrity digital twin platforms like Atlantis's digital twin platform take a different approach — 3D visualization with native NDT, RBI, and API 579 FFS built in from day one rather than layered on top of a general IoT platform. We've published detailed head-to-head comparisons: Atlantis DT vs GE Predix/Vernova APM and Atlantis DT vs Siemens Mindsphere.

Migration Roadmap: Moving Off Predix Without Losing Historical Data

The single biggest risk in any Predix migration is losing years of accumulated inspection and corrosion-rate history. A sound migration plan starts with a full export of asset hierarchy, CML/TML data, thickness readings, and RBI risk scores from the legacy system, followed by a validation pass comparing corrosion rate trends and remaining-life calculations in the new platform against the old ones for a sample of critical assets before cutover. Run both systems in parallel for at least one inspection cycle on high-consequence equipment to confirm the new platform's FFS outputs match engineering expectations. Only after that validation should you decommission the legacy system.

Data Migration Checklist

  • Full asset hierarchy and equipment tag export with CML/TML coordinates
  • Complete UT, RT, MT, PT, TOFD, and phased array inspection history, not just latest readings
  • RBI risk scores and damage mechanism assignments per API 580/581
  • Historian tag mapping for operating temperature/pressure context (OSIsoft/AVEVA PI)
  • EAM work order history linked to affected CMLs (SAP PM / IBM Maximo)
  • Parallel-run validation on at least 10-15% of critical assets before full cutover

Estimating the financial case for migration is worth doing formally rather than on gut feel — the digital twin ROI calculator models inspection efficiency and deferred-failure savings against implementation cost. And if your integrity data also needs a home in a broader ERP context, our asset management ERP module covers the maintenance and work-order side of the equation.

Ready to scope a migration plan against your specific asset portfolio? Get in touch for a technical evaluation session.

Frequently Asked Questions

Q1: Is GE Predix still available in 2026?

A: The original standalone Predix platform was retired in earlier years as GE narrowed focus to Asset Performance Management (APM). Following GE's April 2024 corporate split, APM and related industrial software now operate under GE Vernova's Electrification Software segment.

Q2: Which GE entity owns asset integrity software after the 2024 split?

A: GE Vernova, the energy-focused company created in the split, owns GE's industrial software portfolio including Asset Performance Management. GE Aerospace and GE HealthCare are separate, unrelated entities focused on aviation and medical technology respectively.

Q3: How long does migrating off Predix/GE Vernova APM typically take?

A: A well-scoped migration with historical data validation typically runs 3-6 months for a single asset class, with full parallel-run verification on critical equipment, and longer for enterprise-wide portfolios spanning multiple sites and asset types.

Q4: Will I lose historical inspection data when migrating?

A: Not if the migration plan includes a full export and validated import of CML/TML history, thickness readings, and RBI scores. Data loss typically only occurs when teams attempt a rushed cutover without a parallel validation period.

Q5: What should I prioritize when evaluating a Predix replacement?

A: Prioritize native NDT and RBI data integration, built-in API 579 fitness-for-service calculations, proven EAM/historian connectors, and a clear data migration path — these determine whether the new platform actually reduces engineering workload or just relocates the same manual effort.

title: Digital Twin vs APM vs EAM vs Historian Explained
snippet: Digital twin, APM, EAM, and historian sound similar but do different jobs. Here's how they fit together in an asset integrity stack.
content:
A digital twin visualizes an asset's 3D condition using live inspection data; an APM (Asset Performance Management) system analyzes reliability and failure risk across an asset portfolio; an EAM/CMMS (like SAP PM or IBM Maximo) manages maintenance work orders and asset records; and a historian (like OSIsoft/AVEVA PI) stores time-series process data such as temperature, pressure, and flow. They overlap in purpose but serve distinct roles, and most mature asset integrity programs run all four connected together.

Confusion between these categories is common because vendors increasingly bundle capabilities across boundaries — an APM product may include some visualization, a digital twin platform may include some work order features. This guide separates the categories cleanly so you can evaluate what you actually need.

Quick Definitions

SystemPrimary JobExample Products
HistorianStore time-series process dataOSIsoft/AVEVA PI
EAM/CMMSManage maintenance work and asset recordsSAP PM, IBM Maximo
APMAnalyze reliability and failure riskGE Vernova APM, Cognite Data Fusion
Digital TwinVisualize asset condition in 3D with inspection dataAtlantis Digital Twins

What Is a Historian?

A process historian is a time-series database purpose-built to capture and compress millions of sensor readings per day — temperature, pressure, flow, vibration — at high frequency and retain them for years. OSIsoft PI (now AVEVA PI) is the dominant player in oil & gas, refining, and power generation. A historian answers "what was the operating condition of this asset at 3am on a given date," which matters for integrity engineers correlating a corrosion event or crack growth with an upset condition. What it does not do is track physical inspection findings, weld locations, or maintenance history — it has no concept of a CML or a work order.

What Is EAM/CMMS?

Enterprise Asset Management (EAM) and Computerized Maintenance Management System (CMMS) platforms — SAP PM and IBM Maximo are the two dominant enterprise players — manage the operational side of asset care: work orders, preventive maintenance schedules, spare parts inventory, technician assignments, and cost tracking. An EAM answers "what maintenance has been done on this asset and what's scheduled next." It's transactional and workflow-driven rather than analytical. Our work order management module and asset management module cover this layer for NDT-heavy operations specifically.

What Is APM?

Asset Performance Management sits a level above EAM, focused on reliability analytics: failure mode analysis (RCM/FMEA), risk-based inspection (RBI) scoring per API 580/581, and predictive maintenance modeling that flags which assets are trending toward failure before it happens. GE Vernova APM (the successor product line to the original GE Predix industrial platform) and Cognite Data Fusion are two prominent players in this space, each with different strengths — Cognite leans toward data contextualization and engineering at scale, GE Vernova APM leans toward its legacy power-generation and process-industry customer base. An APM answers "which of my 400 pressure vessels is the highest risk this quarter." See our comparisons: Atlantis DT vs GE Predix/Vernova APM and Atlantis DT vs Cognite Data Fusion.

What Is a Digital Twin?

An asset integrity digital twin is the visualization and engineering layer that ties everything above together in a spatial context. It takes NDT inspection data — UT thickness grids, RT and phased array weld results, TOFD crack monitoring — and maps it onto a 3D model of the actual asset, then runs API 579 fitness-for-service calculations directly against that geometry. A digital twin answers "show me exactly where on this vessel the wall thickness is approaching minimum required thickness, and what that means for remaining life." It's the only one of the four categories built around spatial, code-driven engineering assessment rather than tabular or time-series analysis. Explore how this plays out for a specific asset class on our refinery digital twin and pressure vessel digital twin pages.

How They Work Together in an Asset Integrity Stack

In a mature program, the four systems form a data pipeline. The historian captures raw process conditions continuously. NDT inspection results and work order history flow into the EAM as they're completed. An APM layer aggregates historian trends, inspection frequency, and failure history to calculate risk scores and recommend inspection intervals. The digital twin consumes inspection results, RBI scores, and relevant historian context to give engineers a spatial, code-compliant view of exactly where an asset stands — and it's usually the tool an inspector or reliability engineer opens first because it answers the specific "where and how bad" question the other systems can't visualize directly.

Comparison Table: Capabilities Side by Side

CapabilityHistorianEAMAPMDigital Twin
Time-series process dataYesNoPartial (consumes)Partial (consumes)
Work order managementNoYesNoNo
RBI risk scoringNoNoYesOften included
3D spatial visualizationNoNoRarelyYes
API 579 FFS calculationsNoNoRarelyYes (purpose-built platforms)
NDT data ingestion (UT/RT/PAUT/TOFD)NoPartialPartialYes

Which One Should You Start With?

Most operators already have a historian and an EAM in place — those are foundational and rarely the gap. The decision usually comes down to whether to invest in a standalone APM analytics layer, a digital twin visualization layer, or a platform that combines both. If your inspection program generates large volumes of UT/RT/PAUT data that currently lives in spreadsheets or siloed RBI tools, a digital twin with native FFS capability closes that gap faster than adding a separate APM product on top of your existing stack. Use the digital twin ROI calculator to model where the biggest efficiency gain sits for your asset portfolio, and explore the full digital twin platform to see how the layers connect in practice.

Not sure which combination fits your current stack? Talk to our integrity engineering team for a stack assessment.

Frequently Asked Questions

Q1: Can a digital twin replace my EAM system?

A: No. A digital twin visualizes asset condition and runs integrity calculations; an EAM manages work orders, scheduling, and maintenance cost tracking. They serve complementary functions and typically integrate rather than replace one another.

Q2: Is APM the same thing as a digital twin?

A: No. APM focuses on portfolio-level reliability analytics and risk scoring (which assets are highest risk), while a digital twin provides spatial, asset-specific visualization of inspection data and fitness-for-service condition. Some platforms blend both capabilities to varying degrees.

Q3: Do I need a historian before I can use a digital twin?

A: Not strictly. A digital twin can operate primarily on inspection data (UT, RT, MT, PT, TOFD) without a historian feed, though integrating historian data adds valuable operating-context for corrosion rate and fatigue calculations.

Q4: What's the difference between SAP PM and IBM Maximo versus a digital twin platform?

A: SAP PM and IBM Maximo are enterprise asset management systems focused on maintenance workflows and asset records. A digital twin platform is focused on spatial visualization of inspection data and code-based fitness-for-service engineering — they typically integrate via API rather than compete directly.

Q5: Which system should a refinery invest in first if starting from scratch?

A: Most refineries already have a historian and EAM in place from commissioning. The typical next investment is either an RBI/APM analytics layer or a digital twin with native RBI and FFS capability — the latter often delivers faster time-to-value because it combines visualization and engineering calculation in one system.
