title: PAUT Equipment Selection — What Actually Matters When You Buy
author: Atlantis NDT
metaDescription: A buyer-side guide to phased array ultrasonic equipment for inspection companies: channels, probes and wedges, encoders, software and data handling, and the specification traps that cost money later.
snippet: Channel count sells instruments. Probe inventory, encoder discipline and what happens to the data are what decide whether the purchase earns.
content:
Buy for the scopes you actually win

Phased array purchases go wrong at the start, when the specification is written around the most demanding job the company might ever bid rather than the work it does weekly. The instrument is the smallest part of the decision; the probe and wedge inventory, the encoder discipline and the data workflow decide whether the capability earns.

The instrument

Channels and aperture. More channels buy larger apertures and better focusing at depth. Weld inspection on common wall thicknesses is well served by mainstream configurations; thick-section, coarse-grained or high-attenuation material is where higher channel counts stop being marketing. Specify against your actual material and thickness range, and be honest about how often the extreme case appears.

TFM and total focusing capability. Genuinely superior imaging on the right applications, and slower and more data-hungry on all of them. Useful as a characterisation tool over an area of interest, rarely as a primary scanning mode. If a vendor demonstrates only TFM, ask to see the conventional PAUT workflow you will actually run daily.

Battery, ruggedness and screen legibility outdoors. Unglamorous, and the specifications technicians complain about within a month.

Probes and wedges — where the budget really goes

An instrument with two probes covers a narrow slice of work. Frequency, element count and pitch determine what you can resolve; wedge angles and curvature determine what you can couple to. Curved-surface wedges for the pipe diameters in your scope are not an accessory, they are the difference between winning and declining that work. Budget for the inventory to grow, and treat probes as consumables with a life, not capital that lasts forever.

Encoders and repeatability

Unencoded phased array is a detection tool. Encoded phased array is an evidence tool — position-tied data you can compare against the same weld next year, which is what in-service monitoring requires and what codes expect for recordable examinations. If any part of your work is repeat inspection or corrosion monitoring, encoding is not optional.

The part buyers underestimate: the data

An encoded shift produces file sets that dwarf conventional UT records. Ask where those files live, how they are named, who can open them without a licensed seat, and whether the analysis is reproducible by a second analyst months later. Companies that solve acquisition and improvise storage end up unable to answer a client question about an indication from two years ago. ISO 18563 on PAUT equipment characterisation covers this in more depth, and inspection software is where the provenance problem is actually solved.

Before you sign

Run your own specimens, not the vendor's. Have the technician who will use it daily do the demo, not the manager buying it. Confirm the calibration and service path in your region — an instrument out for weeks is a scope you cannot staff. And confirm export: your scan data should leave in a form another platform can read.

Related: phased array inspection services · PAUT defined · where TOFD outperforms it.

title: Pipeline Audit Preparation — What Operators and Regulators Actually Check
author: Atlantis NDT
metaDescription: How to prepare for a pipeline integrity audit: the records that get pulled first, the operator-qualification trap, and the findings that recur across contractors.
snippet: Audits rarely find bad inspection. They find records that cannot be produced — and on a pipeline contract, that is the same thing as a finding.
content:
What an audit is really testing

A pipeline integrity audit — whether from the operator, a regulator, or a client's own assurance team — is not primarily testing whether the inspection was competent. It is testing whether you can demonstrate that it was, from records, without the person who did the work in the room. That distinction decides how you prepare.

The records pulled first

Personnel qualification. Every technician on the contract: method certifications with levels and expiries, vision records, and — the one contractors most often miss — operator qualification for the covered tasks they performed. OQ is a separate regime from NDT certification, task-based, and an inspector certified to the hilt in UT can still be unqualified for the covered task they were assigned. Auditors know this and check it early.

Procedures and their approval. The procedure that governed the work, at the revision in force on the day, approved by a named Level III. A current revision does not prove the work followed it.

Equipment calibration. Instruments in calibration at the time of examination, with certificates traceable, and the daily verification checks the procedure requires — not just the annual certificate.

The examination records themselves. Readings with location identity, technician and instrument attribution, and the evaluation against acceptance criteria. Unattributed data is data an auditor discounts.

The findings that recur

A certification that expired mid-contract with work performed after the date. Field data transcribed from paper with no original retained. Location identity that changed between campaigns, so no trend can be built. Procedure revisions with no evidence anyone was retrained on the change. Subcontracted crews whose records were never brought inside the contractor's own system.

Every one of these is administrative, and every one of them lands on the prime contractor regardless of who performed the work.

Preparing properly

Audit yourself against the contract's own requirements, not against a generic checklist — the requirements that bite are the operator's specific ones. Do it on a sample of completed jobs, tracing each backwards from report to records, because that is the direction an auditor works. Fix the record-keeping process, not just the sample; a corrected file with an uncorrected process fails the next audit.

The structural fix is having one system where certifications, calibration and examination records live together — which is what makes audit preparation retrieval rather than reconstruction. How that is set up · the audit evidence-pack checklist · qualification and calibration register.

Related: MFL pipeline inspection · risk-based inspection programme design · audit-readiness review.

title: The US NDT Inspection Services Market — How It Is Actually Structured
author: Atlantis NDT
metaDescription: How the US non-destructive testing services market is segmented, who buys what, where the consolidated majors compete against regional specialists, and what that means for a growing inspection company.
snippet: A clear-eyed map of who buys NDT in the United States, how work is bought, and where a smaller provider can actually win against a national contractor.
content:
Who buys, and how

US NDT demand concentrates in a small number of buying patterns, and they behave differently enough that a provider should choose deliberately rather than chase all of them.

Refining and petrochemical buy on turnaround cycles and long-term site contracts, dominated by API-driven programmes. Work is large, scheduled far ahead, and increasingly awarded to contractors who can staff a surge without importing unfamiliar crews. Pipeline operators buy against integrity-management obligations, with operator-qualification requirements layered over NDT certification. Fabrication buys per project, decides fast, and rewards report turnaround above almost everything. Power generation buys around outage seasons in concentrated windows. Aerospace and defence buy under NAS 410 and Nadcap and change suppliers slowly, which cuts both ways.

The structural split

The market runs on two tiers that rarely compete head-on. Consolidated national providers win multi-site master agreements where a single supplier across many locations is the point. Regional specialists win on responsiveness, technique depth, and knowing a specific plant — and typically hold those relationships for years, because switching an inspection contractor who knows your equipment carries real cost for the owner.

The genuine competitive question for a growing company is therefore not "how do we beat the majors" but "which tier are we in, and are we investing accordingly". Trying to price like a national contractor while operating regionally is the failure mode.

Where a smaller provider actually wins

Advanced technique depth. Encoded PAUT, TOFD, corrosion mapping and tube inspection are capabilities many regional providers lack, and asset owners pay for them because the alternative is more repairs. Documentation speed. Owners describe report turnaround as a recurring frustration with large contractors; a provider who turns them around in hours wins repeat work without competing on rate. Audit-grade records. As owners tighten contractor assurance, the provider who produces the evidence pack on request differentiates on something the buyer feels immediately.

All three are operational capabilities, not sales positions — which is why the back office matters more to competitiveness than most inspection companies assume. The systems side of this.

What is changing

The workforce is the constraint, not demand: an aging technician population and a thin pipeline mean the companies that can develop their own Level IIs will out-grow those bidding for scarce experienced hires. Digital deliverables are moving from differentiator to expectation, with owners increasingly asking for structured data rather than PDFs. And owner assurance teams are auditing contractor personnel records directly, which turns administration into a qualifying criterion.

Related: what the workforce actually earns · developing technicians in-house · Level III authority without a full-time hire.

title: Building an In-House NDT Team vs Contracting It Out — The US Decision
author: Atlantis NDT
metaDescription: How US asset owners and fabricators should decide between developing in-house NDT capability and contracting it: the volume threshold, the hidden obligations of certifying your own people, and the hybrid most companies land on.
snippet: The question is rarely "which is cheaper". It is which obligations you are willing to own — and most companies discover those only after they have committed.
content:
The question behind the question

Companies usually frame this as a cost comparison and then discover the comparison was never the point. Contracting buys a service. Building in-house buys a programme — a Written Practice, a Level III authority, examination records, calibration management, and the audit exposure that comes with certifying your own people. The right question is not which costs less this year; it is which set of obligations fits how your business actually runs.

Where in-house genuinely wins

Continuous, predictable volume. If inspection work is happening most weeks at the same facility, an employed technician beats a mobilised one on cost and on familiarity — knowing the plant's equipment history is worth more than most owners credit.

Response time as a production issue. Where waiting a day for a contractor stops a line or extends an outage, having the capability on site pays for itself in avoided downtime rather than in inspection savings.

Retaining knowledge. Contractor crews rotate. Your own technicians accumulate a mental model of your equipment that never appears in a report and is genuinely valuable at the third repeat inspection.

Where contracting genuinely wins

Method breadth you cannot justify employing. Encoded PAUT, TOFD, tube inspection and specialist techniques require equipment and current competence that intermittent use erodes. A technician who runs a technique twice a year is not competent in it, whatever the certificate says.

Surge capacity. Turnarounds need many technicians for a few weeks. No sensible headcount plan covers the peak.

Independence. Some clients, insurers and jurisdictions want the examination performed by a party that does not report to the operations manager whose schedule it might delay. This is not cynicism; it is why third-party inspection exists.

The obligation most companies underestimate

Certifying your own NDT personnel under SNT-TC-1A means you are the certifying body. You write and maintain the Written Practice, you need a Level III with real technical authority behind it, you administer and retain examinations, and you produce all of it when a client audits. Companies that budget for salaries and equipment and not for that programme end up with certified technicians and an indefensible programme — the worst of both. What running that programme actually involves.

The hybrid most companies land on — and why it works

In-house Level II capability for the routine, high-frequency methods your equipment demands weekly; contracted specialists for advanced techniques and turnaround surges; and the Level III authority engaged rather than employed, because the role is continuous but the workload is not. That last piece is the one most often got wrong: companies either appoint a Level III who is too busy performing examinations to exercise the authority, or they have no Level III at all and discover it during an audit. How outsourced Level III authority works.

A test you can apply this week

Count the inspection days you bought last year, by method. Any method with continuous demand is a candidate for in-house. Any method below that line stays contracted — and the technician you were about to hire for it would have spent most of the year not doing it.

Related: developing technicians in-house · how the US contractor market is structured · the workforce constraint behind both options.

title: How to Vet an NDT Contractor in the US — What Actually Predicts Quality
author: Atlantis NDT
metaDescription: A buyer-side vetting guide for US asset owners selecting an NDT inspection contractor: the records to demand, the questions that separate capability from marketing, and the warning signs that appear before the problems do.
snippet: Certificates prove someone passed an exam. These are the checks that predict whether the work will hold up when it is questioned.
content:
Start with the records, not the capability statement

Every contractor's brochure lists the same methods. What differs — and what predicts whether findings will survive scrutiny — is the state of their records. Ask for four things before the technical conversation:

The Written Practice. Their actual document, not a reference to SNT-TC-1A. Read whether the hour and examination requirements have been engaged with or left at the published defaults, and check the named Level III is someone who can describe the programme.

Personnel files for the crew they would assign. Not a summary — certifications with levels and expiry dates, vision records with dates, and documented experience hours. Ask specifically for the people who would work your site, because the crew that shows up is often not the crew in the proposal.

Calibration evidence. Instrument certificates in date, and the daily verification checks their procedures require. Annual certificates alone tell you nothing about the day your job runs.

A redacted sample report from work like yours. Look for whether findings are traceable to locations, technicians and instruments, and whether the evaluation cites the acceptance criteria it applied.

Four questions that separate capability from marketing

"Who is your Level III and what did they approve most recently?" Hesitation here is the single most informative moment in the meeting.

"How do you deliver data — PDF, or structured records our system can consume?" The answer predicts whether you can ever build a trend across campaigns, or whether each inspection is an isolated document.

"What happens when your technician finds something outside the scope we contracted?" You want a contractor whose answer involves telling you immediately, not one whose answer involves a change order.

"Show me a job where the finding was disputed." Every experienced contractor has one. How they describe it — records produced, technique defended, or blame relocated — tells you what happens when it is your asset.

Warning signs that appear early

A proposal that names no personnel. Equipment lists without probe and wedge detail for your geometry. Willingness to commit to a schedule before seeing the scope. Reports quoted in days when the crew size implies otherwise. And the quiet one: a contractor who never says no to a scope. Specialist work that a firm cannot actually staff gets subcontracted to someone you did not vet, under your contract, with your name on the finding.

What to write into the contract

Personnel qualification evidence on request throughout the contract, not just at award. Notification when assigned personnel change. Structured data delivery alongside the report. And the right to audit their records — rarely exercised, but its presence changes how records are kept.

Related: what auditors check on a contractor · the evidence-pack checklist · how the US contractor market splits · independent review of a contractor's programme.

title: Who Actually Has Authority Over Pressure Equipment in the US
author: Atlantis NDT
metaDescription: How US pressure equipment inspection authority is really divided between the National Board, state and city jurisdictions, API certification and owner-user programmes — and why an API certificate alone does not always satisfy the law.
snippet: API 510 makes you a certified inspector. It does not, by itself, make you the authority in every US state — and the difference has caught competent inspectors out.
content:
Three systems that overlap and are frequently confused

The jurisdiction. Most US states — and a few cities — have boiler and pressure vessel laws administered by a chief inspector, and those laws decide what must be inspected, how often, and by whom. This is statute, not industry practice, and it varies by state.

The National Board. Registers pressure equipment, commissions inspectors who work for jurisdictions and authorised inspection agencies, and publishes NBIC for in-service inspection, repair and alteration. A National Board commission is what lets an inspector act on the jurisdiction's behalf.

API certification. An industry certification demonstrating competence against API 510, 570 or 653. Widely required by owners and contracts, and in some jurisdictions recognised for owner-user programmes — but it is not a commission from a jurisdiction.

Where inspectors get caught out

The common error is assuming an API certificate confers authority everywhere. In practice the jurisdiction decides who may perform the statutory inspection of a registered vessel, and depending on the state that may require a commissioned inspector rather than an API-certified one — or may accept an owner-user programme with API-certified inspectors, provided the programme itself is accepted. Two facilities in different states can run legitimately different arrangements for identical vessels.

The second error is treating an owner-user programme as automatic. Where states permit an owner to inspect its own equipment, that permission is typically conditional on a documented programme, qualified personnel and jurisdictional acceptance. It is a status you are granted, not a default you assume.

What this means practically

For asset owners: confirm the requirement per state where you operate, not once at head office. A multi-state programme that assumes uniformity will be non-compliant somewhere. Where you run an owner-user programme, keep its acceptance documentation as carefully as the inspection records.

For inspection contractors: know which of your scopes are statutory and which are owner-driven. They carry different qualification requirements and different consequences when a finding is contested.

For inspectors: API certification is the foundation, and a National Board commission is a distinct and additional credential that opens work API certification alone does not. Whether pursuing it is worth your time depends entirely on whether you intend to perform statutory inspection.

The unglamorous conclusion

There is no single national answer, and any source telling you otherwise is simplifying something with legal consequences. The authoritative sources are the National Board's synopsis of state rules and the jurisdiction itself — check both, per state, and record what you were told.

Related: NBIC decoded · API 510 certification · API 510 vs API 570 · programme review and jurisdictional readiness.

title: The NDT Liability Chain — Who Is Actually Exposed When an Inspection Is Wrong
author: Atlantis NDT
metaDescription: When an examination misses something that later fails, responsibility distributes across technician, Level III, contractor and owner in ways most parties have not thought through. What the records decide, and how exposure is actually managed.
snippet: The question is never only "who was negligent". It is "what can each party produce" — and that is decided long before anything fails.
content:
Why this is worth thinking about before it happens

Most inspection work is never questioned. When it is — a failure, an injury, an insurance dispute — the investigation follows a predictable path, and the parties who fare well are those whose records were in order on an ordinary day months earlier. Nobody assembles a defence after the event; they either have one or they do not.

How responsibility distributes

The technician is answerable for performing the examination per the procedure and reporting what was found. The defence is the record: certification current at the time, instrument in calibration, procedure followed, findings documented with attribution. A technician with those things is in a strong position even if the flaw was genuinely undetectable.

The Level III is answerable for the procedure and for the personnel qualification. If the technique could not reliably detect the flaw type that failed, the question moves to who wrote and approved it. This is the exposure Level IIIs most often have not considered — signing a Written Practice is signing for the competence of everyone certified under it.

The contractor is answerable for who they assigned, whether that person was qualified for the scope, and whether their programme was what they represented at tender. Subcontracted crews do not transfer this; if your name is on the contract, the finding is yours.

The owner is answerable for the inspection programme itself — whether the right equipment was inspected at the right interval by the right method, and whether findings were acted on. An excellent inspection whose recommendation nobody actioned moves exposure squarely back to the owner.

The three failures that turn a defensible position into an indefensible one

A certification that lapsed before the examination. Administrative, fatal, and the most common finding of all — it converts a competence question into a compliance one, which is far harder to defend.

Missing calibration evidence. If the instrument's status on the day cannot be shown, the data's reliability becomes arguable.

Findings reported but not escalated. A recommendation buried in the body of a report that nobody read is a live dispute about whether it was communicated. Anything that changes the risk picture belongs where the reader cannot miss it, with a record of who received it.

What actually reduces exposure

Not disclaimers — records. Certification currency tracked so nothing lapses unnoticed. Calibration traceable per examination. Procedures under revision control with evidence people were trained on changes. Findings communicated in a way that leaves a trail. Every one of these is an operational discipline, which is why companies running one system of record are in a structurally better position than companies running six spreadsheets. How that record-keeping is set up · what changes when you consolidate.

This is general commentary on how responsibility typically distributes in inspection work, not legal advice — take questions about a specific matter to counsel in the relevant jurisdiction.

Related: vetting a contractor's records · the employer's certification obligations · Level III authority and what it carries.

title: What a US Refinery Turnaround Demands From an NDT Contractor
author: Atlantis NDT
metaDescription: Turnaround NDT judged from the planner’s side: mobilisation and qualification evidence, discovery-work capacity, reporting speed inside the critical path, and the failures that cost schedule.
snippet: Turnarounds are won and lost on logistics and reporting speed, not on technique. Here is what the planner is actually measuring you against.
content:
The planner's view of your crew

A turnaround compresses a year of inspection into weeks, on a critical path where a day lost is expensive and visible. From the planner's side, an NDT contractor is judged on four things — and technique quality, while assumed, is not usually the differentiator.

1. Mobilisation without administrative failure

Dozens of technicians arriving with current certifications, vision records, site-specific safety training and contractor-portal clearance. The most common turnaround failure is not technical: it is a technician turned away at the gate because a record lapsed, on a day when that method was on the critical path. Contractors who track certification expiry against the turnaround calendar months ahead do not have this problem; those who check on mobilisation week reliably do.

2. Capacity for discovery work

Every turnaround finds things nobody planned for. When a vessel is opened and the condition is worse than expected, the scope expands mid-window and the contractor who can surge — additional crews, a different method, an advanced technique to characterise what conventional examination found — protects the schedule. The one who cannot forces a decision between waiting and accepting uncertainty, and neither is welcome at that stage.

3. Reporting inside the critical path, not after it

This is where contractors most often lose the next contract. If the repair decision needs the examination result and the report arrives two days later, the inspection did not serve the turnaround — it documented it. Findings must reach the planning team fast enough to influence what happens while scaffolding is still up. Contractors who capture data digitally at the equipment and report from it same-shift are structurally advantaged; those retyping field sheets in the evening are not. Why reporting speed is a systems question.

4. Records that close out the event

When the unit restarts, the owner needs the complete evidence package — every examination, personnel qualifications, calibration certificates, findings and dispositions — for the jurisdiction, the insurer and the next turnaround's planning. Contractors who deliver this as an organised package within days are remembered; those who deliver it in fragments over weeks are remembered differently.

What to fix before the next season

Map certification expiries against next season's calendar now, not in the mobilisation week. Establish which advanced techniques you can actually staff at surge, and be honest about it at tender. Time your own report turnaround from probe-off to issued, because that number is what the planner experiences. And build the close-out package as the work happens rather than assembling it afterwards.

Related: turnaround inspection planning · the systems that make mobilisation and reporting reliable · how turnaround work is bought in the US · the Gulf Coast turnaround market.

title: NDT in US Data-Centre Construction — What Actually Gets Inspected
author: Atlantis NDT
metaDescription: The inspection scope on hyperscale data-centre construction in the US: structural steel to AWS D1.1, mechanical cooling piping, generator and fuel systems, and why schedule pressure changes how QA has to work.
snippet: The fastest-moving construction sector in America has an inspection scope most NDT companies have never bid. Here is what it actually contains.
content:
Why this sector behaves differently

Hyperscale data-centre construction moves faster than industrial work and is judged on energisation dates that do not move. That schedule pressure shapes everything about the inspection scope: the work is conventional, the volume is high, and the intolerance for documentation delay is greater than most contractors expect coming from plant work.

What actually gets inspected

Structural steel. The largest single scope — moment connections, base plates and the long-span framing over data halls, examined visually and volumetrically to AWS D1.1 acceptance. High weld count, repetitive geometry, and acceptance criteria that vary with the connection's loading classification.

Mechanical piping. Cooling systems are the sector's defining feature and its growing inspection load. Chilled water, condenser water and increasingly liquid-cooling distribution — welded piping to the governing code for the service class, with pressure testing and joint examination on the critical path to commissioning.

Generator and fuel systems. Standby generation at scale brings fuel storage tanks, fuel piping and exhaust systems, each with its own code family — and tank work brings API-adjacent requirements into a construction project.

Electrical support structures and anchorage. Equipment pads, seismic anchorage where applicable, and the embed and anchor verification that follows a design change late in the programme.

What contractors get wrong on their first project

Underestimating documentation volume. Thousands of welds across a campus means the weld map and traceability discipline matters more than technique. Contractors who arrive with a plant-work mentality — thorough examination, leisurely paperwork — fall behind in the first month.

Missing the commissioning interface. Inspection is not the last step; it feeds mechanical completion and turnover packages on a defined sequence. Findings that arrive after a system is turned over create rework nobody budgeted.

Staffing for peak without planning the surge. These projects ramp hard. The crew that starts is a fraction of the crew at peak, and every additional technician needs qualification evidence the owner's QA will check.

What wins repeat work

Same-day reporting, because the schedule is the client's dominant concern; clean traceability from weld map to report, because turnover packages are audited; and the ability to add qualified crews without a qualification scramble. All three are back-office capabilities more than technical ones — which is why data-centre work rewards contractors whose records systems are in order. The systems side · training crews for this sector.

Related: AWS D1.1 acceptance criteria · where this fits in the US market · how owners vet contractors for this work.

title: Sponsoring an Employee Through NDT Certification â€” What the Employer Actually Commits To
author: Atlantis NDT
metaDescription: The full commitment behind sponsoring a technician through NDT certification in the US â€” training hours, documented experience, examination, the Written Practice obligation, and the retention risk nobody budgets for.
snippet: Most employers budget for the course and are surprised by everything else. The course is the smallest part of what sponsorship actually commits you to.
content:
What does it cost an employer to sponsor an NDT certification?

The honest answer is that the course is the smallest part. Sponsorship commits an employer to four separate things â€” classroom or online training hours, documented on-the-job experience under supervision, examination, and the certification programme that issues the credential. Three of those four are internal obligations that continue long after the training invoice is paid, and they are where sponsorship programmes actually fail.

The four commitments, in the order they bite

1. Training hours. This is the part employers price. Hours differ by method and by level, and â€” this is the part that surprises people â€” the required number is set by your own Written Practice, not by ASNT. SNT-TC-1A recommends; the employer adopts. If your Written Practice specifies more hours than the recommendation, that is now your binding requirement.

2. Documented experience. The candidate needs supervised experience hours in the method, recorded in a form that survives an audit. This cannot be compressed, bought, or substituted with more classroom time. It is the constraint that sets the real timeline, and it requires a certified person available to supervise â€” which is why companies with one overworked Level II struggle to grow a second.

3. Examination. General, specific and practical examinations, with the practical the one candidates most often fail. The employer administers or arranges these under its own programme.

4. The programme itself. Someone must own the Written Practice, approve the examinations, and sign the certification. Under SNT-TC-1A that is a Level III. If you do not employ one, you cannot certify anybody, no matter how much training you buy.

The commitment employers consistently underestimate

Not money â€” supervision capacity. Every candidate accumulating experience hours consumes the attention of someone already certified and already busy. A company sponsoring three technicians at once against a single Level II is not running three programmes; it is running one bottleneck. Sequencing candidates against real supervision capacity is the single most useful thing an employer can do before committing.

What happens if the employee leaves

Employer-based certification does not transfer. Under SNT-TC-1A the credential is issued by you and is valid within your programme; a technician who leaves does not carry it to the next employer as a portable qualification, and the new employer will certify them again under its own Written Practice. This cuts both ways. It means a departing employee does not take a portable asset you paid for â€” but it also means your investment produced nothing you can point to once they are gone.

Employers who care about portability look at central certification under ISO 9712 instead, where a third-party body issues the credential and it moves with the individual. That changes the calculation, and for companies working internationally it often changes the answer.

A realistic sequence

Establish or fix the Written Practice first â€” everything downstream inherits its requirements. Confirm you have Level III authority to approve and sign; if not, resolve that before enrolling anyone, either by training your own or by contracting the Level III function. Then sequence candidates against supervision capacity rather than against budget.

Atlantis delivers training on-site to your crew and supports the programme behind it. Discuss a sponsorship plan.

title: An Inspector Failed the Certification Exam Twice â€” The Employerâ€™s Options
author: Atlantis NDT
metaDescription: What a US employer should do when a technician fails an NDT or API certification examination a second time â€” diagnosing which part failed, retake rules, and when reassignment is the right answer.
snippet: A second failure is information, not a verdict. What it tells you depends entirely on which part of the examination was failed.
content:
What should an employer do when an inspector fails a certification exam twice?

Treat the second failure as a diagnosis rather than a verdict, and start by establishing which part failed. General, specific and practical examinations fail for completely different reasons, and the remedy for one is useless against the others. Employers who respond by simply rebooking the same course usually get the same result.

Read the failure before buying more training

General examination. This tests method fundamentals â€” physics, principles, common terminology. Repeated failure here usually signals a genuine knowledge gap rather than nerves, and more supervised time on the tools will not close it. Structured study on the underlying method is the answer.

Specific examination. This tests your procedures, your equipment and your codes. Failure here is frequently an employer problem: procedures that are hard to follow, equipment the candidate rarely touches, or a Written Practice that specifies something the working reality does not match. Before blaming the candidate, read the specific exam against what the person actually does each day.

Practical examination. The most common failure and the most fixable. It tests whether the candidate can set up, calibrate, examine and evaluate on real hardware. It fails on repetition â€” not enough hands-on time on the specific configuration being tested. That is a supervision-capacity problem, not an aptitude problem.

Retake rules are set in two places

For employer-based certification under SNT-TC-1A, the retake and waiting-period rules are whatever your Written Practice says. Many employers copy the recommended practice without noticing they have adopted a mandatory waiting period they now have to honour. Read your own document before scheduling anything.

For API individual certification programmes the rules belong to API, are published by them, and change from time to time â€” check api.org for current retake and eligibility conditions rather than relying on what was true at the last attempt. The exam schedule and delivery arrangements also affect how quickly a retake can realistically happen.

When reassignment is the right answer

Some competent technicians are simply not suited to a particular method. A strong MT and PT inspector who cannot pass UT is not a failure â€” ultrasonics demands a different kind of spatial reasoning, and pushing someone through repeated attempts damages both the person and the programme. Moving them to a method they are genuinely good at, and certifying them properly there, is usually better for everyone than a third attempt.

The exception is where the failed method is contractually required for the work you have won. In that case the honest options are to develop somebody else, hire the qualification, or subcontract the scope â€” not to keep re-examining the same candidate.

What good employers do differently

They diagnose the failed part before booking anything. They check whether the specific examination reflects the real job. They give practical candidates more repetitions on the exact configuration rather than more classroom hours. And they treat repeated failure across several candidates as a signal about the programme, not about the people.

Talk to us about targeted re-preparation for a specific failed examination part.

title: Certifying a Crew Across Multiple States â€” NDT Training for Nationwide US Contracts
author: Atlantis NDT
metaDescription: How a US inspection contractor keeps one consistent NDT certification programme across multiple states and client sites â€” one Written Practice, portable records, and the audit exposure of running several.
snippet: Winning national work is one problem. Proving the same certification standard at every site, to every client auditor, is a different and harder one.
content:
How does a contractor keep NDT certification consistent across multiple states?

By running one certification programme, not one per region. Under SNT-TC-1A the certifying entity is the employer, so a company operating in six states still has a single Written Practice, a single Level III of record structure, and a single set of records. Companies that let regional offices drift into local variants create the exact inconsistency a national client's auditor is looking for.

Why NDT certification is not state-licensed â€” and what is

NDT personnel certification under SNT-TC-1A carries no state licensing component; it is an employer credential and it travels with your programme, not with a jurisdiction. What is jurisdictional is pressure-equipment inspection: states and localities operate their own boiler and pressure vessel programmes, and API in-service inspection intersects with those. Confusing the two produces either unnecessary duplication or a compliance gap. The practical rule is that your technicians' method certifications are national to your company, while the equipment inspection regime changes with the address.

What a national client's auditor actually checks

Consistently, four things. That the Written Practice exists and is current. That every certified technician's file contains training hours, documented experience, examination results and a current vision test. That the person who signed the certification had the authority to do so. And that the procedures used on their site are the approved ones, at the current revision.

The failure mode in multi-site contractors is almost never the technical work â€” it is records that live in different systems in different offices, so the file for a technician who transferred between regions cannot be produced in one piece. An auditor who cannot follow one technician's history through your records will not accept the programme, regardless of how good the inspection was.

The mobilisation problem

National contracts move crews between sites at short notice, and each client may add its own approval gate on top of your certification â€” operator-specific orientation, site-specific technique qualification, sometimes performance demonstration before a technician can work. Building that lead time into mobilisation planning is the difference between a crew that starts on Monday and one that watches from the gate.

Practical structure

Keep one Written Practice and version-control it centrally. Hold personnel records in one system that any office can produce from, rather than in regional folders â€” this is the single change that most improves audit outcomes, and it is why contractors increasingly move certification tracking into a system rather than spreadsheets. Maintain Level III coverage for every method you certify in, and confirm it does not lapse when one person leaves â€” the most common cause of a suddenly invalid programme. Where in-house Level III coverage is thin, contracting the function keeps the programme valid while you recruit.

Atlantis delivers training to crews on-site wherever they are working, under one consistent programme. Discuss a multi-site training plan.

title: Accepting One NDT Certification In Lieu of Another â€” Writing the Policy
author: Atlantis NDT
metaDescription: How to write a defensible company policy on accepting ASNT, ISO 9712, PCN or API qualifications in lieu of one another â€” what is genuinely equivalent, what is not, and how to word the exception.
snippet: Equivalence is a scope question, not a prestige question. The schemes qualify different things, and a policy that ignores that will not survive an audit.
content:
Can we accept ASNT Level III in lieu of an API qualification?

Generally no â€” and the reason matters more than the answer. The two qualify different things. An ASNT Level III demonstrates method authority: the ability to establish techniques, approve procedures and interpret results in a specific NDT method. An API individual certification demonstrates knowledge of an in-service inspection code â€” how to assess a vessel, piping system or tank against API 510, 570 or 653. Neither substitutes for the other because neither is a stronger version of the other.

A policy that treats one as outranking the other will produce exactly the wrong outcome: a Level III signing inspection reports on equipment they are not code-qualified to assess, or an API inspector approving NDT procedures they are not method-qualified to approve.

The right question to ask about any equivalence

Not "which certification is better" but "what does this scope actually require someone to do?" Write the requirement against the task:

  • Approving an NDT procedure or technique â€” method authority, so a Level III in that method.
  • Performing an examination and evaluating indications â€” Level II in that method, per your Written Practice.
  • Assessing in-service equipment condition against a code and signing the inspection â€” the relevant API certification.
  • Judging weld quality against a fabrication code â€” a welding inspection qualification such as CWI, which is again a different scope.

Once the requirement is written this way, most equivalence arguments answer themselves.

Where equivalence genuinely does apply

Between personnel certification schemes covering the same method and level, there is real comparability â€” ASNT and PCN, and ISO 9712 against SNT-TC-1A, qualify the same technical competence through different administrative routes. The structural difference is who certifies: SNT-TC-1A puts it on the employer, ISO 9712 and PCN on a third-party body. For an employer accepting an incoming technician, a central certification is easier to verify; an employer-based certification from a previous company is not transferable and the technician must be certified under your own programme regardless of what they hold.

Aerospace is its own regime â€” NAS 410 and EN 4179 govern there, with customer approval frequently layered on top, and a general industrial certification does not carry across.

Wording that survives an audit

State the requirement by scope and name the acceptable qualifications for it explicitly. Say who has authority to approve an exception, require it in writing against the named scope, and keep the record with the personnel file. Avoid open-ended phrases like "or equivalent" with no named approver â€” an auditor reads that as no policy at all. And state plainly that certifications issued by a previous employer are re-established under your own Written Practice, because that is the single most common misunderstanding when experienced technicians join.

Reviewing a written practice or a certification policy is one of the more common Level III consulting engagements we take. Ask us to review yours.

title: Building a US NDT Crew From Scratch â€” The Certification Sequence That Works
author: Atlantis NDT
metaDescription: The order to certify a new US NDT crew in â€” which methods first, how Level III authority gates everything, and why supervision capacity rather than budget sets the timeline.
snippet: Most new inspection companies certify in the wrong order and stall. The constraint is never the training budget.
content:
What order should a new inspection company certify its crew in?

Level III authority first, surface methods second, volumetric methods third â€” and sequenced against supervision capacity rather than against budget. Companies that start by sending several people on a UT course usually stall, because nothing they do can be certified until somebody has the authority to certify it.

Step one: the authority to certify anybody at all

Under SNT-TC-1A the employer certifies its own people, and a Level III must own the Written Practice, approve examinations and sign certifications. Without that, training hours accumulate and produce no certified technician. A new company has two routes: develop a Level III internally, which is slower but builds a permanent asset, or contract the function while the internal candidate qualifies. Most companies that grow successfully do both â€” contract first so work can start, develop in parallel so the dependency ends.

Step two: surface methods, because they build the base

MT and PT are the sensible first certifications. They cover a large share of routine scope, the practical examinations are more forgiving, and they let a new crew accumulate genuine documented experience quickly. VT belongs here too and is undervalued â€” it is the examination that decides where every other method gets deployed, and a crew strong in visual inspection wastes far less volumetric time.

Step three: volumetric, where the contracts are

UT is where inspection contracts are actually won, and it is also where practical examinations fail most often. It needs the most supervised repetition, which is why it comes after the crew has a supervision base rather than before. RT brings a whole additional layer â€” radiation safety, source logistics, exclusion zones and regulatory obligations that exist for no other method â€” so treat it as a business decision about whether to offer it at all, not simply the next certification.

Advanced techniques such as phased array come after conventional UT is genuinely solid. They are a technique layered on top of the method, and a crew that is shaky on conventional ultrasonics will not be rescued by better equipment.

What actually sets the timeline

Not money â€” documented experience hours under supervision. Those cannot be compressed, and every candidate accumulating them consumes a certified person's attention. Two candidates against one supervisor is workable; five is a queue. The single most common planning error is budgeting for five courses and discovering the company can only supervise two people at once.

Getting the paperwork right from day one

Write the Written Practice before certifying anybody, and write it to match what the company will actually do rather than copying a template wholesale â€” every hour and every requirement in it becomes binding on you. Keep personnel records complete from the first candidate: training, experience, examinations, vision tests. Retrofitting records for an early crew before a first client audit is miserable work, and it is why growing contractors move certification tracking into a system early.

Atlantis trains new crews on-site and supports the programme behind them. Talk to us about a crew development plan.

title: Can a Welder Become a Certified NDT Tech Without a Degree? Yes â€” Here Is the Actual Route
author: Atlantis NDT
metaDescription: A welder with no college degree can absolutely become a certified NDT technician â€” no US NDT certification requires a degree. What transfers from welding, what must be learned, and the CWI-vs-NDT fork.
snippet: No NDT certification in the United States requires a college degree. For a welder, the real questions are what transfers, what must be learned fresh, and whether CWI or NDT is the better fork.
content:
Can a welder with no college degree realistically become a certified NDT tech?

Yes â€” and more realistically than almost any other trade. No US NDT certification requires a college degree: under SNT-TC-1A the requirements are training hours, documented supervised experience, examinations and a vision test, all achievable while employed. A welder starts with the single most valuable asset in weld inspection â€” knowing how defects are actually made.

What transfers from welding â€” more than you think

NDT examines welds more than any other product form, and the examiner who has made the defect finds it faster. Lack of fusion, undercut, porosity clusters, crater cracks, slag lines â€” a welder knows which joint configurations produce them, which positions make them likely, and what a rushed root pass looks like from the inside. That intuition is what Level II judgment is built from, and candidates without a trade background take years to develop it.

Procedure discipline transfers too. A welder who has worked to a WPS understands qualified procedures, essential variables and why deviation is forbidden â€” which is exactly how NDT procedures work. So does code exposure: if you have welded to AWS D1.1 or ASME IX, you already know the acceptance-criteria world your future examinations live in.

What does not transfer â€” learn these fresh

The physics is new: ultrasound propagation, radiation interaction, magnetic flux behaviour, capillary action. It is teachable â€” the training-hours requirement exists precisely to teach it â€” but do not expect trade experience to shortcut the theory examination. Documentation habits are also different in kind: an inspector's product IS the record, and the evidence chain matters as much as the finding. And impartiality is its own skill â€” you will sometimes reject a colleague's weld, and the job is to be right, not popular.

The route, step by step

Pick the first method for the market you are already in. For a structural welder that is usually VT then MT â€” visual inspection is judged against the codes you already weld to, and MT finds the surface defects you already understand. For a pipe welder heading toward plant work, VT then UT is the stronger long-term stack â€” the method-order trade-offs in full.

Get the training hours. Delivered by an employer's programme, an NDT school, or on-site training like Atlantis delivers. Hours per method and level are set by the employer's Written Practice â€” the document that will govern your certification â€” so a specific universal number would be wrong to print.

Accumulate supervised experience. This is the real timeline-setter, and it favours the employed: a welder already inside a fab shop or plant can often log experience in a trainee role while still earning. The Level I and Level II pages carry the requirements end to end.

Pass the examinations â€” general (theory), specific (your employer's procedures), practical (on real specimens, where your hands are your advantage).

The fork every welder asks about: CWI or NDT Level II?

They are different jobs. A CWI (AWS Certified Welding Inspector) is a welding-quality generalist: procedures, welder qualifications, visual acceptance â€” the natural fork for someone who wants to stay in the welding world with authority over it. An NDT Level II is a method specialist who examines far more than welds: castings, forgings, corrosion, in-service damage. NDT stacks methods over a career and reaches into in-service inspection, where the API codes take over. Many inspectors eventually hold both; if you must choose one first, choose by where you want to work in ten years, not by which examination looks easier this year â€” and read how employers treat the two scopes before assuming either substitutes for the other.

What it pays off in

The salary guide carries the bands; the short version is that a multi-method Level II out-earns most welding positions with less physical wear, and the ceiling â€” Level III â€” is a career welders reach regularly. Veterans coming through a welding rating should also read the military-to-NDT route, which overlaps this one.

Atlantis delivers method training on-site under ASNT Level III oversight â€” ask about a route in, whether you are one welder or a shop qualifying a crew.

title: How to Choose ERP Software for an NDT Inspection Company (2026 Buyer's Guide)
snippet: A practical 2026 buyer's guide to ERP software for NDT inspection companies: certification tracking, calibration management, job costing, and a real RFP checklist.
content:
Why the spreadsheet-and-QuickBooks stack stops working around ten technicians

Most NDT companies start the same way. A founder with an ASNT Level II or Level III background wins a few refinery turnaround contracts, hires two or three technicians, and runs the business out of QuickBooks, a shared Excel workbook for calibration due dates, and a folder of Word-based report templates. It works. Then the company adds a UT crew, picks up a pipeline integrity contract that requires API 1163 documentation, wins a marine survey line of business, and suddenly the owner is chasing down which gamma source is due for its quarterly leak test, whether a technician's PT Level II is still current for a job starting Monday, and why the job-costing numbers in QuickBooks don't match what the crew actually billed in the field.

This is the point where "we'll figure it out with more spreadsheets" stops being a viable strategy. An NDT inspection company is not a generic professional services business — it is a business built on regulated personnel qualifications, traceable equipment, radioactive material licensing in some cases, and reports that have legal and safety weight. Generic ERP or plain accounting software has no concept of any of that. This guide walks through what to actually evaluate when shopping for ERP software built for — or configurable to — an NDT, inspection, or calibration services company in 2026.

What "ERP for NDT" actually needs to cover

Enterprise resource planning, in the generic sense, means finance, inventory, and sometimes HR in one system. For an NDT company, that's the floor, not the ceiling. The system also needs to model the things that make this industry different from a landscaping company or a marketing agency.

Technician certification and qualification tracking tied to actual work assignment

Under ASNT SNT-TC-1A (the recommended practice most US NDT companies write their written practice around) or the ASNT Central Certification Program (ACCP), a technician's authority to perform and sign off a given method — UT, RT, MT, PT, VT, ET, or an advanced method like Phased Array or TOFD — depends on documented training hours, experience hours, vision exam currency (near and far acuity, typically re-verified annually per SNT-TC-1A recommendations), and a passing exam score at the correct level. A spreadsheet can hold this data. It cannot stop a scheduler from assigning a technician whose PT Level II lapsed eleven days ago to a Monday job, or flag that a technician's annual vision exam is due before a shutdown starts. An ERP built for this industry ties certification records directly to the scheduling and dispatch module, so the system itself throws a hard stop — not a "hopefully someone remembers to check the binder" soft stop.

Calibration and equipment traceability

Every UT flaw detector, thickness gauge, radiation survey meter, and MT/PT accessory has a calibration interval, usually annual for instrument function calibration with NIST-traceable reference standards, plus daily/per-shift verification the technician logs in the field. If your company holds or is pursuing ISO/IEC 17025 accreditation for a calibration lab function, or your client base requires ISO 9001:2015 clause 7.1.5 (monitoring and measuring resources) evidence, you need calibration records that are queryable, not buried in a binder that lives in whichever truck last used the gauge. This is one of the most common gaps we see when auditing a new client's systems — equipment goes into the field with an expired cal sticker because nobody had a single source of truth linking asset ID, cal due date, and current job assignment.

Radiation source and isotope tracking

Companies running industrial radiography under a 10 CFR 34 or equivalent state Agreement State license carry real regulatory exposure here. Source inventory, leak test intervals (typically every six months per NRC/Agreement State rules), transport documentation, and radiographer certification all have to reconcile constantly. An ERP that treats a Co-60 or Ir-192 source like a generic inventory SKU is not solving the actual problem — it needs a dedicated radiation safety module or at minimum custom fields and automated alerts an RSO can rely on.

Job costing by method, crew, and site — not just by invoice

A turnaround job might run three UT technicians, one Phased Array specialist, and a Level III reviewing reports, billed at different rates, with per diem, equipment rental, and consumables layered in. Generic accounting software gives you a single job total. What operations managers actually need is margin visibility by method and by crew so they know that the PAUT line of business is running healthy margins while the basic MT/PT work on a fixed day-rate contract is bleeding money on travel time.

Report generation, revision control, and client delivery

Inspection reports carry signatures, calibration references, and acceptance criteria tied to a code — ASME Section V, API 510/570/653, AWS D1.1, or a client-specific procedure. When a report gets revised, there has to be a controlled trail: who changed it, what changed, and which revision the client actually received. This is a natural integration point between ERP and dedicated NDT reporting software — the ERP should own the job, the crew, and the client relationship, while the reporting tool owns the technical document, and the two need to talk to each other rather than live as two disconnected silos.

Consumables and inventory that actually reflects field reality

Film, chemicals for MT and PT, couplant, replaceable probes, TOFD wedges — these get consumed on jobs and need reordering before a crew shows up to a site without them. Inventory modules built for retail or manufacturing usually assume a warehouse-to-shelf flow that doesn't match a truck-and-jobsite reality.

Vertical-fit ERP vs. generic "big name" ERP

The temptation for a growing NDT company is to reach for a recognizable name — NetSuite, a QuickBooks Enterprise upgrade, or an SAP Business One reseller pitch. The problem isn't that these platforms are bad software; it's that none of them ship with a concept of an ASNT certification record, a calibration due date tied to an asset, or a radiation source register. Every one of those gaps becomes a custom development project, usually billed at a systems integrator's hourly rate, and every future change to how you track qualifications becomes a change order.

This is where a flexible, open platform like Odoo has a structural advantage for a services business this specific: the underlying framework is built to be extended, and the cost of building an NDT-specific certification tracker, calibration module, or radiation source register on top of it is a one-time configuration effort rather than a locked proprietary black box. It's also why "generic ERP" and "NDT-specific ERP" aren't really two categories — the real question is whether the platform and the implementation partner understand the domain well enough to configure it correctly the first time. Our own Atlantis NDT ERP is built on exactly this premise: a proven, extensible ERP core configured specifically around certification tracking, calibration management, and NDT job costing, rather than a generic system with NDT bolted on as an afterthought.

Data ownership, security, and multi-site rollups

Once a company operates across more than one office or branch — say a Houston headquarters with a Gulf Coast field office and a satellite crew based out of Corpus Christi — the ERP conversation shifts from "does it track certifications" to "does it give leadership one consolidated view while still respecting who should see what." A branch manager needs visibility into their own crews, equipment, and jobs. A company owner or COO needs a rolled-up view across every location: total active jobs, aggregate margin by method, and a company-wide certification expiration calendar that doesn't require logging into three separate systems or calling three separate office managers for a status update. Role-based permissions matter here for a second reason beyond convenience — client data separation. If your company works for two competing refiners in the same market, contractual confidentiality terms often require that each client's job data, pricing, and scope details stay walled off from anyone outside that account team, and the ERP's permission model needs to support that without becoming an administrative burden every time a new job gets created.

Data ownership deserves equal weight in the decision. Ask directly: if you terminate the contract in three years, what do you walk away with? A vendor that can only hand you a generic CSV export of customer names, stripped of certification history, calibration records, and job-level detail, is not offering real data portability — it's offering a courtesy gesture. A platform built on an open core, where your data lives in a standard, documented database schema rather than a proprietary format only the vendor's own tools can read, gives you a fundamentally stronger negotiating position for the life of the relationship, not just at the point of exit.

What a realistic budget conversation should sound like

Because Atlantis doesn't publish flat pricing — every implementation depends on technician count, method mix, number of locations, and how much of the existing spreadsheet and paper-based history needs to be migrated — the useful exercise isn't comparing a headline number across vendors. It's comparing total cost of ownership over a realistic five-year horizon: license or subscription cost, implementation and configuration cost, the cost of any custom development needed to fill gaps the platform doesn't cover out of the box, and the ongoing cost of change requests as your certification matrix or reporting requirements evolve. Enterprise suites built for a much larger generic industrial customer base — SAP Business One, Microsoft Dynamics 365 Business Central, and comparable platforms — are frequently quoted to mid-market industrial services companies with implementation budgets that run into six figures once industry-specific customization is scoped in, according to figures commonly cited across the ERP consulting industry for comparable vertical builds. A configurable, open-core platform built by a team that already understands NDT certification structures and calibration compliance generally arrives at the same functional outcome without that same custom-development premium, because the domain-specific configuration is additive rather than a ground-up build. Whatever platform you're evaluating, ask every vendor for a project-scoped quote that specifically covers certification tracking, calibration management, and radiation source compliance — not just a generic per-user licensing number — because that's where the real cost difference between platforms actually shows up.

A practical RFP checklist

Before signing anything, put these questions in front of every vendor you're evaluating, including us:

  • Can the system block scheduling a technician onto a job if their certification for that method has lapsed, and can it flag certifications expiring within a configurable window (30/60/90 days)?
  • Does calibration tracking live on the equipment asset record, with automated alerts before due dates, not just a report you have to remember to run?
  • Can job costing break out labor, equipment, consumables, and travel by method and by individual technician, not just by invoice line?
  • Is there a client-facing portal or controlled document delivery mechanism for reports, or does every report go out as an email attachment with no audit trail?
  • How does the system handle multi-site, multi-crew dispatch — can a scheduler see technician availability, certification status, and equipment location on one screen?
  • What does data ownership look like if you leave the platform? Can you export your certification history, calibration records, and job history in a usable format?
  • What's the actual implementation timeline, and who owns configuration — an implementation partner who understands NDT workflows, or a generalist consultant learning your industry on your dime?

Where implementations actually go wrong

The single biggest failure mode isn't the software — it's treating ERP selection as an IT project instead of an operations project. Systems get selected by an office manager or a finance lead without input from the Level III who knows what a real qualification record needs to contain, or from the scheduler who knows that crews get reassigned mid-week and the system has to handle that gracefully. The second most common failure is under-scoping data migration: certification histories, calibration logs, and open job data from the old spreadsheet system need to land in the new system accurately, or technicians stop trusting it within the first month and quietly go back to their own tracking methods.

A realistic implementation for a company in the 10-75 technician range runs through discovery (mapping your actual certification matrix, equipment fleet, and job types), configuration, data migration, a parallel-run period where both systems operate together, and a cutover — typically eight to sixteen weeks depending on how much custom configuration is needed and how clean the source data is. Vendors who promise a two-week turnkey rollout for a multi-method NDT company are usually underestimating the qualification-and-calibration data model, not moving faster than everyone else.

Adoption is the failure mode that gets the least attention in vendor sales conversations and causes the most quiet damage after go-live. A field technician who's used a paper daily log for fifteen years is not automatically going to trust a tablet-based data entry workflow, especially if the first version they see is clunky, slow on a jobsite with weak cell signal, or requires more taps than the paper process did. If office staff and technicians don't trust the new system in the first few weeks, they build workarounds — a shadow spreadsheet "just in case," a habit of texting the dispatcher directly instead of updating job status in the app — and those workarounds quietly reintroduce the exact data fragmentation the new system was bought to eliminate. The fix isn't a one-time training session at launch; it's involving a handful of respected senior technicians and the office staff who'll use the system daily in the configuration process itself, so the workflow reflects how they actually work rather than how a sales deck assumed they work, and so they have a stake in making it succeed rather than a reason to resist it.

Making the call

The right ERP for an NDT company is the one that treats certification tracking, calibration management, and radiation source control as first-class data — not custom fields bolted onto a generic services template — while still giving you real financial visibility and a system your office staff and field technicians will actually use. If you're evaluating platforms, it's worth walking through your specific certification matrix, equipment fleet, and job mix with a team that has actually run NDT operations rather than one learning the industry from your requirements document. Affordable, accessible, and fully customizable only means something if the vendor understands what "customizable" needs to include for a business built around ASNT qualifications and calibrated equipment — not just invoicing and payroll.

Pairing the right ERP with disciplined NDT training and certification tracking practices and sound ASNT Level III consulting on your written practice closes the loop between what your system says a technician is qualified to do and what your written practice actually requires.
