title: Odoo vs Generic ERP for NDT Companies: What Actually Matters
snippet: Odoo vs. generic ERP for NDT companies: what the platform choice actually changes for certification tracking, calibration management, and total cost of ownership.
content:
The wrong question most NDT companies ask

"Should we use Odoo or a bigger-name ERP?" is the wrong first question. The right first question is: does this platform's underlying architecture let us model certification-gated scheduling, calibration-linked equipment records, and method-level job costing without paying a systems integrator to bolt on custom modules for the next three years? Odoo keeps coming up in these conversations because it answers that question well — it's an open, modular platform where the accounting, inventory, project, field service, and HR apps share one data model, which matters enormously for a business where a technician's certification record, their calibrated equipment, and their assigned job all need to talk to each other in real time. But the platform choice is only half the story. What actually determines whether an NDT company ends up with a system it uses for the next decade or a system it abandons in eighteen months is how it gets configured.

What "generic ERP" gets wrong for inspection companies

Large horizontal ERP suites — think SAP Business One, Microsoft Dynamics 365 Business Central, or NetSuite — are built for a median customer that looks like a light manufacturer, a distributor, or a professional services firm with fairly generic billable-hours logic. None of them ship with a native concept of an ASNT SNT-TC-1A qualification record, a radiation source leak-test interval, or a calibration due date that has to block a scheduling action. Every one of those becomes a custom development request, and in a licensed, proprietary platform, custom development means paying the vendor's certified partners at integrator day rates, often with the customization living in a layer that breaks on the next major version upgrade.

Enterprise suites also tend to price and package around company-wide user counts and module tiers that assume a much larger back office than most NDT companies run. A 25-technician inspection company doesn't need the full financial consolidation and multi-entity intercompany accounting stack that a mid-market manufacturer needs — it needs tight field operations, qualification tracking, and job costing, with accounting that's solid but not the main event.

Why Odoo's architecture fits this industry specifically

One data model across departments

In Odoo, a technician record, a project task, a timesheet entry, an inventory item, and an HR skill/certification field all live in the same underlying database and can reference each other directly. That means a certification expiry date on an employee record can be surfaced as a warning on a project task assignment without custom middleware syncing two separate systems. In a lot of "big name" ERP-plus-bolt-on-HR-system setups, that same integration requires an API connector, ongoing maintenance, and a real risk that the two systems drift out of sync.

Open-source core means configuration, not black-box customization

Because Odoo's core modules are open source, building an NDT-specific certification tracker, calibration register, or radiation source module is a configuration and extension exercise on a known, documented framework — not a request into a vendor's proprietary black box where you're dependent on their roadmap and their pricing for the next change. This is the structural reason a configured Odoo implementation can be dramatically more cost-effective over a five-year horizon than an enterprise suite: the customization is yours, built on a platform you're not locked out of.

Modular rollout matches how NDT companies actually grow

A ten-technician shop doesn't need multi-warehouse inventory or manufacturing resource planning on day one. Odoo's app-by-app structure means you can start with project management, timesheets, and basic accounting, then add field service dispatch, calibration tracking, and a client portal as the company grows — without re-platforming. Enterprise suites often require you to buy into a much larger initial footprint because their pricing and implementation methodology assume a bigger, more complex organization from the start.

Where a generic ERP — Odoo included — still falls short out of the box

It's worth being honest here: vanilla Odoo, installed with default settings, does not know what an ASNT Level II qualification is any more than SAP does. No off-the-shelf platform ships with NDT-specific logic. The difference is what it costs and how long it takes to get there. A few concrete gaps that any implementation needs to close:

  • Certification matrices with method, level, and technique granularity — UT general vs. UT Phased Array vs. UT TOFD are different qualifications, and the system needs fields and workflow rules that reflect that distinction, not a single generic "certified: yes/no" checkbox.
  • Calibration intervals that vary by instrument type and client specification — some clients require more frequent verification than the ASNT/ASME baseline, and the system needs to support client-specific overrides.
  • Radiation source compliance — leak test scheduling, transport index calculation support, and license renewal tracking need dedicated fields most generic field-service modules don't have.
  • Report linkage — the ERP job record should link out to the actual inspection report and revision history, which usually means integration with purpose-built NDT reporting software rather than trying to force report generation into a generic ERP document module.

A side-by-side on what actually matters

Total cost of ownership over five years

Enterprise suite licensing for a mid-market industrial services company commonly runs into significant annual per-user fees plus implementation costs that can reach well into six figures once customization for industry-specific workflows is included — figures reported across the ERP consulting industry for SAP and Dynamics rollouts at this scale are frequently cited in that range. An Odoo-based implementation, particularly one configured by a partner who already has the NDT data model built rather than starting from a blank slate, generally has a materially lower total cost of ownership because the customization work is additive to an already-open platform rather than integrator time spent working around a closed one. Atlantis doesn't publish flat pricing because every company's technician count, method mix, and integration needs are different — but the honest comparison point is: ask any enterprise ERP vendor for a project-scoped quote covering certification tracking and calibration management specifically, and compare that number to a quote for a purpose-configured Odoo implementation covering the same scope.

Speed to a usable system

Because Odoo's modules are pre-built and the customization is additive configuration rather than ground-up development, implementation timelines for a mid-size NDT company tend to run shorter than enterprise suite rollouts of comparable functional scope, where change requests often have to go through a formal integrator change-order process.

Vendor lock-in risk

With an open-core platform, your data, your workflows, and even your custom modules are portable in a way that proprietary enterprise software generally isn't. If you ever need to migrate implementation partners, or bring configuration in-house, you're not dependent on one vendor's exclusive access to the platform's source.

What migrating off a legacy or generic system actually looks like

Most NDT companies evaluating Odoo aren't starting from a blank slate — they're migrating off QuickBooks plus a pile of spreadsheets, or in some cases off an enterprise suite that never got properly configured for their industry in the first place and has been quietly abandoned in favor of workarounds. The migration path matters as much as the platform choice. Certification records need to move over validated against actual supporting documentation, not just copy-pasted from the old spreadsheet as-is, because a migration is exactly the moment latent data quality problems surface — an expired certification nobody caught, a calibration record with a gap nobody explained. Job and client history should migrate far enough back to preserve meaningful trend data (equipment usage patterns, recurring client scope, historical margin by job type) without dragging over years of stale, low-value records that just add noise to the new system.

A sensible sequencing looks like: get core financials and the certification/calibration data model live first, since those touch compliance risk most directly, then layer in project costing and client portal access, then finally retire the legacy system once a full billing cycle has run cleanly through the new one. Companies that try to migrate everything simultaneously — finance, HR, scheduling, calibration, client-facing reporting — in a single cutover weekend tend to create exactly the kind of chaotic transition that makes staff distrust the new system before they've even had a chance to learn it.

Hosting, data residency, and security considerations

Odoo can run as a cloud-hosted subscription or be self-hosted on a company's own infrastructure or a private VPS, which is a genuine architectural advantage for companies with specific data residency requirements — a consideration that matters more each year as clients in oil and gas, defense-adjacent manufacturing, and critical infrastructure sectors tighten vendor security questionnaires around where inspection and asset data physically lives. A proprietary enterprise suite generally locks you into the vendor's own cloud infrastructure and data center regions, full stop. With an open-core platform, the deployment model is a genuine choice rather than a take-it-or-leave-it term in a vendor contract, and that flexibility extends to backup strategy, disaster recovery planning, and how quickly you can respond if a client audit asks detailed questions about where their inspection data is stored and how it's protected.

Questions to ask before you commit to any platform, Odoo included

  • Has the implementation partner actually built certification tracking and calibration management for an NDT or calibration lab client before, or are they learning the domain on your project?
  • Who owns the customized modules after go-live — can you take them to a different partner, or are they proprietary to the implementer?
  • What does the upgrade path look like when Odoo (or whichever platform) releases a new major version — does your customization survive, or does it need to be rebuilt?
  • Does the vendor understand the difference between a UT technician's certification and a radiographer's NRC/Agreement State license, and can the system's compliance logic reflect that?

What the sales conversation with an enterprise vendor usually leaves out

An enterprise ERP sales team pitching an NDT company almost never opens with "here's what it costs to build a certification tracking module that blocks scheduling on an expired qualification." They open with the platform's brand recognition, its financial reporting depth, and its scalability story for a much larger organization than most NDT companies actually are. The certification, calibration, and radiation-source gaps get positioned as "easy customizations we can scope after the contract is signed" — which is exactly backwards for a decision this consequential. Those gaps aren't peripheral features; for an NDT company, they're the core operational requirement the entire system exists to serve, and they should be the first thing scoped and quoted, not an afterthought handled in a change order six months into a rollout that's already over budget and behind schedule.

This is worth naming directly because it's the single most common regret we hear from companies that previously implemented a generic enterprise suite before coming to a vertical-fit conversation: the accounting and inventory modules worked fine, and the parts of the business that actually created compliance risk — technician qualification enforcement, calibration-linked equipment dispatch — never got built to the standard the company actually needed, because nobody scoped them as the priority they were from day one.

What "customizable" needs to mean, concretely

Every ERP vendor claims to be customizable — it's one of the least differentiated words in enterprise software marketing. The useful question isn't whether a platform is customizable in the abstract; it's what specific NDT workflows have already been built and proven, versus what would need to be scoped and built from scratch on your project's timeline and budget. A platform where certification tracking, calibration management, and method-level job costing already exist as configured, tested modules — ready to be tailored to your specific method mix and client requirements — is a fundamentally different starting point than a platform where "customizable" means "we can build that for you" as an open-ended, unscoped promise. Ask any vendor to show you the actual configured module, not a roadmap slide, before treating "fully customizable" as a meaningful differentiator rather than marketing language every competitor uses identically.

The bottom line

Odoo isn't automatically the right answer because it's open source, and a generic ERP isn't automatically the wrong answer because it's proprietary. What matters is whether the platform and the team configuring it actually understand ASNT qualification structures, calibration compliance, and NDT job economics — and whether the resulting system is something your technicians and schedulers will use daily rather than work around. Atlantis NDT builds its ERP implementations on exactly this premise: an open, extensible core configured by people who have run NDT operations, not a generic template with your company's name on it.

If you're weighing platforms, it's worth pairing that evaluation with a look at how your asset and inspection data will eventually need to connect to broader integrity management, and how your technician certification pipeline feeds directly into whatever system you choose.

title: Certification Tracking Software for NDT Technicians: Why Spreadsheets Fail at Scale
snippet: Why spreadsheet-based certification tracking breaks down as NDT companies scale, and what SNT-TC-1A compliance actually requires from a real tracking system.
content:
The spreadsheet that runs your compliance exposure

Walk into almost any NDT company under fifty technicians and ask to see the certification tracker. Nine times out of ten, it's an Excel workbook — one tab per technician, or one master sheet with a row per person and columns for UT, RT, MT, PT, VT, ET, and maybe Phased Array or TOFD, each cell holding a level and an expiration date. Someone updates it when they remember to, usually the office manager or the Level III who also has a dozen other responsibilities. It works fine at eight technicians. It becomes a genuine liability at twenty-five, and by fifty it's not a question of if something slips through, it's a question of how often.

This isn't a knock on the people running these systems — it's a structural problem. A spreadsheet has no concept of a dependency. It can't stop a scheduler from assigning a technician to a job requiring a certification that expired last week, because the spreadsheet and the scheduling process are two completely disconnected activities that happen to share an office. The only thing preventing a compliance failure is a human remembering to cross-reference two systems before every single job assignment, every single week, forever.

What's actually at stake under SNT-TC-1A and ACCP

Under ASNT SNT-TC-1A, the employer's written practice is the governing document — it defines training hour requirements, experience hour requirements, examination requirements (general, specific, and practical), vision acuity testing (near and far, typically Jaeger Number 2 near and 20/30 far or better, re-verified annually), and recertification intervals, which the recommended practice sets at a maximum of five years for most methods with annual capability verification in between. Under the ASNT Central Certification Program (ACCP), certification is issued by ASNT directly with its own renewal and recertification cycle. Either way, a technician performing work outside their current, documented qualification isn't a paperwork technicality — it's a direct finding waiting to happen in a client audit, an API-authorized inspection agency review, or worse, a real finding after a missed indication on an in-service asset.

Clients in the oil and gas, power generation, and aerospace sectors routinely audit their NDT vendors' certification records as part of vendor qualification and periodic surveillance. An auditor who finds one technician's PT Level II certification eleven days expired on a report signed last month doesn't treat that as an isolated clerical error — it calls into question the reliability of every certification record the company holds, and in the worst case, it puts the validity of every report that technician signed during the lapse period in question. For a company whose entire value proposition to E&C firms, refineries, and fabricators is the integrity of the reports it produces, that's an existential risk, not an inconvenience.

Where the spreadsheet model actually breaks

No connection between qualification and scheduling

The certification data and the job assignment process live in different tools maintained by different people on different update cycles. Nothing structurally prevents the gap between them from becoming a live compliance failure.

No visibility into what's expiring soon — only what's already expired

A well-maintained spreadsheet might get checked weekly, which means you find out a certification lapsed after it already happened, not with enough runway to schedule a recertification exam, book the Level III's time to proctor it, or line up a replacement technician for an upcoming job.

No audit trail

When a client asks "prove this technician was qualified to perform TOFD on this vessel on this date," a spreadsheet with editable cells and no version history is a weak answer. Who changed the expiration date, and when, and based on what supporting document? A spreadsheet can't answer that. A real system with a document attachment, a change log, and a timestamp can.

No connection to training records and experience hour accumulation

SNT-TC-1A qualification isn't just about the exam date — it's built on documented training hours and experience hours accumulated over time, per method, per technique. Tracking that in a spreadsheet means manually tallying hours from timesheets or job records, a process that tends to get "trued up" once a year rather than maintained continuously, which means a technician approaching a certification level upgrade often doesn't know they're close until someone does the math.

Single point of failure

One person owns the spreadsheet. When that person is out, on a job site, or leaves the company, institutional knowledge about who's tracking what goes with them, and the file itself — sitting on a local drive or a shared folder with no real permissions model — is one accidental deletion or corrupted save away from a genuinely bad week.

What a real certification tracking system needs to do

  • Hard-stop scheduling integration — the system should refuse, or at minimum flag with a required override and reason code, any attempt to assign a technician to a job requiring a certification they don't currently hold.
  • Rolling expiration alerts — automated notifications at 90, 60, and 30 days before any certification, vision exam, or recertification deadline, routed to both the technician and whoever schedules their work.
  • Method and technique-level granularity — separate records for UT general, UT Phased Array, UT TOFD, RT film, RT digital, and so on, because a technician can be current in one and lapsed in another.
  • Document attachment and audit trail — exam results, vision test results, training hour logs, and experience hour documentation attached directly to the qualification record, with a timestamped change history.
  • Experience and training hour accumulation tied to actual job records — hours should populate from timesheets and job assignments automatically rather than requiring manual reconciliation.
  • Client-facing export — the ability to generate a clean, auditable qualification summary for a client vendor audit in minutes, not a day of manually compiling records.

What a client vendor audit actually checks

Large industrial clients — refiners, EPCs, fabrication shops supplying pressure equipment — routinely run vendor qualification audits on their NDT suppliers, and certification records are almost always item one on the checklist. A typical audit will sample a handful of recent reports, pull the technician who signed each one, and ask for documented proof of current qualification at the time the work was performed: the exam record, the vision test, the training and experience hour log, and evidence the written practice's recertification interval was actually followed. Auditors don't just check whether a certification is current today — they check whether it was current on the specific date the report was signed, which means a system that only shows present-tense status and doesn't retain historical point-in-time records is a real liability. If a technician's certification lapsed for three weeks eight months ago and then got renewed, a spreadsheet with the current expiration date overwritten in place has destroyed the evidence needed to answer "was this person qualified on this specific date" — a properly built system retains that full history instead of just the latest value.

This point-in-time requirement is one of the more subtle but consequential differences between a spreadsheet and a real system. Spreadsheets are, by design, mutable records of current state. Audit-grade certification tracking needs to be closer to an append-only ledger — every change timestamped, attributed, and retained — so that six months or two years later, the company can reconstruct exactly who was qualified to do exactly what on any given date, without relying on anyone's memory of what the spreadsheet looked like at the time.

Multi-crew and multi-site complexity compounds the problem

A single-location company with five technicians can, with real discipline, keep a spreadsheet reasonably current because one person effectively owns the whole picture. A company running crews out of three offices, supplementing with subcontracted technicians during turnaround season, and supporting multiple advanced methods per technician has a fundamentally different data management problem — one where a single owned spreadsheet becomes either a bottleneck (everything routes through one person) or a consistency problem (each office keeps its own version, and they inevitably drift apart). This is precisely the scale at which the absence of a real system stops being an inconvenience and starts being close to inevitable that something falls through. A centralized system with role-based access — where a branch manager sees and updates their crew's records in real time, and those updates roll up automatically to a company-wide certification dashboard — is what actually scales past the point where one person's memory and diligence is the only thing holding compliance together.

What this looks like inside a real ERP

This is exactly the kind of workflow that belongs inside a company's core operating system rather than as a standalone app that has to be manually synced with everything else — which is one of the main reasons certification tracking is built as a core module inside Atlantis NDT ERP rather than treated as an afterthought. When the certification record, the scheduling module, and the job costing module share the same underlying data, a technician's qualification status is a live fact the system checks automatically, not a lookup someone has to remember to perform. The same structure that prevents a scheduling error also makes recertification planning proactive: a Level III or training coordinator can see, at a glance, every technician approaching an expiration window across every method, and plan exam sessions and refresher training around that instead of reacting to lapses after they happen.

It's worth being precise about what this solves and what it doesn't. Software tracks and enforces the qualification records you feed it — it doesn't replace a sound written practice, and it doesn't replace the judgment of a Level III reviewing whether your qualification structure actually meets the intent of SNT-TC-1A or your client's specific requirements. Getting that foundation right is a written-practice and procedure question, which is exactly where dedicated ASNT Level III consulting earns its keep — building or auditing the written practice that the software then enforces.

Recertification planning as a proactive exercise, not a reactive one

Under SNT-TC-1A, recertification generally depends on continued satisfactory performance, an annual or periodic capability verification (near/far vision, and often a practical demonstration depending on the written practice), and re-examination at the interval the written practice specifies, capped at five years for most methods. A system with real visibility across the whole technician roster lets a training coordinator batch recertification activity sensibly — scheduling a group vision exam session for six technicians whose annual checks fall in the same month, or planning a Level II re-examination sitting three months ahead instead of one technician at a time as each deadline arrives individually. This batching isn't just an efficiency gain; it reduces the number of individual deadlines a training coordinator has to track manually, which is itself one of the more common points where something gets missed in a fast-growing company.

The transition from spreadsheet to system

Moving off a spreadsheet doesn't require a rip-and-replace event that disrupts operations. A realistic path looks like: audit every current technician's certification record against actual supporting documentation (this step alone often surfaces the first real gaps), migrate clean records into the new system, run both in parallel for a scheduling cycle or two so the office staff and Level III build trust in the automated alerts, then retire the spreadsheet once nobody's checking it as a backup anymore. Companies that skip the parallel-run step and just cut over cold tend to see technicians quietly keep their own personal tracking, which defeats the purpose — the goal is one source of truth everyone actually relies on, not a system that exists alongside the old habits instead of replacing them.

Practical evaluation questions to ask a certification tracking vendor

  • Does the system retain a full point-in-time history for every qualification change, or only the current status — can you prove who was qualified on a specific past date?
  • Can scheduling be configured to hard-block, not just warn, when a technician lacks the current qualification a job requires?
  • How are training and experience hours captured — manually re-entered, or pulled automatically from timesheets and job assignment records?
  • Can the system generate a clean, exportable qualification summary formatted for a client vendor audit without hours of manual compilation?
  • Does the platform distinguish qualification by method and technique granularity, or only a single generic certification field per person?

Why this matters more every year, not less

As NDT companies add advanced methods — Phased Array, TOFD, automated ultrasonic scanning — the certification matrix per technician gets more complex, not simpler. A technician who's UT general Level II, PAUT-qualified, and working toward TOFD qualification has three separate tracks to manage simultaneously, each with its own training hours, experience hours, and renewal timeline. The spreadsheet model that barely worked with five methods per technician does not scale to that complexity. Investing in a real certification tracking system before it becomes a crisis — rather than after a client audit finding forces the issue — is one of the highest-leverage operational decisions a growing NDT company can make.

title: Calibration Management Software for Instrument Labs: A Practical Buying Guide
snippet: A practical buying guide to calibration management software for NDT instrument labs, covering ISO/IEC 17025 traceability, as-found/as-left data, and audit readiness.
content:
Calibration isn't a back-office chore — it's the thing your reports depend on

Every measurement an NDT technician takes is only as good as the calibration behind the instrument that took it. A UT thickness gauge reading that's off by half a millimeter because the instrument was calibrated against the wrong reference block, or run six weeks past its due date, doesn't just create a bad data point — it can put a corrosion rate calculation, a remaining-life estimate on a pressure vessel, or an API 653 tank bottom assessment on the wrong side of a fitness-for-service decision. Calibration management software exists to make sure that never happens quietly. This guide covers what an instrument lab — whether it's an internal cal function inside an NDT company or a standalone third-party calibration lab — actually needs from a software system, separate from the marketing language every vendor uses.

The regulatory and standards backdrop that shapes requirements

If your lab holds or is pursuing accreditation under ISO/IEC 17025 (General requirements for the competence of testing and calibration laboratories), the software isn't optional infrastructure — it's part of your quality management system evidence. Clause 6.4 (equipment) and clause 7 (process requirements) both drive documentation expectations an auditor from A2LA or ANAB will actually check: unbroken calibration history per asset, traceability to NIST or another recognized national metrology institute, uncertainty budgets where applicable, and a clear record of out-of-tolerance events and their disposition. Separately, if your company operates under ISO 9001:2015 as its base quality system, clause 7.1.5 (monitoring and measuring resources) requires that measuring equipment be calibrated at specified intervals, identified to allow its calibration status to be determined, and protected from adjustments that would invalidate results. A calibration management system is how you produce that evidence on demand instead of assembling it under pressure during an audit.

What to actually evaluate

Asset-level calibration history, not a flat spreadsheet log

Every gauge, flaw detector, radiation survey meter, and reference standard needs its own asset record with a complete calibration history — not a row in a master spreadsheet that gets overwritten each cycle. You need to be able to pull up a single UT thickness gauge and see every calibration event across its service life, including which reference standard was used, who performed it, and what the as-found and as-left readings were.

As-found / as-left data capture

A calibration record that only shows "passed" isn't enough for a rigorous lab. Recording as-found readings before adjustment tells you whether the instrument was drifting within tolerance or had already gone out of spec — which matters enormously if a client later asks whether any data collected before the last calibration might be suspect. This is the difference between calibration software that's built for real metrology work and one that's just a scheduling reminder tool wearing a calibration label.

Automated interval tracking with configurable rules per instrument type

Calibration intervals aren't one-size-fits-all. A UT flaw detector might run on a 12-month cycle for full function calibration, a radiation survey meter might need a shorter interval per license conditions, and a client contract might specify a tighter interval than your default. The software needs to support per-asset interval rules, not a single global default that gets manually overridden constantly.

Traceability chain documentation

NIST traceability isn't a checkbox — it's a documented, unbroken chain from your working standard back through reference standards to a national metrology institute. The system should let you attach or link the calibration certificates of your reference standards, so that when a client or auditor asks to see the traceability chain for a specific measurement, you can produce it in minutes.

Out-of-tolerance workflow and impact assessment

When an instrument comes back from calibration out of tolerance, the real question is what else it affects — every job that instrument was used on since its last known-good calibration. A mature system flags every job or report associated with an asset during the period in question, so you can actually assess impact instead of hoping nothing important happened in between. This single capability is often the difference between a contained non-conformance and a client relationship crisis.

Integration with scheduling and dispatch

An instrument with a calibration due date three days from now shouldn't get dispatched on a two-week offshore job. Calibration status needs to be visible — and ideally enforced as a hard stop — at the point equipment gets assigned to a job, the same way a technician's certification status should be.

Handling out-of-tolerance events without hiding the impact

Every calibration program eventually finds an instrument out of tolerance — it's not a sign the lab is failing, it's a sign the verification process is actually catching real drift, which is the entire point of running the schedule in the first place. What separates a mature program from a weak one is what happens next. A weak process quietly recalibrates the instrument, files the certificate, and moves on without ever asking what that drift might have affected. A mature process treats an out-of-tolerance finding as a trigger for a documented investigation: how far out of tolerance was the reading, over what period could the drift plausibly have developed, and which jobs used that instrument during that window. Software that automates the third step — cross-referencing an asset's job history against a calibration date range — turns a task that could otherwise take a technician or quality manager hours of manual log review into a query that returns an answer in seconds, which matters enormously when a client is waiting on an answer about whether their inspection data might need to be re-verified.

Internal cal function vs. sending equipment to a third-party lab

Many NDT companies run a hybrid model: routine function checks and daily verification happen in-house, while full calibration against NIST-traceable standards goes to an accredited third-party lab annually. If that's your setup, the software still needs to track outbound shipment dates, expected return dates, and — critically — flag when equipment is sitting at a calibration vendor longer than planned, because that equipment gap can quietly become a scheduling problem for an upcoming job. Companies running their own accredited lab under ISO/IEC 17025 need the fuller metrology feature set: uncertainty calculations, measurement traceability documentation, and proficiency testing record management, which is a materially deeper requirement than what a company just tracking its own field equipment needs.

What a client calibration audit actually checks

When a refinery, fabrication shop, or EPC runs a vendor qualification audit on an NDT provider, calibration records are checked with almost as much scrutiny as technician certifications, and for the same reason: the audit isn't really about whether a piece of paper exists, it's about whether the client can trust the numbers in your inspection reports. A typical calibration audit sample will pull a recent report, identify the specific instrument used, and ask for that instrument's calibration certificate valid on the date the work was performed — not the instrument's current status, its status on that specific date. This is the same point-in-time requirement that governs certification audits, and it means a calibration system that only shows "current status" without a retained, timestamped history for every asset is going to struggle to answer the actual question an auditor is asking.

Auditors will also frequently trace the traceability chain itself — not just "is this NIST-traceable" as a checkbox, but actually reviewing the chain of calibration certificates from your working instrument back through your reference standard's own calibration, verifying there's no gap and no expired link anywhere in that chain. A system that stores reference standard certificates as attached, linked documents rather than requiring someone to physically locate a paper certificate in a filing cabinet turns what can be a multi-day audit response into something you can produce inside the audit meeting itself.

Proficiency testing and inter-laboratory comparison records

Labs operating under ISO/IEC 17025 accreditation are also expected to participate in proficiency testing or inter-laboratory comparison programs periodically, per clause 7.7 of the standard, as an independent check on measurement competence beyond routine internal quality control. These results — along with any corrective actions taken in response to an unsatisfactory result — need to be documented and retained as part of the lab's ongoing competence evidence. A calibration management system that has no place to record proficiency testing participation and outcomes is missing a real piece of the accreditation documentation picture, forcing that record-keeping into yet another disconnected file outside the system that's supposed to be the single source of truth for lab quality evidence.

Common mistakes in the buying process

  • Treating calibration tracking as a standalone point solution. A dedicated calibration app that doesn't talk to scheduling, job costing, or certification tracking creates the same disconnected-systems problem that spreadsheets create — just in a nicer interface. The value comes from calibration status being visible everywhere equipment gets used, not from a prettier calendar of due dates.
  • Underestimating migration effort. Every existing asset's calibration history needs to be captured accurately when moving to a new system. Rushing this step means starting your new system with gaps in exactly the historical record an auditor will want to see.
  • Ignoring who actually uses the system day to day. Field technicians need a fast, simple way to log daily verification checks from a phone or tablet at the jobsite — not a desktop-only interface that requires them to remember details after the fact.
  • Assuming a generic asset management tool is close enough. Generic maintenance or asset management software tracks things like "next service date" for equipment in general. It typically has no concept of as-found/as-left readings, uncertainty, or traceability chains — the specific data a metrology function actually needs.

Reference standards need their own calibration discipline

A working reference standard — an IIW block, a step wedge, a set of reference thickness plates — sits at the top of a lab's internal traceability chain, and it's easy to treat these as permanent fixtures that don't need the same tracking rigor as active field instruments. That's a mistake. Reference standards wear, get nicked or corroded through handling, and in some cases need their own periodic recertification against a higher-tier standard to maintain the validity of everything calibrated against them. A calibration management system that only tracks field instruments and treats reference standards as static, permanently valid fixtures has a structural gap at exactly the point where an error would propagate to every instrument calibrated against that standard — which is precisely why the strongest programs put reference standards on their own tracked recalibration schedule, with the same due-date alerting as any other tracked asset, rather than assuming they're good indefinitely once purchased.

What good looks like in practice

A well-run calibration function, properly supported by software, means a Level III or quality manager can answer three questions in under a minute at any moment: which instruments are currently out of calibration or approaching their due date, what jobs and reports each instrument touched during any given period, and whether the full traceability chain for any specific measurement can be produced on request. If any of those three questions currently takes more than a few minutes — or requires digging through paper certificates and separate spreadsheets — that's the clearest sign the calibration management approach needs to change before an audit or a client review forces the issue.

Mobile capture for field verification checks

Daily or per-shift verification checks — the quick function check a technician performs before using a gauge or flaw detector each day, distinct from the full periodic calibration — are the highest-volume calibration-adjacent data point most labs generate, and they're also the easiest to skip when logging them is inconvenient. A mobile-friendly capture method, where a technician can log a verification check in under thirty seconds from a phone at the jobsite against a reference block photo or barcode-scanned asset ID, produces dramatically better compliance than a paper log clipped inside a truck's glove box that only gets transcribed back at the office once a week, if at all. This is a small workflow detail that has an outsized effect on whether daily verification actually happens consistently versus becoming a formality nobody takes seriously.

Where this fits into the bigger operational picture

Calibration management shouldn't be an isolated system bolted onto your operation — it's one piece of the same operational backbone that handles technician certification tracking, job scheduling, and job costing. Building it as a core module of a broader NDT ERP system rather than a standalone point tool means calibration status, certification status, and job assignment all reference the same live data, which is the only way to reliably prevent the scenario every quality manager dreads: equipment or a technician going out on a job that they shouldn't have been eligible for. If your lab is working toward ISO/IEC 17025 accreditation or preparing for a client's vendor quality audit, it's worth pairing your software evaluation with ASNT Level III consulting to make sure your written procedures and your software configuration are actually aligned — software enforces the rules you give it, and those rules need to be right first.

title: RBI and Corrosion Tracking Software: What a Real Risk-Based Inspection Program Needs
snippet: What a real API 580/581 risk-based inspection program needs from corrosion tracking software, beyond a due-date calendar, and where most plants' data actually breaks.
content:
Why RBI programs live or die on data infrastructure, not methodology

Every refinery, chemical plant, and midstream operator running a risk-based inspection program already knows the methodology — API RP 580 lays out the framework, API RP 581 gives the quantitative risk calculation approach, and most fixed-equipment integrity groups can recite the probability-of-failure and consequence-of-failure logic in their sleep. What actually determines whether an RBI program produces defensible, current risk rankings — or slowly drifts into a stale exercise nobody trusts — is whether the underlying corrosion and inspection data feeding those calculations is complete, current, and accessible. An RBI methodology is only as good as the thickness readings, corrosion rate calculations, and inspection history behind it, and that's a data infrastructure problem before it's an engineering problem.

The data an RBI program actually depends on

Thickness monitoring location (TML) history

Every corrosion monitoring location on a vessel, piping circuit, or tank needs a full history of readings over time, not just the most recent value. Corrosion rate — whether calculated as short-term rate from the last two readings or long-term rate from the full history — depends on having clean, correctly-referenced historical data tied to the exact same TML location every time, which sounds simple and is actually one of the most common sources of bad RBI data when TML numbering isn't rigorously maintained across inspection cycles and different inspection companies.

Corrosion loop and circuit definitions

API 581 risk calculations happen at the circuit or corrosion loop level — a defined section of piping or equipment expected to experience similar damage mechanisms and rates. If your data system tracks individual components but doesn't maintain the circuit grouping consistently, calculating a defensible corrosion rate and remaining life at the circuit level becomes a manual reconciliation exercise every single assessment cycle instead of a query.

Damage mechanism identification

API 571 (Damage Mechanisms Affecting Fixed Equipment in the Refining Industry) catalogs the damage mechanisms — sulfidation, hydrogen-induced cracking, chloride stress corrosion cracking, and dozens more — that drive both probability-of-failure calculations and the selection of appropriate NDT methods for each asset. This isn't a field you can leave blank or default to "general corrosion" for convenience; the wrong damage mechanism assignment cascades into the wrong inspection method selection and the wrong risk ranking.

Inspection results tied back to the risk model, not filed separately

This is where a lot of programs actually break down operationally. The RBI risk software calculates a next-inspection-date and recommended scope. The inspection gets performed — often by a third-party NDT provider — and the results land in a PDF report that gets emailed, filed, and referenced manually by an engineer updating the RBI model months later. Every manual handoff in that chain is an opportunity for a finding to get lost, a corrosion rate to be calculated from the wrong prior reading, or an updated risk ranking to lag behind reality by a full inspection cycle.

Where software actually needs to do more than track a due-date calendar

A genuinely useful RBI and corrosion tracking system needs to close the loop between inspection execution and risk model updates, not just remind an inspector when a vessel is due. Concretely, that means:

  • Direct data entry paths from field NDT work into the corrosion database — thickness readings captured during a UT scan should be able to flow into the TML history without manual retyping from a PDF report, which is both a time sink and a transcription-error risk.
  • Automated corrosion rate recalculation whenever a new reading is added, with configurable logic for short-term vs. long-term rate selection per API 581 guidance.
  • Remaining life and next-inspection-date calculation that updates automatically rather than requiring an engineer to manually recompute after every inspection cycle.
  • Flagging for accelerated corrosion — when a new reading produces a rate significantly higher than the historical trend at that location, the system should surface that immediately rather than waiting for the next scheduled program review.
  • Circuit and unit-level rollups so an integrity engineer can see risk ranking trends across an entire process unit, not just asset by asset.
  • Audit-ready documentation for both internal management-of-change processes and external regulatory review, since RBI programs used to justify inspection interval extensions under jurisdictional rules (many US states and the National Board follow API 510/570/653 inspection interval guidance, with RBI-justified extensions subject to jurisdictional approval in many cases) need a clear, defensible data trail.

Where API 570, API 653, and API 510 intersect with RBI data

Piping inspection under API 570, aboveground storage tank inspection under API 653, and pressure vessel inspection under API 510 each define baseline inspection intervals and methods independent of RBI. What a mature RBI program does is use accumulated condition data to justify interval adjustments within what the applicable code and jurisdiction allow — extending intervals on genuinely low-risk, low-corrosion-rate circuits while tightening scrutiny on circuits showing accelerated degradation. That justification only holds up under an internal or third-party audit if the underlying data — every TML reading, every corrosion rate calculation, every damage mechanism assessment — is traceable and complete. An RBI program with gaps in its inspection history isn't just an inconvenience; it undermines the entire basis for any interval extension the program has approved, which is exactly the kind of finding that turns a routine PSM or mechanical integrity audit into a much longer conversation.

A concrete scenario that shows where the gaps actually bite

Consider a mid-size crude unit piping circuit inspected annually under an API 570 program, with six years of UT thickness readings across four TMLs. In year four, a new inspection contractor performs the annual survey and, because TML location wasn't precisely re-established from the prior contractor's sketch, records readings roughly eighteen inches from the original monitoring points. The corrosion rate calculation that follows looks anomalous — either a sudden acceleration or an implausible deceleration, depending on local wall thickness variation — and an integrity engineer now has to decide whether that's a real change in the corrosion mechanism or a data quality artifact from inconsistent TML location. Resolving that ambiguity, if it's even caught before it flows into a flawed remaining-life calculation, requires digging through years of inspection sketches and reports from multiple contractors to reconstruct exactly where each historical reading was actually taken. A corrosion tracking system with GPS-referenced or clearly diagrammed, persistent TML location records — carried forward automatically regardless of which contractor performs the next survey — prevents this exact failure mode instead of relying on institutional memory and hand-drawn sketches to preserve monitoring location integrity across contractor changes and personnel turnover.

Management of change and PSM program alignment

For facilities operating under OSHA's Process Safety Management standard (29 CFR 1910.119), mechanical integrity is one of the fourteen required program elements, and RBI-driven inspection interval decisions typically need to tie back into the site's broader management of change (MOC) process — particularly when an RBI reassessment recommends extending an inspection interval beyond what a prior baseline schedule specified. A corrosion tracking and RBI system that can generate the specific data package an MOC review needs — corrosion rate trend, remaining life calculation, damage mechanism basis, and inspection history supporting the recommendation — turns what can be a slow, manual compilation exercise into something closer to a standard report the system produces on demand. Facilities that treat RBI data management and PSM/MOC documentation as separate, disconnected processes tend to find that connecting them after the fact, during an audit or incident investigation, is far more painful than building the connection into the system from the start.

The integration problem most plants actually have

In practice, a lot of sites run three disconnected systems: a dedicated RBI/risk software package (commercial platforms exist specifically for API 581 calculations), a separate corrosion/TML tracking database, and inspection reports arriving from NDT service providers as standalone PDF documents. Each system is individually fine. The gaps between them are where risk actually hides. An inspection provider whose reporting software can export clean, structured thickness data — rather than only a formatted PDF — removes one of the most common manual bottlenecks in this chain. This is one of the practical reasons the format and structure of your NDT provider's report output matters as much as the quality of the inspection itself: a report that's accurate but locked in an unstructured PDF still forces someone to retype data into the system that actually drives your risk model.

External vs. internal corrosion, and why the data model needs to distinguish them

Not every damage mechanism behaves the same way over time, and a corrosion tracking system that treats every TML the same regardless of the underlying threat will eventually produce misleading trend data. Internal corrosion under a naphthenic acid or sour water service, for example, tends to correlate with process conditions — feedstock changes, temperature excursions — in ways that a purely time-based trend line can miss entirely. External corrosion under insulation (CUI), a damage mechanism specifically called out in API 571 and a persistent driver of unplanned piping failures across the refining and petrochemical industry, often doesn't show up on routine internal UT monitoring at all and needs its own inspection program — insulation removal at representative locations, or increasingly, guided wave or pulsed eddy current screening — tracked as a distinct data set rather than folded into the same TML history as internal wall loss monitoring. A system that lets damage mechanism drive which inspection technique and which monitoring cadence apply, rather than forcing every circuit through the same generic thickness-monitoring template, produces a program that actually reflects how these different threats behave.

What to ask when evaluating a corrosion tracking or RBI-adjacent system

  • Can thickness and inspection data be imported directly from field data collection tools or NDT reporting software, or does everything require manual entry?
  • Does the system recalculate corrosion rates and remaining life automatically when new data arrives, or is that a manual engineering task performed periodically?
  • How does the system flag anomalous readings — a rate spike, a reading that breaks trend — for engineering review rather than letting them sit unnoticed until the next scheduled assessment?
  • Can you produce a full, exportable audit trail for a specific circuit's inspection and corrosion history on demand, in a format a jurisdictional inspector or internal auditor can actually review?
  • Does the platform support damage mechanism tagging per API 571, and does that tagging drive inspection method recommendations, or is it a free-text field with no downstream logic attached?

Data quality is a bigger risk to program credibility than methodology choice

It's worth stating plainly: no software fixes bad field data. If a technician records a thickness reading against the wrong TML number, or a corrosion rate gets calculated from two readings that were never actually taken at the same physical location, the most sophisticated API 581 risk calculation engine in the world will still produce a confidently wrong answer. The software's real job is reducing the number of places that kind of error can creep in — structured data entry that forces a valid TML selection rather than free text, automated flags when a new reading breaks sharply from historical trend, and a clean chain of custody from field collection through to the risk model — not replacing the underlying discipline of accurate field data collection. Programs that invest heavily in RBI software while treating the field data collection process as an afterthought tend to discover, usually during an external audit or after a genuine near-miss, that their risk rankings were only ever as good as the weakest link in that data chain.

Where this connects to broader asset integrity strategy

Corrosion and RBI data is also exactly the kind of information that becomes far more useful when it's visualized spatially against the actual asset rather than buried in a spreadsheet or a standalone risk software report — seeing TML locations, historical readings, and current risk ranking mapped directly onto a 3D model of a vessel or piping run gives an integrity engineer a fundamentally different, faster way to spot patterns than scrolling through tabular data. That's the specific gap a digital twin platform is built to close, layering inspection and corrosion history directly onto asset geometry so risk isn't just a number in a spreadsheet but something you can see. Getting the underlying inspection data collection right in the first place — accurate, consistently referenced, and delivered in a structured format — is the foundation everything downstream depends on, whether it's an RBI recalculation, a digital twin overlay, or a jurisdictional audit response. Pairing rigorous field data collection through modern NDT reporting software with a properly configured inspection management ERP is what actually keeps an RBI program defensible year over year instead of turning into a once-a-decade re-baselining project.

title: ERP for Marine Survey Companies: Managing IACS, Class Society, and Vetting Workflows
snippet: ERP for marine survey companies: how to manage IACS class society surveys, OCIMF SIRE/TMSA vetting workflows, and dual technician/surveyor credentialing in one system.
content:
Marine survey operations don't fit a generic services ERP template

A marine survey and inspection company — whether it's running hull thickness gauging on bulk carriers calling at Houston and Gulf Coast ports, condition surveys ahead of a sale, or NDT work supporting newbuild inspection at a shipyard in Canada — operates under a set of workflow requirements that don't map onto a typical field-services business. Surveyors work against class society rules that differ by flag state and society, vetting inspections follow tanker-industry-specific protocols, and a single vessel call might require coordinating a surveyor's travel, port agent scheduling, tide and berth windows, and same-day report turnaround before the vessel sails. Generic ERP or job-management software built for landside industrial inspection work usually has no concept of any of this. Here's what actually needs to be built into a system supporting marine survey and inspection operations.

Class society and IACS structure, and why it matters to your data model

The International Association of Classification Societies (IACS) is the umbrella body whose member societies — ABS, DNV, Lloyd's Register, Bureau Veritas, ClassNK, RINA, and others — set and enforce classification rules that determine a vessel's structural and mechanical fitness to operate under a given flag. Each society publishes its own rules for hull surveys, and the timing of special surveys (typically every five years), intermediate surveys, and annual surveys is governed by the vessel's class notation and age, with additional requirements kicking in under the IACS Common Structural Rules and enhanced survey programs for older tonnage. A survey company doing thickness gauging or structural NDT work in support of these surveys needs its records organized around vessel identity (IMO number, not just a job number), class society, survey type, and due-date windows that are vessel-specific and society-specific — not a generic "next inspection date" field borrowed from a plant-inspection template.

This matters practically because a single survey company might be working under an ABS special survey scope on one vessel and a DNV intermediate survey scope on another in the same week, each with different reporting formats, different acceptance criteria for gauging results (IACS Unified Requirement UR Z10 series governs hull survey and thickness measurement standards that member societies reference), and different documentation the class surveyor attending on behalf of the society will expect to review.

Vetting workflows: a separate discipline from classification surveys

Tanker vetting inspections — run under frameworks like OCIMF's SIRE (Ship Inspection Report Programme) and TMSA (Tanker Management and Self Assessment), or the dry-bulk equivalent RightShip inspections — are commercial risk assessments charterers and oil majors use to decide whether to fix a vessel, and they operate on an entirely different cadence and documentation standard than class surveys. A survey or inspection company supporting vetting work needs to track inspector accreditation separately (SIRE inspectors, for instance, go through OCIMF's own accreditation and observation process, distinct from ASNT NDT qualifications), manage report submission into the SIRE VIQ (Vessel Inspection Questionnaire) database format, and handle much faster turnaround expectations — a vetting inspection often needs to be reported within days because it's gating a charter decision, not a five-year class cycle.

Running both classification-support NDT work and vetting-adjacent inspection work through the same operational system means the ERP needs to cleanly separate these workflows rather than force them into one generic "inspection job" template. Mixing up a class survey due date with a vetting inspection expiration is the kind of error that looks small on a spreadsheet and becomes a real commercial problem when a charterer finds an expired vetting report during a fixture negotiation.

Newbuild and shipyard inspection coordination

Survey and NDT work supporting newbuild construction — increasingly relevant for companies working with shipyards in the US and Canada, as well as coordinating remote or third-party inspection oversight on vessels built overseas — follows yet another distinct workflow from in-service class surveys or vetting inspections. Newbuild NDT typically involves weld inspection (radiography and ultrasonic testing on hull and structural welds per the applicable class society's construction rules and often referencing AWS D1.1 or an equivalent structural welding code for specific joint types), progressive inspection hold points tied to the build schedule, and close coordination with a resident class surveyor who's tracking the vessel's construction against the classification society's approved plans. A survey company supporting this work needs scheduling and reporting structured around build milestones and hold points rather than the vessel's operational calendar, since a newbuild doesn't have "port calls" in the operational sense — it has a fixed sequence of fabrication and inspection stages that a delay in one stage cascades through the entire schedule. Tracking which hold points have been inspected, which are pending, and which NDT results are still outstanding against a specific block or section of the hull is a fundamentally different data structure than tracking recurring survey due dates on an operating vessel.

Insurance, P&I club, and flag state documentation

Beyond class society and vetting requirements, marine inspection and survey data frequently feeds into insurance underwriting and Protection and Indemnity (P&I) club requirements, particularly for older tonnage or vessels renewing hull and machinery coverage. Underwriters and P&I clubs often want condition survey history, not just a pass/fail class certificate, when assessing risk on a vessel — which means a survey company's ability to produce a clean, chronological condition history for a specific vessel, across multiple surveys and multiple years, can directly support (or complicate) a client's insurance renewal process. Flag state administrations layer on their own statutory survey and documentation requirements as well, which can differ meaningfully from the classification society's own rules even though the two are often coordinated. A system that can't cleanly distinguish class society requirements, flag state statutory requirements, and insurance-driven condition survey requests — treating them as one undifferentiated "vessel inspection" bucket — makes it much harder to respond quickly when a client's broker or P&I correspondent asks for a specific type of documentation on short notice.

What a marine-survey-capable ERP actually needs

Vessel-centric records, not job-centric records

The core entity in the system should be the vessel — tracked by IMO number for permanent identity regardless of name changes or flag changes — with survey history, class society, gauging history, and vetting inspection history all attached to that vessel record across every port call and every survey company engagement, not scattered across disconnected job files.

Port call and scheduling logic that accounts for tight windows

Marine survey work happens against vessel arrival and departure windows, not a standard nine-to-five job schedule. A dispatcher needs to coordinate surveyor travel, port access credentials, and equipment mobilization against a berth window that might be twelve hours, and the system needs to support that kind of tight, date-and-time-specific scheduling rather than a generic weekly calendar.

Technician and surveyor qualification tracking across multiple credentialing bodies

A marine NDT technician typically holds ASNT SNT-TC-1A qualifications for the actual gauging and inspection methods, while a surveyor attending on behalf of a class society or conducting vetting work holds separate accreditations from that society or from OCIMF. The system needs to track both without conflating them — a common and costly error when companies try to force marine credentials into a template built for land-based ASNT tracking alone.

Multi-currency and multi-jurisdiction invoicing

A survey company working ports on both sides of the US-Canada border, or handling international vessel calls, needs invoicing that handles USD and CAD cleanly, along with the documentation requirements that differ by port state and flag state.

Fast report turnaround with structured data, not just PDF generation

When a vetting inspection report needs to reach a charterer or the SIRE database within days, or a class surveyor needs gauging results formatted to a specific society's reporting template before the vessel sails, the speed and structure of report generation is a commercial necessity, not a nice-to-have. This is exactly where the connection between the operational ERP and dedicated NDT reporting software pays off — structured thickness data captured in the field should flow directly into a report formatted to the class society's or client's specification, rather than requiring a survey team to manually reformat gauging results after every job.

Equipment logistics unique to marine work

Marine NDT equipment — UT thickness gauges, MPI yokes for weld inspection, sometimes portable radiography equipment for newbuild weld verification — has to travel to the vessel, often through port security and terminal access procedures that add real time to mobilization, and sometimes overseas for vessels calling at foreign yards for repair or drydock work. Equipment calibration status needs the same rigor covered elsewhere for any NDT operation, but marine work adds a logistics layer: an ERP tracking equipment for marine survey work benefits from being able to flag when a piece of equipment scheduled for a vessel call is still in transit from its last job, physically at a different port, or held up in customs on an international mobilization, rather than only tracking calibration due dates in isolation from physical location and transit status.

Why the vessel identity problem trips up more systems than expected

A vessel's name, and sometimes its flag and owner, can change multiple times over its operating life — a bulk carrier delivered under one owner's naming convention might be sold, renamed, and reflagged two or three times over a twenty-year hull life. Software built around name-based identity, rather than the IMO number that stays permanently assigned to the hull regardless of ownership changes, will silently fracture a vessel's survey history every time it changes hands — the "new" vessel under its new name shows up as having no inspection history at all, even though the physical hull has a complete gauging record under a previous name. This sounds like an edge case until you consider how common vessel sales and renaming actually are in the secondhand tonnage market that a large share of independent survey work serves. Getting vessel identity right at the data model level, from day one, is the difference between a survey company that can pull up twenty years of hull condition trend data on request and one that effectively starts every relationship with a "new" vessel from a blank slate.

Common operational failure points

  • Treating every survey job identically. A special survey scope, an intermediate survey scope, and a vetting inspection have different documentation requirements, different turnaround expectations, and different qualification requirements for who can perform them — a system that flattens all of this into one generic job type creates confusion at exactly the moments precision matters most.
  • Losing vessel history across engagements. If a vessel's gauging history from three years ago lives in a closed job file rather than attached to a persistent vessel record, the next survey team has to start from scratch reconstructing trend data that should have been immediately available.
  • Underestimating scheduling volatility. Vessel arrival times shift constantly due to weather, port congestion, and operational delays. A scheduling system built for predictable land-based job timing will fight against marine operations rather than support them.

Language, documentation format, and working with a multinational crew

Marine survey work in North American ports frequently involves interacting with vessel crews, port agents, and terminal operators from a wide range of nationalities and primary languages, and class society and vetting documentation itself often needs to satisfy both the operator's expectations and the specific formatting conventions a given class society or the SIRE VIQ database requires. A system that supports standardized, code-referenced reporting — thickness readings tied to a specific frame or station number, findings referenced against the applicable class rule or VIQ question number — produces documentation that's unambiguous regardless of who on the vessel or in the charterer's office is reviewing it, which matters more in marine work than in most facility-based inspection contexts where everyone involved typically shares a single employer's internal documentation conventions.

Building this the right way

None of this requires a marine-industry-specific proprietary platform costing a fortune to license — it requires an ERP flexible enough to be configured around vessel-centric records, dual credentialing tracks, and tight scheduling windows, built by a team that actually understands the difference between a class survey and a vetting inspection. That's the specific configuration work behind Atlantis NDT ERP for marine-sector clients: the same extensible core used for land-based inspection companies, configured around IMO-number vessel tracking, dual qualification paths for technicians and surveyors, and report generation aligned to class society and OCIMF formatting expectations. Pairing that operational backbone with rigorous technician qualification tracking and, where a company is building out its written practice for marine NDT work, ASNT Level III consulting, closes the loop between what the system enforces and what your written practice actually requires — which matters just as much on a bulk carrier hull survey as it does on a refinery turnaround.
