title: ERP for Pipeline Integrity Services: PHMSA, API 1163, and ILI Data in One System
snippet: ERP for pipeline integrity services: managing PHMSA compliance deadlines, API 1163 ILI data, linear referencing, and dig verification NDT in a single system.
content:
Pipeline integrity data is a different animal from a single job report

A refinery turnaround produces inspection reports on a defined population of vessels and piping circuits within a fixed outage window. A pipeline integrity program produces a continuous, decades-long stream of data across hundreds or thousands of miles of buried and above-ground pipe — in-line inspection (ILI) runs, direct assessment digs, hydrostatic test records, and direct examination NDT results from excavations — all of which has to reconcile against a single, continuously updated integrity model for the line. Companies providing integrity services to pipeline operators, or operators managing this work internally, need a system built around that reality, not a generic job-tracking tool repurposed for pipeline work.

The regulatory framework driving the data requirements

PHMSA (the Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration) regulates pipeline integrity management under 49 CFR Part 192 for gas transmission and gathering lines and Part 195 for hazardous liquid pipelines. Both frameworks require operators to identify High Consequence Areas (HCAs), assess threats to pipeline integrity, and run structured integrity management programs with defined reassessment intervals — for gas transmission lines in HCAs, the baseline reassessment interval is a maximum of seven years under Part 192, subject to the specific risk-based adjustments the operator's program justifies. API 1163, "In-Line Inspection Systems Qualification," sets the standard for how ILI tool performance is qualified and how ILI data quality is validated — which matters enormously because everything downstream, from anomaly identification to repair prioritization, depends on the reported accuracy of the ILI vendor's tool for that specific run. A system supporting this work needs to track ILI tool qualification and reported tolerances alongside the actual anomaly data, not just the anomaly list on its own.

On top of PHMSA's federal framework, API 1160 (Managing System Integrity for Hazardous Liquid Pipelines) and the broader integrity management practices referenced across API RP 1173 (Pipeline Safety Management Systems) shape how operators structure their programs. None of these standards care what software you use — but every one of them drives a documentation and data-traceability expectation that a well-built system needs to satisfy by design, not by heroic effort during an audit.

What the data model actually needs to handle

Linear referencing, not point-in-space job records

Pipeline data is fundamentally linear — every anomaly, every dig, every ILI feature is located by distance along the line (often reconciled to a station or engineering stationing system, sometimes tied to GPS coordinates as well) rather than as an independent point location. A system built for plant or facility inspection, where every asset has a fixed tag number and location, doesn't naturally support this — pipeline integrity software needs linear referencing as a core data structure, with the ability to correlate features found in different ILI runs or different excavation digs to the same physical location on the line even as the referencing system gets refined over time.

ILI run management and feature correlation

Each ILI run — magnetic flux leakage (MFL), ultrasonic (UT) tools, or geometry/deformation tools — produces a feature list that has to be correlated against prior runs to calculate corrosion growth rates and against dig verification data to validate the ILI vendor's sizing accuracy. This correlation exercise is one of the most data-intensive and error-prone parts of pipeline integrity work when it's done manually across spreadsheets pulled from different ILI vendor formats over multiple run cycles.

Direct examination and dig verification NDT data

When an ILI-reported anomaly gets excavated for direct examination, the field NDT work — UT wall thickness measurement, MT for crack-like indications, sometimes phased array for more detailed crack sizing — needs to feed back into the same system that holds the original ILI call, so the integrity engineer can compare reported vs. actual and adjust confidence in that ILI tool's performance for the rest of the run. Treating the dig NDT report as a standalone document disconnected from the ILI feature record defeats the entire purpose of the verification dig.

Repair and remediation tracking against regulatory deadlines

Once an anomaly is confirmed and classified — immediate repair condition, scheduled repair, or monitored — PHMSA timelines apply (for gas transmission, immediate repair conditions generally require action within five days of discovery per Part 192 criteria, with scheduled conditions carrying longer but still defined windows). A system supporting integrity work needs to track these deadlines explicitly against each confirmed anomaly, not rely on an engineer's memory or a separate compliance spreadsheet running in parallel to the technical data.

Cathodic protection and coating condition data

External corrosion — one of the primary threats pipeline integrity programs manage — depends on cathodic protection system performance and coating condition, both of which get surveyed separately (close-interval surveys, DCVG, ACVG) from ILI and direct examination work but feed into the same overall threat assessment for a given segment. A system that silos CP survey data away from ILI and dig data makes integrated threat assessment — which is the actual point of an integrity management program — much harder than it needs to be.

Seam weld data and legacy pipe considerations

A meaningful share of the US pipeline network, particularly older gas transmission and hazardous liquid lines installed before modern seam weld quality controls, carries longitudinal seam types — low-frequency electric resistance welded (LF-ERW), lap-welded, or flash-welded seams among them — with known susceptibility to seam-related threats like selective seam corrosion or long-seam fatigue cracking. PHMSA's integrity management rules require operators to specifically consider seam type and vintage when selecting ILI technology, since not every ILI tool detects every seam threat with equal reliability — an MFL tool optimized for corrosion detection isn't necessarily the right tool for a crack-like seam threat, which typically calls for a UT crack-detection tool or electromagnetic acoustic transducer (EMAT) technology instead. A system managing pipeline integrity data needs pipe seam type and vintage as a queryable attribute at the segment level, because that single data point drives which ILI technology and which direct examination NDT methods are actually appropriate for a given stretch of line — treating every segment as interchangeable for tool selection purposes is a documented cause of missed threats industry-wide.

Coordinating data handoffs with ILI vendors and integrity engineering firms

Pipeline integrity work rarely involves just one company end to end — an ILI vendor runs the in-line tool and delivers a feature list, a separate integrity engineering firm may perform the threat assessment and prioritize digs, and an NDT services company performs the actual field verification at each dig site. Each of these parties typically uses its own internal systems, and the data handoff points between them are exactly where information gets lost, reformatted with errors, or delayed. A services company that can accept ILI feature data in the vendor's native export format, correlate it automatically to prior runs and dig history inside its own system, and hand back structured direct examination results in a format the integrity engineering firm can ingest directly — rather than a standalone PDF report requiring manual re-entry on the other end — becomes a measurably easier company for an operator to work with across a multi-vendor integrity program. This kind of interoperability is often an underrated factor in how pipeline operators evaluate and retain integrity services providers over multi-year program relationships.

Where a services company fits into this picture

For an NDT or integrity services company supporting pipeline operators rather than operating the line itself, the practical challenge is usually managing multiple clients' data cleanly — each with different pipeline systems, different ILI vendor relationships, and different reporting formats — while maintaining the crew certifications, equipment calibration, and job costing discipline that applies to any NDT operation. This is where a purpose-configured ERP system earns its keep: the same platform handling technician SNT-TC-1A certification tracking and equipment calibration for a refinery turnaround crew can be extended to handle dig-site scheduling, direct examination data capture, and client-specific reporting formats for pipeline integrity work, rather than running an entirely separate, disconnected system for this line of business.

Right-of-way access, landowner coordination, and scheduling reality

Excavation and direct examination work on a buried pipeline right-of-way involves logistics that plant-based inspection work simply doesn't: landowner notification and access agreements, agricultural or seasonal access restrictions in some regions, one-call/utility locate coordination before any excavation, and often significant travel between dig sites spread across long linear distances rather than a compact plant footprint. Scheduling software built for facility-based inspection work — where every job happens at a fixed, known-access site — doesn't map cleanly onto this reality. A system supporting pipeline integrity field work benefits from tracking access agreement status, locate ticket numbers and their expiration windows (most one-call locate tickets are valid for a limited period before requiring renewal), and realistic travel time between dispersed dig sites as explicit scheduling constraints, the same way certification and calibration status function as hard constraints elsewhere in NDT operations.

Reporting to state and federal regulators without a scramble

Beyond routine integrity management documentation, PHMSA reporting requirements include incident and safety-related condition reports under defined timelines, and state pipeline safety agencies operating under certification from PHMSA often layer their own reporting expectations on top of the federal baseline. When a reportable condition is identified — whether from an ILI call, a direct examination finding, or an in-service event — having the supporting integrity data (inspection history, prior run comparisons, repair history at that location) already organized and retrievable inside one system meaningfully shortens the time it takes to assemble an accurate, complete regulatory submission. Operators and the integrity services companies supporting them that discover during a live reporting deadline that key supporting data is scattered across old spreadsheets, email attachments, and a prior contractor's now-inaccessible files are working under exactly the wrong conditions to produce a careful, accurate submission.

Practical evaluation questions for a pipeline-integrity-capable system

  • Does the system support linear referencing natively, or would pipeline location data have to be forced into a point-asset model built for plant equipment?
  • Can ILI feature data be imported and correlated across multiple run cycles to calculate corrosion growth rates automatically, or does that stay a manual spreadsheet exercise?
  • Does direct examination NDT data from a verification dig link back to the specific ILI-reported feature it's validating?
  • Can the system track PHMSA repair condition classifications and their associated regulatory deadlines as first-class data, with alerts before deadlines lapse?
  • How does the system handle multi-client data segregation if you're providing integrity services to more than one operator?

Field data capture and the reporting layer

A dig crew performing direct examination in the field needs a fast, reliable way to capture UT thickness grids, MT indications, and photographic documentation on-site — often in remote right-of-way locations with limited connectivity — and have that data structured well enough to flow directly into both the client's integrity report and the ERP's job record without manual re-entry. This is precisely the gap purpose-built NDT reporting software closes, particularly when it supports offline data capture that syncs once the crew has connectivity again, which matters enormously for pipeline right-of-way work where cell coverage is often unreliable.

Geographic information system integration

Most pipeline operators maintain a GIS layer representing their system's geographic footprint, and integrity data ultimately needs to reconcile against that same spatial reference so that a corrosion feature, a dig location, or a repair record can be viewed in context alongside population density (relevant to High Consequence Area determination), waterway crossings, and other pipelines or infrastructure in the vicinity. A services company whose data stays purely in a linear-referencing, station-based format without any GIS export capability creates extra translation work for the operator's own integrity team every time that data needs to be layered into a broader system view — while a system that can export located features in a standard geospatial format removes a recurring friction point in what's usually a long-term, multi-year client relationship built on regularly recurring data handoffs.

The bottom line for integrity services companies

Pipeline integrity work rewards precision and traceability more than almost any other NDT services segment, because the consequence of a missed repair deadline or a mishandled ILI-to-dig correlation isn't a bad report — it's a real risk to a line carrying hazardous liquid or gas through populated areas. Building operations on a system that natively understands linear referencing, ILI run management, and regulatory deadline tracking — integrated with the same certification and calibration discipline that governs every other NDT service line — is what separates an integrity services company that scales cleanly from one perpetually reconstructing data from vendor spreadsheets. Getting the underlying qualification structure right for crews performing this specialized work is also where ASNT Level III consulting and rigorous technician training pay dividends well beyond the software layer.

title: Work Order Management Software for Multi-Crew NDT Companies
snippet: Work order management software for multi-crew NDT companies: how to dispatch crews and equipment without double-bookings, scope creep, or lost billing data.
content:
The point where a company outgrows "the owner keeps it all in their head"

Every NDT company has a moment where the informal system stops working. For a two-crew shop, the owner or ops manager can hold the whole picture in their head: who's on what job, what equipment is where, what's due when. Somewhere around four or five simultaneous crews — especially once they're spread across a turnaround site, a fabrication shop inspection, and a standalone field service call — that mental model breaks down, and it breaks down in specific, predictable ways: double-booked technicians, equipment that's supposed to be on two jobs at once, work orders that exist as a text message thread instead of a documented record, and a Friday afternoon scramble to figure out who's actually available for a Monday job that just came in. Work order management software exists to solve exactly this problem, but only if it's built around how multi-crew NDT operations actually function — not a generic field service template borrowed from HVAC or plumbing dispatch.

Why NDT work orders are structurally different from typical field service work

A generic field service work order usually needs: a customer, an address, a technician, and a time window. An NDT work order needs all of that plus a method or combination of methods (a single job might require UT and MT on the same components), a required certification level per method, specific equipment with current calibration status, applicable code or client procedure references, and — critically — a defined scope that often isn't fully known until the crew is on site and finds more indications than the original scope anticipated. A work order system that can't flex to capture scope changes mid-job, tie those changes back to accurate billing, and still maintain a clean audit trail of what was originally ordered versus what was actually performed isn't built for this industry.

What multi-crew dispatch actually requires

A single view of technician availability, certification, and location

A dispatcher managing five active crews needs to see, on one screen, who's currently assigned where, who's free, what each available technician is certified for, and roughly where they're located relative to a new job that just came in. Toggling between a certification spreadsheet, a separate scheduling calendar, and a group text thread to answer "who can I send to this job tomorrow" is exactly the failure mode that causes double-bookings and certification mismatches.

Equipment allocation tracked alongside technician allocation

Equipment doesn't move itself — a Phased Array unit or a radiography source assigned to a job in one city can't simultaneously be dispatched to a job three states away, and a work order system needs to treat equipment scheduling with the same rigor as technician scheduling, including calibration status checks at the point of assignment.

Real-time status visibility, not end-of-day reconciliation

When a crew arrives on site, starts work, encounters a scope change, or completes a job, that status needs to be visible to the office in near real time — not reconstructed the next morning from a technician's memory of what happened the day before. This matters for two concrete reasons: it lets a dispatcher redeploy a crew that finishes early to a same-day emergency call, and it means job costing and client updates are based on what's actually happening, not what happened a day ago.

Scope change and additional work documentation

NDT work orders change scope constantly — a UT thickness survey that finds unexpected wall loss triggers additional MT on adjacent welds, or a client asks for extra coverage once the crew is already mobilized. The system needs a clean way to document scope changes with client approval trails, both to protect billing accuracy and to maintain an honest record of what was actually inspected versus what was originally scoped, which matters if a report is ever questioned later.

Multi-site coordination for large turnarounds

During a major refinery or petrochemical turnaround, a single client engagement might involve a dozen or more technicians working across multiple units simultaneously, often coordinated with the client's own turnaround management system and multiple other contractors on site. Work order software needs to support this scale — grouping work orders under a master project, tracking crew rotation across shifts, and rolling up progress reporting the client's turnaround coordinator actually needs without your office staff manually compiling a daily update from scratch every evening.

Safety documentation and permit tracking belong on the work order, not in a separate binder

Industrial jobsites — refineries, chemical plants, fabrication yards — almost universally require site-specific safety documentation before a crew can start work: a job safety analysis (JSA), a hot work permit if radiography or any spark-producing activity is involved near a process unit, confined space entry permits for vessel internal inspections, and site-specific orientation records proving each technician has completed the client's HSE onboarding. When this documentation lives separately from the work order — a paper permit in a site trailer, an orientation record in an HR file — there's no single place to confirm, before dispatch, that every technician assigned to a job has what they need to legally and safely start work on arrival. A work order system that attaches permit status, JSA completion, and site orientation currency directly to the job and to each assigned technician turns "does this crew have everything they need for Monday" into a question the system can answer instantly, rather than a scramble the day before mobilization when someone discovers a technician's site orientation expired and needs to be redone.

What poor dispatch actually costs, beyond the obvious

The most visible cost of poor work order management is the double-booking everyone remembers — a technician showing up to find another crew already on site, or equipment arriving at the wrong location. The less visible, more persistent cost is the accumulation of small inefficiencies: technicians sitting idle for an hour because the next job's paperwork wasn't ready, crews routed inefficiently because nobody had visibility into geographic clustering of same-day jobs, or a piece of specialized equipment sitting unused in a warehouse while a job three hours away rents an equivalent unit because nobody checked availability first. None of these individually looks like a crisis. Collectively, across a fleet of five or more crews running continuously, this kind of friction is often the single largest drag on utilization — and utilization, not the headline day rate, is what actually determines whether a crew is profitable over a quarter.

Job costing that comes out the other side of dispatch, not bolted on separately

The real payoff of well-run work order management isn't just avoiding scheduling chaos — it's that clean dispatch data becomes clean job costing data automatically. When technician time, equipment usage, and consumables are captured against a specific work order as the job happens, rather than reconstructed from memory at invoicing time, the company gets accurate margin visibility by job, by crew, and by method without a separate manual costing exercise. This is one of the most underrated benefits of getting dispatch right: most NDT companies that struggle to answer "which lines of business are actually profitable" aren't missing an accounting problem, they're missing accurate field data capture at the point of work, which is a dispatch and work order problem first.

Client-facing visibility as a competitive differentiator

Large industrial clients running multi-contractor turnarounds increasingly expect their inspection vendors to provide real-time status visibility rather than end-of-shift phone updates — some turnaround management offices now run their own dashboards pulling contractor status feeds directly. An NDT company whose work order system can generate a live, accurate status feed of crew location, job progress, and completion percentage — without a project manager manually compiling that information from field calls every few hours — has a genuine competitive advantage when competing for large multi-crew turnaround contracts against companies still coordinating by phone and clipboard. This isn't a hypothetical nice-to-have; procurement teams evaluating NDT vendors for major turnaround work increasingly ask directly about reporting cadence and status transparency as part of the vendor selection criteria, alongside the more traditional questions about certifications and safety record.

Common failure patterns as companies scale past a handful of crews

  • Dispatch by group chat. Text message and phone-call-based dispatch works until it doesn't — there's no record, no certification check, and no way for a second dispatcher to step in and cover for the first without losing context.
  • Paper work orders that get data-entered later. Delayed data entry means the office is always working from information that's hours or days old, which defeats the purpose of trying to manage active operations in real time.
  • No connection between scheduling and certification/calibration status. As covered in depth elsewhere on this site, this is the gap that produces the worst outcomes — a technician or piece of equipment dispatched to a job it shouldn't have been eligible for.
  • Treating every job as a one-off instead of building a client and asset history. Recurring clients — a refinery running quarterly PT on specific vessels, for example — benefit enormously from a system that remembers the asset history and can pre-populate a new work order from the last one, rather than starting from scratch every time.

Handling emergency and short-notice work orders without derailing the planned schedule

Multi-crew NDT companies live with a constant tension between planned, scheduled work booked weeks in advance and short-notice or emergency requests — a suspected leak, an unplanned shutdown finding requiring immediate verification — that can't wait for the normal booking cycle. A work order system needs a clear process for slotting urgent work into an already-committed schedule without simply overwriting a planned job and hoping nobody notices the conflict later. That means visibility into which planned jobs have genuine schedule flexibility (a recurring low-urgency PT inspection that could reasonably shift a day) versus which are fixed and non-negotiable (a turnaround window that won't move regardless of what else comes up), so that an emergency request gets absorbed by adjusting the right job rather than the first one a dispatcher happens to see on the calendar.

Reporting rollups for owners and operations managers

Beyond the day-to-day dispatch function, the accumulated work order data becomes the raw material for the reporting an owner or operations manager actually needs to run the business: utilization rate by technician and by crew, on-time job start percentage, average time between job completion and report delivery, and revenue per crew per week. Most companies running informal dispatch processes can't answer these questions with real numbers — they can offer an impression, based on whoever's loudest about being busy, rather than data. A work order system that captures accurate timestamps automatically as jobs move through their lifecycle turns these questions into a report that runs in seconds instead of a guess based on anecdote, and that visibility is often what first reveals which crews or which service lines are genuinely driving profit versus which are quietly underperforming behind a busy-looking schedule.

What to look for in a system

The core test for any work order management system for a multi-crew NDT operation is simple: can a dispatcher, in under a minute, answer "who is qualified, available, and geographically sensible to send to this job, with what equipment, and is that equipment currently in calibration?" If the answer requires checking three separate systems, the software isn't actually solving the problem, regardless of how polished its calendar view looks. This is why work order and dispatch management is built as a core function of Atlantis NDT ERP rather than sold as an isolated scheduling app — because the answer to that question depends on certification data, calibration data, and job history all living in the same system, cross-referenced automatically rather than manually.

Onboarding new crews and new clients without breaking what already works

Growth itself puts pressure on a work order system in ways that are easy to underestimate. Adding a new crew, opening a new regional office, or winning a large new client with its own specific documentation and reporting requirements all mean new configuration — new certification requirements to track, new client-specific procedures to reference on work orders, sometimes new equipment types entirely. A system that requires a developer or the original implementation partner to make every configuration change becomes a bottleneck exactly when the company needs to move fastest — onboarding a new client relationship or standing up a new crew shouldn't take weeks of vendor back-and-forth. Evaluating how much day-to-day configuration your own office staff can handle directly, versus what genuinely requires outside development support, is worth clarifying with any vendor before signing, because that answer determines how much friction growth itself will create.

Scaling past the crisis point

Companies that get work order management right before they hit the crisis point of double-bookings and missed certifications tend to scale crew count far more smoothly than companies that wait until the pain forces the decision. The investment pays for itself less through any single avoided incident and more through the compounding effect of a dispatcher who can confidently take on more simultaneous jobs without the operational risk growing linearly with crew count. Pairing solid work order infrastructure with disciplined technician certification management and, for companies building out or refining their operational procedures, ASNT Level III consulting, is what actually lets a multi-crew NDT company grow without its quality and safety margins eroding along the way.

title: Inspection Scheduling Software: Dispatching NDT Crews Without the Spreadsheet Chaos
snippet: Inspection scheduling software for NDT crews: why certification, calibration, and travel-time constraints matter more than a pretty calendar, and how to fix dispatch.
content:
Scheduling is the daily operational bottleneck nobody budgets for

Ask an operations manager at a mid-size NDT company what actually eats their week, and dispatch and scheduling usually tops the list — not because any single scheduling decision is hard, but because it happens constantly, under constraints that shift by the hour: a technician calls in sick, a client pushes a job start time back four hours because a vessel isn't ready for entry, a shutdown job runs long and the crew scheduled for tomorrow's job is still on site tonight. A shared calendar or a whiteboard with magnets handles the easy version of this problem. It falls apart the moment you're juggling more than a handful of simultaneous jobs, because none of those tools actually encode the constraints that make an NDT scheduling decision valid in the first place: is this technician certified for this method at this level, is the required equipment calibrated and physically available, and can this person realistically get from yesterday's job site to today's on time.

Inspection scheduling software, done right, isn't a fancier calendar. It's a constraint-checking engine that happens to have a calendar view on top of it.

The constraints a real NDT scheduling decision has to satisfy

Certification match, not just headcount

"Do I have a free technician tomorrow" is the wrong question. The right question is "do I have a technician free tomorrow who's currently qualified for the specific method and technique this job requires" — UT general competency doesn't qualify someone for a Phased Array scope, and a lapsed vision exam disqualifies a technician regardless of how current their method certification otherwise is. A scheduling tool that shows availability without cross-referencing certification status is showing you an incomplete, and potentially dangerous, picture.

Equipment availability and calibration status

The technician being free doesn't help if the flaw detector, gauge, or radiography source the job requires is currently on a different job, in for calibration, or approaching a due date that will lapse mid-job. Equipment needs to be a first-class scheduling constraint alongside people, not an afterthought checked separately after the technician assignment is already locked in.

Geography and travel realism

A technician finishing a job in one part of a metro area at 3 PM cannot realistically start a new job ninety minutes away at 3:30. Scheduling software that ignores travel time between jobs produces schedules that look clean on a screen and fall apart in reality, which erodes trust in the system fast — technicians and dispatchers both learn to route around a tool that keeps generating impossible assignments.

Shift patterns and fatigue management on extended jobs

Turnaround and shutdown work often runs extended hours or rotating shifts over multiple weeks. Scheduling needs to track cumulative hours per technician not just for payroll accuracy but for fatigue and safety management — many client site safety programs impose hour limits or mandatory rest periods, and a scheduling system that can't track and flag against those limits pushes that responsibility back onto a supervisor's memory during exactly the highest-pressure, highest-fatigue period of the job.

Recurring versus one-off work

A refinery client running quarterly PT inspections on a defined set of vessels needs recurring scheduling logic — the system should be able to project future recurring jobs, flag when a recurring client's equipment or technician assignment history suggests a preferred crew, and prompt renewal scheduling before the interval lapses. A one-off emergency call-out needs the opposite: fast, ad hoc slotting into the schedule with immediate visibility into who's actually available right now.

Where spreadsheet and whiteboard scheduling actually fails

The failure isn't usually dramatic — it's a slow accumulation of small errors that eventually adds up to a real problem. A dispatcher assigns a technician to two overlapping jobs because the spreadsheet didn't show the first assignment clearly enough. A piece of equipment gets sent to a job three hours from where it's actually needed the next day because nobody cross-checked the following day's schedule before dispatching it. A technician's certification lapses mid-week and nobody catches it until the report gets signed, because the certification spreadsheet and the scheduling spreadsheet are two different files maintained by two different people. None of these errors show up as a dramatic system failure — they show up as a client complaint, a missed billing opportunity, or in the worst case, a compliance finding traced back weeks later to a scheduling decision nobody remembers making carefully.

What good scheduling software actually delivers

  • A single schedule view that encodes constraints, not just availability. When a dispatcher looks at open slots, the system should already have filtered out technicians who aren't certified for the job or whose travel time makes the slot unrealistic — not display every technician and rely on the dispatcher to manually check each one.
  • Mobile access for field crews. Technicians need to see their assignments, accept or flag issues with a job, and update status from a phone at the jobsite — not call the office to report they've arrived or finished, which ties up office staff and introduces a lag between what's happening in the field and what the schedule shows.
  • Automatic conflict detection. The system should refuse, or at minimum loudly flag, any attempt to double-book a technician or piece of equipment, rather than silently accepting a conflicting assignment that someone discovers the hard way.
  • Change propagation. When a job's start time shifts, everyone affected — the technician, the equipment allocation, any downstream job that technician was scheduled for next — needs to see that change immediately, not learn about it from a separate phone call or text message that may or may not happen.
  • Recurring job projection. For clients with standing inspection contracts, the system should surface upcoming recurring work far enough in advance to schedule proactively rather than reactively.

Weather, site access, and the constant need to replan

Outdoor and offshore-adjacent NDT work — pipeline right-of-way digs, tank inspections, structural work on offshore platforms or at marine terminals — is routinely disrupted by weather in ways that plant-floor inspection work generally isn't. A lightning warning halts elevated work and radiography immediately under most site safety programs. High wind can suspend crane-supported access equipment needed for tank shell inspection. A scheduling system that has no mechanism for rapidly replanning a full day's crew assignments when weather forces an unplanned stoppage leaves that replanning entirely to a dispatcher working the phones under pressure, often while several other jobs are simultaneously affected by the same weather system. Software that supports rapid bulk rescheduling — reassigning an entire day's disrupted jobs to the next available window, factoring in which technicians and equipment are already committed elsewhere — turns a stressful, error-prone scramble into a structured process, even though it can never eliminate the underlying disruption weather causes.

Emergency and on-call scheduling

Beyond planned work, most NDT companies maintain some on-call capacity for emergency inspection requests — a suspected leak requiring immediate UT verification, an unplanned shutdown requiring rapid mobilization. On-call scheduling has different constraints than planned dispatch: it needs to identify, in minutes rather than hours, which currently off-duty technician is both qualified for the likely scope and reasonably positioned to respond quickly, and it needs to respect labor rules and fatigue limits so an on-call callout doesn't inadvertently push a technician past a safe consecutive-hours threshold before their next planned shift. A scheduling system that maintains an accurate, current picture of technician certification and recent hours worked — the same data it already needs for planned dispatch — can support this decision in real time instead of requiring a manager to manually call down a mental list of who might be available.

Handling subcontracted and 1099 technicians

Many NDT companies supplement their core crew with subcontracted technicians during peak turnaround season. Scheduling software needs to handle this cleanly — tracking a subcontractor's certifications with the same rigor as an employee's, managing their availability and rate structure separately from payroll technicians, and making sure a subcontractor assigned to a job is held to the exact same certification and calibration verification standard as anyone else on the crew. Treating subcontractor scheduling as an informal, off-system process is a common gap that undermines the entire point of having rigorous scheduling controls in the first place — the standard has to apply to everyone touching a report, regardless of employment status.

Forecasting crew capacity before it becomes a hiring crisis

Beyond day-to-day dispatch, a well-built scheduling system doubles as a capacity planning tool. If a dispatcher can see, three months out, that recurring client commitments plus seasonal turnaround demand will require more UT-Phased-Array-qualified technicians than the company currently has certified and available, that's a hiring and training lead-time problem best identified early — qualifying a technician to a new method or technique takes months of documented training and experience hours under SNT-TC-1A, not something that can be solved with a week's notice. Companies that only discover a capacity gap when they're already turning down work because nobody's available are, in effect, using missed revenue as their capacity planning signal. A scheduling system with visibility into projected recurring work and current certification coverage across the whole technician roster turns that into a proactive planning exercise instead of a reactive scramble every time demand spikes.

What the transition period actually feels like

Moving a company off phone-and-spreadsheet dispatch onto a real scheduling system rarely feels like an immediate improvement in week one, and it's worth setting that expectation honestly rather than overselling a smooth transition. Dispatchers who've built years of mental shortcuts around which technicians work well together or which clients need extra hand-holding have to learn to trust a new tool instead of their own memory, and the first few weeks often involve double-checking the system's suggestions against gut instinct before confidence builds. That trust-building period is normal and shouldn't be read as a sign the system isn't working — the real signal to watch for is whether double-bookings and missed certification conflicts drop measurably once the certification and calibration data underlying the system is fully populated and accurate, which typically takes a full scheduling cycle or two to stabilize after go-live.

The connection to job costing and client communication

Accurate scheduling data — who actually worked when, on what job, using what equipment — is also the raw material for accurate job costing and client billing. When scheduling and actual field status live in the same system, invoicing reflects reality rather than an office administrator's best reconstruction of the week. It also means client-facing status updates — "your crew arrived on site at 7 AM and gauging is underway" — can be generated from live data instead of a phone call to the field, which matters a great deal for clients managing a tight turnaround schedule of their own and needing real-time confidence that their inspection scope is on track.

Balancing crew preference against pure optimization

A purely algorithmic dispatch approach that optimizes strictly for geographic efficiency and certification match can miss a factor that matters just as much to long-term retention: technicians generally perform better and stay longer at companies that give some weight to consistency and preference, not just optimal routing on paper. A technician who's built a working relationship with a specific client's site contacts, or who prefers a particular rotation pattern for family reasons, represents real value a purely mechanical scheduling algorithm won't capture unless the system is configured to weight those factors deliberately. The best scheduling software supports this as a configurable input — preferred client-technician pairings, rotation preferences — rather than treating every assignment as an interchangeable optimization problem with people as the variable being optimized.

Building this without over-engineering it

The trap a lot of growing NDT companies fall into is either staying on spreadsheets far too long, or jumping straight to an expensive, overbuilt enterprise scheduling suite designed for a much larger field service operation with completely different constraints. The right target is scheduling functionality that's tightly integrated with certification tracking, equipment calibration, and job costing — because those three things are exactly what makes an NDT scheduling decision valid — without carrying the overhead of a system built for an industry that doesn't share these constraints. This integrated approach is the core design principle behind the scheduling and dispatch functionality in Atlantis NDT ERP: one system where a scheduling decision is automatically checked against certification and calibration data, rather than three separate systems a dispatcher has to manually reconcile under time pressure. For companies also investing in asset visualization for their larger clients, that same scheduling and inspection history becomes part of a much richer picture of asset condition over time — but getting the day-to-day dispatch mechanics right is the foundation everything else builds on.

title: Document Control Software for ISO 9001 NDT Companies
snippet: How ISO 9001:2015 Clause 7.5 applies to NDT companies: controlled vs. uncontrolled field copies, SNT-TC-1A linkage, and what auditors ask for at the document station.
content:
When "Rev 3" Isn't What's in the Truck

A UT technician shows up to a refinery turnaround with a laminated procedure in his gear bag — the same one he's used on the last four jobs. What he doesn't know is that the quality manager revised it six weeks earlier after a client audit flagged a calibration reference that no longer matched the equipment fleet. The revision went out by email to a distribution list that hadn't been updated since two technicians left. His copy is Rev 2. The controlled copy is Rev 3. Nobody catches it until the client's inspection engineer cross-checks the procedure number during report review, and now the shop is explaining why three days of UT data may need re-verification against the correct acceptance criteria.

This is not a hypothetical. It's the most common finding an ISO 9001:2015 surveillance auditor or a client pre-qualification auditor writes up against small and mid-sized NDT companies, and it's almost never a competence problem — it's a document control problem, one generic file storage was never built to solve. This piece covers what Clause 7.5 requires in NDT-specific terms, where version control breaks in the real world, how it intersects with your SNT-TC-1A written practice, and what separates a folder of PDFs from a system an auditor will trust.

What ISO 9001:2015 Clause 7.5 Actually Requires

Clause 7.5, Documented Information, is short in the standard's text but expansive in what it obligates a certified NDT company to do day to day. It splits into two jobs: creating and updating documented information (7.5.2) and controlling it once it exists (7.5.3.1, 7.5.3.2). For an NDT shop, "documented information" isn't abstract — it's your UT/MT/PT/RT/ET procedures, written practice, calibration records, inspection reports, certification files, NCR/CAPA forms, and quality manual.

Creating, Updating, and Controlling Documents

7.5.2 requires identification and description (title, date, author, reference number — what lets you tell Rev 2 from Rev 3 at a glance), an appropriate format, and review and approval for suitability before a document goes live. In practice, every revision needs a named technical reviewer (usually your ASNT Level III) and a documented approval step before it reaches a technician's hands — not an approval created retroactively for an audit.

7.5.3.1 and 7.5.3.2 are where most shops fail. The standard requires documented information to be available where and when needed, and protected from loss of confidentiality, improper use, or loss of integrity, through specific controls: distribution, access, retrieval and use; storage and preservation including legibility; control of changes; and retention and disposition. A shared drive with folders named "Procedures" and "Procedures OLD" satisfies almost none of that checklist, because a folder structure doesn't control access, doesn't track who changed what, and doesn't prove an obsolete file was pulled from circulation rather than just renamed.

Retention and Disposition Aren't One Rule

Quality records — calibration certificates, certification records, inspection reports, NCR/CAPA files — typically have retention periods driven by contract terms, client specs, or code requirements (API 510/570/653 inspection records, for example, are often retained for the life of the asset plus a defined period, per the owner-user's fitness-for-service program). Controlled procedures work differently: once superseded, the current revision must be removed from active circulation immediately, but the superseded revision is often retained as a historical record — if a client questions a report from eighteen months ago, you need to show which revision was in force that date, not what the procedure says today. A document control system needs to distinguish those states cleanly: obsolete-and-inaccessible-for-use versus obsolete-but-retained-for-traceability. Conflating them is a common finding.

Controlled vs. Uncontrolled Copies in the Field

The controlled-copy/uncontrolled-copy distinction is old quality-manual language, but it maps directly onto NDT field reality. A controlled copy is one the system guarantees is current — distribution is tracked, and when the document changes, every controlled copy is updated or recalled. An uncontrolled copy is a snapshot, valid the moment it was printed or downloaded, no guarantee after. Almost all NDT field work happens on uncontrolled copies by default: a technician on a shutdown, often without reliable signal, isn't refreshing a live document viewer between shots — he's working from a printed binder, a PDF saved to a tablet before leaving the yard, or a laminated card that's been in his bag for a year.

ISO 9001 doesn't forbid this — it requires the risk be managed. The two accepted approaches: stamp printed copies "UNCONTROLLED COPY — VALID AT TIME OF PRINTING ONLY" and force re-verification against the master before each job; or give technicians live access to the controlled master through a mobile-capable system that checks revision status the moment connectivity is available, even if offline during the inspection itself. The first depends entirely on technician discipline at the point of use — exactly where the refinery scenario above breaks down. The second is what a document-control module inside an NDT ERP platform does: sync the current revision to the device before the crew leaves the shop, flag anything stale, and log the check automatically.

Where Version Control Actually Breaks at NDT Shops

The failure modes are consistent industry-wide, and worth naming specifically because they're what an auditor probes for:

  • The turnaround scenario. A procedure revises mid-outage — a new acceptance criterion, a corrected reflector size, a scan pattern change — and the distribution list is stale or the notice sits unopened in a busy supervisor's inbox. Technicians keep working the old revision because nothing at the point of use tells them otherwise.
  • The superseded written practice still in a drawer. A company updates its SNT-TC-1A written practice — a re-test interval, an exam matrix for a new method — but old printed copies stay in truck cabs because no formal recall ran. An auditor pulls a random copy off a shelf and it doesn't match current certification records.
  • Parallel "master" files. Two people each believe they hold the master calibration procedure because both have edit access to the same shared folder, each making small, undocumented edits over time — no single source of truth, and metadata most cloud drives don't reliably preserve across downloads.

None of these are competence failures. The document was correct and the approval was correct — the control meant to keep the two in sync didn't exist or wasn't followed.

Document Control and the SNT-TC-1A Written Practice

The written practice sits at the intersection of two obligations: it's a controlled document under Clause 7.5, and the governing document for your entire personnel certification program under ASNT's Recommended Practice SNT-TC-1A. Get the document control wrong and you don't just have an ISO nonconformance — you have a defensibility problem for every certification issued under that written practice's authority.

A properly controlled written practice needs its own revision history (a method added, an experience-hour requirement adjusted), formal approval by the person with that authority — typically your Level III — and a documented link between each certification record and the revision in effect when it was issued or renewed. If your written practice moves to Rev 5 and you can't show which certifications were qualified under Rev 4 versus Rev 5, those certifications are hard to defend during an audit or dispute. This is the kind of record a document-control capability inside an operations platform handles cleanly: the revision is timestamped and linked, and the chain is pullable in one query rather than reconstructed from memory. Companies rebuilding certification programs from scratch often lean on outside ASNT Level III consulting to get this linkage right the first time.

The Controlled Forms That Carry the Most Risk

A handful of controlled forms account for most findings and most legal exposure if they're wrong:

  • Inspection procedures (UT, MT, PT, RT, ET, TOFD, Phased Array) — the document defining acceptance criteria, and the one most likely to be field-superseded without proper recall.
  • Calibration records — equipment-specific and date-stamped, tied directly to the validity of every reading taken during that interval. A missing or expired record can invalidate an entire report's data.
  • WPS/PQR references pulled into NDT reports — when RT or UT results are evaluated against a Welding Procedure Specification and its Qualification Record, the report needs the correct, current revision, not whichever version was on file when the job was quoted months earlier.
  • Nonconformance and CAPA forms — auditors trust these least by default, because a shop that never generates an NCR reads as either flawless or not looking. A controlled, trackable CAPA form with closure evidence is one of the fastest ways to demonstrate a functioning quality system.

Every one of these forms benefits from being a controlled template rather than something technicians recreate from an old job. When the form lives inside the same system that generates the inspection report, a field revision propagates automatically instead of depending on someone remembering to redistribute a file — one argument for producing reports through NDT reporting software tied to the same controlled-document backbone as the rest of the QMS.

Electronic Signatures and Audit Trails vs. Wet Ink

Wet-ink workflows are still common in NDT, and ISO 9001 doesn't require electronic signatures — but wet ink creates a specific weakness: a signature only proves someone signed paper, not that the signed version is the one currently in circulation. Reconstructing an approval history means physically locating signed originals, which get lost, filed inconsistently across sites, or signed out of sequence when someone's traveling.

An electronic signature with a real audit trail solves a more useful problem: it captures who approved a specific revision, the exact timestamp, and — done correctly — a user-level log of every view, download, and edit taken afterward. When an auditor asks "show me who approved Rev 4 and when," the answer needs to come back in under a minute from a system record, not a filing cabinet. Response time is read as a proxy for whether a control functions daily or only on paper. A system that can also show Rev 3 was pulled from active device caches at the same timestamp Rev 4 was approved closes the loop auditors are trained to test.

Three Ways to Manage Document Control — And What Each Costs You

Most NDT companies land on one of three approaches, each with real tradeoffs rather than an obvious universal winner:

  • Generic file-sharing (SharePoint, Google Drive, Dropbox folders). Cheap and familiar — fine for a one- or two-person shop with a small procedure library. The failure is structural: these tools weren't built to enforce single-source-of-truth for controlled documents. Version history isn't organized around approval workflows, nothing forces obsolete files out of active use, and permissions loosen over time. It works until an auditor asks for a controlled-document register with approval dates, and someone spends a weekend reconstructing it by hand.
  • A dedicated, standalone QMS document-control module, sold separately from anything else you run. This solves the control problem properly — approval workflows, e-signatures, and audit trails are the whole point. The tradeoff: it's another system of record to keep in sync with operational data. Technician files, job records, and calibration schedules live in one platform while the documents governing them live in another, and someone maintains that mapping manually — reintroducing the sync problem the module was bought to solve, one layer up.
  • Document control built into an ERP that also runs scheduling, job costing, and certification tracking. The advantage is a single source of truth: the procedure revision linked to a job is the same record the scheduler pulled the technician's certification from and the report generator cited for acceptance criteria, no manual reconciliation needed. The honest tradeoff: the module must be genuinely built for ISO 9001 compliance, not bolted on as a generic attachment feature — a folder of PDFs inside job software isn't document control just because it lives inside an ERP. Atlantis NDT ERP treats document control as a first-class module — revision approval, controlled-copy distribution to field devices, audit-trail logging — not a file cabinet bolted onto scheduling software.

The right answer scales with company size and audit exposure. A two-person shop doing local plant work may be fine on disciplined shared folders. A shop running turnaround work for major EPCs, or past the point where one person remembers every open revision by heart, carries real risk on folder discipline alone.

What an Auditor Actually Asks at the Document Control Station

Whether it's an ISO 9001:2015 surveillance audit or a pre-qualification audit before awarding turnaround work, this station follows a predictable script:

  • "Pull up the current approved revision of this UT procedure and the approval record — who approved it, and when." A fast lookup, not a search.
  • "Show me the previous revision has been removed from circulation." The one most shops fail — most systems show the new version exists without proving the old one is gone from every device and binder it reached.
  • "Walk me through what happens when a procedure is revised — who gets notified, how do you confirm the field received it." Auditors listen for a repeatable process, not good intentions.
  • "Show me this technician's certification record and the written practice revision it was issued under." The SNT-TC-1A linkage question, asked more often than shops expect.

Every question tests the same thing: can the system produce a specific, dated, attributable answer quickly, or does it require memory, a phone call, or a manual search. Speed here is read as evidence of whether the quality system is operated for real or maintained for the audit.

Migrating From Paper or Shared Drives

Moving from paper binders or an unstructured shared drive into a controlled system is a real project, and rushing it creates its own risk. A realistic sequence starts with a document inventory — every procedure, form, and written practice in use, current revision confirmed against the master, not assumed from a filename — which becomes the controlled-document register. Next is formal approval of record for each document entering the new system, even unchanged ones, so there's a clean starting point rather than an ambiguous handoff. Field distribution needs a hard cutover date, with old printed copies formally recalled rather than left to expire naturally — "naturally" is exactly how the turnaround scenario at the top of this piece happens.

Historical records don't need to enter the live system at all; they need archiving somewhere retrievable, tagged with retention/disposition dates, separate from the active register. Most shops find the transition faster paired with broader onboarding, refreshing procedures alongside the new system, where NDT training support and Level III oversight catch outdated content before it's carried forward as a "controlled" version of something already wrong.

Document control isn't the most technically demanding part of an NDT quality system, but it's disproportionately where certifications get put at risk — not because the inspection work was bad, but because nobody could quickly prove which version of the rules it was performed under. Building that proof into daily operations, rather than reconstructing it under audit pressure, is the entire point.

title: Quality Management Software for Calibration Laboratories (ISO/IEC 17025)
snippet: How ISO/IEC 17025 calibration labs use QMS software for NIST traceability, uncertainty budgets, interval scheduling, and audit-ready records instead of spreadsheets.
content:
A UT thickness gauge goes out on a piping circuit inspection at a Gulf Coast refinery. The tech grabs it off the shelf, runs a two-point check against the site's step wedge, and gets to work. Three days later, back at the shop, someone notices the gauge's own calibration certificate expired the day before the job. Nobody caught it because it was tracked on a spreadsheet, in a tab nobody opened that week. Every reading on that job is now suspect, and if the lab is A2LA or ANAB accredited, dispatching an expired gauge is a nonconformance that has to be logged and root-caused. This is the scenario calibration lab QMS software exists to prevent — and why spreadsheets and calendar reminders stop being adequate once a lab is running under ISO/IEC 17025:2017 with real accreditation on the line.

For an NDT company that operates its own calibration lab — thickness gauges, hardness testers, MT yokes and ammeters, PT black lights and radiometers, RT densitometers and step wedges — this isn't an abstract IT decision. It's the difference between an audit that takes two hours and one that takes two days, and between field crews who can trust the case they grab off the shelf and crews who have to double-check everything because the tracking system is only as current as the last update.

ISO/IEC 17025:2017 Clauses 6-8: What Actually Drives Software Requirements

ISO/IEC 17025:2017 has eight clauses, but three of them are where a QMS platform earns or loses its keep. Clause 4 (impartiality and confidentiality) and Clause 5 (structural requirements) matter for governance; Clauses 6, 7, and 8 are different — each maps almost line for line onto a feature an assessor expects to see demonstrated on screen, not described in a policy manual.

  • Clause 6 — Resources. 6.2 requires documented competence for every person who calibrates, reviews, or authorizes results. 6.4 requires equipment — including the lab's own reference standards — uniquely identified, on a defined calibration program, and protected from adjustment that would invalidate results. 6.5 is metrological traceability: every result links, through an unbroken chain of calibrations, back to the SI unit via a national metrology institute or an ILAC MRA-recognized lab.
  • Clause 7 — Process. The longest clause and the one with the most software touchpoints: 7.1 review of requests, 7.2 method selection and verification, 7.4 handling of calibration items (receipt, unique ID, condition on arrival, storage), 7.5 technical records, 7.6 evaluation of measurement uncertainty, 7.7 ensuring validity of results (proficiency testing, interlaboratory comparisons, control charts), 7.8 reporting of results, and 7.10 nonconforming work.
  • Clause 8 — Management system. Document control, control of records, corrective action, internal audit, and management review — the same system of record an assessor reviews for document revision history and CAPA closure, not a calibration tracker bolted onto the side of the business.

Every one of those sub-clauses generates a specific artifact — a competency record, a traceability chain, an uncertainty budget, a technical record, a CAPA entry — and assessors are trained to ask for the artifact, not the policy statement describing it.

Metrological Traceability to NIST: The Chain Your System Has to Preserve

Traceability is the most assessor-tested concept in the standard, and the one spreadsheets handle worst because it's relational, not tabular. Every certificate a lab issues has to show the reference standard used — a gauge block set, a multifunction calibrator — was itself calibrated by a source with a documented, unbroken chain back to the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) or another recognized national metrology institute. That chain isn't a single link: a working standard traces to a reference standard, which traces to a calibration from an accredited external lab, whose own standards trace to NIST — each hop with its own certificate number, date, and uncertainty figure that has to be retrievable.

In a spreadsheet system, that chain lives as a scanned PDF filed under an asset number, cross-referenced (if you're lucky) in a column someone typed a cert number into by hand. When an assessor pulls a certificate issued eighteen months ago and asks for the traceability chain behind it, someone walks backward through folders manually. In a properly built QMS, that chain is a data relationship: the certificate links to the reference standard's asset record, which links to its own current and superseding certificates, which link to the accredited supplier's scope of accreditation — a lookup, not an investigation, and one of the fastest ways to keep a routine surveillance visit from becoming a suspended scope.

Calibration Intervals: Fixed Schedules vs. Reliability-Based Adjustment

Most labs start with fixed intervals — annual for a UT thickness gauge, six months for a black light radiometer — whatever the manufacturer or a generic industry table suggests. That's a legitimate starting point, but the standard (via Clause 6.4 and supporting guidance in ILAC-G24 / OIML D 10) expects a documented methodology for adjusting intervals based on actual performance, not habit: "automatic adjustment" (extend or shorten by a fixed ratio depending on whether the last calibration was in or out of tolerance), the "control chart" method (track drift and set the interval where projected drift approaches the tolerance limit), and "in-service time" methods for equipment with variable usage.

For equipment that sees hard field use — an MT yoke dropped on scaffolding, a UT gauge living in a truck through Houston summers — a fixed 12-month interval might be dangerously long if drift data shows out-of-tolerance trending by month eight. A rarely-used reference hardness tester in a climate-controlled lab might legitimately go to 24 months with data behind it, saving real turnaround time. The catch: reliability-based adjustment only works if someone tracks as-found/as-left data every cycle and runs the numbers — longitudinal analysis a spreadsheet resists (formulas break, a cell gets overwritten, the "master" file forks) and a database-backed QMS handles natively. Software that flags equipment off a static due-date is doing the bare minimum; software that shows a drift trend across cycles is doing what 17025 actually asks for.

Measurement Uncertainty Budgets: Why Spreadsheets Break Down at Scale

Clause 7.8.3.1(c) is unambiguous in a way the testing side of the standard isn't: a calibration certificate has to state measurement uncertainty whenever it's relevant to the result's validity or application — for calibration, essentially always. That figure isn't pulled from a spec sheet. Under GUM (Guide to the Expression of Uncertainty in Measurement) methodology, it's a budget: reference standard uncertainty, resolution of the unit under test, environmental drift, operator repeatability, and the reference standard's own drift since its last calibration, combined in quadrature and expanded by a coverage factor (typically k=2, ~95% confidence).

One uncertainty budget for one gauge type is a manageable spreadsheet. The problem is scale: a lab supporting UT, MT, PT, and RT equipment might run budgets across fifteen or twenty instrument types. Every time a reference standard is recalibrated and its stated uncertainty shifts, every downstream budget citing it should technically be revisited — a propagation that doesn't happen automatically in a spreadsheet, because nobody remembers which of thirty tabs reference that standard. That's the stale-data gap an assessor probes by asking when a budget was last reviewed against the standard's current calibration. A calibration-specific QMS that stores uncertainty components as structured data tied to the reference standard's live record can flag every affected budget the moment the parent certificate changes.

What A2LA, ANAB, and PJLA Assessors Actually Pull

US-based calibration labs accredit through one of three ILAC MRA-signatory bodies: A2LA (American Association for Laboratory Accreditation), ANAB (ANSI National Accreditation Board), or PJLA (Perry Johnson Laboratory Accreditation). What gets pulled during a surveillance or reassessment visit is consistent across all three:

  • Scope of accreditation control — is every issued certificate within the lab's accredited scope (parameters, ranges, best measurement capability), with no quiet drift outside it on a one-off job.
  • Proficiency testing and ILC records — Clause 7.7 requires ongoing validity monitoring via PT/interlaboratory comparisons: the provider's report, the lab's z-score or En-number evaluation, and corrective action for any out-of-range result.
  • Technical record completeness — for a randomly selected certificate, can the lab produce raw as-found/as-left readings, logged environmental conditions, the technician's competency record, the reference standard's traceability chain, and the uncertainty budget, all cross-referenced.
  • Nonconforming work handling — Clause 7.10 requires a documented process for identifying, containing, and dispositioning nonconforming calibrations, including client notification, with actual logged instances, not just the procedure.
  • Corrective action closure — evidence that findings from the last audit cycle were root-caused and closed, not just opened.

A lab walking into a reassessment on spreadsheets and a filing cabinet spends the assessment finding things; a lab with a real QMS spends it showing things, which changes both duration and tone.

The Three-Day Gauge Problem: Due-Dates Meet Field Dispatch

Calibration due-date tracking sounds like a back-office concern until it collides with field scheduling, which is where it actually creates risk. An NDT company running UT surveys, MT/PT crack detection, and RT film work needs job dispatch and calibration status living in one system, not two that someone reconciles manually — the failure mode being the scenario at the top of this post: a gauge with three days left goes out on a five-day job and comes back non-compliant, or a radiometer due next week gets grabbed because it's the only one on the shelf.

The risk compounds under API 653, API 510, and ASME code work, where a client's QA specification may require proof of current, traceable calibration for every instrument used — not just at report time, but when the reading was taken. If calibration lapses mid-job, every reading after the lapse is technically unsupportable, which can mean re-inspection, a client complaint, or an integrity decision made on data that can't be defended. This is why due-date tracking belongs inside the same platform that handles scheduling: a scheduler assigning a tech should get an automatic warning if the equipment is inside a defined buffer window of its due date, not find out after the fact. Platforms like Atlantis NDT ERP are built around exactly this integration — calibration status, scheduling, and technician records in one place, so a gauge three days from due can't be assigned to a five-day job without someone consciously overriding a flag, itself a documented decision instead of a silent gap.

Personnel Competency Records: 17025 Is Not the Same File as SNT-TC-1A

This trips up a lot of NDT companies running their own cal labs, because both records answer "is this person qualified," and it's tempting to file them together. They're not the same thing, and an assessor treats them as two separate lines of evidence.

ASNT SNT-TC-1A is a recommended practice for qualifying and certifying NDT personnel — technicians performing UT, RT, MT, PT, ET, VT, or phased array inspections in the field — through documented training hours, experience hours, and a written/practical/general exam under an employer's written procedure. It answers whether a technician is qualified to perform and interpret a given NDT method. ISO/IEC 17025 Clause 6.2, by contrast, concerns the competence of laboratory personnel to perform calibration work specifically — operating calibration equipment, evaluating results, calculating uncertainty, authoring or authorizing a certificate — assessed through defined competence criteria, training records, and often witnessed calibrations, and it applies even to a technician whose SNT-TC-1A qualification has nothing to do with calibration bench work.

A technician can hold a current SNT-TC-1A Level II in UT and still not be competent to calibrate under 17025 if never trained and signed off on the lab's specific procedures and uncertainty methodology — and calibration competence under Clause 6.2 has no bearing on field inspection qualification. A QMS needs to keep these as genuinely separate records — separate criteria, evidence, and renewal triggers — rather than a single "certified" flag on an employee profile. Companies building out both sides often lean on structured NDT training and certification and outside ASNT Level III consulting to keep the two documented correctly and distinct from day one, since conflating them is a common finding on first-time accreditation.

Spreadsheets vs. Standalone Trackers vs. an ERP-Integrated QMS Module

In practice, a calibration lab chooses between three tiers of tooling, each with a real tradeoff profile:

  • Spreadsheets and shared folders. Zero cost and infinitely flexible — and exactly why they're dangerous at scale: no enforced relationship between a certificate, its uncertainty budget, and its traceability chain, no automatic due-date flagging tied to dispatch, no audit trail on who changed what. Workable for a one- or two-gauge shop; a real liability past a few dozen assets.
  • Standalone calibration-management software. Purpose-built trackers handle the calibration-specific work well — due-date automation, certificate generation, uncertainty budget templates, traceability linking — a real improvement over spreadsheets. The gap is integration: they typically sit outside the system handling job dispatch, so someone still has to manually check a separate system before sending a tech out, and the three-day gauge scenario slips through at the handoff.
  • An ERP with a built-in calibration/QMS module. The advantage isn't necessarily deeper calibration features than a dedicated tool — it's that calibration status, technical records, and uncertainty data live in the same database as job scheduling and technician competency, so due-date enforcement happens automatically at dispatch instead of a manual cross-check. For an NDT company where the cal lab supports field operations, that integration usually matters more than deeper standalone features, because it closes the exact gap where nonconformances happen.

The real test of any of these three shows up during a reassessment audit's evidence pull. A typical A2LA or ANAB reassessment has the assessor select a handful of issued certificates at random and ask the lab to reconstruct everything behind them, live: the technical record, the technician's competency file at the time of the work, the reference standard's own current traceability chain, the uncertainty budget with its component values, and confirmation the reference standard was itself current on the job date. In a spreadsheet environment that reconstruction can take twenty minutes per certificate; multiplied across four or five sampled certificates, that's a half-day assessment becoming a two-day one. In an integrated system it's a handful of lookups, because the relationships were built into the data model from the start — and assessors read that speed as a proxy for whether the Clause 8 management system actually functions day to day. For labs also tracking asset condition alongside calibration, a digital twin platform extends that same connected-data logic to the physical equipment itself.

None of this replaces sound calibration technique or a well-written quality manual — software doesn't calibrate the gauge or write the uncertainty methodology. What it does is make sure the paper trail 17025 requires actually exists, stays connected, and can be produced on demand — the difference between a technically sound calibration program and one that survives contact with an assessor.
