title: API 580/581 RBI Consulting: What a Risk-Based Inspection Program Setup Costs in Time
snippet: API 580 vs. 581 explained, with realistic phase-by-phase time ranges for RBI program setup on a mid-size refinery unit or gas plant, from data gathering to intervals.
content:
The question inspection leads and reliability managers actually need answered before committing to a Risk-Based Inspection program isn't "what will this cost" — it's "how long is this going to take, and what does my team need to do during that time." RBI setup is a data and workshop-intensive process, and underestimating the time commitment is the single most common reason RBI programs stall out mid-implementation, six months in, with half the asset register screened and momentum gone. This piece walks through the actual phases of standing up an API 580/581 RBI program, with realistic time ranges for a mid-size refinery process unit or gas plant, so you can plan resourcing and schedule expectations honestly from the start — not a dollar figure in sight, because the real constraint here is calendar time and the availability of the people who hold the process and inspection knowledge you need.

API 580 vs. API 581: Two Documents, One Program

API RP 580 (Risk-Based Inspection) is the practice standard. It defines what an RBI program needs to contain — the organizational elements, the RBI team composition, the data requirements, the process for identifying damage mechanisms, the requirement to assess both probability and consequence of failure, and how risk assessment results should drive inspection planning (method, coverage, and interval). API 580 is method-agnostic in the sense that it accommodates qualitative, semi-quantitative, and fully quantitative approaches to risk assessment — it sets the framework, not the calculation engine. API RP 581 (Risk-Based Inspection Methodology) is the quantitative methodology that most refineries and gas plants actually use to execute what API 580 requires. It provides the calculation procedures: probability of failure (POF) derived from generic industry failure frequencies, adjusted by a damage factor specific to the actual corrosion and cracking mechanisms active in each equipment item (thinning, external damage, stress corrosion cracking, and others per API 571's damage mechanism taxonomy), and further adjusted by a management systems factor reflecting the quality of the facility's mechanical integrity program. Consequence of failure (COF) is calculated separately — for flammable and toxic fluids, typically as a consequence area or financial impact based on modeled release scenarios; for non-hazardous or contained fluids, often as a simpler thinning or production-loss consequence. Multiplying POF by COF produces a risk ranking that API 580 then uses to set inspection intervals and prioritize resources — equipment ranked high-risk gets tighter intervals and more thorough NDT coverage; equipment ranked low-risk can safely extend intervals, freeing inspection resources for where they matter more. The practical result: API 581 does the math, API 580 tells you what to do with the answer. Most engagements reference both simultaneously, because a defensible RBI program needs the 580 framework and the 581 calculation rigor together.

Why Time, Not Cost, Is the Right Lens

RBI program setup is fundamentally rate-limited by three things that money alone can't accelerate: how fast your organization can locate and validate historical inspection and process data, how much time your process engineers and inspectors can free up for damage mechanism screening workshops, and how many equipment items (pressure vessels, piping circuits, exchangers) are in scope. Throwing more consultants at the problem compresses some phases, but data gathering in particular is gated by how quickly your own personnel can pull records, validate corrosion loop boundaries, and confirm process conditions — work that inherently depends on people who know your specific unit's history, not just RBI methodology.

Phase-by-Phase Time Investment for a Mid-Size Unit

The following ranges assume a mid-size refinery process unit or gas plant with roughly 40 to 80 pressure vessels and piping circuits in scope — a realistic size for a single crude unit, a hydrotreater, or a gas processing train. Larger, multi-unit rollouts scale up proportionally, and complexity (sour service, high-temperature hydrogen, amine systems with multiple active damage mechanisms) pushes toward the longer end of each range even at the same equipment count.

Phase 1: Scoping and Team Formation (1-3 weeks)

Defining the asset boundary, assembling the RBI team (process engineer, inspection engineer/Level III, corrosion/materials specialist, and an RBI facilitator), and agreeing on methodology depth (API 581 Level 1 screening vs. Level 2 more detailed analysis for higher-risk items). Short on paper, but this phase determines how smoothly everything after it runs — teams that rush scoping tend to discover mid-program that they scoped the wrong boundary or left out a critical circuit.

Phase 2: Data Gathering (4-16 weeks — typically the longest phase)

This is where RBI programs bog down. You need, per equipment item: equipment design data (material, thickness, design conditions), current operating conditions, corrosion loop definitions (which equipment shares the same process stream and damage mechanism exposure), historical inspection results (thickness readings, CML data, any prior NDT findings), and process history (upsets, changes in feedstock or operating severity). For a facility with well-organized digital records in a modern inspection data system, this can be compressed toward the lower end — roughly a month. For a facility where inspection history lives across paper files, old spreadsheets, and institutional memory of people who've since retired, this phase routinely stretches to three or four months, and it is by far the most common reason RBI implementation timelines slip. Data gaps discovered here (missing CML history, undefined corrosion loops, incomplete P&ID-to-equipment mapping) often require a secondary data reconciliation pass before the team can move forward with confidence.

Phase 3: Damage Mechanism Screening Workshops (1-4 weeks, run in parallel with late data gathering)

Structured workshops — typically following the API 571 damage mechanism framework — where the RBI team walks each corrosion loop and identifies which damage mechanisms are credible given the metallurgy, process conditions, and operating history. Expect roughly half a day to a full day per corrosion loop for a thorough review; a unit with 8-12 distinct corrosion loops might need one to two weeks of dedicated workshop time, though loops with straightforward, well-understood mechanisms move faster than loops with multiple interacting mechanisms (say, a loop with both sulfidation and hydrogen-related cracking exposure).

Phase 4: POF and COF Calculations (2-6 weeks after data is validated)

Once data is clean and damage mechanisms are screened, the actual API 581 quantitative calculations — damage factor determination, POF, and COF for each equipment item — run relatively quickly using RBI software (commercial platforms or a validated in-house calculation tool), assuming the data feeding them is trustworthy. This phase moves fast when data gathering was done well and stalls immediately when it wasn't, because bad inputs surface here as calculation results that don't pass a sanity check against the team's field experience — sending work back to Phase 2 for correction.

Phase 5: Risk Ranking, Interval Setting, and Team Review (1-3 weeks)

Results get compiled into a risk matrix, inspection intervals and required NDT methods/coverage are assigned per API 580's risk-based logic, and the full RBI team reviews the output against field experience and engineering judgment before it's finalized. This is a deliberate checkpoint, not a formality — a risk ranking that contradicts what the inspection team has actually observed in the field needs to be reconciled before the program goes live, or field credibility in the whole RBI output erodes fast.

Phase 6: Integration Into the Inspection Data System (2-8 weeks, can run partially in parallel)

Getting RBI outputs — intervals, required techniques, risk rankings — loaded into whatever system schedules and tracks actual inspection work is what turns an RBI study from a report on a shelf into an operating program. This ranges from a couple of weeks (a facility with a modern inspection data platform where RBI outputs map cleanly into existing equipment records) to two months (a facility integrating RBI into a legacy CMMS with manual data entry and validation).

Total Initial Program: Roughly 3 to 7 Months for a Mid-Size Unit

Adding the phases together, a realistic initial RBI implementation for a 40-80 item unit runs three to five months when data is in reasonably good shape going in, and five to seven months (occasionally longer) when data gathering uncovers significant gaps. A full refinery-wide rollout across multiple units scales toward six months to well over a year, particularly when units are staged sequentially rather than run in parallel due to limited RBI team bandwidth.

The Recurring Cycle: RBI Is Never "Done"

The initial implementation is the beginning of a maintenance cycle, not a one-time project. API 580 calls for periodic reassessment — commonly on a cycle of up to five years for the full quantitative reassessment, but in practice, the risk rankings and inspection intervals should be revisited incrementally every time new inspection data comes in. A thickness reading that comes back showing higher-than-expected corrosion rate on a circuit should trigger a reassessment of that circuit's damage factor and interval immediately, not wait for the next scheduled five-year cycle. Facilities that treat RBI as a living program — where new NDT results flow back into the risk model continuously — get far more value from the framework than those that run it once and file the report. This is also where the time investment shifts character: instead of large discrete phases, ongoing RBI maintenance becomes a smaller, continuous task — updating a handful of circuits' damage factors each time a turnaround or routine inspection campaign produces new data, with a fuller reassessment of the whole unit on the multi-year cycle API 580 recommends. Facilities chronically underestimate this ongoing time commitment and end up with an RBI program that's technically current on paper but hasn't actually absorbed two years of inspection findings — which defeats the entire purpose of a risk-based approach.

What Pushes Timelines Longer or Shorter

Two units of similar equipment count can land at opposite ends of the time range above. The variables that matter most:

  • Record digitization — a unit with inspection history already in a structured database moves through Phase 2 in weeks; a unit relying on filing cabinets and retired employees' institutional memory can take months just to establish what data exists before validating it.
  • Corrosion loop complexity — straightforward loops with one or two well-understood damage mechanisms (general thinning, for instance) screen quickly. Loops with multiple interacting mechanisms — sour water systems with both general corrosion and wet H2S cracking exposure, or amine units with corrosion under insulation alongside process-side thinning — take proportionally longer in both the screening workshops and the calculation review.
  • RBI methodology depth chosen — API 581 supports both a simpler Level 1 (screening-level) analysis and a more detailed Level 2 analysis with equipment-specific inputs. Running Level 2 across every item in scope takes meaningfully longer than screening with Level 1 and reserving Level 2 depth for the items that rank highest-risk on the initial pass — which is also the more common, and often more sensible, approach for a first implementation.
  • Team availability — if the process engineer and inspection lead who hold the institutional knowledge for a unit are also running a turnaround during the RBI kickoff, expect the data gathering and workshop phases to stretch to fit around their actual availability, not the ideal schedule.
  • Software and calculation tooling — teams using an established RBI calculation platform move through Phase 4 faster than teams building spreadsheet-based calculations from scratch, simply because the platform handles the API 581 damage factor lookups and consequence modeling without manual formula-building.

A useful planning exercise before committing to a start date: walk your own unit against this list honestly. A unit that's weak on digitized records but has a stable, available team and straightforward corrosion loops will spend its time differently — and probably land closer to the long end of the data-gathering range but the short end of the workshop range — than a unit with excellent records but complex, interacting damage mechanisms across a dozen loops.

Gas Plant Example: Scoping the Time Investment

Take a gas processing plant with roughly 50 pressure vessels and piping circuits across inlet separation, amine treating, dehydration, and compression — a common mid-size configuration. Inlet separation and compression circuits tend to screen relatively fast: well-understood mechanisms, good historical data because they're high-visibility equipment operators already watch closely. The amine treating loops are usually where the time goes — multiple credible damage mechanisms (amine corrosion, wet H2S cracking susceptibility, potential for corrosion under insulation on chilled or intermittently insulated lines), often less complete historical CML data because amine systems don't always get the same inspection attention as higher-visibility rotating equipment trains. A realistic phasing for this plant: two to three weeks of scoping, six to ten weeks of data gathering (skewed longer if amine loop records are incomplete), two to three weeks of damage mechanism workshops (amine loops taking disproportionate workshop time relative to their equipment count), three to four weeks of calculation, two weeks of risk review, and four to six weeks of system integration — landing at roughly four to five months total for a first-pass implementation, consistent with the mid-size unit range above.

How a Digital Twin / Inspection Data Platform Compresses the Timeline

The single biggest lever for shortening RBI setup time is compressing Phase 2 — data gathering — because it's the phase most exposed to how well your existing records are organized. A digital twin platform that already ties equipment records, corrosion loop definitions, historical thickness data, and inspection findings to a live 3D asset model turns what would otherwise be weeks of manually reconciling P&IDs against paper inspection files into a data export that's already structured and validated. When CML history, equipment metallurgy, and process conditions are already centralized and queryable rather than scattered across formats and departments, the RBI team can move into damage mechanism screening and POF/COF calculation far sooner — often cutting the data gathering phase from months to weeks for facilities that have already digitized their asset and inspection records. The same logic applies to the recurring reassessment cycle: a facility where new inspection results feed automatically into a central system, rather than requiring a manual data pull each time, keeps RBI risk rankings genuinely current instead of stale between the formal multi-year reassessments. Pairing an RBI program with Atlantis NDT ERP for inspection scheduling and record-keeping, and a digital twin for the asset and corrosion loop data layer, means the data gathering phase for future reassessments shrinks close to zero — the information is already where the RBI team needs it, continuously, rather than needing to be reassembled from scratch every time. For facilities weighing whether to build this RBI capability in-house or bring in outside expertise for the initial screening workshops and methodology setup, ASNT Level III consulting support during the damage mechanism screening and calculation phases specifically — where deep familiarity with API 571 mechanisms and 581 methodology directly shortens Phase 3 and Phase 4 — tends to be the highest-leverage place to bring in outside time, rather than trying to accelerate data gathering, which no amount of outside expertise can do faster than your own records allow.

title: Consulting for API 570 Piping Inspection Programs: RBI Integration Done Right
snippet: Why API 570 piping programs and API 580/581 RBI models drift apart, and how a Level III audit finds the CML and corrosion-rate gaps costing turnaround budget.
content:
Why RBI Programs Drift Away From API 570 Reality

Most refineries and chemical plants running a mature Risk-Based Inspection program will tell you their piping circuits are covered under API 580 and API 581. Fewer can tell you, without pulling the file, why a specific Condition Monitoring Location (CML) on a 12-inch carbon steel line was placed where it was, or whether the corrosion rate driving its remaining life calculation still reflects current process conditions. That gap between "we have an RBI program" and "our API 570 inspection intervals are actually risk-justified" is where a lot of turnaround budget gets wasted, and it's the single most common finding when an outside ASNT Level III walks a piping inspection program for the first time.

API 570, the Piping Inspection Code for in-service metallic piping systems, sets the baseline framework: piping is assigned to Class 1, 2, or 3 based on consequence of failure, and each class carries a default external and internal inspection interval. RBI, governed conceptually by API 580 and quantified through API 581, is supposed to modify those default intervals up or down based on actual probability and consequence of failure at the circuit level. In practice, a lot of programs implement RBI once, at commissioning or during an initial mechanical integrity buildout, and then let the risk ranking calcify while the plant itself keeps changing — feed slate shifts, throughput increases, a metallurgy upgrade in one spool but not the adjoining one, a process change that quietly increases hydrogen partial pressure. The RBI model doesn't know any of that happened unless someone tells it.

Where CML and TML Selection Breaks Down

The technical backbone of any API 570 piping program is Condition Monitoring Location and Thickness Measurement Location selection, and this is where damage-mechanism knowledge from API 571 has to drive the plan rather than follow it. A circuit governed by sulfidation corrosion in a crude unit atmospheric column overhead needs CMLs concentrated at low-velocity zones, elbows, and downstream of flow disturbances where sulfur compounds concentrate — not evenly spaced grid points every 20 feet because that's what the spreadsheet template defaults to. A line susceptible to High Temperature Hydrogen Attack (HTHA) in a hydroprocessing unit needs a completely different inspection strategy: HTHA doesn't show up reliably on conventional UT thickness gauging until it's advanced, which is why API 941 (Nelson curves) governs material selection and why advanced UT techniques — backscatter, attenuation, or velocity-ratio methods — matter more than a thickness reading for early detection.

Corrosion Under Insulation (CUI), addressed specifically in API 583, is its own category of failure for API 570 programs, because the damage is invisible without removing insulation, and a plant can't economically strip every insulated line at every turnaround. A defensible CUI program uses a risk-ranked insulation removal plan — typically prioritizing carbon steel piping operating between roughly 25°F and 250°F, areas with damaged jacketing, low points, and dead legs — supplemented by guided-wave (long-range) UT screening to identify candidate locations before committing to insulation removal and conventional UT or profile radiography for confirmation. Amine cracking, naphthenic acid corrosion (which tracks with total acid number and velocity, not just temperature), and wet H2S cracking each carry their own inspection logic, and an RBI model that doesn't encode the specific damage mechanism per circuit is really just a scheduling tool wearing a risk-analysis label.

Matching NDT Method to Damage Mechanism, Not the Other Way Around

One of the most consistent findings in an ASNT Level III consulting review of an API 570 program is a mismatch between the NDT method specified and the damage mechanism actually present. Conventional single-element UT thickness gauging is fast and inexpensive, and it's the right tool for general, uniform wall loss. It is the wrong tool, used alone, for localized pitting, and it's a poor tool for early-stage HTHA. Phased array UT (PAUT) earns its keep on complex geometries — nozzles, weld overlays, thickness transitions — where a single-element probe can't resolve the flaw orientation or where sizing accuracy matters for a fitness-for-service calculation. Guided-wave UT (sometimes called long-range UT or LRUT) is the right screening tool for inaccessible or insulated piping runs, road crossings, and pipe supports, but it's a screening method, not a quantification method — a positive indication still needs a follow-up conventional UT or PAUT scan to size the actual wall loss.

Digital radiography has a narrower but important role in API 570 programs: it remains one of the few methods that can reliably characterize internal corrosion morphology (pitting versus general thinning) on small-bore piping and at tees or fittings where UT access is geometrically difficult. The mistake many programs make is treating method selection as a procurement decision — whichever contractor is cheapest per point — rather than an engineering decision tied to the specific damage mechanism, material, and geometry at each CML. A written practice or inspection plan that doesn't explicitly document the rationale for method selection per circuit is going to struggle in an audit, and more importantly, it's going to miss things.

Remaining Life Calculations: Where Small Errors Compound

Corrosion rate and remaining life calculations look deceptively simple — take two thickness readings at different dates, divide the loss by the time between them, project forward to the minimum required thickness — but the inputs are where programs go wrong. Using a short-term corrosion rate (say, between the last two inspection cycles) when the damage mechanism is cyclical or process-dependent can produce a remaining life estimate that's either dangerously optimistic or needlessly conservative. Using the nominal wall thickness instead of the actual as-built thickness from mill records inflates apparent remaining life. Failing to account for the tmin calculation methodology specified in the applicable design code (ASME B31.3 for process piping, most commonly) introduces errors that compound across every downstream RBI risk calculation, because probability of failure in API 581 is directly sensitive to the remaining life estimate.

This is exactly the kind of gap an outside Level III review is built to catch — not because in-house inspectors lack competence, but because they're close to the data and often inherit calculation templates built years earlier by someone who's since left the company. A consulting engagement typically starts with a sample audit: pull ten to fifteen circuits across different damage mechanisms and criticality classes, trace the CML placement rationale, the corrosion rate calculation, and the resulting inspection interval back to source data, and see where the logic breaks. It's common to find both false economy (Class 1 piping on a wider interval than the actual risk supports) and wasted inspection spend (Class 3 piping inspected as often as Class 1 because nobody revisited the ranking after a decade of clean data).

Digital Twin and ERP Integration: Making the Data Trustworthy Over Time

RBI is only as good as the data feeding it, and the data problem is structural in most plants: thickness readings live in one system, isometric drawings in another, corrosion loop assignments in a third, and the actual RBI risk model in a fourth, often maintained by an external consultant on an annual update cycle. A digital twin platform that ties inspection history directly to a 3D model of the piping system changes the economics of this problem — instead of an inspector or reliability engineer reconstructing context from four systems before every turnaround, the corrosion trend, CML history, and current risk ranking are visible on the model itself, color-coded by remaining life. That doesn't replace the API 581 calculation, but it makes the calculation's inputs visibly traceable, which is exactly what breaks down in most legacy programs.

On the data capture side, moving field crews off paper thickness logs and into an NDT inspection management platform closes a different gap: readings get geolocated to the correct CML automatically, technician certification and procedure revision are captured at the point of collection, and the corrosion rate calculation updates the same day instead of during a batch data-entry cycle weeks later. Programs that make this shift consistently report catching data anomalies — a CML that was apparently never actually surveyed, a thickness reading that's physically impossible given the prior trend — years earlier than they would have on a paper-based or spreadsheet workflow.

What a Level III Consulting Engagement Actually Delivers

A well-scoped engagement for API 570/RBI integration typically covers four things: a sample-based audit of CML selection logic against documented damage mechanisms, a review of the corrosion rate and remaining life calculation methodology against the governing design code, a gap assessment of how the current RBI risk ranking compares to actual process history (feed changes, upset events, metallurgy), and a set of prioritized recommendations — which circuits are genuinely under-inspected, which are over-inspected, and what data or procedural changes would make the next RBI revalidation cycle defensible without a full re-baseline. For plants earlier in the maturity curve, the engagement might instead focus on standing up the CML/TML selection logic and inspection procedures from scratch, aligned to NDT training requirements so in-house technicians and any contracted inspection crews are working from the same technical baseline.

The value isn't in replacing a plant's inspection team — it's in the outside perspective a Level III brings from having reviewed programs across multiple facilities and damage mechanisms, catching the assumptions that get baked in and stop being questioned. Whether the immediate driver is an upcoming turnaround, a fitness-for-service trigger, or simply the sense that the RBI model hasn't kept pace with plant changes, the fastest way to find out where the program actually stands is a focused technical audit rather than a full re-implementation.

How RBI-Driven Scope Changes Ripple Into Turnaround Planning

Every wrong assumption baked into an RBI risk ranking eventually shows up as a turnaround scope decision, and turnarounds are where the cost of getting it wrong is easiest to see. A circuit that's actually running an active damage mechanism but is ranked as low-risk because the corrosion rate calculation used a stale baseline will get deferred past the point it should have been opened, and the plant finds out the hard way — either during the next scheduled inspection when the wall loss is worse than projected, or worse, during an unplanned event. The opposite failure is quieter but still expensive: a circuit with genuinely low risk that's still being inspected on a legacy interval nobody revisited, consuming turnaround scaffolding, isolation, and inspection crew hours that could have gone to a genuinely higher-risk asset.

A disciplined turnaround scoping process ties directly back to the RBI model's risk ranking, but only if the planning team trusts that ranking — and trust has to be earned by the model actually reflecting current plant reality. This is where a Level III's review adds value beyond the technical audit itself: sitting in the scoping meeting and being able to explain, circuit by circuit, why a particular piping run made the cut or didn't, tied to a specific damage mechanism and a specific data trail, changes the character of that meeting from a negotiation over historical precedent into a risk-based technical decision the whole team can stand behind. Plants that go through this exercise once, with a defensible technical rationale attached to every scope decision, tend to find their next turnaround scoping cycle goes noticeably faster, because the arguing-over-assumptions phase has already been resolved.

Common Pushback From Plant Inspection Teams, and How to Address It

An outside review of an established API 570/RBI program almost always generates some defensiveness, and it's worth naming the two most common objections directly because they come up in nearly every engagement. The first is some version of "we've been running this program for years without an incident, so it must be working." That's a survivorship argument, not a technical one — the absence of a failure to date doesn't validate a CML placement methodology or a corrosion rate calculation, it just means the actual risk hasn't caught up with an optimistic assumption yet, or the conservatism built into default Class 1/2/3 intervals has been doing the protective work the risk model gets credit for. The second objection is resourcing: "we don't have the staff to re-baseline the whole program." A properly scoped audit doesn't ask for a full re-baseline — it identifies the highest-consequence gaps first (typically a handful of circuits carrying active damage mechanisms under-represented in the current risk ranking) and lets the plant address those before deciding whether a broader re-baseline is warranted. Framing the engagement this way, as a targeted risk-reduction exercise rather than a wholesale program teardown, is usually what gets a skeptical inspection team to actually engage with the findings instead of shelving the report.

title: Consulting for Marine Survey Companies: IACS UR Z17 Compliance
snippet: IACS UR Z17 governs hull thickness surveys and UTM firm approval. What class societies expect, common written-practice gaps, and how a compliance review fixes them.
content:
The Standard Behind Every Hull Thickness Reading That Counts

A ship's classification society doesn't just want a thickness number — it wants to know the number came from a firm and a technician it has already reviewed and accepted. That is the entire premise behind IACS Unified Requirement Z17, "Procedure Requirements for Thickness Measurements." Every International Association of Classification Societies (IACS) member — ABS, Lloyd's Register, DNV, and the rest — has built UR Z17's minimum requirements into its own class rules for periodical, intermediate, and special or renewal surveys of hull structures. In practice, that means a marine NDT provider doing ultrasonic thickness measurement (UTM) on a hull can be technically excellent with a probe and still fail a survey if the firm itself was never properly accepted by the society, or if its written procedures don't trace back to what Z17 actually demands.

This distinction trips up otherwise capable inspection companies constantly. A firm that has run UT on pressure vessels and piping for years under API and ASME codes can walk into marine survey work assuming the fundamentals transfer directly. Some do. The firm-level approval process, the survey-type-specific extent of readings, and the reporting conventions surveyors expect generally do not — and that gap is exactly where a Z17 compliance review earns its keep.

What UR Z17 Actually Requires of a UTM Firm

Z17 operates at two levels simultaneously: it sets expectations for the individual conducting the measurement, and it sets expectations for the company employing that individual. Most marine NDT providers focus heavily on the first and underinvest in the second, which is usually the part a class society actually audits when it decides whether to accept, renew, or withdraw a firm's approval.

At the firm level, a class society generally wants to see:

  • A documented approval or acceptance process with the society itself — most major class societies maintain their own list of accepted thickness measurement (TM) firms, and being added to that list requires submitting a quality manual, sample reports, and an equipment list, not just a résumé of qualified staff.
  • Written procedures that map measurement extent and location to the specific survey type — annual, intermediate, or special/renewal surveys each call for a different scope of readings, and a generic "we UT hulls" procedure rarely reflects that distinction.
  • A defined responsible-person structure, typically requiring technical oversight from someone qualified at a minimum of NDT Level II in the ultrasonic method under a recognized certification scheme.
  • Defined record retention — survey reports, calibration logs, and personnel files need to be retrievable well after the survey closes out, often for several years, matching the class society's own record-keeping expectations.

Personnel Qualification Expectations

Technicians performing UTM for class survey purposes are typically expected to hold at minimum a Level II qualification in the ultrasonic method under a recognized certification scheme — most commonly ASNT SNT-TC-1A in North America, with ISO 9712 accepted by some societies as an alternative route, particularly for firms working an international fleet. It's worth being precise here: Atlantis trains and certifies technicians to ASNT SNT-TC-1A specifically. ISO 9712 is a real, employer-independent certification scheme that some class societies also recognize, but it is administered by third-party certification bodies, not by Atlantis or by any single training provider — a distinction that matters the moment a surveyor asks which scheme backs a technician's card.

Class societies also generally expect documented evidence that a firm's Level II and Level III personnel didn't just pass an exam once and disappear into the field. Current certification dates, vision exam currency, and a clear chain of who supervises whom on a given job are all things a surveyor — or an auditor from the class society itself — can and will ask to see.

Calibration and Equipment Traceability

Z17-compliant procedures need calibration that's traceable to a recognized national standard — in the US, that means traceability to NIST — using reference blocks appropriate to the method, commonly IIW-type or stepped-wedge blocks for hull plate thickness work. The expectation isn't just "we calibrate the gauge." It's a documented linearity check, a verification of the specific probe-and-instrument combination in use for that job, and a record that ties each measurement session back to a specific calibration event with a date, a block serial number, and a technician signature. Firms that keep calibration certificates in a drawer but can't produce the link between a given reading and the calibration event behind it are one of the most common findings in a firm-level review.

Where Written Practices Fall Apart in Practice

A written procedure that reads well in isolation often collapses the moment it's checked against an actual survey report. The gaps a compliance review typically surfaces include:

  • A generic UT thickness procedure with no method for tying measurement locations back to the vessel's structural drawings or original construction thickness — surveyors need to see where a reading sits relative to as-built thickness and the class society's renewal criteria, not just a bare number.
  • No differentiation between the reading extent required for an annual survey versus an intermediate or special/renewal survey — these are not the same scope, and treating them as interchangeable is a fast way to have a report rejected outright.
  • Reports missing items surveyors expect as a matter of course: hull diagram or zone references, probe type and frequency, coupling method, and any correction applied for coating thickness over the steel.
  • Level II technicians on the roster without a documented near-vision and color-contrast exam on file, or without traceable on-the-job training hours — easy to overlook until an auditor asks for the personnel file, not just the wallet card.
  • Calibration records that exist but aren't cross-referenced to specific job reports, breaking the traceability chain a class society auditor is specifically trained to look for.

None of these are exotic failures. They're the ordinary byproduct of a written practice that was assembled once, years ago, and never re-qualified against the specific requirements of marine survey work as opposed to onshore industrial UT.

How Class Societies Enforce Z17 — ABS, Lloyd's Register, DNV

IACS Unified Requirements set a floor; individual class societies build their own rule sets on top of it and enforce it through their own approval and audit mechanisms. ABS incorporates thickness measurement requirements into its Rules for Survey After Construction and maintains its own process for accepting TM firms and surveyors, with ABS Americas offices serving the Gulf Coast and Great Lakes fleets directly. Lloyd's Register and DNV each run comparable acceptance schemes under their own rule sets — the details of submission and renewal differ from society to society, but the underlying logic is the same: approval isn't permanent, and a firm's status can be reviewed or withdrawn if survey reports start showing the kind of gaps described above.

In practice this means a marine NDT provider's relationship with a class society is ongoing, not a one-time gate. Surveyors spot-check reports during actual surveys, class societies periodically re-verify TM firm approval, and non-conformances found during a vessel's survey can trigger a harder look at the firm behind the numbers — which is precisely the moment a firm doesn't want to discover its written practice has drifted out of alignment with Z17.

US-Flag, Jones Act, and Great Lakes Fleet Realities

US-flag vessels operating under the Jones Act — US-built, US-crewed, US-owned — typically layer US Coast Guard requirements under 46 CFR on top of whichever class society holds the vessel's classification, with ABS historically the dominant class society for the domestic fleet. A UTM firm working Gulf Coast repair yards around Houston or Beaumont needs procedures that satisfy both the class society's Z17-based requirements and whatever the attending Coast Guard marine inspector expects to see cross-referenced in the survey report.

The Great Lakes fleet adds its own operational pressure. Self-unloading bulk carriers typically come out of service for winter layup, giving Great Lakes yards only a narrow window — often just a few weeks — to complete drydock surveys before the shipping season resumes. A UTM firm serving that fleet has to run a Z17-compliant thickness survey against a hard calendar deadline, which is exactly the condition under which shortcuts in extent-of-readings documentation or calibration traceability tend to appear. A firm that has already stress-tested its written practice against Z17 outside of layup season isn't improvising when the schedule gets tight in January.

Canadian Coast Guard and Cross-Border Survey Work

Canadian-flag commercial vessels are typically surveyed under Transport Canada's authority via the Canada Shipping Act, frequently delegated to a recognized classification society operating in much the same role it holds for US-flag vessels — meaning a UTM firm doing hull thickness work in a Canadian yard is still, in practice, working against a Z17-based procedure even though the flag administration is different. Canadian Coast Guard vessels themselves — icebreakers, buoy tenders, and search-and-rescue craft based out of stations from Halifax to Vancouver — typically fall under a separate government fleet maintenance framework rather than commercial classification, a distinction worth knowing before assuming one procedure covers every vessel type calling a Canadian port.

Cross-border mobility matters here too. A US-flag vessel classed by an ABS office in Houston that goes into drydock in Halifax or Vancouver still needs its thickness survey performed by a firm accepted by that same class society, regardless of which country the yard sits in. For a UTM firm trying to grow along both coasts, having a written practice and firm approval status that travels cleanly between US and Canadian yards is a genuine commercial advantage, not just a compliance checkbox.

Trending Diminution Rates Across Survey Cycles

A single thickness survey is a snapshot; what a surveyor and an owner both actually care about is the trend. Comparing readings from the current survey against the prior intermediate or special survey — at the same grid locations, ideally — lets a firm calculate an annual corrosion or wastage rate in millimeters per year for a given plate or structural member. That rate matters for two decisions: whether a member is approaching the class society's renewal threshold before the next scheduled survey, and whether the owner needs to plan a steel renewal or coating intervention sooner than the survey cycle would otherwise dictate.

Renewal thresholds themselves are set by the applicable class rules and vary by vessel type, structural member, and society — there's no single number that applies across the board, and a firm's written practice should point technicians to the specific rule reference rather than a rule of thumb memorized from a different vessel type. What a Z17-aligned written practice should require, though, is a consistent method for recording grid locations so that survey-to-survey comparison is actually possible. Firms that re-gauge at approximate locations each cycle, without a documented grid reference tied to the structural drawing, make trend analysis effectively impossible — which means the owner finds out about accelerating wastage only when a member finally crosses the line, rather than a survey cycle earlier when a coating repair or partial renewal would have been the cheaper fix.

What a Z17 Compliance Review and Remediation Engagement Actually Covers

When Atlantis's ASNT Level III consulting team walks into a marine NDT provider for a Z17 review, the engagement generally follows a consistent sequence: a document review of the existing written practice, sample survey reports, and calibration records; a gap analysis against Z17's requirements and the specific addenda of the class societies the firm works with; a review of personnel files for certification currency, vision exam documentation, and OJT records; a live witness of an actual thickness survey where practical; and a prioritized remediation plan that distinguishes findings that block firm approval from findings that are simply good practice.

Much of what surfaces in that review isn't a technical failure — it's a recordkeeping failure. Firms that store calibration certificates, personnel qualifications, and survey reports across a mix of shared drives, email attachments, and paper folders struggle to produce the traceability chain a class society auditor wants on demand. Moving that structure into a system like Atlantis NDT ERP — where equipment calibration due dates, personnel certification expiry, and job reports are linked records rather than scattered files — turns an audit from a scramble into a five-minute lookup. On the reporting side, standardizing survey report format with NDT reporting software built around the fields surveyors actually expect — zone reference, probe details, coupling method, coating correction — closes a surprising number of the gaps described earlier without touching field technique at all.

Getting — Or Keeping — Your TM Firm Approval

Z17 compliance isn't a document you write once and file away. It's the operating discipline that keeps a marine NDT provider's firm approval active, keeps its survey reports accepted without rework, and keeps its technicians credible in front of a class surveyor who has seen a thousand thickness reports and can tell within a minute whether the one in front of them came from a firm that actually understands the requirement or one that's guessing. A structured compliance review — whether you're pursuing first-time TM firm approval or shoring up a written practice that's drifted over the years — is the fastest way to close that gap before a class society closes it for you.

Before your next survey cycle, it's worth getting a firm-level read on where your written practice actually stands against Z17, rather than finding out from a surveyor mid-drydock.

title: Consulting for Pipeline Integrity Programs: API 1163 and 1160 Compliance Review
snippet: API 1163 ILI qualification and API 1160 integrity management, together: POD/POI validation, dig verification, PHMSA/49 CFR 195, and common program gaps.
content:
Why ILI Data Is Only as Good as the Qualification Behind It

A smart pig can run a flawless inline inspection and still leave a pipeline operator exposed if nobody validated that the tool actually finds and sizes what it claims to find and size, on that specific pipeline, in that specific product, at that specific run speed. That validation gap is precisely what API 1163, "In-line Inspection Systems Qualification," exists to close. It doesn't certify a tool once for all conditions — it defines a qualification process an operator has to run through for the specific application, and it's the piece of a pipeline integrity program most likely to be treated as a formality rather than as the load-bearing document it actually is.

API 1163 doesn't operate in isolation. It sits inside the broader framework of API 1160, "Managing System Integrity for Hazardous Liquid Pipelines," which defines what a complete integrity management program looks like — risk assessment, threat identification, data integration, and repair criteria — with ILI as one input among several. A pipeline integrity consulting review has to look at both documents together, because a technically sound ILI qualification file sitting inside a threadbare integrity management program is still a program with a hole in it.

The two documents also fail independently in different ways, which is part of why a review has to treat them as one exercise rather than two separate checklists. An operator can have an immaculate API 1163 qualification file — a well-built Performance Specification, a defensible validation plan, a properly stratified dig program — and still have an API 1160 program that never actually uses any of it to update risk rankings or reprioritize the next assessment interval. The reverse is just as common: a mature-looking integrity management program with a formal risk model and a documented threat matrix, resting on ILI data nobody ever independently validated against field conditions. Either failure mode produces a program that looks complete on a binder shelf and falls apart the moment a regulator asks to trace one specific anomaly from the ILI report through to the repair decision.

What API 1163 Actually Requires of an ILI Program

API 1163 structures ILI qualification around a Performance Specification — a document, usually built jointly by the operator and the ILI vendor, that states what the tool is expected to detect, identify, and size on the specific pipeline segment being run, under the conditions that segment presents: product type, wall thickness range, diameter, and expected anomaly types. The qualification process then requires that performance be validated in the field, not just asserted on paper.

Tool Qualification and the Performance Specification

A defensible ILI qualification file typically includes the Performance Specification itself, documentation of the tool's prior track record on comparable pipelines with similar diameter and wall thickness range, and — critically — a validation plan describing how the vendor's claimed performance will be checked against real dig data once the tool has actually run. An operator that accepts a vendor's published specification sheet at face value and skips this step has satisfied the paperwork but not the intent of API 1163.

Vintage pipe adds a qualification wrinkle that catches operators off guard. A segment built decades ago on electric resistance welded (ERW) pipe carries a threat profile — long-seam anomalies, hook cracks, hard spots near the seam — that a generic metal-loss tool qualified for corrosion detection was never designed to find. An ILI qualification file that doesn't explicitly address whether the selected tool technology is appropriate for the seam type and vintage of the specific segment being run isn't really qualified for that segment, even if the same tool has a strong track record on newer, seamless pipe elsewhere in the system. This is one of the more consequential findings a compliance review can surface, because it points to a threat category the operator's ILI program may not be covering at all, not just a documentation gap.

POD, POI, and Sizing Accuracy — What the Numbers Actually Mean

Vendors typically publish three categories of performance claims for a metal-loss or crack-detection tool: probability of detection (POD), the likelihood the tool flags a feature that's actually there; probability of identification (POI), the likelihood it correctly classifies what kind of feature it is — external corrosion versus a dent versus a manufacturing anomaly, for example; and sizing accuracy, typically expressed as a tolerance band with an associated confidence level for depth, length, and width. These numbers vary meaningfully by tool technology — magnetic flux leakage (MFL), ultrasonic (UT), and electromagnetic acoustic transducer (EMAT) tools each carry different strengths depending on whether the threat is metal loss, cracking, or geometry — and by pipeline-specific conditions like wall thickness variation and internal coating. The point of API 1163 qualification isn't to memorize the vendor's number; it's to confirm that number holds up on this pipeline, not just on the pipelines the vendor used to build its spec sheet in the first place.

Where API 1163 Meets API 1160: Integrity Management, Not Just Inspection

API 1160 lays out the structural elements of a hazardous liquid pipeline integrity management program: risk assessment, integrity assessment methods (ILI, hydrostatic testing, and direct assessment among them), data integration, repair criteria, prevention and mitigation measures, and performance measurement. ILI results from an API 1163-qualified tool run feed directly into several of these elements — but only if the data integration step actually happens.

Threat Identification and Data Integration

A common design flaw in immature integrity management programs is treating ILI as the entire threat assessment rather than one input into it. API 1160 expects an operator to consider the full range of threat categories relevant to hazardous liquid pipelines — external and internal corrosion, mechanical damage from third-party excavation, stress corrosion cracking, and manufacturing or construction defects among them — and to integrate ILI findings with cathodic protection survey data, coating condition history, and as-built construction records rather than reviewing ILI results as a standalone report.

Dig Verification Programs and Unity Checks

Once an ILI run identifies anomalies, the operator excavates a sample of them to physically verify the tool's calls — this is the dig verification program, and it's where API 1163's qualification claims get tested against reality. A statistically sound dig program stratifies its excavation sample across anomaly types and severities rather than digging only the largest, most obvious calls, and builds a unity chart comparing ILI-reported depth against field-measured depth — often confirmed by UT wall thickness readings taken at the dig site — across that sample. An operator that digs five convenient anomalies and calls the tool "validated" hasn't actually validated anything, and that's one of the most common findings a compliance review turns up.

The dig verification program also has to hold up statistically, not just visually. A unity chart with a handful of points clustered near the origin looks reassuring on a slide but doesn't demonstrate anything about how the tool performs on the anomalies that actually matter — the deeper, more severe calls where a sizing error has the most consequence. A properly built verification program deliberately includes digs across the full range of reported severities, documents the field measurement method used at each dig (UT thickness gauging at multiple points around the anomaly, not a single spot reading), and records enough digs per anomaly category to say something statistically meaningful about that category's actual POD and sizing accuracy on this pipeline — rather than borrowing the vendor's aggregate performance claim and assuming it applies uniformly.

PHMSA and 49 CFR 195 — the Regulatory Backdrop

For hazardous liquid pipelines, PHMSA enforces integrity management requirements under 49 CFR Part 195, with §195.452 specifically requiring an integrity management program for pipeline segments that could affect a high consequence area (HCA) — populated areas, commercially navigable waterways, and other drinking water or ecologically sensitive areas as defined in the regulation. PHMSA's framework leans heavily on the structure API 1160 describes, and PHMSA inspectors reviewing an operator's integrity management program expect to see the same elements: documented risk assessment, a defensible ILI qualification and validation trail per API 1163, an actual dig verification program with statistical grounding, and a change-of-condition process that updates the risk assessment when new information — a failed dig verification, a newly identified threat, a changed operating pressure — comes in.

A PHMSA inspection is not the moment to discover that the ILI qualification file consists of a vendor brochure and an email chain. Operators that treat the qualification and validation documentation as a living file, built and updated as each ILI run and dig program closes out, walk into a PHMSA review in a fundamentally different position than operators trying to reconstruct that history after the fact.

Common Gaps a Pipeline Integrity Compliance Review Finds

  • ILI vendor performance claims — POD, POI, sizing tolerance — accepted from the spec sheet without an operator-side validation plan tied to actual dig data from that specific pipeline.
  • Dig verification programs large enough in raw count to look credible but not statistically stratified — heavily weighted toward the largest, easiest-to-confirm anomalies rather than a representative sample across severity and anomaly type.
  • Threat identification limited to corrosion mechanisms, with mechanical damage, stress corrosion cracking, and manufacturing or construction threats acknowledged in the program document but never actually assessed against pipeline-specific history.
  • ILI data sitting in a standalone report rather than integrated with cathodic protection survey history, coating condition assessments, and as-built records — meaning the integrity assessment technically exists but doesn't inform risk ranking the way API 1160 intends.
  • Repair criteria referenced generically without a clear, documented method — modified B31G, RSTRENG, or an API 579 fitness-for-service assessment — for translating an ILI-reported anomaly into an actual repair or re-inspection decision.
  • No formal management-of-change process to update the integrity assessment when a dig verification contradicts the ILI call, or when operating conditions shift.
  • ILI qualification files that don't address whether the selected tool technology is appropriate for the seam type, vintage, and known threat history of the specific segment being run — as opposed to relying on the tool's general track record elsewhere in the system.
  • Performance measures tracked for regulatory reporting purposes but never actually fed back into the risk model that decides reassessment intervals — turning API 1160's continuous-improvement intent into a static, once-a-year paperwork exercise.

Gulf Coast Corridor Realities

The Gulf Coast pipeline corridor — running through the refining and petrochemical complexes around Houston and Beaumont-Port Arthur, and feeding into major hazardous liquid infrastructure like the Louisiana Offshore Oil Port — presents its own version of these challenges: dense pipeline crossings, a mix of vintage and modern pipe within the same system, and HCA density around populated Gulf Coast metro areas that raises the regulatory stakes on getting threat identification right. Operators running ILI programs through this corridor are also more likely to be running multiple tool technologies across a single system as it ages, which makes consistent qualification documentation across vendors and tool types — rather than a fresh, ad hoc qualification file every time a new vendor is brought in — a genuine operational advantage rather than a paperwork nicety.

What an Atlantis Consulting Engagement Covers

An Atlantis ASNT Level III consulting engagement on pipeline integrity typically starts with a document review — the integrity management program itself, the ILI qualification and Performance Specification files, and the dig verification history — followed by a gap analysis against both API 1163 and API 1160 side by side, since a finding in one document usually has a corresponding gap in the other. From there, the engagement builds a prioritized remediation plan: which gaps are PHMSA-exposure critical, which are simply best-practice improvements, and what sequence closes the most risk fastest.

Where PHMSA exposure is the concern, that remediation plan often includes a mock audit — walking the integrity management program the way a PHMSA inspector would, starting from a single anomaly in an ILI report and tracing it forward through the dig verification record, the repair or re-inspection decision, and the corresponding update to the risk model, to confirm the chain actually holds together end to end rather than existing as disconnected documents that happen to reference the same pipeline segment.

A recurring piece of that remediation work is structural, not just procedural. Dig verification data, ILI qualification records, and repair decisions scattered across vendor portals, spreadsheets, and email threads make it nearly impossible to build the kind of longitudinal unity analysis PHMSA and API 1163 both expect. Centralizing that data — including UT wall thickness readings taken at dig sites, formatted through NDT reporting software built for field verification work — and tracking calibration, personnel, and inspection records inside Atlantis NDT ERP turns a reactive, audit-triggered scramble into a program an operator can actually stand behind on request. For systems where visualizing anomaly history against the physical asset matters — comparing successive ILI runs, dig locations, and repair history spatially along a corridor — a digital twin platform gives an integrity team a single visual layer instead of a stack of disconnected reports.

Building an Integrity Management Program That Holds Up Under Review

API 1163 and API 1160 aren't independent hoops — they're two halves of the same argument, that a pipeline operator actually understands the condition of its asset because it can show its work, from tool qualification through dig verification through documented repair decisions. A program built that way survives a PHMSA audit as a matter of course. A program built by accumulating vendor deliverables without ever stepping back to check whether they add up to a defensible integrity case usually finds out the hard way that they didn't.

If it's been a while since your ILI qualification files and dig verification program were reviewed end to end against API 1163 and API 1160 together, that gap is exactly what a compliance review is built to close.

title: NDT Consulting for Startups: Building Your First Written Practice From Scratch
snippet: Building a first ASNT SNT-TC-1A written practice, personnel program, procedure qualification, and calibration program — in the right order, without first-year mistakes.
content:
The First 90 Days of an NDT Department That Doesn't Exist Yet

Every NDT service provider and every fabricator's in-house inspection department started the same way: zero personnel files, zero procedures, and a founder or quality manager who knows the work needs to be defensible from day one but isn't sure what "defensible" actually requires on paper. The single most consequential document in that first 90 days is the written practice — and it's also the document new companies most often get wrong, because it looks like paperwork when it's actually the decision record for the entire qualification and certification program.

ASNT SNT-TC-1A is a recommended practice, not a mandatory third-party certification standard — which is exactly what makes it easy to underestimate. Unlike ISO 9712 or PCN, where a central certification body issues the credential, SNT-TC-1A puts the employer in the driver's seat: the company writes its own written practice, using SNT-TC-1A's guidelines as the reference framework, and the company — through its designated NDE Level III — makes the actual certification decisions. That's a real responsibility, and a startup that treats the written practice as a template to fill blanks in usually finds out how much was missing the first time a client or a code body's auditor asks to see it.

This employer-based model is also why two companies performing the same method can have legitimately different certification requirements without either one being wrong. A shop doing UT on structural steel welds to AWS D1.1 and a shop doing UT on pressure vessel welds to ASME Section VIII may reasonably set different experience-hour minimums, different practical exam specimens, and different recertification intervals in their respective written practices — because the risk profile, the code requirements, and the client expectations differ. A startup that doesn't understand this flexibility either over-copies a stricter program it can't practically staff to, or under-builds a weaker one that won't survive a client's technical audit.

Step One: The Written Practice Isn't a Template, It's a Decision Document

SNT-TC-1A's guideline tables — minimum classroom training hours and documented experience hours by method and qualification level — are exactly that: guidelines, not mandates. The company's written practice is where those guidelines become the company's actual requirements, adjusted for the methods it performs, the codes its clients require, and the level of risk in the work. A startup that copies another company's written practice wholesale — hour requirements, method list, and all — has adopted someone else's risk decisions without ever making its own.

What SNT-TC-1A Actually Asks the Employer to Own

At minimum, a written practice needs to define which methods the company covers — UT, RT, MT, PT, VT, ET, and others as applicable — and at which qualification levels; the education, training, and experience requirements for each method and level; the examination structure (general, specific, and practical) required before certification; vision examination requirements and renewal frequency, typically near vision and color contrast verified annually; and the certification period and recertification requirements. None of that is filled in from a generic source — it's a set of decisions the company has to make and be able to defend to a client's quality auditor.

Step Two: Personnel Certification Program Structure

Level I, II, and III Responsibilities — and Who Signs What

The three-tier structure isn't arbitrary. A Level I technician performs specific calibrations, tests, and evaluations according to written instructions, under the supervision of a Level II or III, and doesn't independently decide acceptance or rejection. A Level II sets up and calibrates equipment, interprets and evaluates results against applicable codes and standards, organizes and reports results, and provides direction to Level I personnel. A Level III — the role a startup most often underbuilds — is qualified to establish techniques, interpret codes and standards, designate the particular methods and procedures to be used, and has the training and standing to qualify and examine Level I and Level II personnel. In a startup's early structure, it's tempting to let a strong Level II act as a de facto Level III without ever formally qualifying at that level — a decision that looks fine until a client's quality audit or a code compliance review asks who actually holds Level III authority on file, and the honest answer is nobody does.

The Eye Exam and OJT Hours Mistake Almost Everyone Makes

Two personnel-file gaps show up constantly in first-year NDT departments. The first is certifying technicians without a documented annual near-vision and color-contrast exam on file — not just performed, but dated, filed, and tied to the specific technician's certification record. In practice this means a near-vision acuity check (commonly a Jaeger J1 or J2 equivalent chart) and a color-contrast test (an Ishihara plate test is the usual method), administered annually and signed by whoever administered it, with the result sitting in the personnel file next to the certification it supports — not in a separate binder nobody cross-references. The second gap is logging on-the-job training hours as a lump sum rather than as dated entries with supervisor sign-off, which means when an auditor asks to verify that a Level II candidate actually accumulated the required hours under qualified supervision, there's no way to substantiate it after the fact. Both are cheap to do right from day one and expensive to reconstruct a year later.

Step Three: Procedure Qualification, Not Procedure Copying

A written UT or MT procedure borrowed from a previous employer, a client, or a downloaded template is not a qualified procedure for a new company — it reflects someone else's equipment, someone else's personnel, and someone else's material conditions. A procedure has to be demonstrated to work on the company's own equipment, by the company's own qualified personnel, on representative material or welds, with the results documented as a procedure qualification record. This matters most acutely for fabricators bringing NDT in-house to support welding inspection: a UT procedure qualified for one code's acceptance criteria — say, ASME Section VIII — isn't automatically valid for a different code's criteria, such as AWS D1.1 structural welding, even if the equipment and technician are identical. Each code-and-application combination needs its own qualification trail.

A practical example makes this concrete. Suppose a new fabricator's NDT department writes a UT procedure for inspecting groove welds on a specific joint configuration. Qualifying that procedure means running it on a mockup weld with known reflectors — side-drilled holes or notches at documented depths — built in the same material and thickness range the production welds will actually use, and demonstrating that the procedure, in the hands of the company's own certified technician, correctly detects and sizes those known reflectors within the code's acceptance criteria. Only once that demonstration is documented does the procedure count as qualified for that application. Doing this once at startup, for every method-and-code combination the company expects to use in its first year, is far cheaper than doing it retroactively after a client's quality department rejects a report because the underlying procedure was never actually qualified.

Step Four: Equipment Calibration Program

A calibration program needs three things a startup rarely has all of on day one: reference standards traceable to a national standard (NIST, in the US), a defined calibration frequency for each instrument type — commonly annual, with per-use or per-shift verification layered on top — and a documented process for what happens when a piece of equipment is found out of tolerance, including how to handle results generated with that equipment before the out-of-tolerance condition was caught. Skipping that last piece is common and dangerous: without it, a single miscalibrated gauge can quietly invalidate weeks of inspection results with no clean way to identify which reports are affected.

Different instrument types carry different verification routines, and a written practice should spell each one out rather than treating "calibration" as one generic requirement. A UT thickness gauge needs a documented reference block check — typically before each shift and whenever the probe or couplant changes — in addition to its periodic full calibration. A magnetic particle yoke needs a documented lift-test (commonly a pull test against a specified minimum weight) on a defined schedule, not just once at purchase. Penetrant systems need sensitivity verification against a reference panel with known indications on a defined interval, and UV light sources used for fluorescent methods need intensity checks logged against a minimum threshold. A calibration program that only tracks "annual cal due" dates in a spreadsheet, without these method-specific interim checks, is missing exactly the layer that catches equipment drift between full calibrations — which is usually when it actually matters in the field.

Step Five: NDE Level III Oversight — Who's Actually Accountable

Every written practice needs a named, qualified Level III behind it — someone with the standing to write and sign the written practice, resolve interpretation disputes, and take responsibility when a client or code body asks hard questions about a certification decision. Startups without an in-house Level III have two real options: qualify someone internally as the company grows, or bring in Level III oversight as a consulting relationship until that internal capability exists. Neither option is a shortcut around the requirement — a written practice with no genuine Level III behind it is a document that won't survive its first serious audit.

Where This Connects to ISO 9001 and Welding Code Compliance

Most NDT startups eventually run into ISO 9001 from the client side — an EPC or fabricator client requiring its inspection suppliers to operate under a certified quality management system — and the written practice, calibration records, and personnel files built correctly from day one become the objective evidence an ISO 9001 auditor expects to see, rather than a separate project to build later. The same is true for welding inspection specifically: AWS D1.1 and ASME Section IX both reference NDT personnel qualification and procedure requirements as part of weld acceptance, which means a fabricator's in-house NDT department needs its procedures qualified against the exact code its welding program operates under, not against NDT in the abstract. Getting this sequencing right the first time — written practice, then personnel program, then procedure qualification tied to the actual codes in use, then calibration — saves a company from redoing all four once a client's audit or a code compliance review forces the issue.

Common First-Year Mistakes We See Walking In

  • Personnel certified with a training course completion certificate mistaken for the employer's actual SNT-TC-1A certification — the training vendor certifies attendance and competency demonstration; the employer's Level III makes the certification decision.
  • Procedures copied from a previous employer or a generic template with no site-specific or code-specific qualification record behind them.
  • No documented Level III oversight structure — a strong Level II informally treated as the final technical authority with nothing on file to support it.
  • Vision exams performed but not dated, filed, or linked to the specific certification record they're supposed to support.
  • Calibration records kept, but no documented process for what happens to results generated before an out-of-tolerance condition was discovered.
  • A written practice built once at company formation and never revisited as new methods, new codes, or new clients are added.

How an Atlantis Consulting Engagement Sequences This

When a startup NDT provider or a fabricator's new in-house department engages Atlantis's ASNT Level III consulting service, the work is sequenced deliberately rather than tackled all at once: first the written practice itself, built around the company's actual methods and client codes rather than a generic template; then the personnel certification program structure, including the Level I/II/III responsibility matrix and the documentation trail for vision exams and OJT hours; then procedure qualification tied to the specific codes the company's clients require; then the equipment calibration program; and throughout, establishing — or providing, as an interim consulting relationship — genuine NDE Level III oversight. Where it makes sense, that program also gets built directly into Atlantis NDT ERP from the start, so personnel certification expiry, calibration due dates, and procedure qualification records live as linked data instead of a folder of PDFs the company has to reconstruct at audit time, and new technicians coming up through the program can be trained toward ASNT SNT-TC-1A through Atlantis's own NDT training pathway rather than starting that search from scratch.

Building It Once, Correctly

A startup NDT department has one real advantage over an established one: nothing has to be unwound. There's no legacy written practice full of decisions nobody remembers making, no personnel files missing documentation because "that's just how it's always been done here." Getting the sequence right, from the first written practice through the first calibration program, means the company is building a defensible structure from day one instead of retrofitting one under audit pressure two years in — and that difference shows up every time a client's quality team, a code compliance reviewer, or a new prospective customer asks to see how the program actually works.

If you're standing up an NDT department for the first time — or inheriting one that was never built with this structure — that's exactly where a consulting engagement like this starts.
