title: NDT Technician Career Path: From Level I to Running Your Own Crew
snippet: What actually separates a Level II technician stuck at one method from one running turnaround crews: method stacking, certification mechanics, and Level III.
content:
The NDT career ladder looks simple on paper — Level I, Level II, Level III — and almost nobody's actual path matches the paper version. Some technicians spend four years at Level II doing nothing but UT thickness gauging on a single client's tank farm and never touch a second method. Others stack three or four methods inside eighteen months, get pulled into API-related fieldwork, and end up running a crew before they've hit five years in the trade. What determines which path a given technician takes is rarely raw aptitude — it's a combination of which employer they started with, how many methods that employer's written practice actually exposes them to, and whether they treat certification as a box to check or as the mechanism that controls their earning ceiling for the next two decades.

This piece walks the realistic version of that ladder: what Level I work actually involves, where the real judgment development happens at Level II, how the SNT-TC-1A qualification mechanics work compared to ISO 9712 and ACCP, which method combinations actually move the needle on assignability and pay, what changes at Level III, and what it takes to go from senior technician to crew lead to shop owner.

Level I: What the Job Really Looks Like in Year One

Per SNT-TC-1A, a Level I technician is qualified to perform specific calibrations, specific tests, and specific evaluations against written acceptance criteria, under the supervision of a Level II or Level III. In practice, that means a Level I hire spends the first year doing an enormous volume of repetitive, closely supervised work: setting up and running magnetic particle inspection on welds against a clearly defined acceptance standard, performing liquid penetrant testing on castings, prepping surfaces, running calibration blocks, and logging readings — the mechanical execution of a method rather than the interpretation calls that come later. Entry-level pay in most U.S. markets in 2026 runs roughly $18 to $24 an hour depending on region and industry (aerospace and nuclear tend to run higher than general fabrication), and per diem or field pay differentials become a meaningful part of total compensation the moment a technician starts traveling for turnaround work.

The single biggest determinant of how fast a Level I technician advances is exposure breadth. A technician sitting in one shop running PT on castings all year builds real proficiency in that one method but a thin resume. A technician who rotates through MT, PT, and basic UT in the same year — even at Level I depth — walks into the Level II exam with a foundation across multiple methods that compounds later. This is exactly the gap NDT training programs structured around ASNT SNT-TC-1A recommended practice are built to close for technicians whose current employer only exposes them to one or two methods.

Level II: Where the Real Judgment Calls Begin

Level II is where the job changes character. A Level II technician is qualified to set up and calibrate equipment, conduct and supervise tests, and — critically — interpret and evaluate results against applicable codes, standards, and specifications, organizing and reporting NDT results. That last part is the actual inflection point: a Level II technician makes accept/reject calls on real components, and those calls carry consequence. A UT thickness reading that gets misread as sound when a pit has actually dropped wall thickness below the retirement thickness calculated under API 570 doesn't get caught by anyone above the technician unless a Level III happens to audit that specific reading.

Base pay for a solid multi-method Level II technician in U.S. oil and gas or aerospace markets commonly lands in the $28 to $42 an hour range as of 2026, with turnaround and outage work paying meaningfully above that on a per diem and overtime basis — experienced phased array or TOFD-qualified Level II technicians working heavy turnaround seasons can clear well into six figures annually when overtime and per diem are counted. The variance is driven almost entirely by method mix and willingness to travel, not tenure alone. A technician who has sat at Level II doing only basic UT on the same static assets for eight years often earns less than a technician two years into Level II who is qualified in phased array UT, TOFD, and radiographic interpretation and takes turnaround assignments across multiple sites.

Certification Mechanics: SNT-TC-1A vs ISO 9712 and ACCP

Understanding what actually certifies a technician matters more than most people realize, because the three dominant schemes in the U.S. NDT market work fundamentally differently and employers weight them differently.

  • ASNT SNT-TC-1A is a recommended practice, not a certification body itself — the employer writes its own qualification and certification program (the "written practice") that follows SNT-TC-1A guidelines, then certifies its own employees against that written practice after they complete required training hours, experience hours, and a formal examination (general, specific, and practical). Certification under SNT-TC-1A is employer-issued and travels with a technician only as far as the next employer is willing to honor the issuing company's written practice, which is why training documentation and a clean exam record matter enormously when changing employers.
  • ISO 9712 is a third-party personnel certification scheme, common internationally and increasingly requested by clients operating to European or Middle Eastern codes, where certification is issued by an accredited independent certification body rather than the employer, making it portable across employers by design. It exists and is a real, widely required credential in global NDT work — employers in certain regions and industries will specifically require it — but it is administered through accredited third-party certification bodies, not through employer-based training providers.
  • ACCP, the ASNT Central Certification Program, is ASNT's own third-party certification scheme, positioned as a portable alternative to employer-based SNT-TC-1A certification within the U.S. market, with its own examination and renewal requirements administered directly by ASNT.

A technician planning a long career benefits from understanding which scheme the industries they want to work in actually require. A technician staying in U.S. refining, petrochemical, and fabrication almost always operates under employer-based SNT-TC-1A. A technician eyeing international EPC work, aerospace primes, or clients with European parent companies will run into ISO 9712 requirements and should understand that pathway runs through accredited third-party certification bodies specifically, separate from an employer's internal written practice.

Multi-Method Stacking: Which Combinations Actually Pay

Not all method combinations move a technician's assignability and pay equally. The combinations that consistently show up in the highest-demand, highest-pay turnaround and shutdown work are:

  • UT + Phased Array UT (PAUT) + TOFD — the backbone combination for weld inspection on new construction and in-service piping/pressure vessels under ASME Section V and API 510/570, and the single most reliably well-paid stack in industrial NDT.
  • MT + PT —ubiquitous entry-level surface methods, expected as a baseline rather than a differentiator, but still required on nearly every job scope.
  • RT interpretation (film and digital) — fewer technicians hold current radiography qualifications due to radiation safety training and dosimetry requirements, which keeps demand for qualified RT interpreters consistently tight.
  • PEC and guided wave UT — the specialty screening methods used in corrosion-under-insulation programs, in shorter supply because fewer training providers teach them and fewer employers have the equipment to build in-house experience hours.
  • Visual inspection to API 510/570/653 inspector-level knowledge — note that API 510, 570, and 653 inspector certifications are administered directly by API through its own examination program, not by NDT training providers, and sit alongside NDT method certifications as a separate but complementary credential many senior technicians pursue once they're aiming at inspector or crew-lead roles.

A technician who stacks PAUT/TOFD on top of a solid MT/PT/UT base, and adds RT interpretation, becomes assignable to nearly any turnaround scope a contractor bids, which is the actual mechanism behind the pay jump between a generalist Level II and a specialist Level II.

The Jump to Level III: Breaking the Career Ceiling

ASNT NDT Level III certification is administered directly by ASNT and requires passing a Basic exam covering general NDT knowledge (codes, standards, materials science, and metallurgy fundamentals) plus Method exams in each NDT method the candidate wants Level III certification in, on top of documented experience and, typically, a relevant engineering or technical degree or additional years of qualifying experience in lieu of one. A Level III is qualified to establish techniques, interpret codes and standards, designate the methods to be used, and — critically for a career trajectory — to write and approve the employer's written practice under SNT-TC-1A, train and examine Level I and II candidates, and sign off on procedures that Level II technicians execute in the field.

This is the actual ceiling-breaker in the career path, because it moves a technician out of hourly field execution and into the roles that control an inspection company's technical program: quality manager, technical director, procedure writer, and often the person a client's engineering team calls directly when a fitness-for-service question comes up mid-turnaround. Level III professionals frequently move into independent consulting, training delivery, or expert-witness work on top of or instead of a staff role, which is where the earnings ceiling opens up meaningfully beyond even a senior field Level II's turnaround-season income.

Running a Crew: The Skills Nobody Trains You For

Becoming a crew lead or shop supervisor draws on almost none of the technical skill that got a technician promoted into the role. Scheduling a six-person crew across three simultaneous job sites during peak turnaround season, reconciling per diem and overtime against a client's purchase order, tracking every crew member's certification expiration and required continuing education hours before they lapse mid-job, and managing client relationships when a finding gets disputed are logistics and people-management problems, not NDT problems. Companies that run this well typically lean on NDT-specific ERP software to track technician certification expiration dates, equipment calibration due dates, and project assignments in one place rather than in a spreadsheet a crew lead updates from a hotel room at 11 PM — the operational overhead of running a crew is exactly the kind of work that either gets systematized or quietly erodes margin and safety compliance.

Building Your Own Shop: What It Takes

The final rung — starting an independent NDT service company — requires all of the above plus business fundamentals most technicians never touch on the way up: general liability and professional liability insurance, equipment capital (a single phased array unit with probes and wedges is a serious capital outlay, before radiography sources, dosimetry, and transport licensing enter the picture for an RT-capable shop), ASNT written practice development if the shop wants to certify its own Level I and II technicians rather than relying on contract Level IIIs, and the sales and estimating skill to win work against established regional competitors. Most successful shop owners spend several years as a crew lead or operations manager at an existing company first, specifically to absorb the estimating, safety-program, and client-relationship side of the business before betting personal capital on a startup.

Common Derailers: What Actually Slows the Path Down

Certification lapses are the most preventable and the most common. SNT-TC-1A certification under an employer's written practice typically requires periodic recertification — an eye exam on a defined cycle, documented continuing experience hours, and sometimes a re-examination interval — and a technician who lets a certification lapse between employers, or during an extended layoff between turnaround seasons, can find themselves re-sitting exams they'd already passed once, losing months of assignable time in the process. Keeping personal copies of every exam record, training certificate, and experience-hour log, independent of whatever employer issued them, is the single cheapest insurance a technician can carry against this.

  • Injury and physical demands — field NDT work involves scaffolding, confined space entry, elevated work, and carrying equipment in extreme heat; a career-ending or career-limiting injury is a real risk that pushes some technicians toward inspection roles or Level III consulting earlier than planned.
  • Method obsolescence at a single employer — a technician who spends a decade at a shop that never adopted phased array or TOFD can find their method set aging out of demand even while their seniority grows, which is why deliberate cross-training matters more than tenure alone.
  • Geographic immobility — the highest-paying turnaround and shutdown work concentrates around refining and petrochemical corridors (the U.S. Gulf Coast, parts of the Midwest, and West Coast refining clusters); a technician unwilling or unable to travel for peak season work caps their own earning ceiling regardless of certification level.
  • Treating Level III as purely an exam to pass — candidates who cram for the Basic and Method exams without building the underlying codes, standards, and metallurgy knowledge the role actually requires often pass the test and then struggle in the job, because Level III work is judgment-heavy in a way multiple-choice exams only partially capture.

A Realistic Timeline

Compressed but achievable: Level I certification within the first six months to a year of entering the field; Level II in a primary method within eighteen months to two years of steady field experience, assuming an employer's written practice tracks required hours accurately; a second and third method stacked over the following two to three years for a technician who deliberately seeks out cross-training rather than staying in one lane; Level III within roughly seven to ten years for a technician who pursues it aggressively and has or completes the underlying technical education requirement; crew lead responsibility often overlaps with late Level II or early Level III status, driven more by demonstrated reliability and client trust than by certification level alone. None of these timelines are fixed — they compress dramatically for technicians who prioritize multi-method training early, and stretch out indefinitely for technicians who stay in a single-method, single-employer track without ever forcing the issue.

title: Choosing an NDT Service Provider: An Owner's Checklist for 2026
snippet: A working checklist for owner-operators vetting NDT providers in 2026: certifications, calibration records, method depth, reporting quality, and red flags.
content:
An owner-operator picking an NDT service provider is not buying a commodity inspection service — they're buying the data their mechanical integrity program, their RBI intervals under API 580/581, and their next turnaround scope will be built on. A missed indication on a piping circuit governed by API 570, or a tank floor reading that gets logged wrong against API 653 minimum thickness criteria, doesn't surface as a procurement problem. It surfaces months or years later as an unplanned outage, a release, or a failed audit. Yet in practice, a large share of NDT service selection still happens on price and availability alone, with certifications and quality systems verified by nothing more than a checkbox on an RFP response. This checklist is built for 2026 conditions: tighter labor markets for qualified Level II and Level III technicians, more sites running digital, mobile-first inspection data capture, and clients increasingly expecting inspection data to feed directly into RBI software and asset integrity systems rather than arriving as static PDFs.

Certifications: What to Actually Verify, Not Just Ask For

Every provider's marketing material claims certified technicians. The diligence question is which certification scheme, at what level, current or expired, and verifiable how. A provider operating under ASNT SNT-TC-1A should be able to produce its written practice document on request — the internal standard that defines its qualification, training hour, and examination requirements for each method and level — along with current certification records for the specific technicians who will be assigned to the job, not a roster of the company's most senior people who won't actually show up on site. If the scope requires ISO 9712 certification, confirm it is issued by an accredited third-party certification body, since ISO 9712 by design is not something a provider self-issues the way SNT-TC-1A employer certification works. If the scope touches API 510, 570, or 653 inspector sign-off, confirm the individual inspector holds current API certification directly from API — that credential is separate from NDT method certification and is issued and renewed by API itself, not by the NDT provider's internal program.

Ask for certification expiration dates in writing, not verbally, and cross-check that the provider has a system tracking recertification and continuing education hours proactively rather than reactively. A provider whose Level II technicians are routinely certifying at the deadline or slightly past it is signaling a weak internal quality system, regardless of how good any individual technician's field skill is.

Equipment and Calibration Records

Ask for the make, model, and last calibration date of the specific instruments — UT flaw detectors, phased array units, radiography sources, PEC and eddy current instruments — that will be used on the job, not a generic equipment list from the company's marketing packet. Calibration traceability matters for two reasons: it is a direct compliance requirement under most codes (ASME Section V references specific reference block and calibration requirements per method), and it is the single easiest thing for an auditor or a client's own Level III to check after the fact if a finding is disputed. A provider that cannot produce a calibration certificate traceable to a national standards body for a given instrument within minutes of being asked has a records problem that will eventually become the owner's problem when a finding needs to be defended.

Radiography sources carry additional scrutiny: confirm current source activity, leak test records, transport licensing, and that the RSO (radiation safety officer) on the job holds current state or NRC licensing appropriate to the jurisdiction. A lapsed or improperly transferred radioactive materials license is not a paperwork technicality — it is a regulatory exposure that lands on the site hosting the work, not only on the contractor performing it.

Multi-Method Capability vs Method Lock-In

A provider that only offers UT and MT will subcontract or simply skip the phased array, TOFD, RT, or PEC work a turnaround scope actually needs, adding a layer of subcontractor management the owner didn't ask for and often doesn't find out about until the invoice shows a pass-through markup. During the RFP process, ask directly which methods are performed by the provider's own certified staff versus subcontracted, and get the subcontractor's own certification documentation under the same scrutiny as the prime provider's. A provider with genuine multi-method depth — UT/PAUT/TOFD, MT, PT, RT, and CUI-specific screening methods like PEC and guided wave — in house reduces both the coordination burden during a compressed turnaround window and the finger-pointing risk when a subcontracted method's finding gets disputed later.

This is also where equipment capital signals real commitment versus a company renting whatever a given job requires. A phased array unit with a full probe and wedge inventory represents a serious standing investment; a provider that owns rather than rents that equipment has typically also invested in the training hours to use it well, because idle capital equipment is an expensive mistake for a small NDT company to make.

Reporting Quality and Turnaround

The deliverable from an NDT inspection is the report, and report quality varies enormously across providers even when the underlying field data is sound. A strong report ties every reading to a specific, relocatable point on the asset (grid reference, GPS coordinate, or component ID cross-referenced to the P&ID), states the acceptance criteria and code reference used for each accept/reject call explicitly rather than a bare pass/fail, and includes calibration data, technician certification level, and equipment serial numbers as a matter of course rather than only on request. Ask to see a redacted sample report before award, not a sales deck describing the reporting process.

Turnaround time matters more during a live turnaround than at almost any other point in the relationship: a provider still hand-typing field notes into reports two or three days after the crew leaves site is a provider that will bottleneck a compressed turnaround window when engineering needs same-day or next-day accept/reject decisions to close out a work order before the unit comes back up. Providers using mobile, offline-capable NDT reporting software that generates ASNT/ISO-formatted reports directly from field-captured data can typically turn a report same-day; providers still working from paper field sheets routinely run a week or more behind during peak season, which either delays turnaround closeout or forces engineering to make decisions on verbal summaries instead of a signed report.

Data Compatibility With RBI and Asset Integrity Systems

A growing share of owner-operators in 2026 run their mechanical integrity programs through a dedicated risk-based inspection or asset integrity management system, whether that's a commercial RBI platform tied to API 580/581 methodology, an in-house EAM build, or a digital twin platform that overlays inspection history directly on a 3D model of the plant. An NDT provider whose deliverable is a flat PDF, with thickness readings buried in a narrative paragraph rather than structured data, forces the owner's engineering team to manually re-key every reading into the integrity system before it can feed the next RBI interval calculation. That re-keying step is where transcription errors enter a dataset that a turnaround decision will later depend on, and it is a completely avoidable cost if the provider's reporting workflow was evaluated for data compatibility before award rather than discovered after the first deliverable lands.

During the RFP process, ask specifically what format thickness and finding data arrives in — a structured export (CSV, XML, or a direct API feed) that maps cleanly to component IDs in the owner's own CMMS or RBI software is worth real weight in the evaluation, not just a nice-to-have. Ask whether the provider's field technicians capture data on a mobile, offline-capable platform in the field or transcribe from paper afterward, because that single workflow choice is usually the best predictor of both turnaround time and data accuracy. Providers who have invested in modern NDT reporting software built for structured, code-compliant data capture tend to hand over datasets that plug into an owner's integrity program with minimal rework, while providers still running a paper-and-spreadsheet workflow generate a data cleanup burden that quietly erodes whatever price advantage they offered at bid time.

This matters even more for owners running a multi-year RBI program rather than a single turnaround engagement, because trending wall-loss rate at a specific CUI circuit or tank floor grid point across three or four inspection cycles only works if every provider across those cycles — which may not be the same company each time — references the exact same component ID and location convention. Locking that data standard into the contract scope, rather than leaving it to each provider's internal preference, is one of the simplest things an owner can do to protect the long-term value of its inspection history.

Insurance, Safety Record, and Site Access Readiness

Confirm current general liability and workers' compensation coverage at limits appropriate to the site's contractor requirements, and ask for the provider's TRIR (total recordable incident rate) and EMR (experience modification rate) for the past three years, not just the current year — a single good year can mask a volatile safety history. Most refineries, petrochemical plants, and larger fabrication shops require ISNetworld, Avetta, or a similar contractor prequalification system status current before badging a crew onto site; confirm this well before the RFP deadline, because prequalification renewal can take weeks and has stalled more than one otherwise-qualified provider out of a job simply on timing.

Site access readiness also covers less obvious items: does the provider's crew already hold current TWIC cards if the site requires maritime/port access, current H2S and confined space training if the scope includes vessel entry, and radiation worker training and dosimetry badges current if RT is in scope. A provider that has to scramble these credentials after award, rather than maintaining them as standing readiness across its technician roster, will show up as schedule slippage in week one.

Red Flags During the RFP Process

  • Vague answers about which specific technicians (by name and certification number) will be assigned, versus a generic "our certified staff."
  • Reluctance to produce a written practice document or sample calibration certificate on request.
  • Pricing dramatically below the rest of the field with no explanation — frequently a signal of under-qualified staff, expired equipment calibration, or undisclosed subcontracting.
  • No documented quality system or internal audit process for reviewing technician findings before reports go out.
  • Inability to name the specific codes and standards (API 510/570/653, ASME Section V, AWS D1.1, as applicable) the scope will be executed against, beyond generic references to "industry standards."
  • No clear escalation path if a technician's finding is disputed — ask specifically who the Level III of record is and how a second-opinion review gets triggered.

A Scored Checklist You Can Actually Use

A workable evaluation splits roughly into five weighted categories: certification verification and written practice quality (technician-level, not company-level); equipment ownership, calibration traceability, and method breadth; reporting quality, turnaround time, and data format compatibility with the owner's own asset integrity or RBI systems; safety record, insurance, and site prequalification status; and finally price, weighted last rather than first, because the cheapest bid on a scope where the finding quality is wrong costs far more than the bid delta once a missed indication turns into an unplanned event. Score each shortlisted provider against all five categories with the same site visit, reference check, and document request applied uniformly — the providers who resist that scrutiny at the RFP stage are telling the owner exactly how they'll behave once the contract is signed and the leverage shifts.

Making the Final Call

The strongest final-round diligence step most owners skip is a working reference call with another client running a comparable scope — similar asset types, similar code requirements, similar turnaround intensity — asking specifically about report turnaround under schedule pressure, how disputed findings got resolved, and whether technician assignments stayed consistent across the engagement or rotated unpredictably. An owner without an in-house Level III to run this evaluation can bring in independent ASNT Level III consulting to audit a shortlist against the checklist above before award, which is often a fraction of the cost of a single missed finding downstream. Providers on the other side of this evaluation who invest in NDT-specific ERP software for certification and calibration tracking and modern reporting software for field data capture tend to be the ones who pass this kind of scrutiny cleanly, because the systems that make a provider auditable are the same systems that make its findings reliable.

For owners with a large or recurring scope, a limited trial engagement — a single unit, a single tank, or one week of a larger turnaround — before committing to a multi-year contract is worth the modest inefficiency of running a shorter procurement cycle twice. A trial scope surfaces exactly the gaps that a paper RFP response cannot: whether the crew that actually shows up matches the certifications submitted, whether reports arrive on the promised schedule under real field conditions rather than a sales estimate, and whether a disputed finding gets escalated to a Level III promptly or sits unresolved while a turnaround clock keeps running. None of this replaces the certification, equipment, and safety diligence covered above — it confirms that what was promised on paper is what actually shows up on site, which is ultimately the only diligence that protects an owner's mechanical integrity program once the contract is signed.

title: Fitness-for-Service (API 579) Consulting: When You Need an Outside Level III
snippet: How API 579-1/ASME FFS-1 fitness-for-service assessments actually work, what NDT data drives the outcome, and when a plant needs an outside ASNT Level III.
content:
The Call That Starts Every FFS Engagement

It usually starts the same way. A turnaround crew finishes a UT thickness survey on a 12-inch API 570 piping circuit in crude service, and three grid points come back below t-min. The unit engineer needs an answer inside a week: run to the next turnaround, install a clamp, or pull the spool for repair. The plant has good API 510/570/653 inspectors and a capable Level II bench, but nobody on staff has run more than a handful of API 579-1/ASME FFS-1 Level 2 assessments, and this one is trending toward Level 3. That's the moment most owner-operators pick up the phone and look for an outside ASNT Level III with fitness-for-service experience — not because their inspection program failed, but because the assessment in front of them has moved past what a routine mechanical integrity program is built to handle day to day.

Fitness-for-service consulting is a narrow, technical niche inside the broader field of ASNT Level III consulting. It sits at the intersection of NDT data quality, fracture mechanics, and code interpretation, and getting any one of those three wrong produces a defensible-looking report with the wrong answer. This post walks through what API 579-1/ASME FFS-1 actually requires, where the NDT data feeds directly into the calculation, and the specific situations where bringing in outside expertise stops being optional.

What API 579-1/ASME FFS-1 Actually Asks For

API 579-1/ASME FFS-1, jointly published by API and ASME, is not a single procedure — it's a library of part-specific assessment methods, each built around a distinct damage mechanism. Part 4 covers general metal loss, the straightforward case of broad, relatively uniform thinning across a shell or head. Part 5 covers local metal loss (LTAs — local thin areas), which requires mapping the actual footprint of the thin region rather than averaging it away. Part 6 addresses pitting corrosion, using pit-couple and pit-chart methods that are unforgiving of sloppy pit-depth data. Part 7 covers blistering and HIC/SOHIC damage from wet H2S service. Part 9 handles crack-like flaws, where the assessment is a fracture mechanics calculation built on flaw size, orientation, and material toughness. Part 12 covers dents, gouges, and dent-gouge combinations, common in pipeline and piping mechanical damage cases.

Each part uses the same three-tier structure. Level 1 assessments use conservative screening curves that a trained inspector can apply directly from field data — minimum thickness, remaining wall, pit density from a chart. Level 2 requires calculating a Remaining Strength Factor (RSF) and comparing it against a code-allowable RSFa, which demands more precise input data and a working understanding of the underlying equations. Level 3 is reserved for cases where Level 1 and Level 2 don't clear the component, or where the owner-user wants a more accurate, less conservative remaining life instead of walking away from a serviceable asset. Level 3 routinely calls for numerical analysis — elastic-plastic FEA for local metal loss, detailed fracture mechanics for crack-like flaws — and a documented engineering evaluation that a jurisdictional authority or insurer can audit.

Where the Assessment Level Determines Who Should Sign It

API 579-1 Part 2 is explicit that Level 3 assessments require an engineer experienced in the relevant analysis methods, and most owner-user FFS programs pair that engineering sign-off with an independent NDT review, because the entire calculation rests on data an inspector collected in the field. A plant's in-house Level II staff can be excellent at running the scans and just as good at Level 1 screening, and still have never built the flaw characterization package a Level 3 crack-like flaw case needs: precise through-wall depth profiling, tip location, and an uncertainty budget on the sizing technique itself. That gap — not a deficiency in the base inspection program — is what a fitness-for-service consulting engagement is built to close.

The NDT Data an FFS Case Lives or Dies On

Every part of API 579-1 is only as good as the flaw characterization feeding it, and this is where NDT technique selection stops being a formality and starts directly changing the calculated answer.

  • General and local metal loss (Parts 4 and 5). UT thickness grids need spacing tight enough to actually capture the LTA footprint — a grid that's too coarse will either miss the thinnest point or misjudge the flaw's length and width, both of which move the RSF. Corrosion mapping with encoded UT or phased array C-scans gives a defensible thickness profile instead of a handful of spot readings.
  • Pitting (Part 6). Pit-depth accuracy matters more than most inspectors expect, because the pit-couple method is sensitive to the combined depth of adjacent pits, not just the deepest single pit.
  • Crack-like flaws (Part 9). This is the highest-stakes case. TOFD and phased array UT sizing of the crack's through-wall depth feeds directly into the stress intensity factor calculation. A sizing error of even a millimeter or two on a shallow surface crack can swing the calculated Kr ratio enough to change a "fit for continued service" result into a "repair now" result, or vice versa — which is exactly why over-conservative sizing costs money and under-conservative sizing costs safety margin.
  • Weld quality inputs. RT and UT weld examination results feed the flaw type classification — planar versus volumetric — that determines which Part 9 procedure applies in the first place.

Owner-operators who keep a clean, trended history of thickness and flaw data, rather than a folder of disconnected turnaround reports, make every future FFS case faster and cheaper to run, because half the Level 2/3 workload is reconstructing corrosion rate and prior flaw geometry from old records. This is one of the more overlooked reasons plants standardize inspection data in a system like Atlantis NDT ERP rather than in scattered PDFs: when the next FFS case comes up, the corrosion rate trend and prior UT grid data are already in one place instead of buried in five years of turnaround binders.

Real-World Damage Mechanisms That Drive These Engagements

A handful of damage mechanisms account for most of the outside FFS consulting calls we see:

  • HIC and SOHIC in wet H2S service. Amine units, sour water strippers, and coker units running wet H2S service develop hydrogen-induced cracking and stress-oriented HIC that don't behave like ordinary corrosion. Part 7 assessments require a damage survey — often angle-beam UT or specialized HIC-mapping techniques — that a general corrosion-mapping crew isn't necessarily set up to run correctly on the first pass.
  • Brittle fracture screening on older carbon steel. Part 3 brittle fracture screening becomes a live issue every cold-weather startup season for older carbon steel vessels and piping that predate modern Charpy toughness requirements. The MDMT evaluation depends on accurate material identification and thickness data, and getting it wrong in the conservative direction can force an unnecessary preheat or hold, while getting it wrong in the non-conservative direction is a brittle fracture risk during startup.
  • Corrosion under insulation (CUI). CUI produces local thin areas that are invisible until insulation is removed or a scan is run through jacketing, and the resulting LTA geometry is frequently irregular in a way that stresses the Part 5 methodology's assumptions. Getting an accurate footprint on an irregular CUI flaw is a sizing problem before it's ever an engineering problem.
  • Pitting in crude and produced-water tank bottoms. API 653 tank floor and shell pitting assessments lean on Part 6, and the pit-density data quality from an MFL or UT floor scan directly sets how conservative, or how unnecessarily conservative, the resulting RSF comes out.

What a Third-Party Consulting Engagement Actually Looks Like

A well-scoped outside FFS engagement isn't a rubber stamp on whatever the plant's Level II already found. It typically includes an independent review of the raw NDT data and the technique used to collect it — is the sizing method appropriate for the flaw type and material thickness in the first place — a check of which API 579-1 part and level actually applies given the damage mechanism, an independent RSF or remaining-life calculation run in parallel with, not copied from, the plant's internal number, and a documented peer-review sign-off suitable for a jurisdictional inspector, insurer, or corporate mechanical integrity audit. For crack-like flaw cases specifically, that includes confirming the flaw sizing uncertainty was accounted for in the fracture mechanics input, since API 579-1 Part 9 explicitly calls for the assessment to account for NDE sizing error.

The output is a report an owner-user can defend in front of an API inspector or their own corporate engineering review, not just a spreadsheet with a passing number in it. That documentation and review discipline is the same reason plants pair FFS work with organized NDT reporting software — the underlying UT grids, TOFD sizing data, and prior turnaround history all need to be retrievable and auditable years later when the same component comes up for its next assessment.

Common Findings When Reviewing Existing FFS Files

When an outside Level III opens a plant's FFS file for independent review, a handful of issues show up often enough to be worth naming. The first is a Level 1 screening curve applied to a flaw geometry the curve wasn't built for — using a general metal loss curve on what is actually a local thin area, which understates the true severity because the averaging effect of general metal loss doesn't apply to a localized flaw. The second is UT thickness grids sized for a routine CML survey rather than for the specific LTA under evaluation — five-point condition monitoring location data is fine for trending general corrosion, but it's the wrong resolution for defining an LTA's exact footprint for a Part 5 calculation. The third is a corrosion rate calculated from only two data points years apart, which produces an average rate that can mask a recent acceleration from a process change, a new corrosion inhibitor program, or a shift in feedstock. The fourth, specific to crack-like flaw cases, is a flaw sizing report that states a single through-wall depth without any stated sizing uncertainty or technique validation — API 579-1 Part 9 expects that uncertainty to be part of the input, and its absence is one of the first things an independent reviewer will flag.

None of these findings mean the original inspection was done poorly. Most come from a Level II inspector correctly executing a standard turnaround scope that was never designed to produce Level 3 FFS-grade input data in the first place. Recognizing that gap early, ideally before the turnaround window closes, is usually cheaper than discovering it during an independent review months later.

Deciding When You Actually Need Outside Help

Not every below-t-min reading needs a consultant. A straightforward Level 1 general metal loss case that clears the screening curve with margin is well within most in-house programs' capability. Bring in outside expertise when any of the following apply:

  • The damage mechanism is crack-like, HIC/SOHIC, or otherwise outside straightforward metal-loss assessment
  • Level 1 and Level 2 don't clear the component and a Level 3 numerical analysis is the next step
  • No one on staff has run this specific API 579-1 part before, or has run it but has no one to peer-review the result
  • The result changes MAWP, forces a rerate, or affects a run/repair decision with real production or safety consequences
  • A jurisdictional authority, insurer, or corporate audit requires independent, non-plant-employee sign-off

An outside ASNT Level III consulting engagement on an FFS case is typically measured in days of engineering time, not weeks — the value is in getting a defensible, code-correct answer fast enough to make the run/repair decision on the turnaround's actual schedule, not months after the unit is already back on stream.

Working With Your Existing Inspection Program, Not Around It

The most effective FFS consulting engagements don't replace a plant's internal API 510/570/653 program — they plug into it. An outside Level III who understands the plant's existing procedures, prior turnaround history, and corrosion rate trends can scope exactly the incremental NDT work an FFS case needs — an extra TOFD scan here, a tighter UT grid there — instead of re-inspecting everything from zero. That's also where building NDT capability in-house pays off over time: a Level II staff that's been through NDT training specifically oriented around FFS-relevant sizing techniques — TOFD, phased array corrosion mapping, encoded scanning — produces field data that's already close to what a Level 3 case needs, which shortens every future engagement and reduces how often an emergency below-t-min reading turns into a scramble.

For plants weighing whether a specific reading, pit survey, or crack indication needs to go to Level 2 or Level 3, or whether an in-house Level II sign-off is sufficient, the fastest path to a clear answer is usually a short scoping call with an outside Level III before committing engineering hours to a full assessment.

Whether you need a full Level 3 fitness-for-service assessment or just a second set of eyes on a borderline reading, Atlantis NDT's ASNT Level III consulting team can help you scope the right response before your next turnaround window closes.

title: Third-Party NDT Consulting for M&A Due Diligence: What Buyers Actually Check
snippet: What third-party NDT and mechanical integrity consultants actually check in an M&A data room, and how their findings change purchase price and deal terms.
content:
Why NDT Data Shows Up in Every Industrial M&A Data Room

By the time a buyer's technical team gets access to a data room for a refinery unit, a terminal, a fabrication shop, or a pipeline system, financial and legal diligence is usually already well underway. Mechanical integrity and inspection records tend to arrive later, and get less scrutiny than they deserve, because they're technical documents that a corporate development team or a generalist environmental consultant isn't equipped to read critically. That's a mistake. A thickness trending chart that shows a piping circuit approaching t-min in eighteen months, or a fitness-for-service file with an unresolved Level 3 finding, is a liability with a dollar figure attached, sometimes a large one, and it's sitting in the same data room as the environmental Phase I report everyone reads carefully.

Third-party NDT and mechanical integrity consulting during M&A diligence exists to put a technically qualified reader — usually an ASNT Level III with API 510/570/653 and, where relevant, API 579-1 fitness-for-service background — in front of that data before the deal closes, not after.

The Documents Buyers Ask For First

A structured diligence request for an industrial asset's mechanical integrity file typically pulls:

  • Risk-Based Inspection (RBI) program documentation per API 580/581, including current risk rankings and inspection intervals for pressure equipment
  • Thickness monitoring history and corrosion rate trending for all API 570 piping circuits and API 653 storage tanks
  • Open fitness-for-service files under API 579-1/ASME FFS-1, including any component currently operating under a Level 2 or Level 3 assessment with conditions attached
  • Pressure vessel and tank inspection reports for the most recent internal/external cycle, with any deferred recommendations noted
  • Regulatory correspondence — OSHA Process Safety Management (29 CFR 1910.119) citations, state environmental agency notices, or jurisdictional boiler/pressure vessel inspector findings
  • NDT contractor qualification records and current calibration certificates for any owned inspection equipment

Each of these documents answers a different question a buyer's valuation model implicitly assumes has already been answered correctly. The RBI program tells a buyer whether the seller's own inspection cadence matches the actual risk profile of the equipment, not just a fixed calendar interval. The thickness monitoring history is what lets an independent reviewer recalculate a corrosion rate and remaining-life projection independently of whatever conclusion the seller's report states. And the FFS files are, in practice, the single highest-value document in the request: an open Level 2 or Level 3 case with a stated remaining life directly informs how much capital the buyer should expect to spend on that specific component within a defined number of years after close.

The volume alone is the first problem. A mid-size refinery unit can have thousands of condition monitoring locations with years of trending data attached, and no buyer's deal team has the bandwidth or the domain knowledge to read all of it in a four-week diligence window. The job of an outside Level III isn't to read every record — it's to know which records determine whether the asset's remaining useful life matches what the seller's model assumes.

Reading Between the Lines of a Seller's Inspection Reports

Sellers aren't necessarily hiding anything — most mechanical integrity gaps in a diligence file come from years of decent-but-not-rigorous inspection practice rather than concealment. Still, a few patterns show up often enough to check for specifically: recommendations marked "monitor" for multiple consecutive turnaround cycles instead of being resolved, corrosion rates calculated from only two widely spaced data points (which can hide a recent acceleration), and repair or rerate decisions that were made verbally and never formally documented in an FFS file. None of these are necessarily disqualifying, but each one changes what a buyer should assume about near-term capital spend after close.

Independent Verification: What a Third-Party Level III Actually Does

Paper review is step one. A properly scoped diligence engagement also includes a targeted field component — a plant walk with spot UT thickness checks on the highest-risk circuits identified in the RBI program, a sample cross-check of the seller's reported thickness readings against independent measurements, and a review of the actual calibration records for whatever equipment generated the historical data. If the seller's UT data was collected with equipment calibrated against a block that doesn't match the referenced ASTM practice, or with a technician whose ASNT certification lapsed mid-program, that's a data quality problem that undermines every trend built on top of it, and it's the kind of finding a financial or legal diligence team has no way to catch on its own.

This is also where a buyer's own future operating plan matters. If the acquisition includes plans to run the asset longer or harder than the seller did, the existing RBI intervals and corrosion rate assumptions may not hold, and an independent Level III review is the right place to flag that before it becomes a post-close surprise.

Red Flags That Change Deal Terms

A handful of findings consistently move the needle in negotiations:

  • Piping or vessel components operating close to t-min with no documented FFS assessment or repair plan on file
  • RBI intervals that have slipped — inspections overdue relative to the program's own stated schedule
  • A pattern of deferred recommendations across multiple turnaround cycles on the same equipment
  • NDT contractor or in-house technician certification records that don't hold up — expired certifications, missing vision test documentation, or written practice gaps
  • Regulatory notices tied to mechanical integrity that haven't been formally closed out

These findings don't automatically kill a deal. What they do is give the buyer's negotiating team a specific, defensible number to put on the table — an escrow holdback sized to the estimated cost of resolving an open FFS case, a purchase price adjustment reflecting near-term capital spend the seller's model didn't account for, or a closing condition requiring specific repairs before transfer. Without an independent technical review, buyers are negotiating on the seller's own characterization of the asset's condition, which is rarely the position you want to be in on a nine or ten-figure transaction.

When the Target Is an NDT or Inspection Services Company Itself

The other version of this engagement is diligence on an NDT service provider being acquired, increasingly common as the inspection industry consolidates. Here the questions shift from asset condition to organizational capability: does the target's Written Practice meet current SNT-TC-1A or CP-189 requirements, are technician certification and experience-hour records actually maintained and verifiable, is the calibration program for owned equipment (UT flaw detectors, phased array units, radiographic sources) current and traceable, and does the target hold the ISO 9001 and other certifications its contracts represent that it holds. A buyer acquiring an inspection company is effectively buying its certifications and its people's qualifications as much as its equipment, and a gap in Written Practice documentation or a lapsed technician certification can be a direct, quantifiable liability if it surfaces after close on a customer audit.

Diligence on an inspection services company also needs to look at contract concentration and backlog quality specifically through an NDT lens: are the company's largest contracts tied to a single Level III whose departure would jeopardize the Written Practice's interpretation authority, does the equipment fleet's calibration status support the utilization rate the target's financials assume, and are there any customer audit findings in the target's own file, such as a prior nonconformance from a refinery or EPC customer, that never made it into the financial diligence data room because it was treated as a technical rather than a financial issue.

Sizing the Review to the Deal, Not to Every Component

The instinct on a first M&A diligence engagement is often to ask for a full independent review of every pressure component in scope, which is both unaffordable and unnecessary. A better approach mirrors how the seller's own RBI program should already be structured: rank equipment by consequence of failure and probability of failure, then focus the independent NDT review on the highest-risk 10 to 20 percent of components, plus anything already flagged with an open recommendation or an FFS file in progress. That subset typically represents the large majority of the asset's actual integrity risk, and reviewing it thoroughly is far more valuable to a deal team than a shallow pass across everything. For a refinery unit with several hundred RBI-ranked components, this usually narrows the field verification scope to a few dozen high-consequence circuits and vessels, enough for a two- or three-person Level III team to walk in a matter of days rather than weeks, while still producing statistically meaningful confidence in the seller's broader data quality.

This risk-based sizing also gives the deal team a defensible answer when asked why certain equipment wasn't independently verified: the review targeted the components where a wrong answer would actually matter to valuation, not an arbitrary percentage of the total component count.

How Findings Translate Into Deal Terms

The output of a diligence-stage NDT review is only useful if it's written in language the deal team can act on — not a technical memo full of RSF calculations, but a prioritized list with an estimated cost or risk assigned to each item, and a clear statement of which findings are pre-close conditions versus post-close operating items. Some findings belong in the purchase agreement as specific indemnification carve-outs; others are simply added to the post-close capital plan. Getting that translation right is as much a communication skill as a technical one, which is part of why this work usually goes to a consultant who has already sat across the table from corporate development teams, not only from plant engineering.

Coordinating With Environmental and PSM Diligence Workstreams

Mechanical integrity findings rarely exist in isolation from the rest of a diligence effort. A piping circuit with a deferred FFS case is often also flagged in environmental diligence if it's a potential leak source, and it almost always intersects with process safety management diligence under 29 CFR 1910.119, since mechanical integrity is itself one of PSM's fourteen elements for covered processes. The most effective diligence engagements have the NDT/mechanical integrity reviewer coordinating directly with whoever is running PSM and environmental diligence, rather than each workstream producing an independent report that never gets reconciled. A piping circuit that shows up as a "monitor" item in the mechanical integrity file and separately as a fugitive emissions concern in the environmental file is the same underlying risk counted twice in two different reports, or worse, discussed in neither report clearly enough for the deal team to connect the two and understand the actual combined exposure.

Common Pushback From Deal Teams, and Why the Review Still Pays for Itself

The most common objection to scoping an independent NDT review during diligence is timeline pressure — deal teams are reluctant to add another workstream to an already compressed schedule. The second is a belief that the seller's own inspection program, if it's ISO 9001 certified or run by a recognizable engineering firm, doesn't need independent verification. Neither objection holds up well against the actual cost of being wrong. A single overlooked FFS case on a large-diameter piping circuit can represent a repair scope in the high six or seven figures once engineering, fabrication, and unit downtime are factored in, and that's before considering the cost of discovering it during the first turnaround after close, when the buyer no longer has any leverage to renegotiate. A properly scoped review, by contrast, adds days to the diligence timeline, not weeks, when it's scoped early and focused on the highest-consequence equipment rather than an exhaustive review of every record in the file.

Buyers who plan to operate the acquired asset for the long term also use diligence as the moment to plan post-close systems integration — folding the target's inspection history into a digital twin platform for ongoing asset visualization, or migrating scattered contractor reports into a single Atlantis NDT ERP instance so corrosion trending and RBI scheduling don't depend on whichever engineering firm ran the program under the previous owner.

A Practical Diligence Checklist for Deal Teams

  • Request RBI documentation, thickness trending, and all open FFS files at first data room access, not during confirmatory diligence
  • Identify the highest-consequence 10-20 percent of equipment and scope field verification to that subset
  • Cross-check a sample of the seller's reported thickness readings against independent measurements, not just against each other
  • Pull calibration records for the equipment that generated the historical data, not just the equipment currently in the field
  • Coordinate findings with the PSM and environmental diligence workstreams before the findings summary is finalized
  • Translate every finding into a dollar range and a pre-close versus post-close classification before it reaches the negotiating table

Building Diligence Into the Timeline

NDT and mechanical integrity diligence needs to start earlier than most deal teams schedule it, because document requests, plant access for field verification, and third-party review all take longer than a desktop financial model review. A realistic window is three to five weeks from data room access to a findings summary the deal team can use in negotiations, longer if field verification requires plant access coordination through the seller. Bringing in outside ASNT Level III consulting support at the letter-of-intent stage, rather than waiting until confirmatory diligence, gives the buyer's team time to actually use the findings instead of racing a closing date with an incomplete technical picture.

If your deal team needs an independent read on an asset's mechanical integrity, or on an NDT service provider's certifications and quality system, before you sign, Atlantis NDT's Level III consultants can scope a diligence review sized to your timeline.

title: ASNT Level III Consulting for Written Practice Audits: Common Findings
snippet: The written practice compliance gaps an outside ASNT Level III finds most often: vision testing, training hours, experience logs, and exam records.
content:
What a Written Practice Is, and Why Someone Eventually Checks It

Every company that performs nondestructive testing under ASNT SNT-TC-1A is required to establish a Written Practice — the internal document that defines how personnel are trained, examined, and certified in each NDT method the company uses. It's not a form filed away for the sake of having one. The Written Practice is the document an auditor, a customer's quality representative, or a Level III reviewer will ask for first, because it's the foundation everything else in a personnel qualification program rests on: if the Written Practice is wrong or out of date, every certification issued under it inherits the same defect.

SNT-TC-1A is a recommended practice, not a mandatory standard by itself — it becomes binding when a contract, a customer specification, or a code such as ASME Section V invokes it through its personnel qualification requirements. That's exactly why Written Practice audits tend to arrive at inconvenient moments: a new prime contract requires proof of compliance, a customer's quality group schedules a supplier audit, or an ISO 9001 surveillance audit turns up a personnel qualification nonconformance that traces back to the Written Practice itself.

SNT-TC-1A and CP-189 — Two Different Documents, Two Different Audits

SNT-TC-1A is a guideline: each employer writes its own Written Practice based on it, choosing training hours, experience hours, and examination requirements within the recommended ranges, and the resulting document is only as rigorous as the employer chose to make it. ANSI/ASNT CP-189 is a full national standard for a personnel qualification and certification program, with less room for employer discretion. Some customer specifications, particularly in nuclear, aerospace, and certain pipeline work, require CP-189 rather than SNT-TC-1A. An audit finding we see often is a company operating a CP-189-referencing contract against a Written Practice that was originally built for SNT-TC-1A and never fully reconciled to CP-189's stricter requirements — different minimum training hours, different examination administration rules, different Level III qualification requirements. Confirming which document actually governs a given contract, before auditing anything else, is the first step of a competent Written Practice review.

What Actually Triggers These Audits

Written Practice audits rarely happen because a company decides one morning to review its own qualification program from first principles. In practice, four triggers account for nearly every engagement we see: a new prime contract or master service agreement that requires proof of SNT-TC-1A or CP-189 compliance as a condition of award, an ISO 9001 surveillance or recertification audit where the assessor's sampling happens to land on a personnel file with a gap, a corporate merger or acquisition where the acquiring company's own quality group wants independent confirmation before absorbing the target's certified technicians into its own program, and a scheduled internal review that a mature quality function runs on its own cadence rather than waiting for an external party to find the problem first. The first three arrive on someone else's timeline, which is exactly why the fourth, a company-initiated review, tends to produce better outcomes: there's time to fix what's found before a customer or certifying body sees it.

Common Finding: Vision Testing Gaps

This is, by a wide margin, the single most common finding in a Written Practice audit, and the easiest to miss internally because it's administrative rather than technical. SNT-TC-1A requires annual near-distance visual acuity testing — Jaeger J-1 or equivalent at 12 inches, or better — and color vision screening at the time of initial certification, with the ongoing annual requirement often overlooked once someone is a few years into their career. Common gaps: annual vision exams that lapsed by a few months and were never caught because there's no automated tracking, color vision testing that was never repeated after hire even though the Written Practice requires it, and vision test records that exist but don't specify which standard and at what distance was used, which makes the record technically unverifiable even if the test itself was performed correctly. The fix is rarely complicated — a scheduled reminder tied to each technician's certification anniversary closes most of this gap permanently — but until it's tracked systematically, it resurfaces at every audit cycle.

Common Finding: Training Hour Shortfalls by Method

SNT-TC-1A's recommended minimum training hour tables differ by method and by certification level, and they differ again depending on whether the individual holds a degree or prior related certifications that qualify for reduced hours. Audits regularly find Written Practices that copy an outdated hours table from a prior revision of SNT-TC-1A without updating it, or that apply one method's training hours to a different method by clerical error. Phased array UT and TOFD present a specific version of this problem: because they're specialized applications of the base UT method, some Written Practices never clearly state whether PAUT/TOFD requires additional method-specific training hours beyond conventional UT, and if the Written Practice is silent, the company has no defensible answer when a customer auditor asks how a technician became qualified to size cracks with phased array equipment. The remediation here is more involved than the vision-testing fix, because it can mean identifying technicians who were certified against an insufficient hours table and determining whether additional documented training closes the gap retroactively or whether recertification is the only defensible path.

Common Finding: Experience Hour Documentation That Doesn't Hold Up

SNT-TC-1A ties certification level to accumulated hours of experience in each method, and the finding here is rarely that the hours weren't worked — it's that they weren't documented in a way that survives an audit. A technician's personnel file needs a verifiable log connecting specific dated work to specific hours in a specific method, signed off by a qualified supervisor. What auditors commonly find instead is a single summary line — "2,400 hours UT" — with no underlying daily or job-level detail to substantiate it, no clear separation between hours in conventional UT versus PAUT/TOFD, or overlap where an individual is credited with the same working hours toward two different methods without an explanation for how that's possible. None of these findings necessarily mean the technician isn't competent — they mean the paperwork can't prove it, which is a real problem the moment a customer, an insurer, or a jurisdictional authority asks for evidence. Where records genuinely cannot be reconstructed, the only defensible options are a documented statement from a supervisor with direct personal knowledge of the work, or, more conservatively and more commonly, treating the certification as unsupported until new experience hours are logged going forward under a proper tracking system.

Common Finding: Qualification Exam Records and Question Bank Security

SNT-TC-1A calls for general, specific, and practical examinations at each certification level, each scored and retained. Audit findings here cluster around a few patterns: minimum passing grades that don't match what the Written Practice itself specifies — commonly 70% general/specific and 80% practical, though the specific numbers a company sets are its own choice within SNT-TC-1A's guidance and need to be applied consistently — practical exams that don't actually include a real flawed specimen with a documented, known result, and, a finding that surprises people, the same fixed exam given repeatedly for years without rotation, which becomes an integrity problem once technicians have had years to memorize a static answer key. A Level III reviewing exam administration will also check that the person administering and grading the exam holds a qualification level appropriate to do so, and that recertification exams, not just initial certification exams, are actually being given on the interval the Written Practice specifies. Where a fixed exam has clearly been reused for years, the corrective action isn't just writing new questions once, it's establishing a rotation schedule and a documented process for retiring exam versions once they've been administered enough times to be considered compromised.

A Worked Example: How One Gap Cascades

A mid-size fabrication shop's Written Practice audit, prompted by a new EPC contract requiring CP-189 compliance, started with a routine sample of five personnel files out of a technician roster of thirty. The sample turned up one lapsed annual vision test. That alone would have been a minor finding, except pulling the thread showed the same lapse pattern across eleven of the thirty technicians, because vision testing had been tracked on an informal spreadsheet that nobody owned after the original quality coordinator left two years earlier. Because CP-189 is stricter than SNT-TC-1A about continuously valid certification, the eleven technicians' certifications were technically unsupported for the period the vision testing lapsed, which meant every inspection report those individuals signed during that window was, strictly speaking, issued under an invalid certification. The shop didn't have to redo the underlying inspection work — the NDT itself wasn't in question — but it did have to reconstruct a defensible record of when each lapse occurred, retest all eleven technicians immediately, and build a tracking system that made the same failure structurally impossible going forward. What started as one finding in a five-file sample became a company-wide remediation because nobody had checked whether the gap was isolated before assuming it was.

How This Differs From a Broader Quality System Audit

It's worth being precise about scope, because the two get conflated often. A Written Practice audit is narrowly about personnel qualification and certification under SNT-TC-1A or CP-189: training, experience, examination, vision testing, and the documented authority structure behind certification decisions. An ISO 9001 quality system audit is broader, covering calibration control, document control, nonconformance handling, and management review across the entire operation, of which personnel qualification is only one clause. A company can have a fully compliant Written Practice and still fail an ISO 9001 audit on calibration traceability, and the reverse is just as common: a well-run ISO 9001 quality system with a Written Practice that hasn't been touched in years because nobody's internal audit scope ever specifically sampled it. Companies preparing for either kind of audit are usually better served scoping both reviews together rather than sequentially, since the underlying personnel and procedure records overlap substantially.

Common Finding: Level III Interpretation Authority Left Undefined

SNT-TC-1A gives the employer's Level III, or an outside consulting Level III retained for the purpose, responsibility for establishing and interpreting the Written Practice, approving procedures, and having final say on qualification and certification decisions. A surprising number of Written Practices name a Level III as responsible without clearly stating what happens when that individual leaves the company, retires, or is otherwise unavailable, leaving certifications technically ungoverned until a successor is named and the document updated. This becomes a real operational problem for smaller NDT companies and in-house inspection groups that employ exactly one Level III: if that person is unreachable during a customer audit or a certification dispute, there's often no documented backup authority, which is precisely the kind of structural gap that outside ASNT Level III consulting support is commonly retained to cover, either as a standing backup authority or as the reviewer who catches the gap before a customer auditor does.

What a Level III Written Practice Audit Actually Delivers

A structured audit produces more than a pass/fail. It produces a finding-by-finding list mapped to the specific SNT-TC-1A or CP-189 clause each gap violates, a corrective action for each one — revise the document, retrain and re-examine specific individuals, rebuild missing records where recoverable — and, critically, a revised Written Practice that's internally consistent instead of a patchwork of edits made over successive years by different people. Most companies that go through this process discover their Written Practice has been amended piecemeal for a decade: a training hours table updated in one revision cycle, a vision testing clause added after a prior customer finding, a new method added later without fully cross-referencing the rest of the document. An outside review is often the first time the whole document gets read start to finish as a single coherent policy instead of an accumulation of patches.

Keeping the underlying qualification records — training hours, experience logs, exam results, vision test dates — organized in a structured system rather than individual paper files makes the next audit dramatically less painful. Companies that manage technician certification tracking through a system like Atlantis NDT ERP can produce a complete, audit-ready qualification file for any technician in minutes instead of reconstructing it from personnel folders under audit pressure.

Getting Ahead of the Audit Instead of Reacting to One

The companies that handle Written Practice audits well are the ones that schedule an internal or third-party review on their own timeline — annually, or ahead of a known contract renewal — rather than waiting for a customer or certifying body to find the gaps first. A proactive review costs a fraction of what a failed customer audit costs in remediation time, re-examination scheduling, and, in some cases, work stoppage on a contract that requires proof of a compliant qualification program before technicians can be dispatched to a job site. Pairing a Written Practice review with broader technician development through Atlantis NDT Academy gives a company a documented, defensible answer for how its qualification program actually works, not just a policy that reads well until someone checks the underlying records.

If it's been more than a year since your Written Practice was read start to finish by someone outside your own program, an outside ASNT Level III audit is the fastest way to find the gaps before a customer auditor does.
