title: Pipeline Integrity RBI Consulting: Building an API 1160/1163-Aligned Program
snippet: How midstream and pipeline operators build a defensible RBI program that survives a PHMSA audit — API 1160 risk modeling paired with API 1163 ILI tool qualification.
content:
Why Pipeline Operators Are Rebuilding Their RBI Programs Around API 1160 and API 1163

A hazardous liquid pipeline operator running 900 miles of 16-inch and 20-inch line across three states does not fail an integrity audit because nobody ran an inline inspection tool. It fails because the risk model behind the inspection schedule cannot be defended in front of a PHMSA auditor, and because the ILI data validation trail does not connect cleanly to the written practice that says who reviewed it and when. Risk-based inspection consulting for pipelines is not about telling an operator to run more smart pigs. It is about building a defensible, auditable program that ties API 1160 risk assessment methodology to API 1163 inline inspection qualification, and then proving — with document control, not with a binder of PDFs — that the program was actually followed.

Atlantis NDT's ASNT Level III consulting engagements in this space typically start the same way: an operator has an RBI framework on paper, built by a consultant or an in-house engineer who has since left, and nobody currently on staff can explain why a given segment is inspected every 5 years instead of every 7. That gap is the actual finding, more often than any specific wall-loss anomaly.

What API 1160 Actually Requires From a Risk Assessment

API RP 1160, "Managing System Integrity for Hazardous Liquid Pipelines," does not hand operators a single risk formula. It requires a documented, repeatable process that identifies threats — external corrosion, internal corrosion, stress corrosion cracking, third-party damage, manufacturing and construction defects, equipment failures, incorrect operations, and weather-related or outside-force events — and assigns likelihood and consequence to each pipeline segment. The consequence side has to account for High Consequence Areas (HCAs) as defined by 49 CFR Part 195: populated areas, commercially navigable waterways, and unusually sensitive areas (USAs) for drinking water or ecological resources.

Where operators get into trouble is in the likelihood modeling. A defensible RBI program under API 1160 needs segment-level data on pipe age, coating type and condition, cathodic protection history, soil corrosivity, depth of cover, crossing density, and prior inspection findings — not a single corporate-wide corrosion rate applied uniformly across dissimilar segments. When Atlantis Level III consultants review an existing program, the most common finding is a risk model that was built once, five to eight years ago, and never re-calibrated against actual ILI results. API 1160 explicitly calls for the risk assessment to be a living document, reassessed whenever new inspection data, incident history, or changed operating conditions warrant it — and PHMSA inspectors know to ask for the re-assessment date.

API 1163: Where Most ILI Programs Actually Break Down

API 1163, "In-line Inspection Systems Qualification," governs the tool run itself — not just whether a smart pig went through the line, but whether the vendor's tool was qualified for the specific defect types the operator needs to find, and whether the post-run data validation followed a documented process. Three areas cause the most rework on audit:

  • Tool performance specification mismatch. A magnetic flux leakage (MFL) tool qualified for metal loss detection is not automatically qualified for axial or circumferential SCC detection, which typically requires an EMAT (electromagnetic acoustic transducer) or ultrasonic crack-detection tool. Operators sometimes run the wrong tool class for the threat identified in their own API 1160 risk assessment — for example, running an MFL caliper run on a segment flagged for SCC susceptibility near a compressor station discharge, where the threat is cracking, not metal loss.
  • Unvalidated tolerance claims. API 1163 requires the ILI vendor's stated tolerances (depth, length, width sizing accuracy) to be validated against field data — dig verifications, not just the vendor's factory calibration sheet. Operators who skip the dig-validation step and accept vendor tool-spec sheets at face value cannot defend their reported repair criteria if an auditor asks for the correlation between reported and actual defect dimensions.
  • Data integration into the risk model. ILI results need to feed back into the API 1160 risk assessment as new likelihood data, not sit in a separate report that engineering reviews once and files. Atlantis consultants frequently find that a pipeline's GIS-based risk model and its ILI anomaly database are maintained by different departments on different update cycles, so the "current" risk ranking used to schedule the next inspection is actually 18-24 months stale relative to the most recent tool run.

Building the RBI Program: A Practical Sequence

A pipeline integrity RBI consulting engagement that holds up under a PHMSA or state pipeline safety audit generally follows this sequence, whether the operator is a midstream gathering system, a long-haul crude line, or a refined products pipeline subject to 49 CFR Part 195 integrity management (or Part 192 for gas transmission, where API 1160 principles are commonly adapted alongside ASME B31.8S):

1. Segment the system by threat, not just by milepost

Segmentation should follow changes in threat exposure — coating type transitions, soil resistivity changes, HCA boundaries, crossing density, and known incident or repair history — rather than administrative boundaries like station-to-station mileposts. A 40-mile segment with uniform 1970s coal-tar enamel coating and consistent soil chemistry can often be treated as one risk unit; a segment that crosses from clay soil to sandy, more corrosive soil at mile 12 should be split there.

2. Assign quantitative likelihood scores per threat category

External corrosion likelihood should be driven by coating condition survey data (close-interval survey, DCVG, or ACVG results), cathodic protection rectifier readings, and pipe-to-soil potential trends over time — not a single "medium" rating assigned by engineering judgment alone. Internal corrosion likelihood needs product characterization: water cut, CO2/H2S partial pressures, flow velocity relative to erosional velocity limits, and any history of pigging for solids removal.

3. Select the ILI tool class against the dominant threat, and document the selection logic

This is the step API 1163 audits most directly. The written justification for tool selection — why MFL versus ultrasonic wall measurement versus EMAT crack detection — needs to reference the specific threat identified in step 2, not a default "we always run MFL" policy inherited from a prior operator.

4. Validate tool results against dig data before updating the risk model

API 1163 unity plots (predicted versus actual defect depth) should be generated and retained for every dig program, and the resulting confirmed tolerance should be the number that feeds repair criteria — not the vendor's marketing spec sheet.

5. Re-run the risk assessment with new data and reset the reassessment interval

The reassessment interval itself should be justified — API 1160 does not mandate a fixed number, but it does require the operator to show the basis for whatever interval is chosen, tied to the confidence level of the risk data.

Where Multi-Method NDT Fits Inside the RBI Framework

ILI is the backbone of most liquid pipeline integrity programs, but RBI-driven direct examination still relies on conventional and advanced NDT methods at dig sites and above-ground facilities: phased array ultrasonic testing (PAUT) for girth weld and seam weld verification, time-of-flight diffraction (TOFD) for crack sizing on suspected SCC colonies, magnetic particle testing (MT) for surface-breaking indications on exposed pipe, and guided wave ultrasonic testing (GWUT) for screening inaccessible or insulated segments such as road and rail crossings and pipe supports at pump stations. A risk-based program should specify which method applies to which finding type — GWUT as a screening tool to prioritize excavation, not as a replacement for direct PAUT sizing once a segment is exposed.

Procedure qualification matters here as much as tool selection. Personnel performing PAUT sizing on ILI-flagged anomalies should hold ASNT Level II or III qualification specific to the PAUT technique per the operator's written practice, and the written practice itself should map to SNT-TC-1A with employer-specific qualification requirements — not a generic template. This is where a lot of midstream and gathering-system operators, who may have a smaller integrity staff than a major interstate carrier, benefit from bringing in outside ASNT Level III consulting support to review or author the written practice rather than trying to adapt a template built for a different operator's threat profile.

Documentation: The Difference Between Passing and Failing an Audit

PHMSA integrity management audits under Part 195.452 (and analogous state pipeline safety programs for intrastate lines) focus heavily on whether the operator can produce, on request, the specific records that show the risk assessment, the inspection method selection rationale, the tool qualification records, the dig verification data, and the repair prioritization logic — all cross-referenced to each other. A common failure mode: the risk assessment says segment 14 is high-risk for external corrosion, the ILI report shows several metal-loss anomalies in that segment, but the dig program record does not show which anomalies were excavated, and the repair log does not tie back to the ILI anomaly IDs. Each document may be individually correct, but the chain between them is broken.

This is precisely the kind of cross-referencing problem that inspection management software is built to solve. An NDT and integrity management ERP that ties inspection work orders, personnel qualification records, and NDT reports to specific asset IDs and anomaly IDs eliminates the spreadsheet-and-shared-drive fragmentation that shows up as findings in almost every PHMSA audit report. Pairing that with a digital twin platform that visualizes the pipeline route with anomaly locations, repair history, and current risk ranking overlaid on the actual GIS alignment gives integrity engineers and auditors a single source of truth instead of reconciling four disconnected systems.

Scoping an RBI Consulting Engagement: What to Ask For

Owner-operators and EPC integrity teams evaluating outside Level III support for an RBI program build-out or gap assessment should expect a scope that includes: a review of the existing risk methodology against API 1160 current edition requirements; a gap analysis of ILI tool qualification records against API 1163; a sample audit of dig verification data and unity plot generation; a review of the written practice governing direct-examination NDT personnel qualification; and a documented recommendation set prioritized by audit exposure, not just technical elegance. A Level III consultant should be able to walk into an existing program, identify which of the five sequence steps above is weakest, and scope a fix that the operator's own staff can maintain going forward — the goal of good consulting is a program the operator owns, not a permanent dependency.

For operators building this capability for the first time, NDT training aligned to ASNT SNT-TC-1A for in-house personnel, combined with a properly scoped written practice, is usually more cost-effective over a multi-year horizon than perpetually outsourcing direct-examination NDT. The consulting engagement and the training build-out are not competing options — the strongest programs use outside Level III expertise to build the framework and qualify the written practice, then train internal staff to execute against it year over year.

Common Findings From Gap Assessments

Across midstream and gathering-system RBI gap assessments, a handful of findings recur often enough to be worth naming explicitly, because each one is inexpensive to fix once identified but expensive to discover during a PHMSA enforcement action.

  • Consequence data frozen at construction. HCA identification is sometimes performed once, at the time a segment is built or acquired, and never refreshed against current population growth data, updated National Hydrography Dataset waterway crossings, or newly designated unusually sensitive areas. A segment that was rural in 2010 may now cross a subdivision, and the risk consequence score needs to reflect that.
  • Corrosion growth rates borrowed from industry defaults. Using a generic 5-10 mil-per-year external corrosion growth rate from an industry handbook, rather than the operator's own re-inspection interval data, understates or overstates risk depending on the actual soil and cathodic protection conditions on that specific segment. Two consecutive ILI runs on the same segment, properly aligned and compared feature-to-feature, give a far more defensible growth rate than any published default.
  • Repair prioritization decoupled from the risk ranking. Some operators maintain a technically sound risk model but prioritize repairs purely by defect severity (percent wall loss) without weighting by the segment's HCA consequence score, which is backwards from what API 1160 intends — a moderate anomaly in a high-consequence area generally warrants faster action than a severe anomaly in a low-consequence rural segment with easy excavation access.
  • No record of who qualified the ILI vendor's personnel. API 1163 places qualification obligations on both the pipeline operator and the ILI service provider. Audits increasingly ask operators to show how they verified that the vendor's data analysts and tool operators were qualified for the specific tool and defect type run — not just a general vendor approval letter from years earlier.

Aligning the Program With EPC and Construction-Phase NDT

For new pipeline construction or major looping projects, the RBI program should not start on the day the line goes into service — the baseline risk data begins with construction-phase NDT records: radiographic testing (RT) or automated ultrasonic testing (AUT) results on girth welds, coating holiday detection survey results, and as-built alignment sheets showing actual depth of cover and crossing locations. EPC contractors managing multi-site construction should hand over a digitized NDT record set, not boxes of film or disconnected PDF reports, so the operator's integrity team can load baseline weld quality and coating condition directly into the RBI model from day one rather than treating year-one data as unknown. Atlantis NDT's reporting software is built to produce that structured, exportable record set at the point of construction inspection, which materially shortens the time it takes to stand up a credible RBI baseline once the asset is placed in service.

title: Power Generation NDT Consulting: ASME Section I Boiler Inspection Programs
snippet: Building a damage-mechanism-driven boiler NDT program on an ASME Section I design basis — creep, FAC, and DMW cracking, and why cycling duty rewrites the inspection math.
content:
The Gap Between a Jurisdictional Boiler Inspection and a Real Integrity Program

A coal or gas-fired utility boiler passes its annual jurisdictional inspection under the National Board Inspection Code and the plant's state boiler and pressure vessel regulations, and the plant manager treats that as proof the unit is sound. It isn't, and every power generation reliability engineer who has managed a tube failure knows it. The jurisdictional inspection, performed by an Authorized Inspector, verifies code compliance and safety-relief valve function — it is not a substitute for a condition-based NDT program that tracks creep damage, fireside corrosion, and flow-accelerated erosion across thousands of feet of boiler tubing, headers, and steam piping built to ASME Section I and operated under ASME Section VII guidelines. Power generation NDT consulting exists to close that gap: to translate ASME Section I construction requirements and API 573 (fired heater and boiler in-service inspection guidance, though written primarily for refinery service, is widely adapted for utility and industrial boilers) into a scheduled, risk-ranked inspection program that catches tube wall thinning and creep damage before it becomes an unplanned outage or a tube rupture.

Atlantis NDT's ASNT Level III consulting engagements with independent power producers, cogeneration facilities, and utility maintenance teams typically begin after a forced outage — a superheater tube failure or a header ligament crack — when management asks why the existing inspection program did not catch it. The answer is almost always a combination of the same three gaps: inspection locations chosen by convenience rather than damage-mechanism analysis, NDT methods mismatched to the actual damage mechanism present, and no quantitative remaining-life calculation behind the next inspection interval.

ASME Section I's Role, and Where It Stops

ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code Section I governs the construction of power boilers — material selection, design pressure and temperature ratings, welding procedure qualification, and the original hydrostatic test. It establishes the design basis: minimum wall thickness at construction, the allowable stress values for the specified material at the design temperature, and the stamped MAWP (maximum allowable working pressure). What Section I does not do is tell a plant how to inspect a boiler that has been in service for 25 years and is now running at higher cycling duty than its original baseload design intended. That is the domain of in-service inspection practice — built from NBIC Part 2 inspection requirements, EPRI boiler tube failure reduction guidelines, and API 573 principles adapted for utility service — layered on top of the Section I design basis.

The practical consequence for an integrity engineer: every inspection plan should start by pulling the original Section I data report (the U-1 or equivalent manufacturer's data report) to establish design minimum wall thickness and allowable stress, then compare current measured wall thickness against that baseline to calculate actual corrosion or erosion rate — not against a generic "typical" wall thickness pulled from a vendor catalog for a similar-looking unit.

The Eight Damage Mechanisms That Drive a Boiler NDT Program

EPRI's boiler tube failure research, which utilities have relied on for decades to reduce forced outage rates, groups the large majority of tube failures into a short list of damage mechanisms, and each one calls for a different NDT method and inspection location strategy:

  • Fireside corrosion / waterwall wastage. Common in coal units with reducing atmosphere pockets near burners. Detected with ultrasonic thickness (UT) grid surveys on waterwall tubes at and above the burner zone, tracked over successive outages to establish a wastage rate.
  • Creep damage in superheater and reheater tubes and headers. Long-term exposure above the material's creep threshold temperature causes microvoid formation and eventual creep rupture. Replication metallography (in-situ or removed-sample) combined with dimensional creep-swelling measurement is the primary detection method; advanced ultrasonic backscatter techniques are increasingly used for in-situ creep-void density screening without cutting a sample.
  • Flow-accelerated corrosion (FAC) in economizer and feedwater piping. Single-phase and two-phase FAC thins carbon steel elbows, reducers, and straight runs, typically on the extrados of bends. UT thickness grid surveys following EPRI's CHECWORKS-guided component selection logic are standard; some plants supplement with pulsed-eddy-current (PEC) for insulated piping where removing lagging for every survey point is impractical.
  • Dissimilar metal weld (DMW) cracking at superheater and reheater transitions between ferritic and austenitic tube materials. Phased array ultrasonic testing (PAUT) has largely replaced radiography for these welds because access is one-sided and PAUT gives better sizing of the creep-fatigue cracks that initiate at the weld interface.
  • Hydrogen damage and caustic gouging in waterwall tubes from water chemistry excursions. Detected through a combination of UT thickness surveys showing localized thinning patterns and metallographic sampling to confirm decarburization.
  • Fatigue cracking at attachment welds (tube-to-header, buckstay attachments) from thermal cycling, especially in units that have shifted from baseload to cycling duty to accommodate renewable generation on the grid. Magnetic particle testing (MT) and PAUT are both used depending on access and material.

Scoping the Inspection Plan: RBI Logic Applied to a Boiler

Step 1: Build a damage-mechanism map, not a generic tube survey grid

Every inspection location should be justified by an identified or plausible damage mechanism for that specific zone — burner-zone waterwalls for fireside corrosion, superheater outlet headers for creep, economizer inlet elbows for FAC — rather than a fixed percentage of total tube footage inspected uniformly. A cycling gas-fired unit and a baseload coal unit have almost entirely different damage-mechanism profiles and should never share an inspection template.

Step 2: Match the NDT method to the damage mechanism, not to what the crew already owns

A common finding in Atlantis Level III program reviews is a plant running the same UT thickness survey on every component regardless of damage mechanism, because that is the technique the in-house crew is equipped and qualified for — while creep damage in a superheater header, which UT thickness alone will not detect until very late stage, goes unscreened. A properly scoped program specifies replication metallography or advanced UT creep-screening techniques specifically where creep is the credible mechanism, and reserves conventional UT thickness surveys for corrosion and erosion mechanisms where they are actually diagnostic.

Step 3: Calculate remaining life quantitatively, and set the next interval from that number

For FAC and general corrosion mechanisms, remaining life is a straightforward calculation from measured wall loss rate against minimum required wall thickness per the Section I design basis. For creep damage, remaining life estimation is more involved — Larson-Miller parameter analysis using measured metal temperature history, or direct creep-life-fraction assessment from replication data, both of which require accurate operating temperature records, another reason integrity engineers push for reliable temperature-monitoring data capture as part of the overall program.

Step 4: Document the basis for the next inspection interval in a form an Authorized Inspector and a plant reliability manager can both use

The interval should be defensible on two audiences at once: the jurisdictional Authorized Inspector reviewing code compliance, and the plant's own reliability engineering function planning the next scheduled outage. A written practice or inspection plan that states "next full internal inspection: 4 years, based on measured FAC rate of 12 mils/year against 45 mils of remaining corrosion allowance" satisfies both.

Personnel Qualification: ASNT SNT-TC-1A in a Power Plant Context

Power generation NDT personnel — whether in-house or contracted for an outage — should be qualified under the plant's written practice per ASNT SNT-TC-1A, with method-specific qualification (UT, PAUT, MT, replication/metallography where used) documented against the actual techniques the plant relies on. A written practice built generically for "industrial NDT" without power-plant-specific technique qualification — creep-screening UT, DMW crack sizing by PAUT, FAC-pattern recognition on thickness grids — leaves a gap that shows up exactly when it matters: during a major outage inspection when a Level II technician encounters an indication type they were never specifically qualified to evaluate. ASNT Level III consulting support is commonly brought in to author or upgrade the written practice ahead of a major outage, and to provide Level III review and sign-off on borderline indications discovered during the outage window, when turnaround time directly affects whether the unit returns to service on schedule.

For plants building long-term internal capability rather than relying entirely on contract outage crews, structured NDT training toward SNT-TC-1A qualification in the specific methods the boiler fleet requires — PAUT for DMW welds, advanced UT for creep screening — reduces dependency on outage-season contractor availability, which is often the actual constraint that determines whether a finding gets properly evaluated or gets deferred to "monitor next outage."

Weld Repairs and Section I Re-Qualification

When an inspection finds a rejectable indication — a creep void colony past the acceptance threshold in a header ligament, or a crack at a DMW transition — the repair itself falls back under ASME Section I (or the National Board's R-stamp repair provisions where the repair organization holds that authorization) and requires a qualified welding procedure, PWHT where the material and thickness call for it, and post-repair NDT to verify the weld before the unit is returned to service. Coordinating that sequence during a compressed outage window — metallurgical evaluation, engineering disposition, procurement of replacement material if a cut-out and replace decision is made, welding, PWHT, and final NDT acceptance — is often the actual critical path item that determines whether an outage finishes on schedule, more so than the initial inspection itself. A Level III consultant engaged for outage support should be positioned to render engineering dispositions on borderline indications in real time, rather than requiring findings to be shipped off-site for evaluation and returned days later while the unit sits open.

Managing the Data: Outage Volume Is the Real Bottleneck

A major boiler outage can generate thousands of individual UT thickness readings, dozens of PAUT weld scans, and multiple metallography samples, all collected in a compressed two-to-four-week outage window with inspection crews working around the clock. The integrity risk in that scenario is rarely the NDT technique itself — it is losing traceability between a reading, its exact tube or header location, and the prior outage's reading at that same location, which is what makes trending possible at all. Plants that manage outage NDT data through spreadsheets built fresh for each outage routinely lose that location-to-location traceability, which means a genuinely accelerating wastage rate at one waterwall panel gets missed because nobody could reliably match this outage's grid point 47 to last outage's grid point 47. Inspection management software that stores grid-point geometry and trends readings automatically outage over outage removes that failure mode, and a digital twin platform that overlays wall-loss and creep data on a 3D model of the boiler pressure parts gives reliability engineers and plant management a shared visual reference during outage decision-making, when the question "can we run one more cycle before replacing this header" needs an answer in hours, not weeks.

Cycling Duty Is Rewriting the Inspection Interval Math

A material shift affecting utility and independent power producer boiler programs over the past decade is the move from steady baseload operation to daily or even multiple-times-per-day cycling, driven by the need to balance intermittent wind and solar generation on the grid. A unit designed and inspected on the assumption of continuous baseload running accumulates thermal-fatigue damage at attachment welds, header ligaments, and dissimilar-metal welds far faster under cycling duty than the original design basis or a legacy inspection interval assumed. Reliability engineers who have not re-scoped their NDT program since the unit's duty cycle changed are frequently inspecting the wrong failure mode at the wrong frequency — continuing a corrosion-focused UT thickness survey on the same interval while thermal-fatigue cracking at attachment welds, which cycling duty actively accelerates, goes unscreened between outages. A power generation NDT consulting engagement scoped after a duty-cycle change should explicitly re-derive the damage-mechanism map for the new operating profile rather than simply carrying forward the baseload-era inspection plan.

Scoping a Power Generation NDT Consulting Engagement

Plant reliability managers and asset owners evaluating outside Level III support for a boiler NDT program — whether after a forced outage, ahead of a major turnaround, or as part of a fleet-wide standardization effort across multiple units — should expect a scope covering: a damage-mechanism review against current operating history and any recent water chemistry or fuel-quality excursions; a gap analysis between current inspection locations/methods and the identified mechanisms; a review of the Section I design-basis data against current measured wall thickness to establish accurate corrosion and creep rates; a written practice review or upgrade for personnel qualification under SNT-TC-1A; and a documented, risk-ranked inspection plan with intervals justified by quantitative remaining-life calculations that both the plant's reliability function and the jurisdictional Authorized Inspector can rely on. For fleet operators managing several units of different vintage and duty cycle, a Level III consultant can also standardize the inspection plan template across the fleet while still allowing each unit's damage-mechanism map to reflect its own operating history — avoiding both the failure mode of a single generic template applied everywhere, and the opposite failure mode of every plant engineer building an inspection plan from scratch with no consistency for corporate asset-integrity oversight to review against.

The output of a well-scoped engagement is not just a report — it is a program the plant's own reliability and NDT staff can execute and update outage over outage, with the reasoning behind each inspection location and interval documented well enough that a new engineer inheriting the program two turnovers later can understand why it looks the way it does, rather than treating it as an inherited black box to be carried forward unchanged out of caution.

title: Marine and Offshore NDT Consulting: IACS Class Society Written Practice Requirements
snippet: How shipyards and offshore EPC fabricators build an NDT written practice that satisfies ABS, DNV, and Lloyd's Register without duplicating programs per class society.
content:
Why a Land-Based Written Practice Fails a Class Survey

An NDT written practice built around ASNT SNT-TC-1A for a fabrication shop or a refinery inspection department will not pass muster in front of an ABS, DNV, Lloyd's Register, or Bureau Veritas surveyor reviewing hull and structural NDT on a newbuild or an offshore unit. Not because SNT-TC-1A qualification is wrong — it remains the qualification basis Atlantis NDT trains and certifies personnel against — but because classification society rules layer additional, class-specific requirements on top of it: approved NDT procedures specific to the class society, surveyor witness-point requirements written into the newbuild inspection and test plan, and documentation formats the class society's own database expects. Marine and offshore NDT consulting exists in that gap, translating a shipyard's or offshore fabricator's existing NDT capability into a program a class surveyor will actually sign off without repeated procedure resubmissions that push a keel-laying or hull-erection schedule to the right.

Atlantis NDT's ASNT Level III consulting engagements in marine and offshore work most often come from EPC fabricators and shipyards building floating production units, jack-up rigs, semi-submersibles, or commercial hull sections for class-approved newbuilds, where the yard's existing NDT department is fully competent on API and ASME work but has never had to align a written practice and procedure set to IACS member rules — or has done it once, years ago, for a different class society than the current contract requires, and is now discovering that ABS, DNV, and Lloyd's Register do not treat procedure approvals as interchangeable.

What IACS Member Societies Actually Require

The International Association of Classification Societies (IACS) does not itself certify NDT personnel or approve procedures — each member society (ABS, DNV, Lloyd's Register, Bureau Veritas, ClassNK, RINA, and others) maintains its own rules, though IACS Unified Requirements harmonize core structural and material requirements across members, including UR W-series requirements on welding and NDT of hull structures. In practice, three things vary by society and need to be tracked separately in a written practice serving multi-class work:

  • Procedure approval and NDT operator recognition. Most class societies require NDT procedures used on class-surveyed work to be submitted for review and approval before use, and separately maintain requirements for how NDT personnel qualifications are recognized — commonly referencing ISO 9712 or equivalent national schemes as an accepted qualification basis for personnel performing class-witnessed NDT, alongside or in addition to an employer's own SNT-TC-1A-based written practice. A written practice serving class work needs to document, honestly and specifically, which qualification basis applies to which scope of work, and never blur ASNT SNT-TC-1A employer-based qualification with a third-party personnel certification scheme the yard does not itself administer.
  • Witness and hold points in the newbuild ITP. The inspection and test plan (ITP) approved for a newbuild contract specifies which NDT operations require surveyor witness, which require surveyor notification with hold-point release, and which can proceed on contractor sign-off alone subject to surveyor review of records. Missing a witness point — running a weld's final UT before the surveyor arrives on a day they were scheduled to witness it — is one of the most common and most schedule-damaging errors on a class newbuild, often requiring the weld to be re-exposed or re-tested under witness.
  • Documentation and traceability format. Class societies expect NDT reports traceable to a specific approved procedure number, a specific qualified operator, and a specific structural drawing/weld map location, filed in a format the class surveyor's own record system can absorb — often through the class society's digital survey platform rather than paper reports alone.

Aligning Procedures Across Multiple Class Societies

Offshore EPC fabricators and shipyards frequently work simultaneously under contracts for different class societies — an ABS-classed floating production unit hull section fabricated at the same yard building a DNV-classed offshore wind substation jacket, for example. Running two entirely separate, procedure-for-procedure NDT programs is expensive and increases the risk of a technician using the wrong approved procedure revision on the wrong job. The more defensible approach, and the one Atlantis Level III consultants typically build toward, is a core technique-qualification and equipment-calibration program that is class-agnostic — built to the more conservative requirements across the societies the yard regularly works with — with a thin layer of class-specific procedure cover sheets and witness-point documentation on top, referencing the shared core procedure by revision number. This keeps personnel qualification and equipment calibration records unified in one system rather than duplicated per class society, while still producing the class-specific paperwork each surveyor expects to see.

NDT Methods on Hull and Offshore Structural Steel

Marine and offshore structural NDT draws on the same core method set as onshore fabrication — visual testing (VT), magnetic particle testing (MT), ultrasonic testing (UT) and increasingly phased array UT (PAUT) for weld volumetric examination, and radiographic testing (RT) where geometry and access still favor film or digital radiography over PAUT — but with access and sequencing constraints specific to hull and topside fabrication:

Butt welds in hull plating

Historically inspected primarily by RT, many yards and class societies now accept PAUT as an alternative or supplement, particularly for thicker plate on offshore hull structures where radiography exposure times and radiation-control logistics on an active fabrication yard floor are increasingly impractical. The written practice needs to specify, per class-approved procedure, which joint configurations and thicknesses PAUT is approved for versus where RT remains required.

Fillet welds and T-joints on internal structure

MT is the primary surface method for accessible fillet welds on frames, stiffeners, and bulkhead connections; where subsurface examination of partial-penetration or full-penetration T-joints is required, UT techniques specific to T-joint geometry (distinct from simple butt-weld UT calibration blocks) are needed, and the written practice should call out T-joint-specific calibration reference blocks rather than assuming a standard butt-weld IIW block covers the geometry.

Topside piping and pressure systems on offshore platforms

Process piping on a fixed platform, FPSO, or semi-submersible follows ASME B31.3 for construction and often API 570-derived in-service inspection philosophy once in operation, layered under the platform's overall class and flag-state survey regime — meaning a topside piping NDT program on an offshore asset typically needs to satisfy both the class society's structural/piping survey requirements and the operator's own process-safety inspection program, which are related but administered separately.

Personnel Qualification: Keeping SNT-TC-1A and Class Recognition Straight

This is the point where Atlantis NDT is most precise with clients, because it is also where written practices most often go wrong. Atlantis trains and certifies personnel to ASNT SNT-TC-1A — an employer-based qualification program, not a third-party personnel certification scheme. Some class societies and some international contracts specify ISO 9712 or PCN (or a national equivalent) personnel certification as a requirement for NDT operators performing class-witnessed work, particularly on internationally contracted newbuilds. Where a contract requires that basis, the yard needs personnel holding that specific third-party certification — Atlantis does not deliver, administer, or issue ISO 9712 or PCN certification, and a written practice should never represent SNT-TC-1A qualification as satisfying an ISO 9712 or PCN contractual requirement, because a class surveyor checking certificates against the ITP will catch the mismatch immediately and reject the operator's qualification for that scope. What Atlantis Level III consulting does provide is the analysis of which scopes of a given contract actually require third-party certification versus which can proceed under the yard's own SNT-TC-1A written practice, so the yard invests in third-party certification only where the contract genuinely requires it, and builds everything else on the SNT-TC-1A foundation it already controls through in-house NDT training.

Repair and Retrofit Projects Bring the Same Requirements to Existing Steel

Jumbo conversions, life-extension projects, and major repairs on existing hull or topside structure trigger the same class NDT and written-practice requirements as newbuild work, with an added complication: existing steel condition, prior repair history, and sometimes decades-old original construction records of uncertain completeness. A yard taking on a hull conversion or an offshore platform life-extension project needs its written practice to address not only new-weld NDT but also baseline condition surveys on existing structure — thickness measurement to establish current condition against original as-built minimums, and MT or PAUT screening of existing welds and highly stressed structural details before new work is welded onto them. Class societies scrutinize life-extension and conversion NDT programs closely precisely because the baseline condition data quality determines whether the extended service life assessment is credible, and a written practice that treats a conversion project identically to new fabrication — without the baseline survey component — is one of the more common findings in class plan-approval review for this project type.

Scoping a Class-Ready Written Practice Engagement

Shipyards and offshore EPC fabricators evaluating outside Level III support ahead of a new class-classed contract should expect a scope that includes: a review of the contract's ITP and class rules to identify which NDT scopes require witness points, procedure pre-approval, or third-party personnel certification; a gap analysis between the yard's existing SNT-TC-1A written practice and what the specific class society expects to see; harmonization of procedures across multiple class societies where the yard works under more than one; and a documentation workflow that produces class-submittable records without duplicating data entry across systems. The deliverable should leave the yard's own quality and NDT department able to run the program independently on the next contract, with the class-specific requirements built into their standing written practice rather than re-discovered project by project.

Because newbuild schedules are driven by fixed milestone dates — keel laying, hull erection, float-out, sail-away — a rejected or resubmitted NDT procedure late in a project carries real schedule and liquidated-damages exposure. Getting the written practice and procedure package aligned to the class society's expectations before fabrication starts, rather than discovering a mismatch mid-project, is consistently the highest-leverage point at which outside Level III review pays for itself. Pairing that written practice with inspection management software that tracks procedure approval status, witness-point scheduling, and operator qualification against each class society's requirements in one system — rather than a quality manager's personal tracking spreadsheet — keeps a multi-class fabrication program from quietly drifting out of compliance between class society audits.

In-Service Surveys: The Program Does Not End at Delivery

Class involvement does not stop at sail-away or first oil. Vessels and floating offshore units remain under a periodic survey regime — annual, intermediate, and special/renewal surveys on roughly a five-year cycle for most class societies — that includes close-up structural surveys and thickness measurement surveys targeting known corrosion-prone areas: ballast tanks, cargo tank boundaries on tankers, and topside structural steel exposed to marine atmosphere on offshore platforms. Owners and operators of FPSOs, FSOs, and other long-life floating offshore assets increasingly negotiate risk-based survey schemes with their class society — ABS's dynamic survey scheduling or DNV's equivalent programs — which substitute a data-driven, condition-based thickness measurement and structural survey plan for the traditional fixed five-year cycle, provided the operator can demonstrate a mature in-service NDT and corrosion-monitoring program. Qualifying for a risk-based survey scheme requires exactly the same discipline described earlier for pipeline and refinery RBI programs: documented thickness trending over time, corrosion rate calculation against class-approved minimum thickness diminution limits, and an NDT program executed by qualified personnel under a written practice the class society has reviewed. Operators who invest in that program early recover the cost through reduced dry-docking frequency and shorter survey windows over the asset's life, which for a floating production unit can represent weeks of deferred production avoided per survey cycle.

Coordinating Surveyor Witness Scheduling With Production Throughput

On a high-throughput newbuild program — multiple hull blocks or topside modules progressing through fabrication simultaneously — the operational bottleneck is rarely NDT technician capacity; it is surveyor availability to witness hold points on the schedule the fabrication sequence actually needs. A written practice and quality plan that pre-schedules witness points against the fabrication sequence, and that gives the surveyor advance visibility into which welds will be ready for witness on which shift, measurably reduces the idle time welds spend sitting complete-but-unwitnessed while waiting for a surveyor visit to be arranged. This is a scheduling and documentation-system problem as much as an NDT technique problem, and it is where a digitized inspection record system that the surveyor can review remotely between visits — rather than requiring an on-site walk of physical report binders — measurably shortens the witness-scheduling cycle on a busy fabrication program.

title: Petrochemical Turnaround Consulting: Scoping a Multi-Method Level III Engagement
snippet: Scoping refinery and petrochemical turnaround NDT from API 580/581 risk data — method selection, crew sizing on the critical path, real-time Level III disposition.
content:
The Turnaround Scoping Meeting Where Most NDT Programs Are Already Broken

By the time a petrochemical plant's turnaround steering committee sits down eighteen months out to scope the NDT work list, the inspection strategy is usually already locked in by default — carried forward from the last turnaround with minor edits, sized to whatever contract crew capacity the plant has used before, and built without a hard look at which fixed equipment actually drove the last unplanned outage or near-miss. A cracking unit, an FCC unit, or an olefins plant turnaround that runs 21-35 days and costs the operator lost production measured in tens of thousands of barrels per day of downtime cannot afford an NDT scope built on inertia. Petrochemical turnaround consulting, done properly, is the discipline of building that scope from actual damage-mechanism and API 580/581 risk data, sizing the multi-method NDT crew correctly against the critical path, and having a qualified ASNT Level III on call to disposition findings in real time rather than queuing them for after-turnaround engineering review that the unit cannot wait for.

Atlantis NDT's Level III consulting engagements for turnarounds typically start with a scope review three to six months ahead of the outage — later than ideal, since the best outcomes come from engaging at the eighteen-month planning stage, but still enough runway to fix the most consequential gaps: mismatched NDT method selection, understaffed crack-detection scope on known SCC-susceptible equipment, and no defined real-time disposition path for findings discovered during the turnaround window itself.

Building the Scope From API 580/581 Risk Data, Not From Last Turnaround's List

API RP 580 (risk-based inspection) and the quantitative methodology in API RP 581 give petrochemical operators a structured way to rank fixed equipment — pressure vessels, piping circuits, heat exchangers, and fired heaters — by probability of failure (driven by damage-mechanism susceptibility, wall-thickness margin, and inspection effectiveness history) times consequence of failure (driven by inventory, toxicity, flammability, and business interruption cost). A turnaround NDT scope that is properly risk-ranked concentrates inspection effort and the most capable technique — phased array UT, TOFD crack sizing, automated corrosion mapping — on the highest-risk circuits, while allowing lower-risk, well-understood circuits with strong inspection history to run a lighter-touch conventional UT thickness survey. A scope built by simply repeating last turnaround's list, adjusted for budget, inverts this: it spreads inspection effort evenly across equipment regardless of actual risk ranking, which means the highest-risk circuits — often high-temperature hydrogen attack (HTHA) susceptible reactor circuits, amine or caustic SCC-susceptible piping, or sulfidation-prone crude and vacuum unit piping running high-sulfur crude slates — get the same inspection intensity as a low-risk cooling water line.

Matching Damage Mechanisms to NDT Methods in Real Refinery and Petrochemical Circuits

  • High-temperature hydrogen attack (HTHA) in hydroprocessing reactor circuits, hydrotreater and hydrocracker piping operating above roughly 450°F in hydrogen service, per the API 941 Nelson curves. Advanced UT backscatter and attenuation techniques, sometimes combined with wet fluorescent magnetic particle testing (WFMT) on ground surfaces, are used to screen for the internal fissuring characteristic of early-stage HTHA — conventional UT thickness alone will not detect it since HTHA does not remove wall thickness in early stages.
  • Sulfidation corrosion in crude and vacuum unit piping and heater tubes processing high total-acid-number or high-sulfur crude, evaluated against API RP 939-C guidance. UT thickness grid surveys at flow-disturbance points — elbows, tees, reducers — remain the primary detection method, with corrosion rate trended against prior turnaround data.
  • Amine cracking and caustic SCC in amine treating units and caustic circuits. Wet fluorescent magnetic particle testing on stress-relieved and non-stress-relieved welds, per API RP 571 guidance on damage mechanisms, is the standard detection method, sometimes supplemented by TOFD for subsurface crack sizing on thicker-wall vessels.
  • Creep and creep-fatigue damage in fired heater tubes and high-temperature piping, addressed with replication metallography and dimensional creep-swelling checks, similar in principle to the boiler creep-screening methods used in power generation.
  • Fatigue cracking at nozzle-to-shell welds and small-bore connections subject to vibration, screened with MT or PAUT depending on access, often identified proactively through vibration monitoring data that flags which small-bore connections warrant NDT attention during the turnaround.

Sizing the Multi-Method Crew Against the Critical Path

The single most common scoping error Atlantis Level III consultants find in turnaround NDT plans is crew sizing based on total inspection point count divided by turnaround duration, without accounting for the fact that different NDT methods have very different throughput rates and cannot always run in parallel on the same equipment. Automated UT corrosion mapping on a large-diameter vessel shell can cover substantial area per shift with a two-person crew and a scanner rig; PAUT crack sizing on a suspect weld requires a qualified Level II operator working at a much slower, more deliberate pace per weld; WFMT on amine circuit welds requires surface preparation time that often exceeds the actual test time. A scope document should specify method-specific throughput assumptions and crew counts by discipline, not a single blended "NDT technician" headcount, and should identify which inspection points sit on the actual turnaround critical path — typically the equipment that must be inspected, found acceptable or repaired, and closed out before a specific unit can be pressure-tested and started back up — versus which points have schedule float and can absorb a delay without extending the overall outage.

Real-Time Disposition: Why a Level III Needs to Be On Site, Not On Call

A turnaround inspection crew that finds an indication at 2 a.m. on day 11 of a 24-day outage cannot wait three business days for an off-site Level III to review the data and issue a disposition — every day the unit sits open past its planned duration costs the operator lost production, and every day the crew waits idle for a disposition on one vessel while unable to move to the next scheduled work is a day of contracted crew cost with no progress. Turnaround NDT scopes that hold up under schedule pressure build in either an on-site ASNT Level III for the duration of the critical inspection window, or a clearly defined rapid-response protocol — data transmitted digitally within a defined SLA, disposition returned within a defined number of hours — with named backup Level III coverage so a single person's availability does not become the turnaround's critical path. This is one of the highest-value places to bring in outside ASNT Level III consulting support: not to replace the plant's own inspection department, but to provide surge Level III capacity during the specific multi-week window when finding-disposition speed directly determines whether the turnaround finishes on budget.

Data Capture in the Field: Where Turnarounds Lose Time

Turnaround NDT generates an enormous volume of readings in a short window — thousands of UT thickness points, dozens of PAUT and TOFD weld scans, hundreds of MT and WFMT reports — and the operational bottleneck is frequently not the testing itself but getting results from the field technician's instrument into a reviewable, trendable record before the next shift needs the same equipment cleared for the next work step. Paper field reports transcribed into a spreadsheet after the fact introduce transcription errors and delay the moment engineering can review and disposition a finding. Digital NDT reporting software that lets field technicians submit results directly from the turnaround site, with instrument data attached and prior-turnaround readings for the same location available for immediate comparison, materially shortens the time between a reading being taken and a disposition being issued — often the difference between a finding closed out within the same shift versus one that stalls a work front overnight. Coordinating this at scale, across potentially dozens of contract inspection crews from multiple NDT service providers working simultaneously across different units, is where turnaround inspection management software earns its keep: a single system tracking work order status, crew assignments, and finding disposition across every unit in the turnaround, visible to the turnaround manager in real time rather than reconstructed from end-of-shift phone calls.

Heat Exchanger Turnaround Inspection: A Sub-Scope With Its Own Rules

Shell-and-tube heat exchanger bundles pulled during a turnaround represent a distinct sub-scope that often gets under-resourced relative to its risk contribution. Eddy current testing (ECT) is the standard volumetric method for non-ferromagnetic tube bundles, screening for wall loss, pitting, and cracking across hundreds or thousands of tubes per bundle; remote field testing (RFT) is used instead where tubes are ferromagnetic carbon steel, since conventional ECT loses sensitivity to internal defects in ferromagnetic material; and internal rotary inspection system (IRIS) techniques provide a slower but more precise wall-thickness cross-section where ECT or RFT data is ambiguous and a defensible retirement decision is needed on a specific tube. Turnaround scopes that budget bundle-pull and re-tube time without budgeting adequate ECT/RFT crew time and data-analysis turnaround routinely end up making tube plugging or bundle-replacement decisions on incomplete data, either over-plugging tubes that were actually fine (reducing exchanger thermal performance post-turnaround) or under-plugging tubes that fail in service before the next scheduled turnaround.

Post-Turnaround Data Rollup: Closing the Loop Into the Next RBI Cycle

The turnaround's NDT data has value well beyond the immediate accept/repair/reject decisions made during the outage — every thickness reading, every crack-sizing result, and every tube-plugging decision should feed directly back into the plant's API 580/581 risk model to refine corrosion rates and re-rank equipment for the next inspection cycle. Turnarounds where this rollup happens manually, weeks or months after startup, routinely lose the connection between individual readings and their exact inspection point locations, which degrades the quality of the next risk ranking. Turnarounds where the data capture system is structured from the start to feed the RBI model directly — field readings tagged to the same equipment and location IDs the risk model uses — close that loop automatically, and the plant walks out of the turnaround with a measurably better-calibrated risk model for the next cycle, not just a stack of closed-out inspection reports.

Scoping the Engagement: What Owner-Operators Should Ask For

Refinery and petrochemical reliability and inspection managers evaluating outside Level III support for a turnaround should expect a scoping engagement that delivers: a risk-ranked inspection point list derived from current API 580/581 data (or a recommendation to refresh that data if it is stale); a method-and-crew-size plan tied to the actual turnaround schedule and critical path, not a headcount guess; a defined real-time disposition protocol with named Level III coverage and response-time commitments; and a data-capture plan that gets field results into a reviewable system same-shift. The engagement should also flag any equipment where the existing inspection history is too thin to support a confident risk ranking — newly acquired units, equipment inherited through a merger with incomplete records, or circuits where the operating conditions have changed enough (a crude slate change, a catalyst change) that historical inspection data may no longer predict current damage-mechanism susceptibility. Getting that scope right before the turnaround starts is consistently cheaper than discovering a gap on day 15 of a 24-day outage, when every additional day of schedule extension carries real, measurable cost.

Contract Labor Availability: The Constraint Nobody Prices Early Enough

Turnaround season clusters heavily in spring and fall across the U.S. Gulf Coast, which means the same pool of qualified PAUT, TOFD, and advanced UT technicians is being drawn on by every refinery and petrochemical operator scheduling a turnaround in the same window. Owner-operators and EPCs that finalize their NDT crew sourcing plan only a few weeks ahead of the outage frequently find their preferred inspection service provider's most experienced technicians already committed to another site, and end up with a less experienced substitute crew for the highest-risk inspection scopes — exactly the scopes where technician experience matters most for correctly sizing a crack or distinguishing a real indication from geometric noise. Locking in crew commitments, including named senior technicians for the critical-path crack-detection scopes, at the same eighteen-month mark the overall turnaround scope is being built, rather than treating crew sourcing as a logistics detail to finalize closer to the date, is one of the simplest and most consistently underused levers available to a turnaround planning team.

title: NDT Consulting for EPC Contractors: Managing Multi-Site Written Practices
snippet: How multi-site EPC contractors govern one SNT-TC-1A written practice across varying client specs, rotating crews, and procedure records without losing control.
content:
One Written Practice, Five States, Three Client Codes: The EPC Problem

An EPC contractor running simultaneous fabrication and field-erection work across multiple sites — a modular skid shop in Texas, a field crew erecting piperack at a Gulf Coast petrochemical expansion, and a separate crew doing tank work at a Midwest terminal — does not have one NDT problem. It has as many NDT compliance problems as it has active contracts, because each owner-client may specify a different edition of ASME Section V, a different acceptance criteria reference (ASME B31.3 versus a client's own more conservative internal specification), and a different personnel qualification expectation, all while the EPC's own quality department is trying to maintain one coherent, auditable NDT program across a workforce that rotates between sites. NDT consulting for EPC contractors is fundamentally a governance problem before it is a technique problem: how does a contractor maintain a single, defensible written practice under ASNT SNT-TC-1A that flexes correctly to satisfy each client's specific contractual NDT requirements, without either fragmenting into a different ungoverned practice per project or forcing every project into a one-size-fits-all scope that fails to meet a specific client's more stringent requirement.

Atlantis NDT's ASNT Level III consulting work with EPC contractors most often surfaces this exact tension: a corporate quality department with a solid, SNT-TC-1A-compliant written practice on paper, and multiple project sites where the actual qualification records, procedure revisions in use, and client-specific acceptance criteria have drifted from that corporate baseline — not through negligence, but because each project's site quality lead adapted the practice locally to satisfy an immediate client requirement and never fed that adaptation back into a controlled, centrally reviewed revision.

Structuring a Written Practice That Survives Multi-Client Variation

The written practice itself, per SNT-TC-1A guidance, is the employer's document establishing qualification and certification requirements for NDT personnel — training hours, experience, examination requirements, vision testing, and recertification intervals by method and level. For a single-site fabricator, one document suffices. For a multi-site EPC contractor serving varied clients, the more durable structure separates the document into two tiers:

  • A corporate-level written practice establishing the baseline personnel qualification framework — the training hours, experience logging, and examination standards that apply company-wide regardless of project, controlled through a single revision-controlled document that every site references.
  • Project-specific procedure addenda that layer each client's specific requirements — a particular ASME Section V edition, a client's internal acceptance criteria that is more conservative than the base code, a specific NDT method the client mandates (for example, a client requiring PAUT on all shop butt welds above a certain thickness where the base code would permit RT), or a client-mandated third-party personnel certification requirement — on top of the corporate baseline, without altering the baseline document itself.

This structure lets a technician qualified once under the corporate written practice work across multiple project sites without requalification, while each project's specific procedure package captures what makes that client's requirements different from the baseline. It also gives the corporate quality department a single point of control: when a new project's addendum reveals a genuinely better practice — a more effective acceptance criterion, a technique that catches indications the baseline procedure would miss — that improvement can be evaluated for adoption into the corporate baseline itself, rather than staying trapped in one project's local paperwork.

Procedure Qualification Records: The Other Half of the Governance Problem

Personnel qualification is only half of what an EPC's NDT program needs to govern centrally — the other half is the NDT procedures themselves, each of which requires a Procedure Qualification Record (PQR) or equivalent demonstration that the written procedure reliably detects the indications it claims to, on the actual material thickness, joint configuration, and access conditions found at that site. An EPC running PAUT on both thin-wall shop-fabricated piping and thick-wall field-erected vessel nozzles cannot use a single PAUT procedure qualified only on the thin-wall case and expect it to be valid, or defensible to a client's inspector, on the thick-wall application. Centralizing procedure qualification records — which procedures exist, what material range and joint geometry each is qualified for, which sites are currently using which revision — in a system the corporate Level III can review is what prevents a site from defaulting to "the procedure we always use" when the actual joint configuration in front of them falls outside that procedure's qualified range.

Client Specification Reconciliation: Reading the Contract Before the Steel Arrives

A recurring and expensive failure mode on EPC projects is discovering a client's NDT specification conflict mid-fabrication rather than during contract review — for example, a client specification requiring 100% volumetric examination on a weld category the EPC's standard procedure treats as spot-examination only under the governing code's default sampling rate, or a client acceptance criteria table that is measurably tighter than ASME Section VIII Division 1 Appendix 4 or B31.3 Table 341.3.2 default acceptance limits. Reconciling the client's project specification against the EPC's standard NDT scope and acceptance criteria needs to happen during proposal or early engineering, when a scope gap can still be priced and scheduled, not discovered by a field NDT technician mid-shift comparing the client spec to the shop traveler for the first time. Atlantis Level III consultants engaged during EPC contract mobilization typically perform exactly this reconciliation — a line-by-line comparison of the client's NDT and acceptance criteria requirements against the contractor's standard procedures — and flag every gap that needs either a new procedure qualification, a client-specific acceptance criteria overlay, or a scope clarification back to the client before fabrication starts.

Rotating Workforce, Consistent Qualification: The Practical Mechanics

EPC contractors move NDT technicians between sites as project demand shifts — a Level II ultrasonic technician finishing a shop fabrication scope in one state may be needed on a field erection crew in another within days. That mobility only works cleanly if qualification records, examination results, and recertification due dates are tracked centrally and accessible to whichever site quality lead is receiving the technician, rather than living in a folder at the technician's home site that the receiving project has to request and wait for. Recertification lapses — a technician arriving at a new site with an eye examination or a method recertification that expired weeks earlier without anyone noticing — are one of the most common and entirely avoidable findings in EPC quality audits, and they happen almost exclusively when qualification tracking is decentralized. A corporate personnel qualification database with automated recertification alerts, tied into inspection and workforce management software, removes the dependency on any single site remembering to check before a technician's badge is issued for a new project.

Multi-Site Visibility for Corporate Quality and Client Audits

Owner-clients auditing an EPC contractor's NDT program — whether as part of a pre-award qualification audit or a routine project quality audit — increasingly expect the contractor to demonstrate program consistency across sites, not just compliance at the one site being audited. A contractor that can produce, on request, a real-time view of every active NDT procedure in use across every site, cross-referenced to which client contract requires it and which personnel are currently qualified to execute it, answers that expectation directly. A contractor reconstructing that picture manually from site-level spreadsheets when the audit request lands — which is still the norm at many mid-size EPC firms — spends the audit preparation window doing data reconciliation instead of substantive quality review, and frequently discovers the same drift-from-baseline gaps described earlier in the process. A digital twin or centralized asset and inspection visualization layer that lets corporate quality and a visiting client auditor see inspection status and procedure compliance across every active site from one dashboard turns what used to be a week of audit-prep data-gathering into something a quality manager can pull up in the meeting itself.

Subcontracted NDT Firms: Governing Quality You Don't Directly Employ

Large EPC contractors rarely perform every scope of NDT with directly employed personnel — specialized techniques like automated PAUT corrosion mapping, TOFD crack sizing, or advanced UT backscatter screening are frequently subcontracted to specialist NDT service providers, sometimes different providers on different projects depending on regional availability and client preference. This introduces a third layer of qualification governance beyond the EPC's own workforce and its corporate written practice: verifying that a subcontracted NDT firm's personnel hold qualification equivalent to what the EPC's own written practice requires, that the subcontractor's procedures are reviewed and accepted (not merely assumed compliant because the subcontractor is a reputable firm), and that the subcontractor's reports integrate into the EPC's own project documentation and traceability system rather than existing as a separate, disconnected record set the client's auditor has to request separately. EPC contractors that formalize a subcontractor NDT qualification checklist — applied consistently at every new subcontractor engagement, regardless of how well-known the firm is — avoid the recurring audit finding of a subcontracted scope that technically met the letter of the contract but cannot produce qualification records in the same format and level of detail as the EPC's own workforce.

Onboarding a New Project Site Without Starting From Zero

When an EPC wins a new contract and mobilizes a new site — particularly in a region or for a client type the contractor has not worked with before — the temptation is to build the NDT quality plan for that project from a blank template, because no existing project quite matches the new client's specification set. A more efficient approach, once the two-tier written practice structure described above is in place, is to treat every new project mobilization as a delta against the corporate baseline: identify specifically what this client's specification requires beyond the baseline, draft the addendum covering only those deltas, and qualify only the procedures and, where necessary, the third-party personnel certifications that the delta actually requires. This keeps mobilization timelines shorter and keeps the corporate quality department's oversight burden proportional to what is genuinely new about each project, rather than re-reviewing an entire NDT program from scratch every time the company wins a new contract in a new region or industry vertical.

What to Ask an Outside Level III Consultant to Deliver

EPC contractors evaluating outside Level III support for multi-site written practice governance should expect a scope covering: a corporate written practice review and, where needed, restructuring into the two-tier baseline-plus-addenda model; a procedure qualification record audit confirming every procedure in active use across sites is qualified for the actual material and joint conditions it is being applied to; a client specification reconciliation process built into project mobilization rather than discovered mid-fabrication; and a personnel qualification tracking system that gives every site real-time visibility into a mobile workforce's current qualification status. The objective is not a single rigid program that ignores legitimate client-to-client variation, but a governed program where variation is documented, controlled, and traceable — so the next client audit, and the next project mobilization, both start from a known-good baseline instead of a reconstruction exercise. NDT training aligned to the corporate written practice, delivered consistently across the workforce rather than site by site with local variation, is what keeps that baseline actually reflected in the field once the consulting engagement ends.

Measuring Whether the Governance Model Is Actually Working

A multi-site written practice program is only as good as the evidence a corporate quality department can produce that it is functioning, and a handful of simple metrics tell that story more reliably than a policy document alone: the percentage of active project sites whose local procedure inventory has been reconciled against the corporate baseline within the current review cycle; the number of recertification lapses caught proactively by the central tracking system versus caught reactively during a client audit; and the average time between a new client specification requirement being identified during contract review and the corresponding procedure addendum being issued to the receiving site. Tracking these consistently gives the corporate quality department an early warning when governance is drifting — for example, a rising number of reactive recertification catches signals that the central tracking system's alerts are not reaching site leads in time to act on them — well before that drift shows up as a finding in a client's own audit of the program.
