title: NDT ERP Buyer's Checklist: 25 Questions to Ask Before You Sign
snippet: 25 specific, sharp questions to put to any NDT software vendor before you sign — on data ownership, certification tracking, calibration, integration, and support SLAs.
content:
Most NDT companies choose inspection management software the way they choose a truck: they sit through a demo, like what they see, and sign. The problem is that a demo is built to show the software's best day — a clean UT report generating in thirty seconds, a dashboard full of green checkmarks. It is never built to show what happens eighteen months in, when you need to add phased array to a shop that has only ever run conventional UT, when a client auditor asks you to produce a named technician's full certification package in the middle of a turnaround, or when the vendor's pricing changes and you discover your own inspection data is harder to get out of the system than it was to put in.

This is a procurement document, not a sales page. It is 25 specific, sharp questions organized by the risk category they actually protect against, meant to be sent in writing to any vendor you are evaluating — including us. If a vendor cannot answer a question on this list clearly and in writing, that is itself the answer. The goal is not to find software with the most features; it is to find software that will not become a liability the first time an ASNT Level III reviews your quality system or a client runs a for-cause audit after a field failure.

It's worth saying plainly why a checklist beats a demo for this specific purchase. A demo is a controlled environment: clean sample data, a single happy-path workflow, a salesperson who knows exactly which button not to click. Your actual operation is messier — ten technicians certified across six different methods, three client contracts each demanding a slightly different report format, an Epoch 650 that goes out for calibration every six months and a fleet of reference blocks that need their own tracking. The questions below are designed to surface how the software behaves under that mess, not under a curated slideshow. Put them in writing, send them to two or three vendors side by side, and score the written answers — not the enthusiasm of the person answering them.

Data Model and Method Coverage

The first failure mode in NDT software isn't security or support — it's a data model that was designed for generic field service work and has NDT methods bolted on as free-text fields. That shows up quietly at first (a UT report missing a dedicated field for couplant type or scan pattern) and expensively later (you can't query five years of RT reports for a specific IQI sensitivity level when a client disputes a weld).

  • 1. Does the system support every NDT method we currently run as a native, structured data type — not an unstructured attachment? UT, RT, MT, PT, VT, ET, TOFD, and phased array each require different mandatory fields: RT needs film or digital density and IQI sensitivity per ASME Section V Article 2; UT needs calibration block ID, reference reflector size, and scan pattern; MT needs field strength, yoke spacing, and demagnetization confirmation. A system that treats all of this as one generic "notes" box will not hold up under a client's technical audit.
  • 2. When we add a method later — say phased array to a shop that has only run conventional UT — does that require a paid change order to the vendor, or can our own admin configure the new field set? This tells you whether you're buying a product or subscribing to a permanent consulting relationship.
  • 3. Can the system output reports in the format conventions our clients already require — API 510 thickness survey layout, ASME Section V Article 4/5 UT report format, AWS D1.1 weld inspection report format — without us rebuilding templates from a blank page?
  • 4. Does the system separate raw inspection data (readings, indications, scan data) from the report document itself, so a narrative correction doesn't require altering the underlying data record? This distinction is what makes a report defensible in an audit trail sense — readings should be immutable once captured, while report language can go through review and revision with its own history.
  • 5. Can we restrict what non-technical staff (schedulers, billing admins) see — job status and scheduling without exposure to restricted technical data — and can we configure that boundary ourselves without a support ticket?

Certification and Personnel Qualification Tracking

This is the category where spreadsheets fail most visibly, and where auditors look first. An NDT company's core deliverable is the qualified judgment of a certified technician; if the software can't prove that judgment was qualified at the moment the report was signed, everything downstream is exposed.

  • 6. Does the system track certification by method AND level individually — PT Level II and UT Level II are separate qualifications with separate expiration dates — rather than a single "certified" flag per employee?
  • 7. Will the system automatically block report sign-off by a technician whose certification in that specific method has lapsed, rather than relying on someone remembering to check?
  • 8. Does it distinguish between certification types as separate, non-interchangeable fields — an employer-based SNT-TC-1A certification, an ASNT NDT Level III credential, and, where a client contract specifically requires it, an ISO 9712 or PCN certification? These schemes are not the same thing and conflating them in a personnel file is a documented audit finding on refinery and pipeline work.
  • 9. Can it track the annual near-vision acuity check separately from the 3-to-5-year method recertification cycle, since SNT-TC-1A recommends annual vision screening independent of the broader recertification interval?
  • 10. If a client's QA representative asks to see a specific technician's full certification package during a turnaround, can we produce it in under two minutes — training hours, exam scores, experience log, vision test date — rather than by pulling physical folders from a filing cabinet three states away?

Calibration, Equipment, and Traceability

Equipment traceability is where a paper trail becomes a legal document. If an instrument is later found out of calibration tolerance, you need to know, immediately, every report that instrument touched — not guess.

  • 11. Does the system track calibration due dates for every serialized instrument — Epoch 650s, OmniScan units, reference blocks, yokes — with the NIST-traceable calibration certificate attached, not a note in a shared spreadsheet someone has to remember to update?
  • 12. Will the system prevent a technician from closing out a report against an instrument whose calibration date has expired, the same way it should for a lapsed certification?
  • 13. Can probe and cable serial numbers be logged as line items against specific inspections, so that if a probe is later found defective or out of tolerance, you can pull a complete list of every report where it was used, in minutes rather than days?
  • 14. Does it handle consumable and reference-standard traceability — couplant batch numbers, IQI serial numbers, penetrant and developer lot certificates — where a client specification requires it, which is routine on nuclear and aerospace-adjacent work and increasingly requested on major refinery turnarounds?

Integration, Data Portability, and Exit Terms

The single most consequential question in this entire list is what happens to your data the day you decide to leave. Vendors rarely volunteer this, and it belongs in a contract clause, not a verbal assurance from a sales rep.

  • 15. Can we export our complete historical data — every report, every reading, every certification and calibration record — in a non-proprietary format (CSV, JSON, searchable PDF) on demand, at any point, not just at contract termination?
  • 16. What is the actual mechanism and realistic timeline for migrating our existing archive into the new system, and will migrated historical records remain searchable and reportable, or do they just become static, unindexed PDFs sitting in a folder?
  • 17. Does the system offer a documented API or integration path to our accounting platform, a client's asset management system, or a digital twin platform, without custom development billed at an hourly rate every single time we need to connect something new?
  • 18. If we terminate the contract, what exactly do we retain, in what format, and on what timeline — in writing, in the agreement itself? A vendor who won't put this in the contract is telling you something about how confident they are you'll want to stay.

Security, Audit Trail, and Data Ownership

Oil and gas clients increasingly run their own vendor security questionnaires before they'll accept a service provider's software into their workflow. You need answers to these before that questionnaire arrives, not during it.

  • 19. Who legally owns the inspection data we enter into the system — us or the vendor — and does the contract state that explicitly, rather than leaving it implied?
  • 20. Does every report carry an immutable, timestamped audit trail — who created it, who reviewed it, who approved it, every subsequent edit — sufficient to survive an internal ISO 9001:2015 audit or a client's for-cause investigation following a field failure?
  • 21. Where is data physically hosted, is it encrypted both at rest and in transit, and does the vendor carry its own cyber liability coverage? This has become a standard line item on client vendor-qualification forms in the past two renewal cycles.

Implementation, Support, and Vendor Viability

Software that's technically correct but impossible to actually roll out is not a win. This is where "affordable, accessible, fully customizable" gets tested against reality.

  • 22. What does implementation actually look like week by week — who loads our historical data, who trains our field technicians, and how many hours of our own staff's time does it consume before we're live?
  • 23. What is the support SLA for a production outage — a technician stranded in the field mid-turnaround, unable to submit a report — versus a cosmetic bug, and is that response time written into the agreement rather than described informally in the sales call?
  • 24. How many NDT companies has this vendor actually implemented this software for, and can we speak directly to one as a reference, not read a polished case study on a marketing page?
  • 25. Is the product roadmap driven by how NDT operators actually work — certification cycles, calibration logic, multi-method reporting — or is this a generic field-service or work-order platform with an NDT skin applied after the fact? The difference shows up the first time you hit a workflow the generic tool never anticipated.

Scoring the Answers: A Simple Framework

Once you have written answers from two or three vendors, resist scoring them purely on feature count. Weight the compliance-critical categories — certification tracking, calibration traceability, audit trail, data ownership — more heavily than convenience features like a nicer dashboard. A practical approach: mark each of the 25 questions red (no clear answer, or answer is unfavorable), yellow (partial answer, needs a written follow-up), or green (clear, specific, and in writing). A vendor with three or more reds in the certification, calibration, or data-ownership categories should not advance to contract negotiation regardless of how good the demo looked, because those are the categories where a gap turns into an audit finding, a lost bid, or data you can't get back.

It's also worth having your operations lead, not just your IT or purchasing contact, sit in on the technical answers. The person who will spend a Tuesday morning tracking down whether a UT technician's certification lapsed before a turnaround is the person best positioned to know whether a vendor's answer actually solves the problem or just sounds like it does. If you'd rather have this checklist run against a specific shortlist of vendors, an NDT ERP evaluation session with someone who has implemented these systems for inspection companies specifically — not generic field-service software — tends to surface the gaps faster than doing it solo.

It also helps to pressure-test the answers against a real event, not a hypothetical one. Ask the vendor to walk through, step by step, exactly what the system shows if a client calls on a Friday afternoon asking for the full inspection history and personnel file on a specific weld from eighteen months ago — a request that happens on almost every long-running refinery or pipeline contract sooner or later. If the answer involves "we'd have to check" or a callback the next business day, that's a data point. A system built around how NDT work actually happens should be able to answer that question live, on the call.

None of this is complicated once it's written down. What's expensive is discovering the gaps after the contract is signed, the data is loaded, and switching costs have quietly become the vendor's real product. A vendor confident in its own data model, its own audit trail, and its own exit terms will answer all 25 of these questions in writing without hedging — and that confidence, more than any single feature on a demo screen, is what you're actually buying.

title: The Hidden Cost of Running an NDT Company on Spreadsheets
snippet: Spreadsheets don't show up as a cost on the P&L — they show up as admin hours, missed bids, and compliance exposure. Here's where that cost actually hides.
content:
Nobody budgets for spreadsheets. That's exactly the problem. The Excel workbook tracking technician certifications didn't show up on a purchase order, the shared calibration-due-dates sheet on Google Drive didn't require a capital approval, and the folder of scanned report PDFs didn't need a business case. So when an owner looks at the P&L, "spreadsheet infrastructure" shows up as a cost of exactly zero. It isn't zero. It's just unbilled — paid for in technician overtime, in admin hours, in lost bids, and occasionally in a compliance finding that costs far more than any software contract would have.

This isn't an argument that spreadsheets are always wrong. A two-person shop tracking four active certifications can run on a well-built spreadsheet indefinitely and be perfectly fine. The cost curve bends sharply somewhere between roughly ten and twenty-five technicians, two or more physical sites, or three or more client contracts each demanding a different reporting format. Below that line, the manual system is genuinely the cheaper option. Above it, the hidden cost compounds every month you don't address it.

An Illustrative Scenario: The 25-Technician Multi-Method Shop

Consider a hypothetical shop — not a specific client, just a realistic composite of the kind of operation we talk to constantly — running UT, RT, MT, and PT across two yards and a rotating slate of turnaround contracts. Certifications live in a shared spreadsheet the office manager updates when she remembers to. Calibration due dates for a dozen Epoch and OmniScan units live in a second sheet. Job scheduling lives in a third tool, a shared calendar. Reports get typed in Word from a template that's been copy-pasted and modified so many times that three technicians are now, unknowingly, using three slightly different template versions.

None of this looks broken day to day. It looks broken the week a major client calls asking for a same-day quote on a six-week turnaround needing eight UT Level II techs and two PAUT-qualified techs, and nobody can say, without an hour of cross-referencing three files, exactly who is certified, available, and not already committed to another job. It looks broken again three months later when a client auditor asks to see the calibration certificate for the specific OmniScan unit used on a disputed weld from February, and the answer takes half a day to locate instead of thirty seconds.

It looks broken a third time at year-end, when the office manager who built and maintained all three spreadsheets takes a new job, and the person who inherits the files discovers that the certification tracker hasn't been updated in six weeks, two macros in the calibration sheet reference a column that got deleted, and nobody documented which of the three competing report templates is actually the current, client-approved one. None of this is a hypothetical edge case in a shop that size — it's closer to the default outcome of a coordination system that lives entirely in one or two people's institutional memory rather than in structured, shared data.

Where the Hours Actually Go

The cost isn't one dramatic failure. It's a steady drip of admin time that never shows up as a line item because it's absorbed into salaried hours nobody itemizes. If a scheduler spends even twenty minutes a day reconciling who's certified against who's booked across three disconnected tools, that's roughly ninety hours a year — more than two full work weeks — spent on a task that a system with live certification and availability data would do in seconds. Multiply that by every technician who re-enters the same job or client information into a timesheet, a report header, and an invoice separately, and the duplicate-entry tax alone can run to several hours a week across a mid-sized shop.

Report turnaround time is the more visible cost. A technician who has to manually format a report in Word, attach separately-saved calibration and certification documentation, and route it for review by email loses time a structured reporting workflow would eliminate. On a busy turnaround week, a one- or two-day delay in getting a signed report to the client is often the difference between winning the next scope-add and watching a competitor with faster turnaround get the call instead. NDT reporting software exists specifically to collapse that cycle from days to hours.

The Compliance Exposure Spreadsheets Create

This is the category that turns a productivity problem into a legal and contractual one. A certification expiration that slips through because nobody caught it on a spreadsheet isn't a minor clerical miss — it means a technician signed off on inspection results without a valid credential in that method, under SNT-TC-1A's employer-based certification framework. If that report supports a return-to-service decision on a pressure vessel governed by API 510, or a piping system under API 570, or an above-ground storage tank under API 653, the exposure isn't limited to the inspection company. It follows the asset.

The same pattern applies to calibration. An instrument used past its due date without anyone catching it because the tracking sheet wasn't checked that week invalidates the traceability chain a client's engineering team is relying on. During an ISO 9001:2015 internal or third-party surveillance audit, "we track this in a spreadsheet, mostly" is the kind of answer that generates a documented nonconformance, not a passing note. Owner-operators running their own inspection quality programs under API recommended practices increasingly ask contractors for exactly this kind of proof before a bid is even shortlisted — not after.

The Client-Facing Cost

Large industrial clients — refineries, EPCs, fabrication yards — have been tightening vendor qualification requirements for years. A prequalification questionnaire that asks how certifications and calibrations are tracked, whether reports are generated from a controlled template system, and how data is retained and retrievable is now routine on major turnaround bid packages. A shop that answers "spreadsheets, and a shared drive" isn't automatically disqualified, but it is starting from a weaker position against a competitor who can point to a system with an audit trail, structured records, and same-day retrieval. That's a cost that never appears on an income statement because it shows up as bids you simply don't win, not as an expense you can trace.

There's also a quieter version of this cost: the client relationship that erodes slowly because status visibility is poor. A client project engineer who has to call and ask "where are we on the tank floor scan" instead of checking a live job status is having a worse experience than one working with a shop that gives them visibility without a phone call. Over a multi-year relationship, that friction adds up in ways that show up at contract renewal time, not before.

This shows up especially sharply on multi-site work, where a client running turnarounds at two or three facilities under one master service agreement expects consistent reporting quality and consistent response time across every location. A shop coordinating that spread of work through email and shared drives will almost always show visible seams between sites — one yard's reports formatted slightly differently from another's, one office slower to respond to a status request than the other. A client evaluating whether to consolidate more scope with a single vendor is, whether they say so explicitly or not, evaluating exactly this kind of operational consistency. It's one of the more common reasons a multi-site NDT provider chooses to standardize on a single inspection management platform across every location rather than letting each site run its own local system.

The Invoicing and Utilization Leak

There's a quieter cost that rarely gets discussed because it doesn't announce itself the way a missed audit does: billing leakage. When technician hours, mileage, and per-job costs live in a timesheet that's separate from the job record and separate again from the invoicing spreadsheet, the reconciliation between what a technician actually did in the field and what gets billed to the client depends entirely on someone manually cross-checking three sources before an invoice goes out. Every step in that manual chain is a place where a billable half-day of standby time on a delayed turnaround, a mileage reimbursement, or a consumables charge quietly doesn't make it onto the invoice — not from dishonesty, just from the ordinary friction of moving data by hand between systems that don't talk to each other.

The same disconnection creates a utilization blind spot. Without a live view of which technicians are on a job, available, or sitting on the bench between assignments, a scheduler tends to default to whoever answered the phone first rather than whoever has been idle longest. Over a quarter, that pattern quietly concentrates billable hours on a subset of the team while others sit underutilized — a scheduling inefficiency that's invisible in a spreadsheet because nothing in a spreadsheet flags utilization imbalance; it just requires someone to notice it, and busy people rarely have time to go looking for a problem that isn't announcing itself.

The Growth Ceiling

Spreadsheets don't fail all at once; they fail at specific thresholds. Somewhere around two physical locations, coordination breaks down because there's no single source of truth both offices are looking at — someone in yard A books a technician who yard B has already committed to a different job. Somewhere around three or four concurrent client contracts, each with its own report format requirement, the "copy the old template and edit it" approach starts producing formatting errors that a client's QA reviewer catches and kicks back, adding a rework cycle to every job. Somewhere around 20-30 technicians, the certification and calibration tracking burden exceeds what any single office administrator can reliably hold in their head or catch by memory, regardless of how conscientious that person is.

None of these are hard walls. Plenty of shops push past them anyway, on sheer administrative effort. But that effort is the hidden cost this whole piece is about: it's real, it's recurring, and it scales with headcount in a way that purpose-built NDT ERP software doesn't, because the software absorbs the coordination work that a spreadsheet requires a human to redo, manually, every single time.

What It Actually Costs to Fix This

The honest framing here isn't "software is free and spreadsheets cost a fortune." Migrating to a structured system takes real implementation time — loading historical certification and calibration records, training technicians on new report workflows, and reworking client-specific templates so the switch doesn't disrupt an active contract. That's a genuine cost, and any vendor who tells you otherwise is not being straight with you.

The comparison that actually matters is the ongoing cost, not the one-time switching cost: the admin hours a structured system eliminates permanently versus the admin hours a spreadsheet system consumes every single week, indefinitely, at a growing rate as headcount and contract count increase. A spreadsheet-based tracking system is a cost that compounds with growth. A structured system is a cost that's mostly front-loaded into implementation and then flattens out. For a shop that's already feeling the coordination strain described above, that's usually the more relevant number to run — not "what does this cost," but "what is the current approach already costing, every week, that nobody has itemized."

If you want a straight read on whether your shop has actually crossed that threshold yet, that's a conversation worth having before you buy anything — sometimes the honest answer is "not yet, keep the spreadsheet another year." Other times it's clear the coordination tax has already outgrown what a manual system can carry.

One more thing worth naming honestly: the hidden cost of spreadsheets rarely triggers a decision on its own. Most shops don't switch because someone ran the arithmetic above and got alarmed — they switch after a specific, painful event: a lost bid where the RFP scoring sheet explicitly penalized "manual record-keeping," a client audit finding that took a week of scrambling to close out, or a key admin person leaving and taking undocumented process knowledge with them. If any of those have already happened to your shop in the last year, that's not a coincidence to write off — it's the coordination tax finally sending an invoice. The earlier a growing shop treats structured data as core infrastructure rather than an eventual nice-to-have, the fewer of those invoices it has to pay.

title: NDT Software RFP Template: What to Include When Evaluating Vendors
snippet: A six-section RFP template for evaluating NDT inspection software vendors — what to ask on data ownership, method coverage, integration, support SLAs, and exit terms.
content:
A request for proposal forces vendors to answer questions in writing, on the record, side by side — which is precisely the discipline a software purchase this consequential needs and a verbal sales process rarely provides. A sales demo does the opposite: it lets the vendor control the sequence, skip the workflows that don't flatter the product, and answer follow-up questions verbally in a way that's easy to walk back later if the software doesn't actually do what was implied. For a purchase that will hold years of certification records, calibration history, and client-facing reports, that difference matters. This is a working RFP template — six sections you can copy, adapt, and send to every vendor on your shortlist, including us, so you're comparing the same answers to the same questions instead of comparing polish.

You don't need a procurement department to run this. A structured document with these six sections, sent by email with a two-week response deadline, will get you further than a string of demo calls that all start to blur together by the third vendor.

Before sending it out, decide who on your side actually reads the responses. The mistake most shops make is routing an RFP through whoever handles IT purchasing generally, without input from the people who will use the system daily — the Level II techs filling out reports in the field, the office manager tracking certifications, the ops lead scheduling crews across sites. A technically sound RFP evaluated only for price and general usability will miss the gaps that matter most in this industry: a calibration tracking feature that looks fine in a demo but doesn't actually block sign-off on an expired instrument, or a report template engine that can't reproduce the exact API 653 tank inspection format a specific client contract requires.

Section 1: Company and Method Background

Start by establishing who you're actually buying from. Ask the vendor to state, in writing: how long the company has built software specifically for NDT operations (as distinct from general field-service or asset-management software); which NDT methods the platform natively supports out of the box — UT, RT, MT, PT, VT, ET, TOFD, phased array — versus which would require custom development; and how many active NDT inspection companies currently use the platform in production, with at least one willing to serve as a direct reference. Also ask directly whether the vendor's core product was purpose-built for NDT from the ground up, or is a generalized ERP or field-service tool with NDT-specific fields added on top. Neither answer disqualifies a vendor by itself, but you need to know which one you're evaluating, because the two have very different long-term maintenance profiles.

Section 2: Technical and Functional Requirements

This is the largest section and the one worth the most specificity. At minimum, require the vendor to address, method by method, how the system captures and structures data for each technique your shop runs — not a generic "yes, we support all methods" but the actual field set for each. Require confirmation that mobile data capture works offline in the field (a real requirement on remote pipeline right-of-way or offshore platform work where connectivity is unreliable) and syncs cleanly once connectivity returns. Require the system to generate reports matching established format conventions — ASME Section V Article 4 and 5 UT reporting, API 510/570/653 inspection report conventions, AWS D1.1 weld inspection documentation — either natively or through a configurable template engine your own staff can adjust without a vendor change order. Require certification and calibration tracking to be a first-class, structured feature (individual method-and-level certification expiration per technician, NIST-traceable calibration due dates per serialized instrument) rather than a free-text field or attachment. If your shop does any radiographic work, require explicit confirmation of how digital and film radiography density and IQI sensitivity records are captured and retained, since this is a common gap in generalist platforms.

Go one step further and require the vendor to respond to at least two specific, real scenarios rather than answering only in the abstract. For example: "A UT technician working a scheduled shutdown at a fractionator finds thinning below the retirement thickness on a section governed by API 570 and needs to generate an immediate report flagging the finding for engineering review while still in the field, on a tablet, without connectivity. Walk through exactly how that report gets created, routed, and later reconciled once the technician is back online." Vendors who have actually built for this industry answer concretely. Vendors who haven't tend to answer with generic platform capability statements that don't actually address the scenario.

Section 3: Data, Integration, and Security Requirements

Require the vendor to state explicitly, in the RFP response, who owns the data entered into the system — the client or the vendor — and to confirm this will be stated unambiguously in the contract, not left implied. Require confirmation that the system produces a complete data export, in a non-proprietary format, on request at any point during the contract term, not only at termination. Ask for a description of the data migration process for existing historical records: will old reports be searchable and reportable within the new system, or simply stored as static files? Require a description of available integration paths — a documented API, standard connectors to accounting or ERP systems, and any existing integration with digital twin or enterprise asset management platforms a client might require. On security, require the hosting location, encryption approach (at rest and in transit), backup and disaster recovery policy, and confirmation of the vendor's own cyber liability insurance coverage — increasingly a standard line item on major operator vendor-qualification questionnaires.

Section 4: Implementation, Training, and Support Requirements

Require a week-by-week implementation timeline, stated concretely: who loads historical data, who trains field technicians and office staff, and an honest estimate of how many hours of your own team's time the process will consume before go-live. Require a written support SLA that distinguishes between a production-down issue (a technician in the field unable to submit a report mid-turnaround) and a minor bug, with specific response-time commitments for each — not a general statement that support is "responsive." Ask how ongoing training works for new hires after the initial rollout, since technician turnover is a constant in this industry and a system that requires the vendor's involvement to onboard every new tech doesn't scale.

It's also worth requiring the vendor to describe what happens during their own planned maintenance windows and unplanned outages — specifically, whether field technicians can still capture data offline and sync later, or whether an outage stops fieldwork entirely. A shop running a live turnaround cannot afford a system where a vendor-side outage means no one can submit a report until service is restored. This single question separates platforms genuinely built around field conditions from ones built primarily around an always-connected office use case.

Section 5: Commercial Terms to Request

Ask every vendor on your shortlist to provide a structured, itemized quote reflecting your actual technician count, site count, and method mix — not a single blended number that hides what's driving the cost. Ask specifically what happens to cost as you scale: adding technicians, adding a new method, adding a second site. Ask what's included in the base agreement versus billed as a separate service — implementation, training, data migration, ongoing support, and any custom template work. Most importantly, ask for the contract's exit terms in writing: notice period, data retrieval process and timeline, and any fees associated with leaving. A vendor unwilling to commit exit terms to writing before you've signed is telling you something worth hearing before, not after, you've migrated three years of certification records into their system.

Section 6: References and Proof

Require at least one live reference from a company of comparable size, method mix, and site count to your own, and ask to speak with them directly by phone rather than receiving a written testimonial curated and pre-approved by the vendor's marketing team. Useful reference questions include: how long did implementation actually take versus the original estimate; has the vendor's support SLA held up during a real production issue, such as a technician stranded mid-turnaround; how did the vendor handle the reference's own historical data migration; and, most tellingly, would they choose this vendor again today, knowing everything they know now, or would they shortlist a competitor next time. Also ask the vendor directly how their product has changed in the past 18 months and what's driving the roadmap — a platform actively shaped by real NDT operator feedback behaves very differently over time than one that hasn't meaningfully evolved.

Common Mistakes That Weaken an RFP

The most common failure isn't asking too little — it's asking questions vague enough that every vendor can answer "yes" without differentiating themselves. "Does the system track certifications?" gets a yes from everyone, including a vendor whose "tracking" is a single free-text field. "Does the system support UT reporting?" gets a yes from a generic work-order platform that technically lets you type UT readings into a blank form. Specificity is what makes an RFP useful: ask whether the system blocks report sign-off on an expired certification, not whether it "tracks" certifications; ask whether radiographic density and IQI sensitivity are structured fields, not whether the system "supports RT."

The second common mistake is treating price as the tiebreaker before the technical and compliance sections have actually eliminated any vendors. A lower-cost platform that fails the certification-tracking or data-ownership questions isn't actually cheaper once you account for the audit exposure or the migration cost of switching again in two years. Run the technical scoring first, eliminate anyone who fails the compliance-critical sections outright, and only compare commercial terms among the vendors left standing.

Scoring the Responses

Score each vendor's written response against each of the six sections on a simple weighted scale — for instance, double weight on Sections 2, 3, and 5, since a failure in method coverage, data ownership, or exit terms costs far more over a multi-year term than a rough edge in the training section. Weight compliance-critical sections — data ownership, certification and calibration tracking, and exit terms — more heavily than convenience or interface polish. It's worth involving whoever actually runs day-to-day operations in scoring the technical section, not just IT or purchasing, since they're best positioned to know whether an answer actually solves a real workflow problem or just sounds plausible on paper. A vendor who answers every section clearly, specifically, and without hedging is telling you something about how the relationship will run after the contract is signed — and that predictability is worth more, over a multi-year term, than any single feature demonstrated in a sales call.

If you'd like a second set of eyes on vendor responses before you commit, an ASNT Level III consulting review of the technical sections — specifically the certification tracking, calibration traceability, and reporting compliance answers — is a fast way to catch a gap that a generalist procurement reviewer might not recognize as significant until it becomes one.

Give vendors a realistic response window — two weeks is usually enough for a serious vendor to answer thoroughly without rushing, and it also tells you something: a vendor who responds in two days with generic marketing copy pasted into your document format is showing you how much genuine engineering thought went into the answers, versus one who takes the full window and comes back with specific, scenario-tested responses. Set a hard deadline and hold every vendor to the same one, so you're comparing responses drafted under the same time pressure rather than comparing a rushed answer against a leisurely one.

Finally, keep a written record of every response, not just your own notes on a call. Six months after implementation, when a feature the sales team described verbally doesn't behave the way you expected, the written RFP response is the document you'll want to point back to — both to hold the vendor accountable to what they committed to in writing, and to have an honest record of what you actually evaluated when you made the decision. An RFP process that exists only in scattered email threads and half-remembered calls provides none of that protection. One that exists as a single structured document, answered in writing by every vendor on your shortlist, does.

title: Odoo vs Purpose-Built NDT Software: When Generic ERP Customization Breaks Down
snippet: An honest technical look at where generic Odoo customization for NDT companies breaks down — and what a purpose-built data model actually needs to get right.
content:
This question comes up constantly from NDT company owners who've either inherited an Odoo instance from a prior consultant, or been pitched one by a generalist implementation partner who's never inspected a weld in their life. The honest answer isn't "Odoo is wrong for NDT" — Odoo is a legitimate, widely deployed open-source ERP platform used across manufacturing, distribution, retail, and field service worldwide, and it's a genuinely reasonable technical foundation to build on. The honest answer is that generic customization of Odoo by people who don't understand NDT workflows breaks down in specific, predictable ways, and it's worth understanding exactly where, because that's a different problem than "Odoo doesn't work."

This distinction matters because Atlantis's own NDT ERP is itself built on Odoo 18 — so this isn't an argument against the platform. It's an argument about the difference between a generalist implementation bolting custom fields onto vanilla Odoo, and a purpose-built data model that happens to run on Odoo's core.

It's also worth being direct about why this question keeps coming up specifically in NDT, and not, say, in general contracting or HVAC field service. Most field-service businesses don't need to prove, on demand, that the person who performed a task was legally qualified to perform it at the exact moment they signed off, or that the instrument they used was within a traceable calibration window. NDT does — because the deliverable isn't the service call, it's a certified finding that a piping system, pressure vessel, or storage tank is fit for continued service under a governing code. That single difference is what makes generic ERP customization a materially harder problem here than it is in most industries a typical Odoo consultant has previously worked in, and it's precisely the part most generic implementation proposals underestimate at the scoping stage.

The Question Behind the Question

When an NDT company owner asks "should we just customize Odoo ourselves, or pay a consultant to do it," what they're usually really asking is a narrower, more practical question: "can a generic ERP consultant, or our own admin staff, configure a standard ERP well enough to handle certification tracking, calibration management, and multi-method inspection reporting, without us paying for something purpose-built?" The answer depends entirely on scope. For invoicing, basic inventory of consumables, and general project tracking, vanilla Odoo customization works fine — these are exactly the kinds of workflows Odoo's core modules were designed for, and a competent implementer can configure them in days. For the NDT-specific layer — the part that actually differentiates an inspection company from a generic field service business — generic customization starts to strain, and eventually breaks, in ways that are predictable once you've seen it happen a few times.

Where Generic Odoo Handles NDT Fine

It's worth being fair to the platform before critiquing the customization pattern. Odoo's core accounting, invoicing, inventory, and basic project management modules are mature, well-tested, and genuinely good at what they do. Tracking consumables like couplant, penetrant, and film stock as inventory items works out of the box. Basic job costing, purchase orders for calibration services, and general ledger accounting don't need NDT-specific logic — they need standard ERP logic, and Odoo does standard ERP logic well. A shop that only needs back-office financial operations, with inspection reporting handled by a separate dedicated tool, can often run comfortably on a lightly customized Odoo instance for years without hitting a wall. Vendor and client management, purchase orders for third-party calibration services, and standard project timelines for a multi-week turnaround engagement are all workflows Odoo's project and purchasing modules were built to handle, and they don't require NDT-specific domain knowledge to configure correctly. The failure pattern isn't in these modules — it's specifically in the layer where NDT's regulatory and technical requirements diverge from generic field service.

Where Generic Customization Breaks: Five Failure Patterns

1. Certification-as-a-custom-field

The most common pattern: a generalist implementer adds a "Certification Expiry Date" custom field to the employee record. This looks like it solves the problem the first time it's demonstrated. It doesn't hold up in practice because a single technician typically holds certifications in multiple methods at different levels — PT Level II, MT Level II, UT Level I, each with its own expiration date, its own written practice reference, and its own recertification cycle under SNT-TC-1A's employer-based system. A single custom field can't model that without a proper related data table, and building that related table correctly — with automated expiration alerts, sign-off blocking, and audit history — is a data modeling exercise most generic ERP consultants have never done, because they've never needed to before.

2. Calibration logic bolted on with automation rules that break on upgrade

Odoo's automation studio lets a consultant build workflow rules — "if calibration due date is within 30 days, send an alert" — without touching core code. This works until the next major Odoo version upgrade, when custom automation rules referencing fields or logic paths that changed between versions silently stop firing. A shop discovers this not through a warning, but by realizing months later that calibration alerts simply stopped coming, right around the same time an instrument went out of tolerance and nobody caught it before a job.

3. Report templates that don't survive a version upgrade

Custom report templates built in Odoo's Studio or QWeb templating engine to mimic an API 510 thickness survey format or an ASME Section V UT report layout are functional the day they're built. Odoo's core platform, however, releases a new major version roughly annually, and custom templates frequently require rework after an upgrade because underlying rendering engines and field references shift. A generic implementer who built the template and moved on to the next client isn't available to fix it eighteen months later; the shop either pays for a rebuild or skips the upgrade indefinitely, which creates its own security and support risk. Skipping upgrades indefinitely has its own long-tail cost: security patches stop applying cleanly, third-party module compatibility degrades, and the gap between the shop's frozen version and the current supported release widens every year, eventually forcing an expensive, high-risk jump instead of a series of smaller, routine ones.

4. Method-specific data models that don't actually fit a generic schema

UT, RT, MT, and PT are not variations on the same data structure — they're structurally different. RT inspection records need film or digital image references, density readings, and IQI sensitivity values. UT records need scan patterns, calibration block IDs, and amplitude readings. Forcing all of these into Odoo's generic product or service-order data model, because that's the closest built-in structure, typically means one of two outcomes: either every method gets crammed into the same oversimplified fields (losing the specificity a client audit will look for), or the customization sprawls into a bespoke, undocumented data model that only the original consultant understands.

5. The "who maintains this" problem

This is the pattern that causes the most damage over time. A freelance Odoo consultant or a small local implementation shop builds the NDT customization, gets paid, and moves to the next client. Two years later, the person who understood how the customization actually worked is gone, the documentation is thin or nonexistent, and the NDT company is sitting on a system nobody in-house or on the vendor side can confidently modify without risking something breaking elsewhere. This isn't a knock on Odoo — it's what happens to any generic platform customized by someone without a long-term stake in maintaining that specific domain logic. It's the same pattern that shows up with any generic ERP — SAP Business One, Microsoft Dynamics, NetSuite — when a generalist implementer handles the customization; Odoo isn't uniquely exposed to this, it's simply the most common choice for small and mid-sized NDT shops because it's open-source and comparatively inexpensive to start with, which means more of them have gone down the generic-customization path and discovered these failure modes firsthand.

What "Purpose-Built on Odoo" Actually Means

The distinction that matters isn't platform versus platform — it's data model versus data model. A purpose-built approach starts from the NDT workflow itself: certification tracked as a structured, method-and-level-specific table with automated sign-off blocking; calibration tracked against serialized equipment with NIST-traceable certificate attachment as a core object, not an add-on field; report templates built against the actual structural differences between UT, RT, MT, and PT records, maintained as first-class product features that get carried forward through platform upgrades rather than orphaned custom code. Whether that runs on Odoo's core, on a different open-source ERP framework, or on a fully custom stack is a secondary engineering decision. What matters is whether the people who built the data model understood SNT-TC-1A certification structures and API inspection code requirements before they wrote the first line of configuration — or whether they were configuring a generic employee record and hoping it would hold.

There's a useful analogy in how accounting software handles industry-specific regulatory requirements. Generic accounting software can technically record any transaction, but a construction company still benefits from job-costing modules built specifically for progress billing and retainage, and a healthcare provider still benefits from billing software built around CPT codes and insurance claim structures, even when both run on the same underlying database engine as a generic alternative. Nobody considers that contradictory. The same logic applies here: Odoo's accounting, inventory, and workflow engine is a legitimate foundation; what makes software actually fit for an NDT operation is the domain-specific layer built on top of it by people who've spent time in the field understanding what a calibration record, a certification expiry, and a multi-method inspection report actually need to contain.

This is also why "we use Odoo" and "we use a purpose-built NDT ERP" aren't actually opposites. A platform built by people who understand the NDT domain, using Odoo's proven core as the underlying framework rather than reinventing accounting and inventory from scratch, gets the benefit of a mature, well-supported open-source foundation without the failure patterns above — because the NDT-specific data model was designed as the product itself, maintained and upgraded as a first-class part of the platform, not bolted on afterward by whoever happened to be available.

A Decision Framework: When Generic Customization Is Actually Fine

If your shop is very small — a handful of technicians, one or two methods, no active client contracts requiring structured audit trails — and you already have in-house Odoo expertise or a long-term relationship with a consultant who genuinely understands your workflow, light customization can be a reasonable, low-cost starting point. The calculus changes once you cross roughly the same thresholds that matter for any NDT software decision: multiple methods with materially different data requirements, certification and calibration tracking that needs to survive a client audit, multiple sites needing consistent reporting, or growth that will outlast whichever individual consultant built the original customization. Past that point, the maintenance burden of a bespoke customization tends to exceed what it would have cost to start with a data model built for the job.

The practical test is simple, and you can apply it to any vendor regardless of what platform they're proposing: ask whoever is proposing to customize a generic ERP for your NDT operation to walk through, specifically and in writing, how they'll model multi-method certification tracking with individual expiration dates and automated sign-off blocking, how calibration due-date logic will be enforced rather than merely displayed, and how both survive the platform's next major version upgrade without a separate rebuild engagement. If the answer is vague, that's the failure pattern above, arriving early rather than in eighteen months.

It's also worth asking the reverse question honestly: is a fully custom, non-Odoo, ground-up platform automatically the safer choice? Not necessarily. A narrow, proprietary system built by a small vendor carries its own version of the maintenance risk — if that vendor is acquired, shuts down, or simply stops actively developing the product, a fully custom platform can be harder to migrate away from than an Odoo-based one, precisely because Odoo's underlying core is open-source, widely supported, and not dependent on a single company's continued existence. The safest position, in practice, tends to be a purpose-built NDT data model running on a mature, widely adopted open-source core — you get the domain-specific correctness of purpose-built software without betting your operational records entirely on one small vendor's longevity.

title: Choosing Between NDT ERP, Reporting Software and Digital Twin: What Each Actually Solves
snippet: NDT ERP, reporting software, and digital twin platforms solve three different problems. Here's how to tell which one actually matches your bottleneck.
content:
Ask five different people at an NDT company or an asset-owner engineering department what "NDT software" means and you'll get five different answers, because the term gets used loosely to cover at least three genuinely different categories of tool. An NDT ERP runs the business — scheduling, certification and calibration tracking, invoicing, project management. Reporting software captures and produces the inspection deliverable itself — field readings, images, and the finished report a client signs off on. A digital twin platform gives an asset owner a persistent, visual, asset-level record that accumulates inspection history over the life of the equipment. Buyers frequently shop for one and end up confused about why it doesn't do what they needed from another, because the sales conversation blurred the categories together. This is an attempt to separate them cleanly, so the buying decision matches the actual problem. It matters more than it might seem: buying the wrong category doesn't just waste budget, it delays fixing the actual bottleneck by however long it takes to realize the new software was never going to solve it, and then start the evaluation over.

Three Different Problems, Often Confused as One Purchase

The confusion is understandable, because all three categories touch the same underlying data — an inspection reading, once captured, is relevant to the report a client receives, to the technician's certification record that qualified them to take it, and to the asset's long-term condition history. But "touches the same data" isn't the same as "solves the same problem." A ten-person inspection shop deciding between vendors is usually trying to solve a reporting and scheduling problem. A refinery or pipeline operator managing thousands of assets across a facility is usually trying to solve a different problem entirely: how to see an asset's full inspection and maintenance history at a glance, and predict where the next failure is likely to occur. Treating these as one shopping decision is how companies end up with software that's technically impressive and operationally mismatched to what they actually needed.

A useful way to separate the three: reporting software answers "what did we find, right now, at this specific location on this specific asset." ERP answers "is our business running efficiently and staying compliant while we produce those findings, day after day, across every job and every technician." A digital twin answers "what does this asset's condition look like over its entire history, and where is it heading." All three questions matter to different people, at different points in an asset's life, and a company's actual purchase decision should start from which question is currently unanswered for them — not from which product category happens to have the most compelling demo on a given sales call.

What NDT Reporting Software Actually Solves

Reporting software exists to solve the field-to-deliverable problem: getting a technician's readings out of the field and into a client-ready, code-compliant report as fast and as accurately as possible. That means structured, method-specific data capture — UT amplitude and thickness readings, RT film or digital density and IQI sensitivity, MT field strength and indication mapping, PT dwell times and penetrant batch numbers — captured on a mobile device, ideally offline-capable for remote pipeline or offshore work where connectivity isn't guaranteed. It means report templates that match established conventions: ASME Section V Article 4/5 UT report layouts, API 510/570/653 inspection report formats, AWS D1.1 weld documentation. And it means a review and sign-off workflow that preserves an audit trail — who captured the reading, who reviewed it, who approved the final report — because that chain of custody is what makes the report defensible later if a finding is ever disputed.

Reporting software is the right primary purchase for a shop whose main pain point is slow, error-prone, manually-formatted reports eating technician and reviewer time, or a shop that keeps losing points on client audits for inconsistent documentation. It is not, by itself, a scheduling tool, a certification-tracking system for the whole company, or an asset-history platform — though a well-built one should at minimum export data cleanly into whichever of those systems a company also runs.

What NDT ERP Actually Solves

ERP exists to solve the operate-the-business problem, and it's a materially broader scope than reporting. It's where technician certifications get tracked by method and level with automated expiry alerts; where calibration due dates for every serialized instrument live, tied to NIST-traceable certificates; where job scheduling happens against actual technician availability and qualification, not guesswork; where project costing, invoicing, and client contract terms are managed; and where ISO 9001:2015 document control — procedures, work instructions, calibration records, training files — lives in one auditable place instead of scattered folders. A shop growing past roughly ten to twenty technicians, multiple sites, or several concurrent client contracts each with different reporting requirements is usually the one that feels ERP's absence most acutely — not because reporting got harder, but because coordinating people, equipment, and compliance obligations across a growing operation outgrew what a spreadsheet or a reporting tool alone was built to track.

It's common, and often correct, for ERP and reporting software to be different modules of the same platform, since certification data that blocks a technician's report sign-off in the ERP is the same data a reporting workflow needs to check before allowing that technician to close out a job. But they remain conceptually distinct problems: one runs the business, one produces the deliverable, and a company evaluating vendors should be clear about which gap it's actually trying to close.

What a Digital Twin Platform Actually Solves

A digital twin platform solves a different problem again, and it sits primarily on the asset-owner side of the relationship rather than the inspection-provider side, though NDT companies increasingly need to feed data into one as a client deliverable. Where reporting software produces a single inspection event's report, and ERP tracks the business that produced it, a digital twin gives an asset owner — a refinery, a pipeline operator, a fabrication yard's own facilities team — a persistent, visual, three-dimensional representation of a physical asset with its inspection and maintenance history layered on top, accumulated over the asset's entire service life. Instead of a folder of individual PDF reports for a storage tank inspected every five years under API 653, a digital twin shows the tank's condition trend over time, flags where thickness readings are approaching retirement limits, and increasingly incorporates AI-assisted predictive maintenance modeling to flag where the next inspection or repair is most likely to be needed before a failure occurs.

This category solves a fundamentally different question than the other two: not "did we capture this inspection correctly" or "is our business running efficiently," but "what is the current and trending condition of this specific physical asset, viewed across its entire history, and where should we look next." An asset owner managing hundreds or thousands of pieces of equipment across a facility, or a large inspection provider trying to differentiate itself by offering asset-level visibility as a value-added service rather than just delivering PDF reports, is the buyer this category actually serves.

Where They Overlap, and Why That Causes Confusion

The overlap is real and it's the source of most buying confusion. Reporting software's output — a UT thickness reading tied to a specific location on a tank — is exactly the data a digital twin needs to populate its condition-history view. ERP's certification and calibration records are exactly what an audit-ready digital twin deployment needs to reference when an asset owner wants to confirm that every inspection feeding the twin's model was performed by a qualified technician using a calibrated instrument. This is why the three categories are frequently sold by the same vendors and increasingly built to interoperate — but interoperating is not the same as being interchangeable. A company that buys a digital twin platform expecting it to also solve certification tracking and technician scheduling will be disappointed, just as a company that buys reporting software expecting it to give an asset owner a visual, trending condition history across a whole facility will be disappointed. Each tool is built around a different unit of analysis: reporting software around the inspection event, ERP around the business and its people, and a digital twin around the physical asset over time.

A concrete example makes the distinction clearer than the abstract version. Take a single above-ground storage tank at a petrochemical facility, inspected under API 653 on a recurring interval. Each inspection cycle produces a report — that's the reporting layer, capturing floor and shell thickness readings, settlement survey data, and any recommended repairs. The inspection company scheduling that technician, tracking their API 653-relevant training and current certification status, and invoicing the client for the work — that's the ERP layer, running the business behind the report. Over the following fifteen or twenty years, as that same tank goes through five or six more inspection cycles, an asset owner wants to see the full trend: is the floor thinning faster than projected, is a specific quadrant of the shell degrading disproportionately, does the pattern suggest the next inspection interval should be shortened. That longitudinal, asset-level view, stitched together across every inspection report the tank has ever had, is what a digital twin is actually built to show — something no single inspection report, and no ERP record of who performed the work, was ever designed to provide on its own.

A Decision Framework by Company Profile

A small, single-site inspection shop with a handful of technicians and straightforward client relationships usually gets the most immediate value from reporting software first — it directly addresses the daily pain of slow report turnaround and inconsistent formatting, with ERP-style certification and scheduling features added as the shop grows past the point a spreadsheet can reliably handle. A multi-site service provider juggling several client contracts, dozens of technicians, and multiple physical locations usually needs ERP as the backbone first, since the coordination problem — who's certified, who's available, what's calibrated, what's been invoiced — becomes the binding constraint on growth well before reporting speed does, though the two are frequently purchased together as one integrated platform. An asset owner or operator — a refinery, pipeline company, terminal, or fabrication yard managing its own equipment inventory across dozens or hundreds of pieces of monitored equipment — is the buyer for whom a digital twin platform makes sense as a standalone investment, often layered on top of inspection data the owner is already receiving from one or more third-party NDT providers, regardless of what software those providers use internally.

How They Work Together When You Need More Than One

For companies that need all three — a growing multi-site inspection provider serving asset owners who expect digital twin-level visibility as part of the service — the practical goal is data flowing in one direction without re-entry: a technician's field-captured reading in the reporting layer should be the same reading that populates the ERP's job record and, where relevant, feeds an asset owner's digital twin, without anyone retyping the same number three times into three different systems. That's less a feature checklist and more an architecture question worth asking directly of any vendor, including us: does data captured once flow automatically to every system that needs it, or does each platform require its own manual re-entry, quietly recreating the exact duplicate-entry burden a company bought new software specifically to eliminate? The answer to that question, more than any single feature in any one category, determines whether a company ends up with three tools that work together or three separate silos wearing the same login screen.

If you're not sure which of the three actually matches your current bottleneck, that's worth a direct conversation before shopping vendor by vendor — the fastest way to buy the wrong tool is to start from a product category instead of starting from the specific coordination or reporting problem that's actually costing you time or business today. Naming that problem precisely, before a single vendor call, is the single highest-leverage step in the entire buying process, and it's also the one most companies skip.
